0.title: The Throne of Grace: The Book of 2 Samuel
0.overview:
Second Samuel is the story of a king, but more deeply the story of a covenant. At its center stands one of the great promises of the Old Testament: I will establish the throne of his kingdom forever (7:13). Everything before it, David’s securing of the kingdom, and everything after it, the sins, rebellions and griefs of his later years, is to be read in its light. God's covenant with David is unconditional and permanent, reaching to the end of history; it rests on the character of God, not of David. Sinning kings would be disciplined, not cast off (7:14-15).

Who wrote 2 Samuel? It is the second half of one book with 1 Samuel, divided later because of its length. Its author is not named; it draws on the records of Samuel, Nathan and Gad (1 Chr 29:29). David reigned about 1010–970 BC. Its Hebrew text has more copying slips than most books, and modern Bibles sometimes follow the Greek Old Testament or the Dead Sea scroll of Samuel found at Qumran, as their footnotes show. Chronicles retells much of it later, from the viewpoint of the temple and David’s line.

The first movement (chapters 1–10) traces David's rise: the lament for Saul and Jonathan, the long war with the house of Saul, the coronation over all Israel, the conquest of Jerusalem, the ark brought to the city, and the covenant of chapter 7. Even here the narrative is honest: the ark kills Uzzah, Michal's contempt ends her marriage, the wars are costly. But the dominant note is grace: the shepherd boy from Bethlehem sits on the throne of a united Israel and receives an astonishing promise.

The second movement (chapters 11–20) is the great unraveling. David takes Bathsheba, arranges Uriah's murder, and lives in self-deception until Nathan arrives with a parable and a verdict: You are the man. His repentance, recorded in Psalm 51, stands in permanent contrast to Saul's self-justification. But the consequences are devastating: the child dies, Amnon rapes Tamar, Absalom murders Amnon and launches a coup, and David flees Jerusalem weeping, crossing the Kidron (15:23) as the Son of David would one night in sorrow (John 18:1).

The third movement (chapters 21–24) is an appendix of poems, lists, and a plague that ends at the threshing floor of Araunah, the site of Solomon's temple, which Chronicles calls Mount Moriah (2 Chr 3:1), the name of the land where Abraham offered Isaac (Gen 22:2). The book ends not with David's triumph but with his sacrifice, and with the mercy that stops the destroying angel above Jerusalem: the gospel in miniature.

Again and again 2 Samuel points forward to Christ. The covenant of chapter 7 is the seedbed of the New Testament's proclamation that Jesus is the Son of David (Matt. 1:1; Luke 1:32–33; Rom. 1:3; Rev. 22:16). Mephibosheth (chapter 9) is one of the clearest pictures of grace: the crippled heir of a dead dynasty, brought to the king's table, not because of what he was but because of the covenant David made with his father Jonathan. David's cry over Absalom, would I had died instead of you (18:33), is a father's grief for a son who died in rebellion, and many hear in it, by contrast, the Father who did give his Son for those at war with him (Rom 5:10). And the threshing-floor offering that David insists must cost him something (24:24) points to the costliest offering of all: God did not spare his own Son (Rom 8:32).

1.overview:
The book opens some eighty miles from where the last one ended, in a burnt town, with David, who does not yet know that Saul is dead. On the third day a messenger arrives with torn clothes and earth on his head, carrying Saul's crown and a story that he killed the king himself. It is false, and he is an Amalekite, of the nation Saul lost the kingdom for sparing.

David gives the whole day to grief before he passes any sentence. Then he enforces, on his first day with power, the principle he held for years when it cost him everything: nobody puts out a hand against the LORD's anointed.

Then comes the Song of the Bow, ordered taught to Judah: a poem honouring the man whose crown he is about to wear, composed by the one person in Israel who had most reason to write a bitter one.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–10 — A Man Came from Saul's Camp
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: On the third day after Ziklag a man arrives with his clothes torn and earth on his head (vv. 1-2). The army has fled, and Saul and Jonathan are dead (vv. 3-4). Asked how he knows, he tells a detailed story of finding Saul on Gilboa and killing him at his own request, and produces the crown and the armlet (vv. 5-10).
verseByVerse.theology: The story is false, and the reader knows it: Saul fell on his own sword, and his armour-bearer saw that Saul was dead (1 Sam. 31:4-5). This man is a scavenger who stripped the royal insignia off the body and invented a part for himself.
verseByVerse.examples: And he is an Amalekite. Saul lost the kingdom for sparing that nation (1 Sam. 15), and David has come to Ziklag straight from cutting down the Amalekites who burned it (1 Sam. 30). The narrator offers no comment whatever.

verseByVerse.quote: After the death of Saul, when David had returned from striking down the Amalekites, David remained two days in Ziklag. And on the third day, behold, a man came from Saul's camp, with his clothes torn and dirt on his head. And when he came to David, he fell to the ground and paid homage. David said to him, "Where do you come from?" And he said to him, "I have escaped from the camp of Israel." And David said to him, "How did it go? Tell me." And he answered, "The people fled from the battle, and also many of the people have fallen and are dead, and Saul and his son Jonathan are also dead." Then David said to the young man who told him, "How do you know that Saul and his son Jonathan are dead?" And the young man who told him said, "By chance I happened to be on Mount Gilboa, and there was Saul leaning on his spear, and behold, the chariots and the horsemen were close upon him. And when he looked behind him, he saw me, and called to me. And I answered, 'Here I am.' And he said to me, 'Who are you?' I answered him, 'I am an Amalekite.' And he said to me, 'Stand beside me and kill me, for anguish has seized me, and yet my life still lingers.' So I stood beside him and killed him, because I was sure that he could not live after he had fallen. And I took the crown that was on his head and the armlet that was on his arm, and I have brought them here to my lord."
verseByVerse.commentary:
After the death of Saul (v. 1). Two books meet in that sentence. 1 Samuel ended on Mount Gilboa with a body on a wall and the men of Jabesh-gilead walking all night to take it down. This one opens some eighty miles south, in a burnt town, with a man who does not yet know any of it. Note where he has just been: striking down the Amalekites. Keep that in mind until verse 8.

Earth on his head (v. 2). Torn clothes and earth on the head are the recognised signs of a man carrying a disaster, and they are also, in this case, a costume. He falls on his face, which is what you do before a king, not before a mercenary captain in a burnt village, and the gesture shows that he thinks he is greeting the next king.

How did it go (vv. 3-4). A short question, and everything hangs on it. He answers in the right order, worst last, and the last words are the ones that matter to the man he is speaking to.

How do you know (v. 5). The right question, and it is a lawyer's question. David does not take the news on the strength of torn clothes; he wants to know what the man saw.

By chance (v. 6). Nobody happens to be on a battlefield by chance. Men are on a battlefield after the fighting for one reason, and it is to go through the pockets of the dead.

I stood beside him and killed him (vv. 7-10). It is a good story, told with detail, and it is not true. The reader has already seen it. The previous chapter reports Saul's death at close range: the archers found him, the armour-bearer refused out of fear, so Saul took his own sword and fell upon it. And when his armor-bearer saw that Saul was dead, he also fell upon his sword and died with him (1 Sam. 31:4-5). There was no Amalekite in that account, and no breath left in Saul to negotiate with.

So what probably happened is this. A scavenger came over the ridge after the fighting, found the king's body, took the crown off the head and the armlet off the arm, and walked south for three days working out what to say. He calculated what a rival for the throne would pay for: not the news, which anyone could bring, but the deed. Everything about the invention shows how he read David. He assumed that the years of being hunted had made David bitter, as such years usually do, and that a crown and a corpse were a business opportunity. He was wrong about all of it, and it kills him.

Then there is the word he uses to identify himself, and the writer leaves it entirely alone: I am an Amalekite. Saul lost the kingdom over Amalek, the command he would not carry out at Gilgal and the reason Samuel gave at Endor (1 Sam. 15:1-23; 28:18). David has just come back from killing the Amalekites who burned this town, and four hundred of them got away on camels. Here is one, holding Saul's crown, claiming to have finished the man who spared his people. The narrator puts the facts next to each other and lets whoever is reading carefully do the rest.
verseByVerse.note: The Amalekite’s story contradicts 1 Samuel 31, where Saul fell on his own sword; he was probably lying to win David’s favour.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 11–16 — Your Own Mouth Has Testified Against You
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: David and his men tear their clothes, and mourn and fast until evening for Saul, for Jonathan, and for the people of the LORD (vv. 11-12). Then he asks the messenger how he was not afraid to destroy the LORD's anointed (vv. 13-14), and has him struck down on his own testimony (vv. 15-16).
verseByVerse.theology: The order of the day matters. Hours of public grief come first, and the sentence afterwards, and the list he mourns for runs outward: Saul, Jonathan, the people of the LORD, the house of Israel.
verseByVerse.examples: He is condemned on his testimony, not his deed, and he almost certainly did not do it. And the principle enforced is the one David held through seven chapters of being hunted: nobody puts a hand on the LORD's anointed.

verseByVerse.quote: Then David took hold of his clothes and tore them, and so did all the men who were with him. And they mourned and wept and fasted until evening for Saul and for Jonathan his son and for the people of the LORD and for the house of Israel, because they had fallen by the sword. And David said to the young man who told him, "Where do you come from?" And he answered, "I am the son of a sojourner, an Amalekite." David said to him, "How is it you were not afraid to put out your hand to destroy the LORD's anointed?" Then David called one of the young men and said, "Go, execute him." And he struck him down so that he died. And David said to him, "Your blood be on your head, for your own mouth has testified against you, saying, 'I have killed the LORD's anointed.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Until evening (vv. 11-12). Before he says a word he tears his clothes, and his men tear theirs. The whole day goes to grief, and the list runs outward from the personal to the national. For Saul first, and the man had hunted him for the better part of a decade. For Jonathan his son, and there is a whole life in that clause, which will get its own verses at the end of the chapter. For the people of the LORD, and for the house of Israel: the army is gone and the northern towns have been abandoned to the Philistines.

A reader is entitled to wonder whether this is a performance, and the signs say it is not. There is no audience but his own men, who know exactly what Saul did to him, and every one of them lost everything at Ziklag days ago. He also does the grieving before he does the judging. The Amalekite is standing there the whole time.

The son of a sojourner (v. 13). The question is put a second time, and the answer is fuller: a resident foreigner, living under Israel's law without being of Israel. A ger was bound by the same law as the native-born and protected by it (Lev. 24:22). By his own account he is a man who lived under that law and put his hand on the king.

Not afraid (v. 14). Anybody who has read 1 Samuel has heard this before. It is what David said in the cave at Engedi: the LORD forbid that I should do this thing to my lord, the LORD's anointed, to put out my hand against him (1 Sam. 24:6). It is what he said to Abishai over the sleeping king: who can put out his hand against the LORD's anointed and be guiltless? (1 Sam. 26:9). He held that principle for years when it cost him everything, with two clear opportunities to end it in an afternoon and his own men arguing with him. Now he has the crown in front of him and no one to answer to, and he enforces the same rule now that the power is his. That is the test that matters. Almost anyone can hold a principle while it is costing them. The question is whether it survives the day the power arrives, when keeping it costs nothing.

Go, execute him (v. 15). It is done immediately and by somebody else, and both are deliberate: David will not let the sentence look like private revenge.

Your own mouth (v. 16). Read that carefully, because it tells you David knows. He does not say "you killed the king". He says "you said you killed the king". The sentence is passed on the confession, not on the act, and the act in all likelihood never happened. The man has said, unprompted and in front of witnesses, that he killed the king, and David treats the man exactly as the man has described himself. There is a hard justice in it that Scripture does not soften. He came looking to be paid for claiming a thing, and he was paid for it. A man who will invent a murder to advance himself has told you what he is.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 17–24 — Tell It Not in Gath
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: David composes a lament, the Song of the Bow, and orders it taught to Judah (vv. 17-18). The refrain, how the mighty have fallen, opens it (v. 19). Let the Philistine cities not rejoice (v. 20); let the mountain where Saul's shield was defiled have no rain (v. 21). Saul and Jonathan are praised as warriors (vv. 22-23), and the women are called to weep for the king who clothed them in scarlet (v. 24).
verseByVerse.theology: A shield's leather was rubbed with oil to keep it supple and turn a blade. Saul's lies on Gilboa unattended, a king's gear left to rot in the rain, which is why the same verse asks the rain not to come.
verseByVerse.examples: In verse 24 David remembers Saul's reign for what it actually gave the nation, and he says it to the women who once sang the song that nearly got him killed.

verseByVerse.quote: And David lamented with this lamentation over Saul and Jonathan his son, and he said it should be taught to the people of Judah; behold, it is written in the Book of Jashar. He said: "Your glory, O Israel, is slain on your high places! How the mighty have fallen! Tell it not in Gath, publish it not in the streets of Ashkelon, lest the daughters of the Philistines rejoice, lest the daughters of the uncircumcised exult. "You mountains of Gilboa, let there be no dew or rain upon you, nor fields of offerings! For there the shield of the mighty was defiled, the shield of Saul, not anointed with oil. "From the blood of the slain, from the fat of the mighty, the bow of Jonathan turned not back, and the sword of Saul returned not empty. "Saul and Jonathan, beloved and lovely! In life and in death they were not divided; they were swifter than eagles; they were stronger than lions. "You daughters of Israel, weep over Saul, who clothed you luxuriously in scarlet, who put ornaments of gold on your apparel.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Teach it to Judah (vv. 17-18). He does not just grieve. He writes it down and has it taught, so that what a generation feels about Saul's death will be shaped by what David felt about it. Consider what he could have taught them instead. He is about to be made king of Judah, and there is an obvious version of this moment in which the incoming man lets the old regime be remembered badly without saying a word. He composes a poem that honours Saul without qualification and orders it memorised. The Book of Jashar is an older collection Israel drew on, cited once before in Joshua (Josh. 10:13) and lost to us. This poem survived because it was copied into Scripture.

How the mighty have fallen (v. 19). The poem is built around this refrain, which comes three times: here, at verse 25, and in the last verse.

Tell it not in Gath (v. 20). The line has passed into the language, and most people who use it have no idea it is about Saul. Here it is concrete. The runners have already gone out to carry the good news to the house of their idols and to the people (1 Sam. 31:9), and there will be dancing in those streets tonight. David of all people knows what it looks like when the women of a city sing about a battle, and he knows Gath from the inside.

You mountains of Gilboa (v. 21). He curses the ground. This is the language of grief in a poem, not a teaching about the land. The mountain is where it happened, so let nothing grow there again. Then the detail that carries the grief is a piece of equipment: the shield of Saul, not anointed with oil. Oiling it was part of a soldier's routine, before a battle and after it, and nobody is going to oil Saul's again. That is how the poem says he is dead: a picture of good gear left out in the weather, because the man who looked after it is not coming back. And anointed is the word the whole of 1 Samuel turns on, used of Saul over and over, and what David called him five verses ago. Here it is, in its ordinary sense, about a shield.

The bow of Jonathan (v. 22). Both men are praised as soldiers, and the praise is true. Jonathan's bow is the right instrument to remember him by: the weapon he used to signal David in the field on the day they parted (1 Sam. 20:20-22).

Not divided (v. 23). That is more generous than the bare facts. Saul threw a spear at Jonathan across a dinner table for defending David, and Jonathan left in fierce anger and did not eat (1 Sam. 20:33-34). Jonathan made a covenant with the man his father was hunting and told him he would have his father's throne. David knew every bit of that; most of it was done for his sake.

He is saying the largest true thing rather than the most exact one. In the end they were not divided: the son stood in his father's line on his father's mountain and died there with him, when he had every reason to be somewhere else. This is not dishonesty. He is choosing, out of everything he could accurately report about a dead man, the part that is honourable, in a poem he intends the nation to memorise, about a king whose crown he is about to wear. Nearly everyone, given a grievance and an audience, will tell the truth in the way that does most damage. David had more material than anybody and used none of it.

Daughters of Israel (v. 24). These are the women who came out of the cities singing Saul has struck down his thousands, and David his ten thousands (1 Sam. 18:7), the song that put a spear in Saul's hand and nearly cost David his life twice. He calls those women to weep for Saul. And what he tells them to remember is the prosperity. Scarlet and gold meant a country secure enough for ordinary women to be well dressed, and that was Saul's doing: he beat the Philistines at Michmash and the Ammonites at Jabesh, and for forty years Israel had a king and an army and something in the barn. It is the true good thing, and David goes looking for it and says it out loud.
verseByVerse.note: The Book of Jashar was an old collection of poems, now lost.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 25–27 — Your Love to Me Was Extraordinary
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The refrain returns, and the poem narrows to Jonathan (v. 25): David's distress for his brother, whose love surpassed the love of women (v. 26). The refrain a third time ends it (v. 27).
verseByVerse.theology: David is comparing two different kinds of love, not two amounts of the same love. Jonathan and David were sworn brothers under a covenant made three times before the LORD, and the loyalty that held it is hesed; David says he has never met its equal.
verseByVerse.examples: David can grieve a friend without needing to explain the loss; so may we.

verseByVerse.quote: "How the mighty have fallen in the midst of the battle! "Jonathan lies slain on your high places. I am distressed for you, my brother Jonathan; very pleasant have you been to me; your love to me was extraordinary, surpassing the love of women. "How the mighty have fallen, and the weapons of war perished!"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jonathan lies slain (v. 25). The refrain comes back, and then the poem narrows to one name.

My brother Jonathan (v. 26). Everything before this has been public. This is not. I am distressed for you uses a word for being hemmed in and pressed; it is grief felt as a physical weight. They were brothers-in-law by a marriage Saul dissolved by force, and brothers by covenant, which was the tie that held. Very pleasant have you been to me: not "useful", not "loyal", though he was both past all reckoning. Being with him was good.

Then the line people stop at, and it deserves a plain answer rather than an argument. The comparison in surpassing the love of women is between two kinds of love, sworn friendship and marriage, not two amounts of one kind. What Jonathan gave David was covenant loyalty, hesed, the word for love that keeps its promises after the reasons have gone, sworn before the LORD three times.

Look at what it consisted of. The heir to the throne took off his own robe and armour and sword and belt and handed them to a shepherd (1 Sam. 18:4). He defended that shepherd to a king who threw a spear at him for it. He said I shall be next to you, a renunciation of everything he was born to. He walked into a wilderness his father's army was searching, to strengthen a frightened man's hand in God. And then he went home and died in his father's lost battle. David is saying he never met anything like it anywhere else, and he had a wife who loved him and saved his life by lowering him through a window (1 Sam. 19:12).

Nothing in the text points this at anything other than what it says: a man grieving the friend who kept faith with him at the cost of a kingdom. Reading it as erotic imports a meaning the passage gives no sign of; covenant friends in that world spoke of love in just these words (1 Sam. 18:1-3). And a king wrote it down, put his grief in the first person, and had it taught to a nation, which is not a thing men in his position generally do in any century.

The weapons of war perished (v. 27). The last line is about equipment again, as verse 21 was, and it means more than swords: the men who were Israel's defence are lying on a hill.

Now read the whole thing back, and look for two things that are not in it. The first is David. Nine verses, and not one word about what any of this means for him: no relief, nothing about the throne he has waited years for, no hint that the man who spent a decade trying to kill him is conveniently dead. He has every reason to feel some of that, and he is not a man who hides his feelings; the psalms are full of him saying exactly what is in him, including things people would rather he had not written down. Here there is nothing for himself at all. Whatever relief he felt, this is not where he put it.

The second absence is stranger: there is no mention of God in the poem. No the LORD gave, and the LORD has taken away, no appeal, no theology of any kind, from a man who cannot get through eight verses of a psalm without addressing God directly. Scripture keeps it exactly as it came out.

Anybody who has been made to feel that grief must be tidy or theological before it is permitted should sit with that. This is the man after God's own heart, and on the day the news came he wrote a poem full of scarlet cloth and eagles and an unoiled shield, with no doctrine in it and nothing about himself, and God preserved it in Scripture. Sometimes the godly thing is not to explain the loss. It is to say plainly how good the dead were and how much it hurts.

1.theology:
A misreading that kills (vv. 6-16). The Amalekite's story is false, and the reader knows it from the chapter before. He calculated that a rival claimant would pay not for the news but for the deed, which shows how he expected years of being hunted to have shaped David. He was wrong, and he was judged by the account he chose to give of himself.

The principle survives the arrival of power (v. 14). How is it you were not afraid to put out your hand to destroy the LORD's anointed? puts to the Amalekite the principle David stated in the cave at Engedi (1 Sam. 24:6) and to Abishai over the sleeping king (1 Sam. 26:9). He held it while hunted, hungry and living in caves, and twice stopped his own men from breaking it. Almost anyone can keep a principle while it is costing them and feel righteous doing it; the test is the day it costs nothing and nobody would notice its absence.

Choosing which true thing to say (vv. 17-24). An incoming king could simply have let the old regime be remembered badly. Instead David writes a poem honouring Saul and has it taught to Judah, choosing out of everything he could accurately report about a dead man the part that is honourable.

Grief that is allowed to be grief (vv. 25-27). The poem says nothing about David and nothing about God, and Scripture keeps it as it came. That matters a great deal to anybody made to feel that grief must be tidy or theological before it is permitted.

A crown he would not take over a body (vv. 10, 14-16). The Amalekite brought David a crown lifted off a corpse and expected thanks for the death. David would not have the throne that way. The Son of David met the same offer on a grander scale, all the kingdoms of the world for one act of worship, and refused (Matthew 4:8-10). He did not take his throne over anyone else’s body; he came to it through his own, obedient to the point of death, and was therefore highly exalted (Philippians 2:8-9). And the grief David puts in the poem without explaining it is grief the Lord himself shared: at the grave of his friend, before he raised him, Jesus wept (John 11:35).
1.examples:
Then: A man walked three days south carrying a dead king's crown and a story he had made up on the road, expecting to be paid for claiming a murder, and was executed on the strength of his own account by the one person in Israel who had twice refused to commit it when he had the chance.

Now: Two things. The Amalekite is a study in misreading somebody: he assumed that years of persecution had made David into the kind of man who would reward the news. People will tell you what they think you are by what they think will please you. And the lament is the harder lesson. David had more accurate, damaging material about Saul than any person alive, an audience ready to hear it, and every political reason to let it out, and instead he went looking for what was genuinely good about the man and taught it to a nation. That is not pretending. It is choosing which true thing to say. Christians can afford to speak that way about those who wronged them because God has dealt that way with us: in Christ he does not keep the record of our worst, and the Spirit he gives produces a love that covers a multitude of sins.

2.title: Two Kings in Israel
2.text: <sup>1</sup>After this David inquired of the LORD, "Shall I go up into any of the cities of Judah?" And the LORD said to him, "Go up." David said, "To which shall I go up?" And he said, "To Hebron."<sup>2</sup>So David went up there, and his two wives also, Ahinoam of Jezreel and Abigail the widow of Nabal of Carmel.<sup>3</sup>And David brought up his men who were with him, everyone with his household, and they lived in the towns of Hebron.<sup>4</sup>And the men of Judah came, and there they anointed David king over the house of Judah. When they told David, "It was the men of Jabesh-gilead who buried Saul,"<sup>5</sup>David sent messengers to the men of Jabesh-gilead and said to them, "May you be blessed by the LORD, because you showed this loyalty to Saul your lord and buried him.<sup>6</sup>Now may the LORD show steadfast love and faithfulness to you. And I will do good to you because you have done this thing.<sup>7</sup>Now therefore let your hands be strong, and be valiant, for Saul your lord is dead, and the house of Judah has anointed me king over them."<sup>8</sup>But Abner the son of Ner, commander of Saul's army, took Ish-bosheth the son of Saul and brought him over to Mahanaim,<sup>9</sup>and he made him king over Gilead and the Ashurites and Jezreel and Ephraim and Benjamin and all Israel.<sup>10</sup>Ish-bosheth, Saul's son, was forty years old when he began to reign over Israel, and he reigned two years. But the house of Judah followed David.<sup>11</sup>And the time that David was king in Hebron over the house of Judah was seven years and six months.<sup>12</sup>Abner the son of Ner, and the servants of Ish-bosheth the son of Saul, went out from Mahanaim to Gibeon.<sup>13</sup>And Joab the son of Zeruiah and the servants of David went out and met them at the pool of Gibeon. And they sat down, the one on the one side of the pool, and the other on the other side of the pool.<sup>14</sup>And Abner said to Joab, "Let the young men arise and compete before us." And Joab said, "Let them arise."<sup>15</sup>Then they arose and passed over by number, twelve for Benjamin and Ish-bosheth the son of Saul, and twelve of the servants of David.<sup>16</sup>And each caught his opponent by the head and thrust his sword in his opponent's side, so they fell down together. Therefore that place was called Helkath-hazzurim, which is at Gibeon.<sup>17</sup>And the battle was very fierce that day. And Abner and the men of Israel were beaten before the servants of David.<sup>18</sup>And the three sons of Zeruiah were there, Joab, Abishai, and Asahel. Now Asahel was as swift of foot as a wild gazelle.<sup>19</sup>And Asahel pursued Abner, and as he went, he turned neither to the right hand nor to the left from following Abner.<sup>20</sup>Then Abner looked behind him and said, "Is it you, Asahel?" And he answered, "It is I."<sup>21</sup>Abner said to him, "Turn aside to your right hand or to your left, and seize one of the young men and take his spoil." But Asahel would not turn aside from following him.<sup>22</sup>And Abner said again to Asahel, "Turn aside from following me. Why should I strike you to the ground? How then could I lift up my face to your brother Joab?"<sup>23</sup>But he refused to turn aside. Therefore Abner struck him in the stomach with the butt of his spear, so that the spear came out at his back. And he fell there and died where he was. And all who came to the place where Asahel had fallen and died, stood still.<sup>24</sup>But Joab and Abishai pursued Abner. And as the sun was going down they came to the hill of Ammah, which lies before Giah on the way to the wilderness of Gibeon.<sup>25</sup>And the people of Benjamin gathered themselves together behind Abner and became one group and took their stand on the top of a hill.<sup>26</sup>Then Abner called to Joab, "Shall the sword devour forever? Do you not know that the end will be bitter? How long will it be before you tell your people to turn from the pursuit of their brothers?"<sup>27</sup>And Joab said, "As God lives, if you had not spoken, surely the men would not have given up the pursuit of their brothers until the morning."<sup>28</sup>So Joab blew the trumpet, and all the men stopped and pursued Israel no more, nor did they fight anymore.<sup>29</sup>And Abner and his men went all that night through the Arabah. They crossed the Jordan, and marching the whole morning, they came to Mahanaim.<sup>30</sup>Joab returned from the pursuit of Abner. And when he had gathered all the people together, there were missing from David's servants nineteen men besides Asahel.<sup>31</sup>But the servants of David had struck down of Benjamin 360 of Abner's men.<sup>32</sup>And they took up Asahel and buried him in the tomb of his father, which was at Bethlehem. And Joab and his men marched all night, and the day broke upon them at Hebron.
2.overview:
One short sentence opens the chapter, and it is the difference between this king and the last one: David inquired of the LORD. There is no living person whose permission he needs, and he asks anyway. His first act as king of Judah is a thank-you to Jabesh-gilead for burying Saul.

Then the pool of Gibeon, where both armies are Israelite. Abner proposes a contest to keep a war small, and all twenty-four champions die in the same second, settling nothing, so the armies fight anyway. Asahel chases the enemy commander and will not turn aside, and Abner's backward jab with the butt of his spear goes straight through him. The best line of the day comes from the man most responsible for it: shall the sword devour forever? Both armies march all night in opposite directions, and nothing has been decided.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–7 — David Inquired of the LORD
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: David asks the LORD whether to go up into Judah, and then which city; he is told Hebron (v. 1). He goes up with his wives and his men's households, and Judah anoints him king (vv. 2-4). Told that the men of Jabesh-gilead buried Saul, he sends them a blessing (vv. 5-7).
verseByVerse.theology: Being told he may go is not being told where, and David will not choose the place himself and call that God’s guidance.
verseByVerse.examples: His first recorded act as king is a thank-you to the town that buried Saul. Kindness to people who loved our opponents can be both sincere and wise.

verseByVerse.quote: After this David inquired of the LORD, "Shall I go up into any of the cities of Judah?" And the LORD said to him, "Go up." David said, "To which shall I go up?" And he said, "To Hebron." So David went up there, and his two wives also, Ahinoam of Jezreel and Abigail the widow of Nabal of Carmel. And David brought up his men who were with him, everyone with his household, and they lived in the towns of Hebron. And the men of Judah came, and there they anointed David king over the house of Judah. When they told David, "It was the men of Jabesh-gilead who buried Saul," David sent messengers to the men of Jabesh-gilead and said to them, "May you be blessed by the LORD, because you showed this loyalty to Saul your lord and buried him. Now may the LORD show steadfast love and faithfulness to you. And I will do good to you because you have done this thing. Now therefore let your hands be strong, and be valiant, for Saul your lord is dead, and the house of Judah has anointed me king over them."
verseByVerse.commentary:
David inquired of the LORD (v. 1). One short sentence, and it is the whole difference between this man and the last one. Consider what he is holding while he asks: the crown of the dead king, brought by the Amalekite; Samuel's anointing at Bethlehem; six hundred men and the tribe of Judah waiting. Saul and his heir are dead, and there is no living person he needs permission from. He asks anyway.

And then he does something more instructive still. He gets a yes, go up, and he does not run with it. He asks a second question: to which shall I go up? Being told he may go is not being told where, and he is not going to choose the place himself and call the whole thing God’s guidance.

Set this against the last large decision we watched him make: Then David said in his heart, "Now I shall perish one day by the hand of Saul. There is nothing better for me than that I should escape to the land of the Philistines" (1 Sam. 27:1). No priest, no ephod, no prophet, and all three were in the camp. Same man, opposite move. The difference is Ziklag: he asked for the ephod standing in the ashes of his own town (1 Sam. 30:7), and he has not stopped since.

Hebron is the right answer and he could not have known it. It is the oldest covenant ground in the country: Abraham bought the field and the cave there, and Abraham and Isaac and Jacob are all in that ground (Gen. 23; 49:31). It is a city of the Levites and a city of refuge (where a man who had killed by accident could flee for safety), at the centre of Judah's territory. He is not told why. He is told where.

His two wives (vv. 2-3). Six hundred households move at once, and the writer counts the wives. Abigail is here, who talked him out of a massacre. Ahinoam is here. Michal, his first wife, is not: Saul gave her to another man, and getting her back will be a condition in the next chapter.

King over the house of Judah (v. 4). The second anointing, and each is given by a wider circle. Samuel poured the oil at Bethlehem in front of seven passed-over brothers (1 Sam. 16:13). Now his own tribe does it publicly. Seven and a half years from now the elders of all Israel will do it a third time (5:3). God keeps confirming the same thing in front of larger audiences, and each confirmation arrives only when the man has waited for it.

The men of Jabesh-gilead (vv. 4-5). His first recorded act as king is a thank-you letter to the men who buried his enemy. They walked all night through occupied country, took four bodies off a public wall at Beth-shan, carried them home, buried the bones under a tamarisk and fasted for a week, for a king who had been failing them for years, with no possible reward (1 Sam. 31:11-13). And they did it because of one night forty years earlier, when the Spirit of God rushed on a young man behind a plough and he marched all night to save their town (1 Sam. 11). David sees exactly what that was and names it.

Steadfast love and faithfulness (v. 6). The first word is hesed, love that keeps its promises when the reasons for keeping them have gone. It is what Jonathan asked David to show his descendants. It is what Jabesh-gilead did. He asks God to do to them what they did to Saul.

Saul your lord is dead (v. 7). And then, at the end, the politics, and it would be dishonest to pretend it is not there. He tells the most fiercely pro-Saul town in the country that Saul is dead and Judah has crowned him, and asks them for nothing. Every word is weighed. The gratitude and the politics are both real, and the text is comfortable with that. The gratitude is real: he wrote a lament for Saul nobody made him write. And he understands that the north is watching to see whether the new king regards them as the enemy, and he has chosen the one gesture that answers the question before it is asked. Godly and shrewd are not opposites. They are simply harder to hold together than either one on its own.
verseByVerse.note: David was anointed three times: privately by Samuel, then king of Judah at Hebron, then king of all Israel.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 8–17 — Let the Young Men Compete Before Us
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Abner makes Saul's son Ish-bosheth king over the north at Mahanaim, while Judah follows David (vv. 8-11). The two forces meet at the pool of Gibeon (vv. 12-13). Abner proposes a contest of twelve against twelve, and all twenty-four kill each other at once (vv. 14-16). The battle that follows is very fierce (v. 17).
verseByVerse.theology: Both armies are Israelite. This is a civil war, and Abner, not Ish-bosheth, is the real power in the north.
verseByVerse.examples: Measures meant to contain a quarrel can feed it when neither side will accept a result it does not like.

verseByVerse.quote: But Abner the son of Ner, commander of Saul's army, took Ish-bosheth the son of Saul and brought him over to Mahanaim, and he made him king over Gilead and the Ashurites and Jezreel and Ephraim and Benjamin and all Israel. Ish-bosheth, Saul's son, was forty years old when he began to reign over Israel, and he reigned two years. But the house of Judah followed David. And the time that David was king in Hebron over the house of Judah was seven years and six months. Abner the son of Ner, and the servants of Ish-bosheth the son of Saul, went out from Mahanaim to Gibeon. And Joab the son of Zeruiah and the servants of David went out and met them at the pool of Gibeon. And they sat down, the one on the one side of the pool, and the other on the other side of the pool. And Abner said to Joab, "Let the young men arise and compete before us." And Joab said, "Let them arise." Then they arose and passed over by number, twelve for Benjamin and Ish-bosheth the son of Saul, and twelve of the servants of David. And each caught his opponent by the head and thrust his sword in his opponent's side, so they fell down together. Therefore that place was called Helkath-hazzurim, which is at Gibeon. And the battle was very fierce that day. And Abner and the men of Israel were beaten before the servants of David.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Abner took Ish-bosheth (vv. 8-9). Read the verbs: Abner took him, brought him over, and made him king. Ish-bosheth does nothing in that sentence, and very little in the rest of the book. He speaks once, makes an accusation that destroys his own kingdom, and is murdered asleep at his noonday rest. Abner holds the real power; the son of Saul supplies the royal name. And they go to Mahanaim, across the Jordan: the heartland is not safe enough to be crowned in.

Two years, seven and a half (vv. 10-11). The numbers make a point. Ish-bosheth’s reign is short and David's Hebron years are long, so David sat in Hebron for the better part of eight years as king of one tribe out of twelve, waiting. He had been waiting a long time already. The two figures do not match, and the question is taken up at the end of this section.

The pool of Gibeon (vv. 12-13). Two armies sit down on opposite sides of a water tank and look at each other. Archaeologists at Gibeon have dug out a great rock-cut shaft with a spiral stair inside it, probably this pool or part of the same system. It is a real place and this is a real day, and the picture is of men waiting for somebody to decide something. And they are all Israelites. Every man on both sides is a son of Jacob; some fought in the same line at Michmash. Joab is David's nephew and Abner is Saul's cousin, and the war they are about to start is a family quarrel with armies.

Let the young men compete (v. 14). The word is the ordinary one for a game. Abner proposes a representative contest, a fixed number of champions from each side with the result standing for the whole, a recognised way of settling a matter without committing two armies. Goliath had proposed exactly this (1 Sam. 17:8-9). The intention is not bloodthirsty: two generals who know this war cannot really be won are looking for a way to keep the cost down.

They fell down together (vv. 15-16). All twenty-four die at once. It is one of the more terrible pieces of writing in the book, told simply by describing the movements. Each man grabs his opposite number by the head and puts a sword in his side, and they go down in pairs. There is no winner and not even a fight worth describing. Helkath-hazzurim means something like the Field of Sword-Edges, and Israel put that name on the ground and kept it. Abner proposed a contest to avoid a battle; it produced twenty-four dead and settled nothing, because both teams lost.

Very fierce that day (v. 17). So the armies go in anyway, and then a war runs for years. It is a common pattern. A measure adopted to contain a conflict becomes the thing that ignites it, because the men involved were never willing to accept a result they did not like. Abner would not have gone home if his twelve had lost. Neither would Joab. The contest was a pretence they both agreed to while the swords were still sheathed.

How do two years and seven and a half fit? Ish-bosheth was probably made king some years after Saul’s death, once Abner had regained the north; his two years fell within David’s seven and a half at Hebron, and the war between the houses ran through the whole period (3:1).
verseByVerse.note: Ish-bosheth means “man of shame,” probably a scribal replacement for Esh-baal (“man of Baal”). “Helkath-hazzurim” means “the field of sword-edges” (ESV note).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 18–23 — Turn Aside from Following Me
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Asahel, Joab's brother, is as swift of foot as a wild gazelle, and he goes straight for Abner and will not turn to right or left (vv. 18-19). Abner warns him twice to break off, for fear of what Joab would do (vv. 20-22). He will not, and Abner strikes him with the butt of his spear, and he dies where he falls (v. 23).
verseByVerse.theology: Abner is the most experienced soldier in Israel and he does not want this killing. He can see the whole feud coming.
verseByVerse.examples: A blow meant to stop a young man, driven home by his own speed, becomes the fuse for a murder at the gate in the next chapter and for Joab's own execution more than thirty years later (1 Kings 2:5-6). One death in anger can set off a chain of others for a generation.

verseByVerse.quote: And the three sons of Zeruiah were there, Joab, Abishai, and Asahel. Now Asahel was as swift of foot as a wild gazelle. And Asahel pursued Abner, and as he went, he turned neither to the right hand nor to the left from following Abner. Then Abner looked behind him and said, "Is it you, Asahel?" And he answered, "It is I." Abner said to him, "Turn aside to your right hand or to your left, and seize one of the young men and take his spoil." But Asahel would not turn aside from following him. And Abner said again to Asahel, "Turn aside from following me. Why should I strike you to the ground? How then could I lift up my face to your brother Joab?" But he refused to turn aside. Therefore Abner struck him in the stomach with the butt of his spear, so that the spear came out at his back. And he fell there and died where he was. And all who came to the place where Asahel had fallen and died, stood still.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The three sons of Zeruiah (v. 18). They are David's nephews, and between them they will run his army, win his wars, and cause him more trouble than any of his enemies. Asahel is introduced by the one thing everybody knew about him. He could run.

Neither to the right nor to the left (v. 19). He picks the commander-in-chief of the opposing army and goes after him in a straight line. The phrase is normally a compliment in Scripture, said of a king who keeps the law. Here it describes a young man who has decided on a target and will not be talked out of it.

Is it you, Asahel (v. 20). Abner knows him by name. Of course he does: they are one nation, and everyone knew who the fast one was.

Turn aside (v. 21). The first warning, and note its shape: not go home but "take somebody else." He offers the boy an honourable way out with plunder in his hands, so that nothing has to be explained afterwards.

Your brother Joab (v. 22). The second warning, and the reason given foretells much of the rest of the book. Abner can see exactly what is coming. He is not worried about the fight itself, since he could kill this boy in a second and both of them know it, but about what follows. Blood between families does not stay where it falls. If he kills Asahel, Joab will come for him, whatever the circumstances were. He is not begging for his life. He is warning a young man that his death will start something neither of them can stop. And Asahel keeps running.

The butt of his spear (v. 23). That detail shows what Abner intended. He does not turn and put the point through him. He jabs backwards with the butt, which looks like a blow meant to stop him rather than kill him. Spear butts were often shod with a metal point for planting in the ground, so even that end could kill. And Asahel was running flat out and ran onto it. Abner was still trying not to kill him at the moment he killed him.

All who came stood still (v. 23). Men come round the shoulder of the hill, see who is lying there, and cannot go on. Everyone knows the face, knows whose brother he is, and understands in the same instant what has been set in motion. In the next chapter Joab will call Abner aside at the gate of Hebron and put a blade in his stomach, the same wound in the same place. More than thirty years later, dying, David will still be talking about it and tell Solomon what to do: you also know what Joab the son of Zeruiah did to me, how he dealt with the two commanders of the armies of Israel, Abner the son of Ner, and Amasa the son of Jether, whom he killed, avenging in time of peace for blood that had been shed in war (1 Kings 2:5-6). Joab dies holding the horns of the altar (1 Kings 2:28-34). All of it comes out of a boy who could run fast and would not turn aside.
verseByVerse.note: Zeruiah was David’s sister: Joab, Abishai and Asahel were his nephews.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 24–32 — Shall the Sword Devour Forever?
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Joab and Abishai pursue until sundown, and Abner's men rally on a hill (vv. 24-25). Abner calls down: shall the sword devour forever? (v. 26). Joab blows the trumpet and stops (vv. 27-28). Abner marches all night back across the Jordan (v. 29). Nineteen of David's men and Asahel are dead, and three hundred and sixty of Abner's (vv. 30-31). They bury Asahel at Bethlehem and march all night to Hebron (v. 32).
verseByVerse.theology: The best sentence in the chapter comes from the person most responsible for the day.
verseByVerse.examples: A victory that changes nothing is still paid for in lives.

verseByVerse.quote: But Joab and Abishai pursued Abner. And as the sun was going down they came to the hill of Ammah, which lies before Giah on the way to the wilderness of Gibeon. And the people of Benjamin gathered themselves together behind Abner and became one group and took their stand on the top of a hill. Then Abner called to Joab, "Shall the sword devour forever? Do you not know that the end will be bitter? How long will it be before you tell your people to turn from the pursuit of their brothers?" And Joab said, "As God lives, if you had not spoken, surely the men would not have given up the pursuit of their brothers until the morning." So Joab blew the trumpet, and all the men stopped and pursued Israel no more, nor did they fight anymore. And Abner and his men went all that night through the Arabah. They crossed the Jordan, and marching the whole morning, they came to Mahanaim. Joab returned from the pursuit of Abner. And when he had gathered all the people together, there were missing from David's servants nineteen men besides Asahel. But the servants of David had struck down of Benjamin 360 of Abner's men. And they took up Asahel and buried him in the tomb of his father, which was at Bethlehem. And Joab and his men marched all night, and the day broke upon them at Hebron.
verseByVerse.commentary:
On the top of a hill (vv. 24-25). The dead man's two brothers keep going until sundown. Abner's men rally, and the pursuers now face troops drawn up on high ground, so an attack will cost both sides many lives.

Shall the sword devour forever (v. 26). That is the best thing anybody says in this chapter. The picture is of a weapon that eats, with an appetite of its own that does not stop when the reason for drawing it has gone; anybody who has watched a quarrel outlive its cause knows the image is exact.

Do you not know that the end will be bitter? He is not appealing to mercy. He is telling a professional soldier something a professional soldier already knows: this ends badly for your side too, and the taste of it lasts.

And the pursuit of their brothers is the true description of the whole day: not enemies, but brothers.

Now the honesty the passage requires. Abner started this. Twenty-four young men are dead because of a suggestion he made, and he is calling for peace from a hilltop because he is about to be overrun. All of that is true, and the sentence is still true. Right words are not always spoken by people with nothing to gain, and self-interest does not automatically make a thing false. Abner is manoeuvring, and he is also correct, and Joab knows it.

If you had not spoken (v. 27). Joab's answer is colder than it looks. He does not disagree. He says that if Abner had not spoken, the pursuit would have gone on all night: I would not have stopped; you stopped me. It is either a complaint or a confession, and probably both. And there is not a word in it about Asahel, from a man who will settle that account in the next chapter with a knife.

Joab blew the trumpet (v. 28). He stops it immediately. Whatever else is true of Joab, and a great deal is, he does not lose control of himself or his troops.

Nineteen and Asahel (vv. 29-31). The writer counts both sides. Three hundred and eighty Israelites dead in one day at a water tank, and one name among them, because that is the one that will cost more than all the rest. David's side won convincingly, eighteen to one, and it changed nothing. The war will go on a long time (3:1).

The tomb of his father (v. 32). The chapter ends with two night marches in opposite directions. Abner is crossing the Jordan in the dark. Joab is carrying his brother to Bethlehem, burying him in their father's tomb, and walking through the night to Hebron, and the sun comes up on him as he arrives.

Both armies spend the same night walking away from a battle that decided nothing. It is a bleak, exact ending, and the writer offers no comment on any of it. The kingdom is coming to David. This is what it costs while it comes, and most of the cost is being paid by people who never chose either side.

2.theology:
He asks, and then he asks again (v. 1). His claim to the throne was beyond dispute and the moment had plainly come, and he still put it to God; and having been told go up, he would not treat that as an answer to where. He is told where to go but not why, and Hebron turns out to be the oldest covenant ground in the country. What changed this man was Ziklag, where he called for the ephod standing in the ashes.

Each confirmation after the waiting (v. 4). Samuel's oil among his brothers, his own tribe now, and in time the elders of all Israel (5:3): God keeps confirming the same word in front of larger audiences, and each confirmation arrives only after the waiting.

Godly and shrewd together (vv. 5-7). The thank-you to Jabesh-gilead is real gratitude and also a careful word to the watching north, and the text is comfortable with both.

Peace-keeping that starts a war (vv. 14-17). A contest meant to keep a war small settles nothing, because neither general would have accepted a losing result. And Abner, who did not want to kill Asahel, kills him all the same, and that one death runs forward through the rest of David's life (see the note on v. 23).

A king recognised by one tribe (vv. 4, 8-11). David is the anointed king, crowned in Hebron, and for seven and a half years most of Israel follows someone else. His kingdom grows not by his seizing it but because God swore it, and his first act toward the doubtful north is a message of kindness, not a sword. That is the New Testament’s picture of the Son of David now. He is already crowned, yet at present, we do not yet see everything in subjection to him. But we see him... crowned with glory and honor (Hebrews 2:8-9), and he reigns until he has put all his enemies under his feet (1 Corinthians 15:25). Meanwhile he gathers rebels by a gracious word, as David wrote to Jabesh.

The right words from a man with something to gain (v. 26). Abner is calling for peace because he is about to be overrun, and the sentence is still true: the sword does devour, it is bitter in the end, and they are brothers. Self-interest does not automatically make a thing false.
2.examples:
Then: Two Israelite armies sat down on opposite sides of a rock-cut water tank and agreed to settle the matter with twelve men a side, and every one of the twenty-four caught his opposite number by the head and put a sword in his ribs at the same instant, so that nothing at all was decided. They named the ground the Field of Sword-Edges and then fought the battle anyway.

Now: Verse 1 is the practical lesson: David got a clear yes and still would not assume it answered the next question. Most bad decisions made by people who genuinely want to obey are made in exactly that gap, a real leading about whether quietly extended to cover where, when and how. God has not left his people to guess: he gives his word, and the Spirit who leads us through it, and he answers those who keep asking, as he answered a man who had not asked for sixteen months. Abner's line is the other lesson: a quarrel does not stop when its cause has been dealt with, because the sword has an appetite of its own. Somebody usually has to call across the valley and say so, and it is very often the person least entitled to. Christians can be that voice because the Son of David has already made peace for us at his own cost.

3.title: Abner's Defection and Joab's Revenge
3.text: <sup>1</sup>There was a long war between the house of Saul and the house of David. And David grew stronger and stronger, while the house of Saul became weaker and weaker.<sup>2</sup>And sons were born to David at Hebron: his firstborn was Amnon, of Ahinoam of Jezreel;<sup>3</sup>and his second, Chileab, of Abigail the widow of Nabal of Carmel; and the third, Absalom the son of Maacah the daughter of Talmai king of Geshur;<sup>4</sup>and the fourth, Adonijah the son of Haggith; and the fifth, Shephatiah the son of Abital;<sup>5</sup>and the sixth, Ithream, of Eglah, David's wife. These were born to David in Hebron.<sup>6</sup>While there was war between the house of Saul and the house of David, Abner was making himself strong in the house of Saul.<sup>7</sup>Now Saul had a concubine whose name was Rizpah, the daughter of Aiah. These men, the sons of Zeruiah, are more severe than I. The LORD repay the evildoer according to his wickedness!"
3.overview:
One flat verse covers years of civil war and gives away the ending, and a list of David's sons, dropped in like an administrative note, holds most of the sorrows still to come in this book.

Then the chapter turns on two men. Abner, insulted by the king he himself made, changes sides and quotes the oath of God he had known all along. Joab, with a brother to avenge and a position to keep, murders him in the gate at Hebron. Between them stands Michal, David's one condition for peace, whom nobody asks anything.

It ends with the king walking behind the coffin, weeping and fasting, and confessing in public what he cannot do: these men, the sons of Zeruiah, are more severe than I.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–11 — What the LORD Has Sworn to Him
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The long war tilts steadily toward David (v. 1). Six sons are born to him at Hebron by six different women (vv. 2-5). Then Ish-bosheth accuses Abner over Rizpah, Saul's concubine, and Abner in his fury swears to bring about what the LORD promised David, which dooms the northern kingdom (vv. 6-11).
verseByVerse.theology: The list of sons looks like a routine record, but these sons bring trouble for the rest of the book.
verseByVerse.examples: Abner's change of side in verse 9 comes from wounded pride, not from repentance, and God's purpose moves forward through it all the same.

verseByVerse.quote: There was a long war between the house of Saul and the house of David. And David grew stronger and stronger, while the house of Saul became weaker and weaker. And sons were born to David at Hebron: his firstborn was Amnon, of Ahinoam of Jezreel; and his second, Chileab, of Abigail the widow of Nabal of Carmel; and the third, Absalom the son of Maacah the daughter of Talmai king of Geshur; and the fourth, Adonijah the son of Haggith; and the fifth, Shephatiah the son of Abital; and the sixth, Ithream, of Eglah, David's wife. These were born to David in Hebron. While there was war between the house of Saul and the house of David, Abner was making himself strong in the house of Saul. Now Saul had a concubine whose name was Rizpah, the daughter of Aiah. And Ish-bosheth said to Abner, "Why have you gone in to my father's concubine?" Then Abner was very angry over the words of Ish-bosheth and said, "Am I a dog's head of Judah? To this day I keep showing steadfast love to the house of Saul your father, to his brothers, and to his friends, and have not given you into the hand of David. And yet you charge me today with a fault concerning a woman. God do so to Abner and more also, if I do not accomplish for David what the LORD has sworn to him, to transfer the kingdom from the house of Saul and set up the throne of David over Israel and over Judah, from Dan to Beersheba." And Ish-bosheth could not answer Abner another word, because he feared him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Verse 1 covers years, and it does two things at once.

It tells us this went on a long time. Not a season of skirmishing but a war, between two halves of the same nation, with the pool of Gibeon somewhere near the beginning of it.

And it tells us the outcome before it happens, in the flattest possible way. Stronger and stronger; weaker and weaker. There is no drama in the sentence at all, and that is the point. What God said would happen is happening, at the pace of ordinary events, while people fight about it.

Verses 2 to 5 list six sons by six mothers, dropped into a war report like an administrative note. Three of the names fill much of the rest of this book.

Amnon will rape his half-sister Tamar and be murdered at a sheep-shearing feast two years later (ch. 13). Absalom will do the murdering, flee to his grandfather in Geshur, come back, steal the hearts of Israel at the city gate, drive his father out of Jerusalem barefoot, sleep with his father's concubines on the palace roof in daylight, and die hanging in an oak with three javelins in his chest (chs. 13-18). Adonijah will try to take the throne while David lies dying, and be executed by Solomon (1 Kings 1-2).

Every one of them by a different woman.

The law had said this to Israel's king, in advance, in one sentence: he shall not acquire many wives for himself, lest his heart turn away (Deut. 17:17). The rule is not only about desire. A household of rival wives and rival sons splits into factions, and when it is the royal household the factions fight for the throne.

Note also who Absalom's mother is: Maacah the daughter of Talmai king of Geshur. A foreign princess, which means the marriage was a treaty. And when Absalom kills his brother and runs, he runs to Geshur, to his grandfather, and stays three years (13:37-38). The alliance David made to secure a border produced the son who nearly took his throne, and the hiding place the son escaped to.

The narrator says none of this. He gives a list of names between a war summary and a palace quarrel, and lets it sit.

The accusation (v. 7) looks domestic, but it is about the throne.

In that world, taking a dead king's women was a claim on his throne, and everybody understood it. It is not a private matter that happens to be embarrassing; it is the recognised public gesture for saying "the succession is mine". Absalom will do it deliberately, on a roof, in front of the whole city, on Ahithophel's advice, precisely because it is unmistakable (16:21-22).

So Ish-bosheth is accusing his general of moving on the crown, and he may well be right.

He is also finished the moment he says it. Abner is the army, the administration and the reason Ish-bosheth is king at all. Insulting him is the only independent decision this man makes in the entire book, and it destroys him.

Abner does not deny it (v. 8).

His answer is a list of services rendered and a complaint about ingratitude, and nowhere in it does he say the thing did not happen. What he says is: after everything I have done for your father's house, you are going to raise this?

A dog's head is about as low as the insults of that culture went, and the sneer at Judah is deliberate.

The key sentence of the chapter is in verse 9: what the LORD has sworn to him.

Abner has known all along, and known that God swore it. He can quote it, including the geography, from Dan to Beersheba, which is the whole country from top to bottom.

Now count what he has done with that knowledge. He served a king God had rejected. He took Saul's surviving son across the Jordan and crowned him. He ran a civil war for years against the man God had sworn to enthrone. Three hundred and eighty Israelites died at the pool of Gibeon because of a proposal he made, and Asahel died on the end of his spear.

He did all of it knowingly.

And what changes his mind is not conviction, not repentance, not the word of God he has just quoted. It is being spoken to disrespectfully about a woman.

This is more common than a dramatic change of heart. Very few people who resist what they know to be right are converted by an argument. They are moved when the arrangement they were defending finally insults them, and then they discover that they had known all along, and they say so, loudly, as though the knowledge were new.

God's purpose goes forward through it. He is using a furious general with wounded pride and no change of heart whatever, and the kingdom moves a step closer to the man Abner has been fighting for years.

And Ish-bosheth could not answer Abner another word, because he feared him (v. 11). That is the measure of this king: at the one moment that mattered, he had nothing to say.

Did God approve David’s many wives? No. God’s design is one man and one woman (Gen 2:24), and the law told Israel’s king not to acquire many wives for himself, lest his heart turn away (Deut 17:17). Scripture records David’s polygamy without approving it, and the following chapters show its fruit: rape, murder and rebellion among his sons.
verseByVerse.note: The same claim lies behind Absalom on the palace roof (16:21-22) and behind Adonijah's request for Abishag, which cost him his life (1 Kings 2:13-25).

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Abner opens negotiations, and David's one condition is Michal; she is taken from Paltiel, who follows her weeping to Bahurim (vv. 12-16). Abner works the elders of Israel and Benjamin, comes to Hebron with twenty men, is feasted, and leaves in peace (vv. 17-21).
verseByVerse.theology: David's demand for Michal is both politics and a husband's claim, and the cost of it falls on two people who are never consulted.
verseByVerse.examples: Abner's diplomacy with the elders is skilful, and the narrator's triple in peace makes sure we remember the safe conduct he was given.

verseByVerse.quote: And Abner sent messengers to David on his behalf, saying, "To whom does the land belong? Make your covenant with me, and behold, my hand shall be with you to bring over all Israel to you." And he said, "Good; I will make a covenant with you. But one thing I require of you; that is, you shall not see my face unless you first bring Michal, Saul's daughter, when you come to see my face." Then David sent messengers to Ish-bosheth, Saul's son, saying, "Give me my wife Michal, for whom I paid the bridal price of a hundred foreskins of the Philistines." And Ish-bosheth sent and took her from her husband Paltiel the son of Laish. But her husband went with her, weeping after her all the way to Bahurim. Then Abner said to him, "Go, return." And he returned. And Abner conferred with the elders of Israel, saying, "For some time past you have been seeking David as king over you. Now then bring it about, for the LORD has promised David, saying, 'By the hand of my servant David I will save my people Israel from the hand of the Philistines, and from the hand of all their enemies.'" Abner also spoke to Benjamin. And then Abner went to tell David at Hebron all that Israel and the whole house of Benjamin thought good to do. When Abner came with twenty men to David at Hebron, David made a feast for Abner and the men who were with him. And Abner said to David, "I will arise and go and will gather all Israel to my lord the king, that they may make a covenant with you, and that you may reign over all that your heart desires." So David sent Abner away, and he went in peace.
verseByVerse.commentary:
To whom does the land belong? He means: we both know the answer, and we both know I am the only person who can deliver it.

David sets one condition (v. 13), and it is a woman.

Michal. Saul's younger daughter, who loved David: the narrator said so outright, and it is a thing the narrator says of no other woman in either book of Samuel. She warned him the night the assassins came, let him down through a window, put an idol in his bed with goats' hair at its head to buy him time, and lied to her father's face about it (1 Sam. 18:20; 19:11-17).

Then Saul gave her to another man while David was in the wilderness, as though the marriage had never happened (1 Sam. 25:44).

Why does David want her back? Both reasons are real and the text will not sort them out.

She is Saul's daughter, and a king of Judah married to Saul's daughter is a king with a claim in the north that the northern tribes can recognise. That is politics, and it is the reason he raises it in a negotiation about the kingdom rather than at any point before.

And she was his wife, taken from him by force by a man who was trying to kill him, and he has never accepted it. That is not nothing.

David also sends to Ish-bosheth himself (v. 14), so that the return is lawful, and he cites the bride-price.

That price was Saul's idea, and its purpose was to get David killed: a hundred Philistines was expected to be the end of him (1 Sam. 18:25). He brought two hundred (1 Sam. 18:27; the Greek Old Testament there reads a hundred, and David here names the price that was asked). David is reminding the house of Saul that he paid what Saul asked, twice over, and that the marriage was lawful.

Did taking her back break the law? Deuteronomy 24:1–4 forbids taking back a wife after she has been divorced and married another. Michal had not been divorced by David; Saul took her and gave her to Paltiel against the law (1 Sam 25:44). David reclaimed his own wife. That answers the legal question, and it does not answer the human one.

Verse 16 is the hardest thing in the chapter.

Paltiel gets no dialogue, no protest, no argument. He walks behind the party, crying, all the way to Bahurim, until a general who has killed men with a spear says two words to him. And he turns round and goes home.

He had been married to her for years. Nobody consulted him and nobody compensated him. There is no suggestion he did anything wrong; he was given a wife by his king and he loved her, and now two governments have agreed on something and he is walking back to Gallim on his own.

Nobody asks Michal.

She is not addressed by anyone at any point. She is taken from her husband by Ish-bosheth, delivered by Abner, and handed to David, and she does not speak in this chapter or the next. The last time she spoke she was lying to her father to save David's life. The next time she speaks, three chapters from now, it will be to despise him from a window, and the writer will tell us she had no children to the day of her death (6:16-23).

Something happened to that woman between the window she lowered David from and the window she despised him from, and this chapter is a large part of it.

Anyone who has been treated as a piece in other people’s bargains, handed on without being asked, should know that Scripture records this without approving it. The God of Israel is the God who sees the one nobody consulted (Genesis 16:13).

It would be easy, and wrong, to hurry past this. Scripture does not excuse it, and neither should a reader. David is not accused here by the narrator, but the narrator does not usually accuse anybody, and he has just made sure we watch a man weep all the way to Bahurim.

Abner wins over the elders (vv. 17-18), and he does it by telling them what they already wanted.

For some time past you have been seeking David as king over you. So the northern enthusiasm for David was there all along, and Abner was the man holding it back. He now presents himself as the one making it possible.

And again he quotes God. A second word from God, this time about rescue from the Philistines. He knows what God has said, and always did.

Benjamin gets a separate conversation, because Benjamin is Saul's own tribe and has the most to lose.

And he went in peace.

The phrase comes three times in three verses, which is the writer’s way of stressing it. Abner came under safe conduct, ate at the king's table, and left with the king's word on him.

Everything that is about to happen is a violation of that.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 22–30 — In the Midst of the Gate
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Joab returns from a raid, tells the king Abner came to deceive him, and without David's knowledge brings Abner back and kills him in the gate for the blood of Asahel (vv. 22-27). David declares himself and his kingdom guiltless before the LORD and curses Joab's house (vv. 28-30).
verseByVerse.theology: Joab's murder is planned down to its place and manner, and the narrator's quiet line that David did not know about it is the hinge of the whole affair.
verseByVerse.examples: David's first concern is to clear himself and his kingdom of the blood before the LORD; his second is a curse; and there is no third.

verseByVerse.quote: Just then the servants of David arrived with Joab from a raid, bringing much spoil with them. But Abner was not with David at Hebron, for he had sent him away, and he had gone in peace. When Joab and all the army that was with him came, it was told Joab, "Abner the son of Ner came to the king, and he has let him go, and he has gone in peace." Then Joab went to the king and said, "What have you done? Behold, Abner came to you. Why is it that you have sent him away, so that he is gone? You know that Abner the son of Ner came to deceive you and to know your going out and your coming in, and to know all that you are doing." When Joab came out from David's presence, he sent messengers after Abner, and they brought him back from the cistern of Sirah. But David did not know about it. And when Abner returned to Hebron, Joab took him aside into the midst of the gate to speak with him privately, and there he struck him in the stomach, so that he died, for the blood of Asahel his brother. Afterward, when David heard of it, he said, "I and my kingdom are forever guiltless before the LORD for the blood of Abner the son of Ner. May it fall upon the head of Joab and upon all his father's house, and may the house of Joab never be without one who has a discharge or who is leprous or who holds a spindle or who falls by the sword or who lacks bread!" So Joab and Abishai his brother killed Abner, because he had put their brother Asahel to death in the battle at Gibeon.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Joab has been out of town, which is the reason there was a deal at all. When he returns he rebukes the king to his face (vv. 24-25), in the king’s own house, and nothing happens to him.

The charge is that Abner was a spy. There is not a word anywhere in the chapter to support it, and Joab does not offer any evidence. It is the excuse that lay to hand, not the real reason.

The reason is a body in a tomb at Bethlehem. Abner killed Asahel at Gibeon, and Joab buried his brother and walked all night to Hebron and has been waiting ever since.

There is also a second motive, and it would be naive to leave it out. If Abner delivers the northern tribes, Abner becomes the most important man in the kingdom after the king, and Joab is currently the most important man in the kingdom after the king. The spy story is a pretext for a blood feud, and the blood feud is running alongside a rank he does not intend to lose.

But David did not know about it.

The writer puts that in deliberately, and it is the hinge of the whole affair. Everything that follows is done in the king's name, with the king's messengers, from the king's town, without the king's knowledge.

Abner turns round and comes back because he has no reason not to. He has eaten at David's table and been sent away in peace. A summons from Hebron means the king wants another word.

Verse 27 holds four separate outrages, stated without raising the voice.

The first is the place. Hebron. Turn to Joshua 20 and there is a list of six cities set aside by God's own command as cities of refuge, and Hebron is the first one named in the south (Josh. 20:7). Their purpose was exact: a man who killed somebody without intent could run to one of them and be safe from the avenger of blood (the dead man’s nearest kinsman) until there had been a proper hearing.

And Abner’s killing of Asahel is a clear case of it. He warned the boy twice, offered him another target, said out loud that he did not want to face Joab afterwards, and struck backwards with the blunt end of a spear to wind him. Asahel's own speed drove it through. If any death in Scripture was manslaughter rather than murder, it is that one.

The city that existed to protect exactly this man is where he is killed for exactly this death.

The second is the spot. Into the midst of the gate. The gate was the courthouse. It is where the elders sat, where property changed hands, where a case was heard and witnesses stood. Boaz settled the redemption of Ruth in a gate with ten elders watching. It is the most public and most legally protected ground in the town.

The third is the method. To speak with him privately. He is murdered by the offer of a confidential word: the exact gesture of trust, used as the weapon. Abner has to lean in for it to work.

The fourth is the wound. He struck him in the stomach. That is where Abner's spear went into Asahel, and everybody involved would have known it. It is more than a killing; it is a debt repaid in kind.

Joab is not a hot-tempered man. He waited, he chose the ground, and he matched the wound.

David’s first concern (v. 28) is guilt, and specifically guilt resting on the whole kingdom.

This is more than a public statement, though it works as one. In Israel, shed blood defiled the land and lay on the community until it was answered, and a killing done by the king's commander in the king's city with the king's messengers would ordinarily lie on the king. David is declaring before God that it does not.

Then he curses him, comprehensively and permanently, and does absolutely nothing else.

That gap is the point of the chapter's last verse, and we will come to it.

The narrator's verdict in verse 30 sets Joab’s excuse aside: the reason was not spying but Asahel. And in the battle matters: this was a death in war, and Joab has answered it in peacetime, which is the precise thing David will still be naming on his deathbed (1 Kings 2:5).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 31–39 — The Sons of Zeruiah Are More Severe Than I
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: David makes Joab tear his clothes and mourn, follows the bier himself, weeps and laments at the grave, and fasts until sundown, so that all Israel understands the killing was not his will (vv. 31-37). Then he tells his servants a prince has fallen, and confesses that the sons of Zeruiah are too hard for him (vv. 38-39).
verseByVerse.theology: David's public mourning is real grief and shrewd statecraft at once, and the narrator does not make us choose between them.
