verseByVerse.examples: Verse 39 is David naming his own weakness in public, and it is the truest thing he says all chapter.

verseByVerse.quote: Then David said to Joab and to all the people who were with him, "Tear your clothes and put on sackcloth and mourn before Abner." And King David followed the bier. They buried Abner at Hebron. And the king lifted up his voice and wept at the grave of Abner, and all the people wept. And the king lamented for Abner, saying, "Should Abner die as a fool dies? Your hands were not bound; your feet were not fettered; as one falls before the wicked you have fallen." And all the people wept again over him. Then all the people came to persuade David to eat bread while it was yet day. But David swore, saying, "God do so to me and more also, if I taste bread or anything else till the sun goes down!" And all the people took notice of it, and it pleased them, as everything that the king did pleased all the people. So all the people and all Israel understood that day that it had not been the king's will to put to death Abner the son of Ner. And the king said to his servants, "Do you not know that a prince and a great man has fallen this day in Israel? And I was gentle today, though anointed king. These men, the sons of Zeruiah, are more severe than I. The LORD repay the evildoer according to his wickedness!"
verseByVerse.commentary:
David makes the murderer walk in the funeral (v. 31).

Joab is ordered to tear his clothes, put on sackcloth and mourn in public for the man he has just killed, in front of the whole town. It is not justice and David knows it is not justice. It is the only thing he can make him do.

Then the king walks behind the coffin.

Think about who is in that procession. David is following the bier of the general who fought against him for years, crowned a rival, ran the war, and killed David's own nephew. He is grieving for the commander of the opposing army, publicly, at the head of his people.

A second lament, and this is the second poem in three chapters David has composed for a man on the other side.

Should Abner die as a fool dies?

The protest is not that he died. It is how. A soldier of that rank should fall in the line with a weapon in his hand, and there is an honour in that which his whole world recognised.

Your hands were not bound; your feet were not fettered. He was not a prisoner. He had not been taken, tried, condemned, or led out. He was a free man walking into a gate under safe conduct to hear what the king wanted.

As one falls before the wicked you have fallen. That is the verdict, and the word wicked is aimed at somebody standing in the crowd in sackcloth.

He fasts, and he swears an oath about it in front of everybody.

Verse 37 says what the day was for. This is politics as well as grief, because the text says so.

Think about the position David is in. Abner has just persuaded the northern tribes to come over, and before he has even got home Abner is dead in David's own city, killed by David's own commander, brought back by messengers who came from David's house. Every man in the north is asking one question, and if the answer they settle on is "the king had him killed", the union is finished before it starts and the war goes on for another decade.

So David makes it impossible to believe. He curses Joab publicly, walks behind the coffin himself, weeps at the graveside in front of witnesses, composes a lament, and swears an oath not to eat.

And here is the thing that has to be held alongside it: none of that means the grief is false. The man wrote a lament for Saul with nothing in it for himself, and he wrote this one too. He is capable of meaning every word and of knowing exactly what it will accomplish, at the same time, which is what it is to be a public man with a real heart.

The alternative was available and it was easy. He could have said nothing, accepted the convenient death of the one man who might have rivalled Joab, and let people think what they liked. Plenty of kings would have. It would have cost him the north.

A prince and a great man. Said of an enemy general, to his own staff, on the record.

David has a habit by now, and it should be named: he is very good at saying the true good thing about people who have cost him a great deal. Saul got scarlet and gold and eagles. Abner gets a prince and a great man. Neither of them had earned it from him personally.

The last verse of the chapter is David admitting he cannot control his own army, and it is the most honest sentence he speaks all day.

I was gentle today, though anointed king. The word can also mean weak, and he is not paying himself a compliment. He is saying: I am the anointed king of Judah and a murder was committed under my nose by my own commander and I have done nothing about it except make him wear sackcloth.

These men, the sons of Zeruiah, are more severe than I. His own nephews. Joab and Abishai are harder men than he is, they command the loyalty of the army, and he needs them.

The LORD repay the evildoer according to his wickedness. It is what he said in the cave at Engedi, may the LORD judge between me and you, and it is not the same situation at all. There he was a fugitive with no power and handing the case to God was faith. Here he is the king, the law is his to administer, and handing the case to God is a way of not doing his job.

Scripture lets that stand without comment, and the rest of the book shows what it cost.

Joab, unpunished, will run David's army for most of the reign. He will murder Amasa in exactly the same way: a friendly greeting, a hand on the beard, a blade in the stomach (20:9-10). He will kill Absalom with three javelins while the boy hangs helpless in a tree, in direct defiance of an order the whole army heard (18:5, 14). He will speak to David as no subject should speak to a king, and get away with it, because he knows too much and holds too much.

And at the end, on his deathbed, David will hand the whole unfinished business to a young man who has the strength to do what he never did: you also know what Joab the son of Zeruiah did to me... Act therefore according to your wisdom, but do not let his gray head go down to Sheol in peace (1 Kings 2:5-6).

More than thirty years is a long time to carry a thing you should have dealt with on the day. David named his own weakness accurately in verse 39, in public, and then lived with it for the rest of his reign.

3.theology:
God keeps his oath through people who are not keeping theirs. Hardly anything in this chapter is done from a pure motive. Abner changes sides because he has been insulted, David asks for Michal for reasons of state as well as love, and Joab kills for a brother and for his own position. Yet the LORD's sworn word to David (v. 9) moves forward through all of it. That excuses none of them. It is the reason a reader can trust God's purpose even when the people carrying it forward are compromised, and it is a comfort to anyone who knows their own motives are mixed.

The roots of the later sorrows are already in the ground. Two things in this chapter grow into the rest of the book: a divided household, built against the law's warning to the king (Deut. 17:17), and a commander David would not judge. The narrator comments on neither. He lets the reader watch them grow.

Grief and politics need not be rivals. David's mourning for Abner was meant to be seen, and it was also sincere. A leader can know exactly what his public grief will accomplish and still grieve truly. What the chapter faults is not the funeral but the justice that never followed it.

The king Israel still needed (v. 39). David can name the evil and cannot judge it; he is too weak for his own commanders. The prophets therefore look for a son of David who will with righteousness judge the poor and strike the wicked with the breath of his lips (Isaiah 11:4), a king neither cruel like Joab nor helpless like David. Jesus is that king. When his own disciples wanted fire from heaven on a village that refused him, he turned and rebuked them (Luke 9:54-55), and when Peter drew a sword, he told him to put it away (Matthew 26:52). He restrains the sons of violence, and one day he will judge every hidden murder in the gate with perfect justice.
3.examples:
Then: A general who had spent years fighting a war he knew God had already decided changed sides because his king insulted him, won over the northern elders, ate at his new king's table, and was stabbed before he got home, inside a city of refuge, by a man who had asked for a quiet word.

Now: Two things, pulling in different directions. Abner is the warning: it is possible to know the promise of God, say it accurately, and act on it only when the wrong side stops rewarding you. David is the other: he could name exactly what Joab was and still not act, because acting would cost something today. Naming a problem is not the same as addressing it, and that gap lasted thirty years. None of us is cured of either fault by resolve. The God who kept his oath to David through all of it is the one who forgives our long delays when we confess them, and his Spirit gives the courage to deal with the thing on the day rather than leave it to the next generation.

4.title: Ish-bosheth Murdered
4.text: <sup>1</sup>When Ish-bosheth, Saul's son, heard that Abner had died at Hebron, his courage failed, and all Israel was dismayed.<sup>2</sup>Now Saul's son had two men who were captains of raiding bands; the name of the one was Baanah, and the name of the other Rechab, sons of Rimmon a man of Benjamin from Beeroth (for Beeroth also is counted part of Benjamin;<sup>3</sup>the Beerothites fled to Gittaim and have been sojourners there to this day).<sup>4</sup>Jonathan, the son of Saul, had a son who was crippled in his feet. He was five years old when the news about Saul and Jonathan came from Jezreel, and his nurse took him up and fled, and as she fled in her haste, he fell and became lame. And his name was Mephibosheth.<sup>5</sup>Now the sons of Rimmon the Beerothite, Rechab and Baanah, set out, and about the heat of the day they came to the house of Ish-bosheth as he was taking his noonday rest.<sup>6</sup>And they came into the midst of the house as if to get wheat, and they stabbed him in the stomach. Then Rechab and Baanah his brother escaped.<sup>7</sup>When they came into the house, as he lay on his bed in his bedroom, they struck him and put him to death and beheaded him. They took his head and went by the way of the Arabah all night,<sup>8</sup>and brought the head of Ish-bosheth to David at Hebron. And they said to the king, "Here is the head of Ish-bosheth, the son of Saul, your enemy, who sought your life. The LORD has avenged my lord the king this day on Saul and on his offspring."<sup>9</sup>But David answered Rechab and Baanah his brother, the sons of Rimmon the Beerothite, "As the LORD lives, who has redeemed my life out of every adversity,<sup>10</sup>when one told me, 'Behold, Saul is dead,' and thought he was bringing good news, I seized him and killed him at Ziklag, which was the reward I gave him for his news.<sup>11</sup>How much more, when wicked men have killed a righteous man in his own house on his bed, shall I not now require his blood at your hand and destroy you from the earth?"<sup>12</sup>And David commanded his young men, and they killed them and cut off their hands and feet and hanged them beside the pool at Hebron. But they took the head of Ish-bosheth and buried it in the tomb of Abner at Hebron.
4.overview:
The news from Hebron reaches Ish-bosheth and his hands go slack, which is exactly right for a man whose whole kingship was somebody else's doing. Then the narrator interrupts his own story to tell us about a lame child, Jonathan's son, who will not be mentioned again until a king who has won everything asks whether anyone is left of the house of Saul.

Two of Ish-bosheth's own captains kill him in his bed and carry his head to Hebron, crediting the LORD with the deed. They are right about what God is doing and wrong to think he needed them. David answers by naming the God who has redeemed my life out of every adversity, does justice on the killers, and gives his rival an honourable grave.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Ish-bosheth's courage fails at the news of Abner's death (v. 1). Two of his raiding captains, Benjaminites from Beeroth, are introduced (vv. 2-3), and then, with no explanation, a note about Jonathan's lame son Mephibosheth (v. 4).
verseByVerse.theology: With Abner gone, the son of Saul is no longer really a king; he is a man waiting in a house for whatever comes.
verseByVerse.examples: Verse 4 looks like a digression, but it is placed here to prepare for chapter 9.

verseByVerse.quote: When Ish-bosheth, Saul's son, heard that Abner had died at Hebron, his courage failed, and all Israel was dismayed. Now Saul's son had two men who were captains of raiding bands; the name of the one was Baanah, and the name of the other Rechab, sons of Rimmon a man of Benjamin from Beeroth (for Beeroth also is counted part of Benjamin; the Beerothites fled to Gittaim and have been sojourners there to this day). Jonathan, the son of Saul, had a son who was crippled in his feet. He was five years old when the news about Saul and Jonathan came from Jezreel, and his nurse took him up and fled, and as she fled in her haste, he fell and became lame. And his name was Mephibosheth.
verseByVerse.commentary:
In verse 1 the Hebrew is more physical than the English his courage failed: his hands went slack.

It is the exact image for a man whose support has been taken away. Nothing has happened to him personally; the news is about somebody else in another town. And it finishes him, because Abner was never just his general; his kingship rested wholly on Abner. Chapter 2 said it in the verbs: Abner took him, brought him over, made him king.

Now he has nothing to hold on to and he cannot hold anything.

And all Israel was dismayed. The whole northern kingdom feels it at the same time. They had all been depending on Abner.

In verses 2 and 3 the writer takes trouble over where the two captains come from. These men are Benjaminites, from Saul's own tribe. They are officers in Ish-bosheth's own army, captains of raiding bands, which means trusted men with troops of their own. The king they are about to kill is their tribesman and their employer.

An old grievance is being hinted at and not explained. Something drove the people of Beeroth out of their own town at some point, and they were still living displaced when this was written. Some have wondered whether Saul was responsible, since he massacred the Gibeonites, and Beeroth was one of the Gibeonite towns (Josh. 9:17), a matter that costs Israel three years of famine in chapter 21.

The text does not say, and a reader should not pretend it does. What the aside establishes is that these two had a history, and that their loyalty to the house of Saul may never have been what it looked like.

Verse 4 has nothing to do with the story it is sitting in. In the middle of an assassination, the narrator interrupts himself to tell us about a child who fell years ago. He puts it here because it will matter later.

The scene takes one sentence. A five-year-old boy in a royal household. A runner arrives from Jezreel with the news of Gilboa: the king is dead, his sons are dead, the army is destroyed, and the Philistines are coming. The palace empties. A nurse picks up the child and runs, because in that world the first thing an incoming dynasty does is kill the old king's grandsons.

And she drops him.

She was carrying him at a dead run and she fell, or he fell, and something broke that never set. He is crippled in both feet for the rest of his life, and that is the day it happened: the same day he lost his father, his grandfather, two uncles and a kingdom.

He is Jonathan's son.

Which means that in a story where every surviving member of Saul's house is being systematically removed (Abner dead in a gate, Ish-bosheth about to be killed in his bed), there is one left, and he is a lame boy nobody has mentioned, hidden somewhere east of the Jordan.

The writer says nothing more about him for five chapters. Then a king who has finally won everything will sit in his palace and ask a strange question: is there still anyone left of the house of Saul, that I may show him kindness for Jonathan's sake? (9:1). And the answer will be this child, grown up and terrified, saying what is your servant, that you should show regard for a dead dog such as I?

Verse 4 is here so that when that day comes we already know what it cost to be him.
verseByVerse.note: Mephibosheth is another form of Merib-baal (1 Chr 8:34); like Ish-bosheth, the name probably swaps “shame” (bosheth) for “Baal.”

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 5–8 — Behold, the Head of Ish-bosheth
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The captains enter the house at the midday rest as though to fetch wheat, kill Ish-bosheth in his bed, behead him, and carry the head through the night to David, crediting the LORD with the deed (vv. 5-8).
verseByVerse.theology: He dies as he reigned, passively, killed in his sleep by men he trusted.
verseByVerse.examples: This is the second time in this book someone has brought David a dead rival and expected payment, and this time the claim comes dressed in theology.

verseByVerse.quote: Now the sons of Rimmon the Beerothite, Rechab and Baanah, set out, and about the heat of the day they came to the house of Ish-bosheth as he was taking his noonday rest. And they came into the midst of the house as if to get wheat, and they stabbed him in the stomach. Then Rechab and Baanah his brother escaped. When they came into the house, as he lay on his bed in his bedroom, they struck him and put him to death and beheaded him. They took his head and went by the way of the Arabah all night, and brought the head of Ish-bosheth to David at Hebron. And they said to the king, "Here is the head of Ish-bosheth, the son of Saul, your enemy, who sought your life. The LORD has avenged my lord the king this day on Saul and on his offspring."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Everything here is small and domestic, and it is about to become murder. The heat of the day. A rest after the midday meal, which is what everyone did in that climate. The house rather than a palace or a fortress. There is no guard mentioned, no court, no ceremony: two of his own officers walk in during the quiet hour.

They come in as though on ordinary business. Wheat is the reason officers of a raiding band would be at the king's stores, and nobody would look twice.

And it is a stomach wound, which is the third one in three chapters. Abner killed Asahel that way. Joab killed Abner that way. The writer notes it each time, and it is his way of tying the three deaths together as one chain of bloodshed.

Verse 7 adds the detail that makes it worse: as he lay on his bed in his bedroom.

He never woke up. There was no confrontation, no chance, no last words. The last king of Saul's house dies asleep at his noonday rest and is decapitated where he lies, by men who had sworn to him.

Then they walk all night down the Jordan valley carrying a head, on the long road to Hebron.

It is the same kind of journey the Amalekite made with a crown and an armlet, and the same speech is coming, more sophisticated this time. They do not claim the credit: the LORD has avenged. They put God at the front of the sentence and stand behind him.

They also load the description of the victim: the son of Saul, your enemy, who sought your life. Every word of that is chosen. They describe him not as a person but by labels. And it is not even accurate: Saul sought David's life; Ish-bosheth was a frightened figurehead who never personally did David any harm at all.

Their claim deserves a careful look, because they are not wrong about what God is doing.

God is removing the house of Saul. Samuel said so at Gilgal and again at Endor. Abner quoted the oath himself in the last chapter. Every reader of this book knows that the throne is being transferred by divine decision and that Saul's line is finished.

What they have done is take a true belief about God’s purpose and appoint themselves to carry it out.

That is the error, and it is not a rare one. Knowing what God has purposed does not make a man the instrument of it, and no amount of being right about the direction of history authorises the thing you do next. God had said the kingdom would pass to David. He had never said anything at all to Rechab and Baanah.

David's men made the same mistake in the cave at Engedi, and Abishai made it standing over Saul with a spear, and Saul himself made it at Keilah. In every case the reasoning was sound, the circumstance was real, and the conclusion was catastrophic. In the first two cases David talked them out of it. These two did not ask anybody.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 9–12 — Who Has Redeemed My Life out of Every Adversity
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: David answers with an oath by the LORD who redeemed his life, recalls the Amalekite at Ziklag, and condemns the murder of a righteous man in his bed (vv. 9-11). The killers are executed and displayed by the pool at Hebron; the head is buried in Abner's tomb (v. 12).
verseByVerse.theology: David's opening oath carries the theology of the first four chapters of this book: God is the one who rescues him.
verseByVerse.examples: Justice and generosity come together here: the killers are judged, and the rival is given the honour he is owed.

verseByVerse.quote: But David answered Rechab and Baanah his brother, the sons of Rimmon the Beerothite, "As the LORD lives, who has redeemed my life out of every adversity, when one told me, 'Behold, Saul is dead,' and thought he was bringing good news, I seized him and killed him at Ziklag, which was the reward I gave him for his news. How much more, when wicked men have killed a righteous man in his own house on his bed, shall I not now require his blood at your hand and destroy you from the earth?" And David commanded his young men, and they killed them and cut off their hands and feet and hanged them beside the pool at Hebron. But they took the head of Ish-bosheth and buried it in the tomb of Abner at Hebron.
verseByVerse.commentary:
David begins with an oath (v. 9), and the clause he chooses to describe God by is the answer to their whole speech.

Redeemed is the word used for ransoming a person, and in an oath like this it means rescued: set free by God's own hand. Every adversity: not most, not the big ones. And it is stated as settled history, not as a hope.

He has some evidence. A lion and a bear at the sheepfold. A giant in the Valley of Elah. Three spears from a king. A window in the night. Two ambushes. Three thousand chosen men in the wilderness, twice. A whole army put to sleep so he could walk through it. A Philistine gate he escaped by drooling into his beard. Ziklag burning, and every captive recovered.

Not one of those was arranged by a volunteer with a knife.

So the sentence answers Rechab and Baanah before he has said a word about them. You have come to tell me that God has avenged me. I know what God does; he has been doing it since I was a boy; and he has never once required this.

The Amalekite is an exact precedent, and thought he was bringing good news. That is the whole misjudgment of both episodes in six words. Three men in four chapters have looked at David and concluded that a dead rival would please him, and every one of them has read him by what would have pleased themselves.

And which was the reward I gave him for his news is grim on purpose. He came for payment; he was paid.

The argument runs from the lesser case to the greater, in three steps. First, he calls Ish-bosheth a righteous man: his rival, the man crowned against him, in whose name a long war was fought and hundreds of Israelites died. And David says he was righteous.

It is not a statement about his piety, and it does not need to be. In the legal sense the word means innocent: in the right, guiltless in the matter at hand, and Ish-bosheth was. He never sought David's life. He never fought a battle. He was put on a throne by a general and taken off it by two captains, and in between he said one foolish sentence about a concubine. Whatever else he was, he had done David no wrong.

David gives him the word he is owed.

The second is in his own house on his bed, which is what makes the crime worse. The Amalekite claimed a battlefield killing of a mortally wounded man who asked for it. This is a sleeping man in his bedroom killed by his own officers. Even by the standards of an ugly business, this is worse, and the sentence is heavier.

The third is require his blood at your hand, which is the language of Genesis 9:5-6. Shed blood has a claim on the land and on the person who shed it, and somebody has to answer for it. David is not taking revenge on his own behalf; he is carrying out a duty that has fallen to him as king.

The execution is brutal and deliberately public. The hands did it and the feet carried it all the way to Hebron, and both are removed and displayed. And the pool at Hebron is the town's water supply, the place every household in the city walks to.

He is making a statement that cannot be missed by anybody in Israel, and this is the third time in four chapters he has had to make it. There will be no reward in this kingdom for killing the king's enemies. Anyone thinking of doing David a favour has now seen exactly what such favours are worth.

Was David right to do this? The death sentence itself is what the law required for deliberate murder, with no ransom allowed (Genesis 9:6; Numbers 35:31). Cutting off hands and feet and displaying the bodies was the custom of that age, and the narrator records it without commending it; the law itself forbade leaving a hanged body exposed beyond the day (Deuteronomy 21:22-23). Scripture shows a king of that world doing justice in that world's way, and it does not hand Christians a pattern for punishment. Paul takes that same law about a body hung on a tree and applies it to the Son of David, who became a curse for us (Galatians 3:13), and that is where Christian thinking about justice now begins.

The last sentence of the chapter is a kindness. The head of the rival king is given honourable burial, and it is put in the tomb of Abner, the general who made him king and fought David for years, and who is buried at Hebron because David walked behind his coffin in the previous chapter.

The two men who ran the war against him are now lying in the same grave in David's own city, buried at his order.

Now stand back, because chapters 1 to 4 are a single argument and this is where it closes.

Three times a man has killed a rival of David's and read David by what would have pleased himself. The Amalekite with Saul's crown. Rechab and Baanah with a head in a bag. And in between, Joab, who murdered Abner in a gate and was cursed and made to walk in the funeral and was not executed, because he was David's nephew and ran the army (3:39).

Two were dealt with. One was not, and that exception is the crack that runs through the rest of the book.

But the principle is established, and it is the same one David held in the cave and in the camp when he had nothing: the kingdom of God does not get built by killing the people standing in front of it. He waited long years for a throne he had been anointed to, and he would not receive it over a dead body.

There is a greater Son of David who was offered the kingdoms of the world on a shortcut and would not take them either, and who said to a man with a sword in a garden: put your sword back into its place; for all who take the sword will perish by the sword (Matt. 26:52). He had every right to the throne of the universe and he went to a cross to get it, the long way, on his Father's timing.

4.theology:
Right doctrine, self-appointed execution (v. 8). The murderers' mistake is a religious one, and the chapter takes it seriously. God was removing the house of Saul; everyone knew it. But knowing what God has purposed does not make anyone the instrument of it, and the murder of a sleeping man is no less a murder for being on the winning side of history. The stomach wound, the third in three chapters, ties this killing to the two before it: whatever reasons are given, it is one chain of bloodshed.

A king who will not take his throne over a dead body. David's oath by the God who has redeemed my life out of every adversity (v. 9) answers the murderers before he speaks of them, and his treatment of Ish-bosheth as a righteous man gives an enemy the justice he is owed. The one exception, Joab, will cost David dearly. But the principle stands: the kingdom of God does not get built by killing the people standing in front of it.

And a greater Son of David. Offered the kingdoms of the world on a shortcut, he refused them, and told a man with a sword in a garden to put it away (Matt. 26:52). He had every right to the throne of the universe and went to a cross to get it, on his Father's timing, and he reigns now by the gospel, not the sword.
4.examples:
Then: Two officers killed their own king in his sleep, carried his head all night to Hebron, and laid it before the man they were sure would reward them, who had them executed and buried the head honourably in the tomb of the general who had fought him.

Now: The useful thing here is their error, because it is a religious error and not a crude one. They had the doctrine right, and moved from "this is what God is doing" to "therefore I may do it". Being correct about where history is going does not mean God has sent you to bring it about. And they never asked anybody: not God, not a prophet, not a friend who might have said no. A conclusion you are unwilling to test is usually the one that most needs testing. David could wait because he had learned that the LORD redeems his own; the same Lord, who has already rescued us in Christ, gives his Spirit and his people so that we need not seize by our own hand what he has promised to give.

5.title: King of All Israel
5.text: <sup>1</sup>Then all the tribes of Israel came to David at Hebron and said, "Behold, we are your bone and flesh.<sup>2</sup>In times past, when Saul was king over us, it was you who led out and brought in Israel. And the LORD said to you, 'You shall be shepherd of my people Israel, and you shall be prince over Israel.'"<sup>3</sup>So all the elders of Israel came to the king at Hebron, and King David made a covenant with them at Hebron before the LORD, and they anointed David king over Israel.<sup>4</sup>David was thirty years old when he began to reign, and he reigned forty years.<sup>5</sup>At Hebron he reigned over Judah seven years and six months, and at Jerusalem he reigned over all Israel and Judah thirty-three years.<sup>6</sup>And the king and his men went to Jerusalem against the Jebusites, the inhabitants of the land, who said to David, "You will not come in here, but the blind and the lame will ward you off"—thinking, "David cannot come in here."<sup>7</sup>Nevertheless, David took the stronghold of Zion, that is, the city of David.<sup>8</sup>And David said on that day, "Whoever would strike the Jebusites, let him get up the water shaft to attack 'the lame and the blind,' who are hated by David's soul." Therefore it is said, "The blind and the lame shall not come into the house."<sup>9</sup>And David lived in the stronghold and called it the city of David. And David built the city all around from the Millo inward.<sup>10</sup>And David became greater and greater, for the LORD, the God of hosts, was with him.<sup>11</sup>And Hiram king of Tyre sent messengers to David, and cedar trees, also carpenters and masons who built David a house.<sup>12</sup>And David knew that the LORD had established him king over Israel, and that he had exalted his kingdom for the sake of his people Israel.<sup>13</sup>And David took more concubines and wives from Jerusalem, after he came from Hebron, and more sons and daughters were born to David.<sup>14</sup>And these are the names of those who were born to him in Jerusalem: Shammua, Shobab, Nathan, Solomon,<sup>15</sup>Ibhar, Elishua, Nepheg, Japhia,<sup>16</sup>Elishama, Eliada, and Eliphelet.<sup>17</sup>When the Philistines heard that David had been anointed king over Israel, all the Philistines went up to search for David. But David heard of it and went down to the stronghold.<sup>18</sup>Now the Philistines had come and spread out in the Valley of Rephaim.<sup>19</sup>And David inquired of the LORD, "Shall I go up against the Philistines? Will you give them into my hand?" And the LORD said to David, "Go up, for I will certainly give the Philistines into your hand."<sup>20</sup>And David came to Baal-perazim, and David defeated them there. And he said, "The LORD has broken through my enemies before me like a breaking flood." Therefore the name of that place is called Baal-perazim.<sup>21</sup>And the Philistines left their idols there, and David and his men carried them away.<sup>22</sup>And the Philistines came up yet again and spread out in the Valley of Rephaim.<sup>23</sup>And when David inquired of the LORD, he said, "You shall not go up; go around to their rear, and come against them opposite the balsam trees.<sup>24</sup>And when you hear the sound of marching in the tops of the balsam trees, then rouse yourself, for then the LORD has gone out before you to strike down the army of the Philistines."<sup>25</sup>And David did as the LORD commanded him, and struck down the Philistines from Geba to Gezer.
5.overview:
After seven and a half years the division is settled, not by a battle but by a delegation walking into Hebron with an argument from kinship, from David's record and from the word of God. David makes a covenant with the elders before the LORD and only then is anointed king over all Israel, long years after Samuel's oil, with a delay God explained to nobody.

His first campaign takes Jerusalem, a city no tribe had ever held, and makes it his capital. Verse 12 is the chapter's key sentence: God established him king for the sake of his people Israel. The kingdom was not a reward for patience. The very next verse is that he took more wives, and the narrator says nothing at all.

The chapter closes with two Philistine battles in the same valley. The point of having both is that David inquires of the LORD the second time too, and gets a different answer.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–5 — Your Bone and Your Flesh
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: All the tribes come to Hebron and appeal to kinship, to David's record, and to the LORD's word that he would shepherd Israel (vv. 1-2). The elders make a covenant with him before the LORD and anoint him (v. 3). He is thirty, and reigns forty years (vv. 4-5).
verseByVerse.theology: The elders argue from kinship, from record and from the word of God, and the last of these should have settled the matter years before.
verseByVerse.examples: This is David's third anointing, and the long road between the first and this one is part of what the chapter wants us to notice.

verseByVerse.quote: Then all the tribes of Israel came to David at Hebron and said, "Behold, we are your bone and flesh. In times past, when Saul was king over us, it was you who led out and brought in Israel. And the LORD said to you, 'You shall be shepherd of my people Israel, and you shall be prince over Israel.'" So all the elders of Israel came to the king at Hebron, and King David made a covenant with them at Hebron before the LORD, and they anointed David king over Israel. David was thirty years old when he began to reign, and he reigned forty years. At Hebron he reigned over Judah seven years and six months, and at Jerusalem he reigned over all Israel and Judah thirty-three years.
verseByVerse.commentary:
They come to him. After seven and a half years, the whole thing is settled by a delegation walking into Hebron and making a speech.

The speech has three arguments.

The first is kinship. We are your bone and flesh. It is the language of belonging that Adam used when he first saw the woman, bone of my bones and flesh of my flesh (Gen. 2:23), and here it is applied to a nation and a king. We are not two peoples. Whatever the last seven years looked like, you are one of us.

The second argument is his record, and they are honest about the awkward part of it. When Saul was king over us, they say, naming the man they served, it was you who led out and brought in Israel. Everybody remembers who actually fought the wars.

The third is the word of God, and it is the one that decides the matter. The LORD said to you.

They knew. The elders of Israel could quote God's promise about David, and Abner had reminded them of it in the last chapter: for some time past you have been seeking David as king over you (3:17). This was not news to anyone in the room, and it had not been news for years, and they fought a war anyway, and obeyed God’s word only when it had become politically convenient.

The word they use is shepherd. It is what he was when Samuel sent for him, and it is what God calls the office. A king in Israel is a man who looks after sheep that belong to God, not to him.

He does not simply accept the crown. He makes a covenant with them, before the LORD, and then they anoint him.

That is not what a king with unlimited power does. There are terms, and they are sworn in God's presence, and the king is bound by them as much as the people are. Israel's kingship was always meant to sit under a law rather than over it: the king was required to write out a copy of the law for himself and read it every day of his life (Deut. 17:18-19).

He is thirty. Do the arithmetic, because it is the whole story of the last twenty chapters.

Samuel poured oil on the head of the eighth son of Jesse at Bethlehem, and he was a boy then, young enough that nobody had thought to call him in from the sheep. Say fifteen or sixteen. He is thirty here.

So roughly fifteen years passed between the anointing and the throne, and we know exactly what was in them: a giant, a harp, three spears, a window in the night, a massacre of priests, two caves, three thousand chosen men twice, sixteen months in a Philistine town, a burnt village, and seven and a half years as king of one tribe out of twelve.

God said it and then took fifteen years to do it, and did not explain the delay to anybody.

Forty years in total, and the writer divides them for us before the reign starts: seven and a half years over Judah alone, then thirty-three over the whole nation.
verseByVerse.note: The same figures are given at David's death (1 Kings 2:11; 1 Chron. 29:27).

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: David takes the Jebusite stronghold despite their taunt, and it becomes the city of David (vv. 6-9). He grows greater because the LORD is with him, Hiram of Tyre builds him a house, and David knows why he has been exalted (vv. 10-12).
verseByVerse.theology: Jerusalem is chosen as much for what it is not as for what it is. It is no tribe's city, and for twelve tribes that have just been fighting each other, that is worth more than its walls.
verseByVerse.examples: Verse 12 tells us what David understood about his own throne, and the very next verse puts that understanding to the test.

verseByVerse.quote: And the king and his men went to Jerusalem against the Jebusites, the inhabitants of the land, who said to David, "You will not come in here, but the blind and the lame will ward you off"—thinking, "David cannot come in here." Nevertheless, David took the stronghold of Zion, that is, the city of David. And David said on that day, "Whoever would strike the Jebusites, let him get up the water shaft to attack 'the lame and the blind,' who are hated by David's soul." Therefore it is said, "The blind and the lame shall not come into the house." And David lived in the stronghold and called it the city of David. And David built the city all around from the Millo inward. And David became greater and greater, for the LORD, the God of hosts, was with him. And Hiram king of Tyre sent messengers to David, and cedar trees, also carpenters and masons who built David a house. And David knew that the LORD had established him king over Israel, and that he had exalted his kingdom for the sake of his people Israel.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jerusalem at this point is not an Israelite city. Judah once stormed and burned it (Judg. 1:8), but Israel never kept it.

Judges records the failure plainly: the people of Benjamin did not drive out the Jebusites who lived in Jerusalem, so the Jebusites have lived with the people of Benjamin in Jerusalem to this day (Judg. 1:21). It has been sitting there, unconquered, for the whole period of the judges and the whole reign of Saul, and everybody has learned to live around it.

The Jebusites are confident enough to be funny about it. "Even the blind and the lame could hold this place against you."

They have grounds. The city sits on a spur with steep ravines on three sides and a spring below it, and it had held out against Israel for generations.

A word about that taunt, because commentators disagree and it is better to say so than to invent certainty. It may be simple mockery: our weakest men could stop you. It may be a reference to defenders posted on the walls as an insult. Some have suggested a ritual meaning, disabled figures set up as a kind of oath against attackers. The Hebrew of verses 6 and 8 is genuinely difficult and the ancient versions differ. What is certain is the tone: contempt.

Verse 7 reports the capture in one sentence and does not say how it was done. Verse 8 gives a hint: David’s men may well have climbed in through the water shaft, though the Hebrew word translated that way is uncertain.

The city's water came from the Gihon spring, outside the walls at the bottom of the slope, and there was a shaft cut through the rock so the defenders could reach it without going outside. Tunnels reaching the spring have been excavated on that hill, though which, if any, David's men climbed is still debated. David sends men up the one route the walls do not cover.

The rest of verse 8 is harsh, and the writer records the saying without endorsing it. David turned the Jebusites' taunt back on them, and the saying about the house (v. 8) became a proverb about the Jebusites, not a law barring the disabled from God’s presence; Jesus healed the blind and the lame in the temple (Matt 21:14). Hold on to it for four chapters' time, too: the man David goes looking for in chapter 9, and seats at his own table for the rest of his life, is lame in both his feet (9:13).

His choice of this city is one of the shrewdest decisions in the Old Testament.

In practice Jerusalem belongs to no tribe.

It sits on the line between Judah and Benjamin, and though Joshua's allotment assigned it to Benjamin (Josh. 18:28), no tribe had ever held it. A capital in Judah, his own tribe, would have looked like the south annexing the country; one in Benjamin, Saul's tribe, would have been unbearable. But the moment David captures this foreign city, it belongs to him personally rather than to any tribal inheritance, which is why it is called the city of David and not the city of Judah.

He has just spent seven and a half years watching a nation tear itself in half along exactly those lines. A capital that belongs to nobody is the one thing that can hold twelve tribes who have been killing each other, and he takes it in the first campaign of his reign.

In verse 10 the writer makes sure the credit goes to the right place: David grew great because the LORD was with him. Then a foreign king sends materials and craftsmen, unasked.

Tyre is the great Phoenician port up the coast, and cedar is its export, the timber everyone in the region wanted and only Lebanon had. Hiram is making an investment in a neighbour who has suddenly become worth having as a friend. Hiram was still reigning well into Solomon's time, so many think the writer has placed this notice here because it fits the subject, not because it happened at this point.

Keep that cedar in mind. Two chapters from now the first thing David says to Nathan is that he is living in a house of cedar while the ark of God sits in a tent, and this is the cedar he means. The gift becomes the occasion of the greatest promise in the Old Testament.

Verse 12 is the key sentence of the chapter. He knows two things. The first is that God did this: not the elders, not the covenant at Hebron, not the water shaft, not Hiram's cedar. God established him.

The second is harder and rarer. For the sake of his people Israel.

The kingdom is not a reward for fifteen patient years. It is not compensation for the caves. It was not given to David for David; it was given to Israel, and David is the means by which they get it. He is the shepherd the elders called him in verse 2, and the sheep are the point of the job.

That is the principle underneath every position of authority in Scripture, and it is the exact thing that will fail in chapter 11, when a king who is supposed to be at war stays home and uses the kingdom for himself. Everything good in this reign flows from verse 12, and everything catastrophic flows from forgetting it.
verseByVerse.note: The Chronicler's account adds that Joab was the first man up and so became commander (1 Chron. 11:6).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 13–16 — And David Took More Concubines and Wives
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: David takes more wives and concubines in Jerusalem, and eleven more sons are named, among them Solomon (vv. 13-16).
verseByVerse.theology: The narrator sets David's best insight and his taking of more wives side by side, and leaves the reader to draw the line between them.
verseByVerse.examples: This list adds eleven sons to the six born at Hebron, and two of the new names, Solomon and Nathan, matter far beyond this chapter.

verseByVerse.quote: And David took more concubines and wives from Jerusalem, after he came from Hebron, and more sons and daughters were born to David. And these are the names of those who were born to him in Jerusalem: Shammua, Shobab, Nathan, Solomon, Ibhar, Elishua, Nepheg, Japhia, Elishama, Eliada, and Eliphelet.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Read that immediately after verse 12, because the writer intends you to.

The previous sentence was the finest thing said about David in the book: he understood that God had exalted his kingdom for the sake of the people. The next sentence is that he took more women.

There is no transition, no comment, no rebuke. The narrator sets the two down in order and walks away. That is how Israel's narrators often do their most serious work: they put two facts side by side and trust the reader to see the connection.

He took. Keep that verb in mind.

Israel's king had been given three prohibitions in advance, all in the same short passage. He must not multiply horses, or send people back to Egypt to get them. He must not multiply silver and gold. And in the middle: he shall not acquire many wives for himself, lest his heart turn away (Deut. 17:17).

The reason is stated in the law itself, and it is not mainly about appetite: many wives would draw his heart away from the LORD. Lest his heart turn away.

Two things follow from a household like this, and both of them arrive in this book.

The first is faction. Six sons by six mothers were born at Hebron, and eleven more names are about to be listed here. Those boys grow up as rivals with rival mothers and rival claims, and a palace of half-brothers is a civil war waiting for a trigger. Amnon rapes his half-sister Tamar. Absalom kills Amnon. Adonijah makes his move while the old king is dying. Every one of those crimes is possible because of the arrangement recorded in this verse.

The second is the habit itself. A man who has spent twenty years taking women in marriage whenever he wants them, as kings of that time did, is a man who has practised something. And one spring afternoon he will look down from a roof at a woman washing, and send to find out who she is, and send messengers, and take her (11:2-4). The same verb again.

Eleven names, and two of them matter enormously.

Solomon, who will build the temple David wants to build, and inherit the throne and the covenant.

And Nathan, who is not the prophet but another son, and who is almost never mentioned again. He appears in one other place of consequence: Luke traces the genealogy of Jesus back through David not by way of Solomon but by way of this Nathan (Luke 3:31).

So a list dropped into a chapter as an aside, in a paragraph the narrator declines to comment on, contains the name the Messiah's line runs through.

Did God approve David’s many wives? No. God’s design is one man and one woman (Gen 2:24), and the law told Israel’s king not to acquire many wives for himself, lest his heart turn away (Deut 17:17). Scripture records David’s polygamy without approving it, and the following chapters show its fruit: rape, murder and rebellion among his sons.
verseByVerse.note: Nathan was the son through whom Luke traces Jesus’ line; Solomon the one through whom Matthew does.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Twice the Philistines spread out in the Valley of Rephaim, and twice David inquires of the LORD. The first time he is told to go up, and the LORD breaks through like a flood (vv. 17-21); the second time he is told to circle round and wait for the sound in the balsam trees (vv. 22-25).
verseByVerse.theology: The second battle is recorded because the enemy, the valley and the king are the same, and God's answer is not.
verseByVerse.examples: David waits for the sign he is given rather than the moment he judges right, and the victory is the LORD's before it is his.

verseByVerse.quote: When the Philistines heard that David had been anointed king over Israel, all the Philistines went up to search for David. But David heard of it and went down to the stronghold. Now the Philistines had come and spread out in the Valley of Rephaim. And David inquired of the LORD, "Shall I go up against the Philistines? Will you give them into my hand?" And the LORD said to David, "Go up, for I will certainly give the Philistines into your hand." And David came to Baal-perazim, and David defeated them there. And he said, "The LORD has broken through my enemies before me like a breaking flood." Therefore the name of that place is called Baal-perazim. And the Philistines left their idols there, and David and his men carried them away. And the Philistines came up yet again and spread out in the Valley of Rephaim. And when David inquired of the LORD, he said, "You shall not go up; go around to their rear, and come against them opposite the balsam trees. And when you hear the sound of marching in the tops of the balsam trees, then rouse yourself, for then the LORD has gone out before you to strike down the army of the Philistines." And David did as the LORD commanded him, and struck down the Philistines from Geba to Gezer.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The moment Israel is united, the Philistines move.

They had been perfectly happy with a divided country and with David as their dependant at Ziklag. A single kingdom under the man who killed Goliath is a threat to their very existence, and they come up to end it before it starts.

He asks, and by now this is the established rhythm of the man, and the writer records it every time because it is the difference between David's good years and everything else. He asked before going to Hebron. He asked four times at Keilah. He asked at Ziklag with his town in ashes. He asks here, and he asks the two questions he always asks: shall I go, and will you give them.

He names the ground Baal-perazim, "Lord of breaking through", after what God did. Like a breaking flood: the picture is of a dry riverbed in a sudden storm, or a dam giving way, a wall of water that goes through whatever is in front of it because nothing built by people can stand against that much weight moving at once. That is what happened to the Philistine line, and David says so, and puts it on the map.

In verse 21 they run and leave their gods on the field. The reversal is exact and any Israelite would have caught it. Two generations earlier the Philistines beat Israel at Aphek and carried the ark of God back to the temple of Dagon at Ashdod, and Dagon was found face down before it, and the next morning with his head and hands broken off on the threshold (1 Sam. 5:1-5). Now it is the other way round: the Philistines flee and the gods they carried into battle are picked up off the ground by the men who beat them.

The Chronicler adds what David did with them: he had them burned (1 Chron. 14:12), which is what the law required (Deut. 7:5, 25).

Then the same enemy returns to the same valley, and David asks again. God gives him a different answer, which is why the chapter contains two battles instead of one.

Consider how easy it would have been not to ask. He has a word from God about this exact enemy, in this exact valley, given only recently, and it could not have been clearer: go up, for I will certainly give the Philistines into your hand. He obeyed it and it worked and he named a place after it.

Any reasonable man would treat that as covering the rematch.

He would have been wrong, because this time the answer is you shall not go up. Go round behind them instead. Different approach, different direction, different plan.

Why God changes the instruction is not stated and does not need to be. Perhaps the Philistines were expecting the frontal attack that had beaten them before. What the passage establishes is the principle, and the principle is that a word God gave last time is not a standing order for this time.

Believers get this wrong constantly and in good faith. God blessed a thing once, so it becomes the method, and it can be sincere and grateful and still a way of never asking again, because the answer is already on file.

David had every excuse to run on the previous instruction. He asked.

The sign is not a scouting report or David's own judgment of the moment. He is to wait behind an enemy army until he hears something moving in the tops of the balsam trees, and then go.

For then the LORD has gone out before you sums up the whole chapter in one clause. The sound is not the wind giving David his cue to win a battle; it is the noise of God going out ahead of him. The LORD strikes the Philistine army and David's men follow him into it.

Picture what that waiting was like. Behind the enemy, with the army in position and every soldier's instinct saying go, and the order is to stand still until you hear leaves move.

He does exactly what he was told, and the Philistine power in the hill country is broken from one end to the other.

This is the man at his best. Hold the picture clearly, because six chapters from now there is a spring afternoon when he does not ask anybody anything.
verseByVerse.note: The Chronicler tells both battles in 1 Chronicles 14:8-17.

5.theology:
A throne under the law. David makes a covenant with the elders before he is anointed (v. 3), and that matters. Israel's king was never meant to rule above God's law; he was to write out a copy of it and read it all his life (Deut. 17:18-19), and the terms sworn at Hebron bound him as much as the people.

The shepherd who became our bone and flesh. Kinship and shepherding, two of the elders' claims, are the very things the prophets later promise in a coming king whom they call David: I will set up over them one shepherd, my servant David (Ezekiel 34:23), spoken centuries after David died. Jesus takes that office as his own, I am the good shepherd (John 10:11), and Hebrews says he became our bone and flesh in the plainest sense: since the children share in flesh and blood, he himself shared the same (Hebrews 2:14). Israel came to Hebron and told David he was one of them. In Christ the King came to us first and made himself one of us. And the stronghold David took becomes, in Hebrews, the picture of the city every believer has already come to: Mount Zion and... the city of the living God (Hebrews 12:22).

Authority is held for others. Verse 12 states the principle under every authority in Scripture: the king is the means by which Israel receives the kingdom, not its owner. Everything good in this reign flows from remembering it, and everything catastrophic from forgetting it, as chapter 11 will show. Verse 13, set down at once without a word of comment, is the first sign that David will not always remember it.

Asking again. The two battles in the Valley of Rephaim show that God's guidance is a living relationship and not a file of past answers. David is at his best here because he asked when he thought he already knew. And the Philistine gods left lying on the field show whose battle it was. Two generations before, the Philistines had carried the ark off to Dagon's house (1 Sam. 5:1-5); now their own gods are carried off.
5.examples:
Then: A king who had just been given a clear word from God about how to beat a particular army in a particular valley met the same army in the same valley again, asked again, and was told to do something completely different, and to wait behind them until he heard a noise in the treetops.

Now: Verse 23 is uncomfortable, because the mistake it guards against is made by grateful people. A prayer answered, a method God plainly blessed, and it quietly becomes standing policy, so that the asking stops. Keep asking; the Lord who goes out before his people has not stopped speaking through his word and by his Spirit. Verse 12 is uncomfortable too: every position anybody holds, at work, at church, at home, is held for the sake of others. We hold them badly, and chapter 11 shows what forgetting it costs; but the true Son of David served perfectly where David failed, and in him the failures we confess are forgiven.

6.title: The Ark Comes to Jerusalem
6.text: <sup>1</sup>David again gathered all the chosen men of Israel, thirty thousand.<sup>2</sup>And David arose and went with all the people who were with him from Baale-judah to bring up from there the ark of God, which is called by the name of the LORD of hosts who sits enthroned on the cherubim.<sup>3</sup>And they carried the ark of God on a new cart and brought it out of the house of Abinadab, which was on the hill. And Uzzah and Ahio, the sons of Abinadab, were driving the new cart,<sup>4</sup>with the ark of God, and Ahio went before the ark.<sup>5</sup>And David and all the house of Israel were celebrating before the LORD, with songs and lyres and harps and tambourines and castanets and cymbals.<sup>6</sup>And when they came to the threshing floor of Nacon, Uzzah put out his hand to the ark of God and took hold of it, for the oxen stumbled.<sup>7</sup>And the anger of the LORD was kindled against Uzzah, and God struck him down there because of his error, and he died there beside the ark of God.<sup>8</sup>And David was angry because the LORD had broken out against Uzzah. And that place is called Perez-uzzah to this day.<sup>9</sup>And David was afraid of the LORD that day, and he said, "How can the ark of the LORD come to me?"<sup>10</sup>So David was not willing to take the ark of the LORD into the city of David. But David took it aside to the house of Obed-edom the Gittite.<sup>11</sup>And the ark of the LORD remained in the house of Obed-edom the Gittite three months, and the LORD blessed Obed-edom and all his household.<sup>12</sup>And it was told King David, "The LORD has blessed the household of Obed-edom and all that belongs to him, because of the ark of God." So David went and brought up the ark of God from the house of Obed-edom to the city of David with rejoicing.<sup>13</sup>And when those who bore the ark of the LORD had gone six steps, he sacrificed an ox and a fattened animal.<sup>14</sup>And David danced before the LORD with all his might. And David was wearing a linen ephod.<sup>15</sup>So David and all the house of Israel brought up the ark of the LORD with shouting and with the sound of the horn.<sup>16</sup>As the ark of the LORD came into the city of David, Michal the daughter of Saul looked out of the window and saw King David leaping and dancing before the LORD, and she despised him in her heart.<sup>17</sup>And they brought in the ark of the LORD and set it in its place, inside the tent that David had pitched for it. And David offered burnt offerings and peace offerings before the LORD.<sup>18</sup>And when David had finished offering the burnt offerings and the peace offerings, he blessed the people in the name of the LORD of hosts<sup>19</sup>and distributed among all the people, the whole multitude of Israel, both men and women, a cake of bread, a portion of meat, and a cake of raisins to each one. Then all the people departed, each to his house.<sup>20</sup>And David returned to bless his household. But Michal the daughter of Saul came out to meet David and said, "How the king of Israel honored himself today, uncovering himself today before the eyes of his servants' female servants, as one of the vulgar fellows shamelessly uncovers himself!"<sup>21</sup>And David said to Michal, "It was before the LORD, who chose me above your father and above all his house, to appoint me as prince over Israel, the people of the LORD—and I will celebrate before the LORD.<sup>22</sup>I will make myself yet more contemptible than this, and I will be abased in your eyes. But by the female servants of whom you have spoken, by them I shall be held in honor."<sup>23</sup>And Michal the daughter of Saul had no child to the day of her death.
6.overview:
David's first act with his new capital is to bring the ark of God into it, with thirty thousand men and every instrument Israel had. The intention is entirely right. The method is borrowed from the Philistines, and Israel had the law that said otherwise.

So an ox stumbles, Uzzah reaches out, and God strikes him dead. It is the hardest verse in the chapter, and this commentary does not hurry past it. David is angry with God, then afraid, and the ark goes aside to a foreigner's house and blesses it.

Three months later the ark comes up again, carried as the law commanded, and the king dances before it in a linen ephod, a plain priestly garment, and feeds the whole crowd. One woman watches from a window and despises him. She is wrong, and she has also been badly wronged, and the chapter ends with her.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–5 — They Carried It on a New Cart
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: David gathers thirty thousand men to bring up the ark of the LORD enthroned on the cherubim, sets it on a new cart from Abinadab's house, and all Israel celebrates with every instrument they have (vv. 1-5).
verseByVerse.theology: The impulse is entirely right. After decades in a private house at Kiriath-jearim (1 Sam. 7:2), David wants the presence of God at the centre of the nation's life, and the whole nation shares his joy.
verseByVerse.examples: The trouble lies in one ordinary-sounding phrase, a new cart, and in what the law had said about how this ark was to travel (Ex. 25:14-15; Num. 7:9; 4:15).

verseByVerse.quote: David again gathered all the chosen men of Israel, thirty thousand. And David arose and went with all the people who were with him from Baale-judah to bring up from there the ark of God, which is called by the name of the LORD of hosts who sits enthroned on the cherubim. And they carried the ark of God on a new cart and brought it out of the house of Abinadab, which was on the hill. And Uzzah and Ahio, the sons of Abinadab, were driving the new cart, with the ark of God, and Ahio went before the ark. And David and all the house of Israel were celebrating before the LORD, with songs and lyres and harps and tambourines and castanets and cymbals.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Thirty thousand men for a religious procession: not a delegation but a national mobilisation, for the purpose of moving a box.

The ark’s full title is given in verse 2 because we are meant to remember what this object is.

It is not a relic and it is not a symbol. God had said where he would meet Israel and it was precise: there I will meet with you, and from above the mercy seat, from between the two cherubim that are on the ark of the testimony, I will speak with you (Ex. 25:22). The lid is a throne with the invisible King seated on it, and the chest under it holds the tablets of the covenant.

Now remember where it has been.

The Philistines captured it at Aphek, and it destroyed their god and gave them tumours for seven months until they sent it back on a cart of their own making. It reached Beth-shemesh, where men looked into it and seventy of them died. And the people of Kiriath-jearim came and took it to the house of Abinadab on the hill, and there it stayed. From the day that the ark was lodged at Kiriath-jearim, a long time passed, some twenty years (1 Sam. 7:2).

Twenty years before Saul was even anointed, and then all through his reign, in a private house, on a hill, while Saul reigned and fought and lost a kingdom and never once sent for it. Saul asked for it exactly once, in a panic during a battle, and changed his mind before it arrived (1 Sam. 14:18-19; the Hebrew there reads ark, while the Greek Old Testament, the Septuagint, reads ephod, and many think the Greek is right).

So David's impulse here is the first genuinely good idea anybody has had about the ark in a generation. He is not building a shrine to himself; he wants the presence of God at the centre of the new capital, and he wants the nation to see it come.

The sentence the chapter turns on sounds like transport arrangements: a new cart.

The word new matters. It shows care: not any old farm wagon, but one built for the purpose, unused, clean. Somebody thought about this. Somebody wanted to do it properly.

And a cart is exactly how the Philistines had done it.

In 1 Samuel 6 the lords of the Philistines want the ark out of their country and ask their priests how to send it. The instruction is: now then, take and prepare a new cart and two milk cows on which there has never come a yoke (1 Sam. 6:7). They built the cart, put the ark on it, and let the cows walk. It worked, in the sense that the thing arrived.

They were pagans. They had no revelation, no law, no priesthood of the LORD and no idea; they were improvising a way to get rid of something dangerous, and God bore with their ignorance.

Israel had the book.

The instructions about this object are not obscure and they are not buried. There are rings cast onto the four feet of the ark and poles put through the rings, and about those poles the law says: the poles shall remain in the rings of the ark; they shall not be taken from it (Ex. 25:14-15). They are never removed, so the ark is always ready to be lifted and never needs to be touched.

Who lifts it is also specified. When the wagons were distributed to the Levitical clans at Sinai, the sons of Kohath got none: but to the sons of Kohath he gave none, because they were charged with the service of the holy things that had to be carried on the shoulder (Num. 7:9).

On the shoulder. The one clan whose job was the ark is the one clan that was given no carts.

And there is a warning attached, in the same passage, in as many words: the Kohathites are to come only after Aaron and his sons have covered the holy things, but they must not touch the holy things, lest they die (Num. 4:15).

Every one of those sentences was there to be read. There were priests in the land. There were thirty thousand men present and not one of them said anything.

The joy is real, and the writer lists five instruments to make sure we feel it: a nation just reunited after years of civil war, walking behind the throne of God toward a new capital, singing. There is nothing cynical in it anywhere.

Which is what makes the next verse so hard.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 6–11 — God Struck Him Down There
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: When the oxen stumble, Uzzah takes hold of the ark and God strikes him dead (vv. 6-7). David is angry, then afraid, and leaves the ark with Obed-edom the Gittite, whose household the LORD blesses for three months (vv. 8-11).
verseByVerse.theology: Uzzah's death is a hard verse, and the commentary below takes the objection to it seriously before it answers, beginning with David's own later verdict on what went wrong.
verseByVerse.examples: David's anger is recorded without softening, and so is the fear that follows it. Then the same ark that killed a man brings blessing to a house whose master is called a man of Gath.

verseByVerse.quote: And when they came to the threshing floor of Nacon, Uzzah put out his hand to the ark of God and took hold of it, for the oxen stumbled. And the anger of the LORD was kindled against Uzzah, and God struck him down there because of his error, and he died there beside the ark of God. And David was angry because the LORD had broken out against Uzzah. And that place is called Perez-uzzah to this day. And David was afraid of the LORD that day, and he said, "How can the ark of the LORD come to me?" So David was not willing to take the ark of the LORD into the city of David. But David took it aside to the house of Obed-edom the Gittite. And the ark of the LORD remained in the house of Obed-edom the Gittite three months, and the LORD blessed Obed-edom and all his household.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Threshing floors are flat ground, but they are reached by tracks, and an ox on rough ground stumbles.

The cart lurches. The ark tips. And a man standing beside the wheel does the thing any person would do, in the half second available, without thinking about it at all: he puts his hand out to steady it.

Anybody reading this for the first time stops here, and should.

The reaction almost everyone has is that this is not fair. He was helping. He was trying to protect the ark. He did not steal anything or mock anything; he reacted, and he died for reacting.

That reaction deserves an answer rather than a lecture. The first part is that the sin was the cart, not the hand. Uzzah's hand is not the offence; it is the point at which an offence shared by the whole procession of thirty thousand came into the open. The entire procession was in violation of an explicit law from the moment it left the hill. The poles existed so that no one would ever have to touch the ark. Take the poles away and put the ark on a wagon, and sooner or later an ox stumbles and somebody has to.

The cart made Uzzah's death inevitable. He was simply the man standing nearest when the consequence came.

And this is not a modern reading imposed on the text. It is David's own reading, and he says it out loud when he does it properly three months later. Assembling the Levites, he tells them: because you did not carry it the first time, the LORD our God broke out against us, because we did not seek him according to the rule (1 Chron. 15:13).

We. Not Uzzah. The king says the fault was the nation's and his own.

The second is who Uzzah was.

He is a son of Abinadab, and the ark had been in Abinadab's house on that hill for decades. Uzzah has quite possibly lived his whole life with the throne of God standing in the family property. He grew up walking past it. It was furniture.

That is not stated as an accusation and it should not be read as one. It is simply the most likely explanation of the reflex, and it is the most ordinary danger in the world: the thing you live closest to is the thing you stop seeing. Nobody handles a familiar object carefully.

The third is what the instinct itself assumes, and it is worth looking at closely, because it is the most human moment in the chapter.

Uzzah put out his hand to keep the ark from falling in the dirt.

Think about what is assumed in that. That the ark needed him. That God's throne was in danger from a pothole and a man's hand was the remedy. That holy things are fragile and human hands are safe.

It is exactly backwards, and it is the reflex of every religious person who has ever tried to protect God's reputation by means God did not authorise. The ark had already thrown the god of Ashdod face down in his own temple, with his head and hands broken off on the threshold. It did not need steadying.

And the fourth is the one that will not be argued away, and should not be.

This is a hard verse. It is meant to be. Israel had watched seventy men die at Beth-shemesh for looking into this same box (1 Sam. 6:19), and had learned nothing from it in all the years since. (The traditional Hebrew text, which the KJV follows, reads fifty thousand and seventy men there; most modern translations think the larger figure entered in copying.)

The sense of unfairness most readers feel should be examined rather than suppressed, because of what it measures. It does not tell us that God is harsh. It tells us how small a thing we take holiness to be: that we assume, without ever having decided it, that God's presence is basically safe, and that sincerity covers everything, and that a good motive is a sufficient answer to a plain command.

Uzzah was almost certainly sincere. Sincerity was not the question. He was standing next to the place where the God who made the world had said he would sit, on a cart borrowed from the Philistines, in a country that had his instructions in writing.

None of that makes it comfortable, and it would be dishonest to pretend it does. The narrator does not comfort anybody either. He says the man died there beside the ark of God, and moves on to the king's reaction.

Does God still strike people down for a mistake in worship? The question is natural, and the answer runs through Christ. The ark's lid was the mercy seat, where once a year blood was sprinkled so that a holy God could live among sinners, and Paul uses the Greek Old Testament's word for that lid of Christ himself, whom God put forward as the propitiation by his blood, the sacrifice that turns away God’s just anger (Romans 3:25). The holiness that broke out at Nacon is the same holiness that fell on the Son at the cross, so that those who trust him have confidence to enter the holy places by his blood (Hebrews 10:19). Uzzah's death shows what coming near costs without that blood. It does not mean a believer who stumbles in worship today is in danger of being struck: Hebrews sets the terrors of Sinai beside the joyful assembly of Mount Zion, and still calls us to worship with reverence and awe, for our God is a consuming fire (Hebrews 12:28-29). He is not a fragile God to be steadied, nor a tame one to be handled, but a holy God who has made himself approachable at his own cost.

David is angry with God, and Scripture records it without a syllable of apology.

The word is strong. In Hebrew it is the same verb as the LORD's burning anger one verse earlier. He has just organised the greatest day of his reign, with thirty thousand men and a full orchestra, out of what he was sure was pure devotion, and God has killed a man in the middle of it.

And he names the ground after it. Perez-uzzah, the breaking-out against Uzzah. He puts his grievance on the map, which is what he did with his joy at Baal-perazim one chapter ago, using the same word.

God does not strike him for the anger. He is not rebuked for it here or anywhere. Scripture is not squeamish about people being furious with God. Job is, Jeremiah is, Habakkuk is, the psalms are full of it, and several of those psalms are David's. Anger brought into God's presence is a form of dealing with him. It is not the same as walking away.

The anger turns into fear, and the fear asks the right question.

How can the ark of the LORD come to me? It is the same question the men of Beth-shemesh asked when the seventy died: who is able to stand before the LORD, this holy God? (1 Sam. 6:20). And it is the question the whole episode is meant to raise.

The difference is what each of them does next. Beth-shemesh sent the ark away and asked somebody else to take it. David also sends it away, but he spends three months finding out how it is supposed to be done, and then comes back.

The Gittite. A man of Gath.

That is a Philistine city, Goliath's city, the city David hid in twice. Whether Obed-edom was an ethnic Philistine settled in Israel or an Israelite from a place of that name, the writer chooses to give him that label, and leaves it without comment.

(Chronicles names an Obed-edom among the Levites who served the ark, 1 Chron. 15:18, 24; 26:4-5. Some think he is this man, a Levite from the Levitical town of Gath-rimmon, Josh. 21:24; others think he was a man of Gath settled in Israel. Samuel does not settle it.)

This is the other half of the chapter, and without it the first half would give a false picture of God.

The same ark, in the same country, in the same season, killed an Israelite at a threshing floor and blessed a Gittite's household for three months. The difference is not in the ark.

The presence of God is not a hazard to be managed and it is not a convenience to be used. It is God, and God is not tame, and the same nearness that destroyed a careless man filled a house with blessing until people started talking about it.

That is what gets David moving again. He hears that the thing he is frightened of has been making a family prosper for three months, and he goes back for it.
verseByVerse.note: The Chronicler tells this first attempt in 1 Chronicles 13, and the second in 1 Chronicles 15.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 12–19 — Dancing Before the LORD with All His Might
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Hearing of Obed-edom's blessing, David brings the ark up, carried this time, with sacrifice after six steps (vv. 12-13). He dances in a linen ephod as Michal watches and despises him (vv. 14-16); the ark is set in its tent, and he blesses and feeds all the people (vv. 17-19).
verseByVerse.theology: This time the Levites carry the ark on their shoulders, exactly as Moses commanded, and the procession is punctuated by blood, because the first attempt taught them what it costs to come near.
verseByVerse.examples: The king lays aside what marks him as king, puts on the linen of a worshipper, and ends the day by feeding every person in the crowd.

verseByVerse.quote: And it was told King David, "The LORD has blessed the household of Obed-edom and all that belongs to him, because of the ark of God." So David went and brought up the ark of God from the house of Obed-edom to the city of David with rejoicing. And when those who bore the ark of the LORD had gone six steps, he sacrificed an ox and a fattened animal. And David danced before the LORD with all his might. And David was wearing a linen ephod. So David and all the house of Israel brought up the ark of the LORD with shouting and with the sound of the horn. As the ark of the LORD came into the city of David, Michal the daughter of Saul looked out of the window and saw King David leaping and dancing before the LORD, and she despised him in her heart. And they brought in the ark of the LORD and set it in its place, inside the tent that David had pitched for it. And David offered burnt offerings and peace offerings before the LORD. And when David had finished offering the burnt offerings and the peace offerings, he blessed the people in the name of the LORD of hosts and distributed among all the people, the whole multitude of Israel, both men and women, a cake of bread, a portion of meat, and a cake of raisins to each one. Then all the people departed, each to his house.
verseByVerse.commentary:
