Three months of fear end with a report about the blessing on somebody else's house.

What the news tells him is that the problem was never the ark. God had not withdrawn his presence from Israel; Israel had handled it wrongly. So he goes back, and this time he does it right.

One phrase has changed, and it makes the whole difference: those who bore.

Nobody is driving anything. There is no cart in this procession, and there are no oxen pulling. Men are carrying it, which is what the law said.

Chronicles fills in what David did during the three months. He assembled the Levites and told them plainly: no one but the Levites may carry the ark of God, for the LORD had chosen them to carry the ark of the LORD and to minister to him forever, and he admitted that the first failure was the nation’s and his own (1 Chron. 15:13). And so: the Levites carried the ark of God on their shoulders with the poles, as Moses had commanded according to the word of the LORD (1 Chron. 15:2, 15).

He went and read the instructions.

That is what repentance looks like when it is real and not only a feeling. He was angry, then afraid, and then he found out what God had actually said and did that instead.

After six steps they sacrifice. Whatever the arrangement was for the rest of the route, the point of that first sacrifice is unmistakable. The last time this ark moved, a man died. Before it goes any further than six paces, blood is shed. They have learned what it costs to come near, and they are not going to take another step on the assumption that it is safe.

Now the king dances in the street.

With all his might is the phrase Chronicles uses of the whole nation's celebration on the first attempt (1 Chron. 13:8), now used of one man. This is not dignified swaying. It is whirling, leaping, spending himself.

And look at what he is wearing. A linen ephod is a priest's garment, the simple one, not the high priest's. It is what the boy Samuel wore ministering at Shiloh (1 Sam. 2:18). It is not a royal robe.

He has taken off the clothes that say king and put on the clothes that say worshipper, and he is dancing in front of his entire capital dressed as a servant of the sanctuary.

Was a king allowed to wear it, or to offer sacrifices (vv. 13, 17)? The text does not blame him, and the offerings were very likely made through the priests, as a king is said to do what he orders done (compare 1 Kings 8:62-64). But the picture is striking. In Jerusalem, the city most identify with Melchizedek's Salem, a son of Judah in priestly linen blesses the people in the LORD's name and feeds them. David himself later wrote of a Lord who would be a priest forever after the order of Melchizedek (Psalm 110:4), and Hebrews says that King-Priest is Jesus (Hebrews 7). David wore the linen for a day; his Son holds both offices for ever.

That is the deliberate act his wife is about to call an indecency, and it is the deliberate act he is about to defend.

One person in Jerusalem is not in the street.

Everything about the sentence is set up as a contrast. All Israel is outside with the horn and the shouting; she is inside, behind a window, alone, looking down.

And note what the writer calls her: Michal the daughter of Saul. Not the wife of David. He will use that formula twice more before the chapter ends. She is being identified, in every line, by the house that lost.

We will come to her.

The ark is set in a tent, not a temple, and that is the whole subject of the next chapter, which starts with David noticing it.

He feeds everybody, and the writer specifies both men and women.

Peace offerings were the sacrifice that was eaten, and the meat here is the meat of the offering: the whole nation sits down to a meal in the presence of God. Every person gets bread, meat and a raisin cake: not only the officials, the fighting men or the heads of houses. Everyone.

The last thing the king does on the greatest day of his reign is hand out food to the crowd, in a linen ephod, having danced in front of them.

Should Christians dance in worship? David danced in joy before the ark, and God judged Michal’s contempt, not David. Joy, even exuberant joy, has a place before God. The New Testament gives no rule on dancing in public worship, but it calls for all things to be done decently and in order (1 Cor 14:40). David’s “uncovering” (v. 20) means he laid aside his royal robes for a simple linen ephod.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 20–23 — I Will Make Myself Yet More Contemptible
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Michal mocks the king for uncovering himself before servant girls (v. 20). David answers that it was before the LORD, who chose him above her father, and that he will be humbler still (vv. 21-22). Michal has no child to the day of her death (v. 23).
verseByVerse.theology: Michal is wrong about what the dancing was, and she has also been badly wronged, handed between men and never asked anything. The commentary below holds both together.
verseByVerse.examples: David's answer is true and it is not kind. Above your father is aimed at the wound, and he knows it. And the last verse states a fact and gives no reason for it: the text does not say whether this was God's judgment, David's withdrawal, or simple childlessness, and it is not honest to decide.

verseByVerse.quote: And David returned to bless his household. But Michal the daughter of Saul came out to meet David and said, "How the king of Israel honored himself today, uncovering himself today before the eyes of his servants' female servants, as one of the vulgar fellows shamelessly uncovers himself!" And David said to Michal, "It was before the LORD, who chose me above your father and above all his house, to appoint me as prince over Israel, the people of the LORD—and I will celebrate before the LORD. I will make myself yet more contemptible than this, and I will be abased in your eyes. But by the female servants of whom you have spoken, by them I shall be held in honor." And Michal the daughter of Saul had no child to the day of her death.
verseByVerse.commentary:
He comes home to bless his family and is met at the door.

The sarcasm is expert. How the king of Israel honored himself today: every word of it is a knife. The title is used to point out how far he fell short of it. And her complaint is specific: he exposed himself in front of the servant girls, and he behaved like a common man without shame.

She is not entirely wrong about the facts. Dancing in a linen ephod is not dignified, and a king who spins and leaps in a short garment in a crowd is not maintaining the distance kings maintain. She is right that he looked like any ordinary man, and wrong about what it meant, because standing before God as an ordinary worshipper was the point.

Now, before David answers, she is owed a hearing, which the chapter does not give her and a reader should.

Michal loved David. The narrator states it outright, and it is the only place in Samuel, and perhaps in all Old Testament narrative, where a narrator says it of a woman about a man (1 Sam. 18:20). She married him. When her father sent men to kill him in the night, she let him down through a window, put an idol in the bed with goats' hair at its head to buy him hours, and lied to Saul's face about it, so that Saul said to her, why have you deceived me thus? (1 Sam. 19:11-17).

She saved his life, and he ran, and he did not come back for her.

Her father then gave her to Paltiel the son of Laish, and she lived as that man's wife for years, long enough for him to love her, since he followed the escort weeping as far as Bahurim when she was taken away, and turned round only when Abner told him to (3:15-16).

And why was she taken away? Because David made her return a condition of a political agreement with Abner, at the exact moment when being married to Saul's daughter would help him with the northern tribes. Not before. Not in the years he was king in Hebron with six wives. When it was useful.

Nobody in that entire transaction asked her a single question.

So she stands at a window in a city she did not choose, watching a man she once risked her life for dance in front of a crowd, before the God who took her father's kingdom and gave it to him. Her contempt is genuinely wrong, and she has genuinely been wronged, and both of those are true at the same moment.

The first clause is the answer and it is unanswerable. It was before the LORD.

Everything she said assumed an audience of servant girls. He says the audience was God, and that what she watched from a window was not a performance for anybody in the street.

And then he says something else, and it should not be smoothed over.

Above your father and above all his house is aimed to hurt. He knows exactly where the wound is, and he puts his hand on it. He could have defended the dancing without mentioning Saul at all, and he mentions Saul twice.

This is not the David of chapter 1, who wrote a lament for that same father with nothing in it for himself. It is a man in his own doorway being sneered at by his wife, hitting back with the one fact that hurts.

The great sentence of the chapter is I will make myself yet more contemptible than this. He does not deny that he looked ridiculous. He agrees, and offers to go further. He is saying that he does not humble himself before God reluctantly. He means to go on doing it, and if it costs him her good opinion, he is content to pay that.

There is a Son of David who took this further than anybody, who emptied himself, by taking the form of a servant, and humbled himself to a criminal's execution (Phil. 2:7-8). David’s humbling is small beside that. But the man in the linen ephod is pointing in the same direction, and he humbled himself deliberately.

And the last line of his answer is sharp and shrewd and possibly not gracious: the servant girls she is so worried about will think more of him for it, not less. He is telling her that ordinary people understand this and she does not.

The chapter ends with Michal’s childlessness, stated as a fact with no explanation attached.

Readers reach for one immediately, and there are two on offer. Either God closed her womb in judgment for despising the ark's homecoming, or David never went near her again. The text says neither. It says she had no child, and stops.

What the sentence certainly does is close a door on a dynasty. A child of David by Saul's daughter would have united the two houses in one person and been the obvious heir. There is no such child. The union of the two houses ends here, in a childless woman at a window, and the throne passes entirely to David's line and eventually to a son of Bathsheba.

She is called the daughter of Saul one last time in the last verse of the chapter, and the writer has now done it three times in eight verses. That is his verdict and his epitaph in one phrase: whatever she was at that first window, she died as her father's daughter.

It is a bleak ending to the happiest day of David's reign, and the writer puts it there on purpose. The ark is in Jerusalem, the nation has eaten in God's presence, the king has danced himself breathless, and inside the house there is a marriage that is finished, and a woman nobody ever asked.

6.theology:
Sincerity is not enough, and it is not nothing. Everything about the first procession was right except the method (v. 3). The cart was built with care, and it copied pagans who had no instructions, while Israel had them in writing. Uzzah's reflex, reaching out as though God's throne needed a human hand to keep it from the dirt, is the reflex of every religious person who has tried to protect God's reputation by means God never authorised. And familiarity made it easy: he had very likely grown up with the ark in the house.

The holiness that kills and the holiness that blesses are one. The sense of unfairness most readers feel at verse 7 measures how small a thing we take holiness to be. The same ark killed a careless Israelite and blessed a Gittite's house; the presence of God is neither a hazard to be managed nor a convenience to be used. The answer to the fear it raises runs through the mercy seat and the blood of Christ, discussed at verse 7.

Repentance that reads the instructions. David is furious with God and is not rebuked for it; anger brought to God is still a way of turning to him, not of walking away. Where Beth-shemesh passed the ark on, David spent three months finding out how it was supposed to be done, and came back (vv. 8-15).

Humbled before God. David's reply to Michal has three parts. It was before the LORD cannot be answered. Above your father is cruel. Yet more contemptible is great: he is willing to be humbled further before God, and in that he points toward the Son of David who emptied himself, by taking the form of a servant (Phil. 2:7-8). Verse 23 gives no reason for her childlessness, and this commentary does not choose one.
6.examples:
Then: A nation moved the throne of God on a brand-new cart, copying a method invented by pagans who had never read the instructions; when an ox stumbled and a man reached out to steady it, he died on the spot, and the king went home angry with God.

Now: Uzzah’s death raises the question whether sincerity is enough, and the answer is that it is not: good intentions did not turn a Philistine method into an obedient one. The question worth asking is which of your own well-meant arrangements has never been checked against what God said. And David's three months show the way back: furious, then frightened, then he found out what the rule actually was and did that, which is what repentance looks like when it is more than a feeling. We can come back like that because the holy God has opened the way himself, through the blood of his Son, and the Spirit he gives teaches us to worship him with reverence and joy. David came back, did it the right way, and danced.

7.title: The Throne Forever
7.text: <sup>1</sup>Now when the king lived in his house and the LORD had given him rest from all his surrounding enemies,<sup>2</sup>the king said to Nathan the prophet, "See now, I dwell in a house of cedar, but the ark of God dwells in a tent."<sup>3</sup>And Nathan said to the king, "Go, do all that is in your heart, for the LORD is with you."<sup>4</sup>But that same night the word of the LORD came to Nathan,<sup>5</sup>"Go and tell my servant David, 'Thus says the LORD: Would you build me a house to dwell in?<sup>6</sup>I have not lived in a house since the day I brought up the people of Israel from Egypt to this day, but I have been moving about in a tent for my dwelling.<sup>7</sup>In all places where I have moved with all the people of Israel, did I speak a word with any of the judges of Israel, whom I commanded to shepherd my people Israel, saying, "Why have you not built me a house of cedar?"'<sup>8</sup>Now, therefore, thus you shall say to my servant David, 'Thus says the LORD of hosts, I took you from the pasture, from following the sheep, that you should be prince over my people Israel.<sup>9</sup>And I have been with you wherever you went and have cut off all your enemies from before you. And I will make for you a great name, like the name of the great ones of the earth.<sup>10</sup>And I will appoint a place for my people Israel and will plant them, so that they may dwell in their own place and be disturbed no more. And violent men shall afflict them no more, as formerly,<sup>11</sup>from the time that I appointed judges over my people Israel. And I will give you rest from all your enemies. Moreover, the LORD declares to you that the LORD will make you a house.<sup>12</sup>When your days are fulfilled and you lie down with your fathers, I will raise up your offspring after you, who shall come from your body, and I will establish his kingdom.<sup>13</sup>He shall build a house for my name, and I will establish the throne of his kingdom forever.<sup>14</sup>I will be to him a father, and he shall be to me a son. When he commits iniquity, I will discipline him with the rod of men, with the stripes of the sons of men,<sup>15</sup>but my steadfast love will not depart from him, as I took it from Saul, whom I put away from before you.<sup>16</sup>And your house and your kingdom shall be made sure forever before me. Your throne shall be established forever.'"<sup>17</sup>In accordance with all these words, and in accordance with all this vision, Nathan spoke to David.<sup>18</sup>Then King David went in and sat before the LORD and said, "Who am I, O Lord GOD, and what is my house, that you have brought me thus far?<sup>19</sup>And yet this was a small thing in your eyes, O Lord GOD. You have spoken also of your servant's house for a great while to come, and this is instruction for mankind, O Lord GOD!<sup>20</sup>And what more can David say to you? For you know your servant, O Lord GOD!<sup>21</sup>Because of your promise, and according to your own heart, you have brought about all this greatness, to make your servant know it.<sup>22</sup>Therefore you are great, O Lord GOD. For there is none like you, and there is no God besides you, according to all that we have heard with our ears.<sup>23</sup>And who is like your people Israel, the one nation on earth whom God went to redeem to be his people, making himself a name and doing for them great and awesome things by driving out before your people, whom you redeemed for yourself from Egypt, a nation and its gods?<sup>24</sup>And you established for yourself your people Israel to be your people forever. And you, O LORD, became their God.<sup>25</sup>And now, O LORD God, confirm forever the word that you have spoken concerning your servant and concerning his house, and do as you have spoken.<sup>26</sup>And your name will be magnified forever, saying, 'The LORD of hosts is God over Israel,' and the house of your servant David will be established before you.<sup>27</sup>For you, O LORD of hosts, the God of Israel, have made this revelation to your servant, saying, 'I will build you a house.' Therefore your servant has found courage to pray this prayer to you.<sup>28</sup>And now, O Lord GOD, you are God, and your words are true, and you have promised this good thing to your servant.<sup>29</sup>Now therefore may it please you to bless the house of your servant, so that it may continue forever before you. For you, O Lord GOD, have spoken, and with your blessing shall the house of your servant be blessed forever."
7.overview:
For the first time in his life nothing is trying to kill David, and what troubles him is that God's throne is still under canvas while he sits in Hiram's cedar. Nathan tells him to go ahead, and God corrects Nathan before morning.

God's answer turns on one word used twice. David offered to build God a house and meant a temple; God says the LORD will make you a house and means a dynasty. A man offers a building and is given a family that does not end. The promise lands first on Solomon, who will build the temple and be disciplined when he sins, but its threefold forever reaches much further, and the New Testament says with complete confidence that it is fulfilled in Jesus. Unlike Saul's house, this one will be disciplined but never lose God's steadfast love.

Then David goes in, sits down before the LORD, and for a long while asks for nothing at all.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–7 — Would You Build Me a House to Dwell In?
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: At rest from his enemies, David sets his cedar house beside the ark's tent, and Nathan tells him to go ahead (vv. 1-3). That night the LORD reverses Nathan: he has moved about in a tent since Egypt and never asked anyone for a house of cedar (vv. 4-7).
verseByVerse.theology: Nathan's first answer and God's correction stand in consecutive verses, so that no reader can miss the difference between a good man's judgment and the word of the LORD.
verseByVerse.examples: God has never asked for a house. He has been moving with his people since Egypt, in a tent, by choice.

verseByVerse.quote: Now when the king lived in his house and the LORD had given him rest from all his surrounding enemies, the king said to Nathan the prophet, "See now, I dwell in a house of cedar, but the ark of God dwells in a tent." And Nathan said to the king, "Go, do all that is in your heart, for the LORD is with you." But that same night the word of the LORD came to Nathan, "Go and tell my servant David, 'Thus says the LORD: Would you build me a house to dwell in? I have not lived in a house since the day I brought up the people of Israel from Egypt to this day, but I have been moving about in a tent for my dwelling. In all places where I have moved with all the people of Israel, did I speak a word with any of the judges of Israel, whom I commanded to shepherd my people Israel, saying, "Why have you not built me a house of cedar?"'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Rest. It is the first time that word can be used about Israel in this book.

The Philistines are broken from Geba to Gezer, the civil war is over, the tribes are united, the capital is taken and the ark is home. For the first time in the man's life there is nothing immediately trying to kill him, and he has a house with a roof on it.

What a person does with that is revealing, and what David does with it is the subject of the greatest chapter in the book.

He looks around his own sitting room and is uncomfortable.

The cedar is Hiram's, sent up from Tyre with the carpenters and masons who built the place (5:11). It is the finest building material in the ancient near east and it came as a gift, and David is now sitting in the result of it while the throne of God stands under canvas in the same city.

Note what he does not say. He does not propose anything, does not ask for permission, does not lay out a plan. He states the two facts side by side and leaves them there, and Nathan understands him perfectly.

This is the man at his best. His first thought when the pressure comes off is not what to do with the peace but that God's honour is lagging behind his own comfort.

Nathan's answer in verse 3 is wrong. It is easy to read past, and it is one of the most useful verses in Scripture on guidance.

Nathan is a genuine prophet. He is not a court flatterer and not a fraud; he is the man who will walk in on this same king five chapters from now and say you are the man to a king who has just had someone murdered. He has the courage and he has the office.

And here he gives an answer straight away, and it is his own opinion.

Look at how good the opinion is. The proposal is godly. The motive is pure. The man making it is the LORD's anointed, at the height of his obedience, in a season of obvious divine blessing. Every indicator points the same way. Nathan says what any wise and godly counsellor would say, and adds the clincher: the LORD is with you.

All of it is true, and the conclusion is wrong.

God corrects him before morning, which is a kindness to both of them.

Here is what this establishes, and it should be held clearly. There is a difference between good counsel and the word of God, and the difference is not the godliness of the counsellor. A prophet speaking his own mind is a wise man speaking his own mind, and no more. When he speaks for God the text says so, and it says so here in a way that distinguishes the two in consecutive verses.

Which means several things at once. It means that the LORD is with you is not a guarantee that any particular plan is his. It means that a proposal can be sincerely devout, strategically sound, endorsed by a genuinely spiritual man, and still not be what God wants. And it means the check on all of it is not the quality of the advisers but whether God has actually spoken.

Nathan's willingness to come back the next day and reverse himself in front of the king is worth its own sentence. He does not defend his first answer or quietly let it stand. Verse 17 says he told David all these words, which included the correction of what Nathan himself had said the day before.

The question in verse 5 is not a rebuke, and the tone matters.

Nothing in what follows says David was wrong to want this, and a great deal in it says God is pleased with him. What the question does is turn the whole proposal over. Would you build me a house to dwell in? Notice the order of the words: you, build, me. Is David to provide for God, when all his life God has provided for him?

This is God's own account of the last four hundred years and it is startling.

He is not saying he was homeless or badly served. He is saying that this was the arrangement he chose. The tabernacle was designed to be taken down, carried and put up again, because the people it belonged to were going somewhere and God intended to go with them. Through the wilderness, into the land, through the whole disorder of the judges, God travelled.

A house is a good thing, but it stays in one place. What God is pointing out, gently, is that he chose to move with his people and has never asked for a house.

Verse 7 settles the matter. He never asked.

Four centuries of Israelite leaders (Othniel, Deborah, Gideon, Jephthah, Samson, Samuel), and not one of them was ever told that God wanted a permanent building, or reproached for not providing one. The whole idea is David's, and God is pointing out, without heat, that it did not come from him.

It is entirely possible to want something for God that God has not asked for, and to want it out of real love, and to be wrong. The test of a plan is not how much devotion went into it.

One more thing belongs here, because this chapter does not supply it and readers ask.

Why can David not build the temple? Nothing in 2 Samuel 7 says. The reason is given later, twice, in David's own mouth: the word of the LORD came to me, saying, "You have shed much blood and have waged great wars. You shall not build a house to my name, because you have shed so much blood before me on the earth" (1 Chron. 22:8; and again 28:3).

The man who secured the land by war is not the man who builds the house of peace. His son Solomon will, and Solomon's name means peace.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 8–17 — The LORD Will Make You a House
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God recounts what he has done for David since the sheepfold and promises his people a place (vv. 8-11). Then the LORD will make David a house: an offspring who will build God's house, whose father God will be, disciplined but never cast off as Saul was, with a throne established forever (vv. 11-16). Nathan tells David all of it (v. 17).
verseByVerse.theology: Count the pronouns in verses 8-11. David offered to do something for God, and the reply is a list of what God has done and will do for him.
verseByVerse.examples: Verse 15 is where this kingship parts company with Saul's: David's sons will be disciplined when they sin, but they will not be cast off.

verseByVerse.quote: Now, therefore, thus you shall say to my servant David, 'Thus says the LORD of hosts, I took you from the pasture, from following the sheep, that you should be prince over my people Israel. And I have been with you wherever you went and have cut off all your enemies from before you. And I will make for you a great name, like the name of the great ones of the earth. And I will appoint a place for my people Israel and will plant them, so that they may dwell in their own place and be disturbed no more. And violent men shall afflict them no more, as formerly, from the time that I appointed judges over my people Israel. And I will give you rest from all your enemies. Moreover, the LORD declares to you that the LORD will make you a house. When your days are fulfilled and you lie down with your fathers, I will raise up your offspring after you, who shall come from your body, and I will establish his kingdom. He shall build a house for my name, and I will establish the throne of his kingdom forever. I will be to him a father, and he shall be to me a son. When he commits iniquity, I will discipline him with the rod of men, with the stripes of the sons of men, but my steadfast love will not depart from him, as I took it from Saul, whom I put away from before you. And your house and your kingdom shall be made sure forever before me. Your throne shall be established forever.'" In accordance with all these words, and in accordance with all this vision, Nathan spoke to David.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The answer to David's offer begins with David's biography, and the first three words sum it up.

I took you.

From the pasture. From following the sheep. That is where the messenger found him on the day Samuel came to Bethlehem: the eighth son, not called in, out with the flock because somebody had to be, while seven older brothers were being looked over.

God is reminding a man in a cedar palace where he was standing when this started, and he is doing it right before making him one of the largest promises in the Old Testament.

Now count how often God says “I” in verses 8 to 11, because that is the point.

David came into this conversation offering to do something for God. The reply is a list in which God is the one acting in nearly every line.

And a great name is not a passing phrase. There are two other places in Scripture where that phrase matters. At Babel, men said let us make a name for ourselves, and were scattered (Gen. 11:4). To Abram, God said "I will make your name great", and the whole covenant followed (Gen. 12:2). A great name is a thing men grasp at and God gives, and grasping at it never succeeds.

Before God says anything about David's house, he talks about the people.

That order keeps recurring. The kingdom was exalted for the sake of his people Israel (5:12); David is prince over my people Israel; and here the promise of security is Israel's before it is the king's. The dynasty exists for the nation, not the nation for the dynasty.

Verse 11 is the turning point, and it turns on a single word used twice.

The Hebrew is bayit, and it does the same double duty as the English house. It means a building. It also means a family line: the house of Saul, the house of David, which is how the writer has been using it for six chapters.

David said: I will build you a bayit. He meant a temple.

God says: I will make you a bayit. He means a dynasty.

That exchange sums up the whole chapter. A man offers God a building and is told he is going to be given a family that does not end. He came to give and is comprehensively out-given, which is the recurring experience of anybody who tries to do something for God.

Now the promise begins operating on two levels at once, and both of them are real, and neither one can be dropped.

The immediate level is Solomon. He is the offspring who comes from David's body, he does build the house, and Kings records the completion of it in exactly these terms (1 Kings 8:20). Everything in verses 12 to 15 refers first and plainly to the son who succeeds him.

And then there is a word that does not fit any mortal king. Forever. It occurs three times in five verses, and it is not the language of a normal succession.

Verse 14 has two halves, and they pull in different directions.

I will be to him a father, and he shall be to me a son. That is adoption language, and it is the formula by which a king in Israel is declared God's own son. Psalm 2 uses it: you are my Son; today I have begotten you (Ps. 2:7). And the writer to the Hebrews opens his proof of Christ's superiority to angels with two quotations, and the second of them is this verse: to which of the angels did God ever say... "I will be to him a father, and he shall be to me a son"? (Heb. 1:5).

The second half, when he commits iniquity, cannot be said of Christ. He committed no iniquity (Hebrews 4:15; 1 Peter 2:22).

The honest thing is to keep both and explain neither away, because the New Testament does exactly that. This promise has a near fulfilment and a far one. The near one is Solomon and the line of kings after him: sinners who were disciplined, sometimes disastrously, but never removed. The far one reaches past every one of them to a son of David whose throne actually is forever, and the New Testament writers apply it to Jesus with complete confidence.

Gabriel quotes it to a girl in Nazareth: the Lord God will give to him the throne of his father David, and he will reign over the house of Jacob forever, and of his kingdom there will be no end (Luke 1:32-33). Peter preaches it at Pentecost: David, knowing that God had sworn with an oath to him that he would set one of his descendants on his throne, and applies it to the resurrection (Acts 2:30). And the last chapter of the Bible has Jesus saying I am the root and the descendant of David (Rev. 22:16).

Much Old Testament prophecy works like this. The words come true first in someone close at hand, and then go on to a greater fulfilment in Christ.

And it reaches past the King to his people. Paul takes the words of verse 14 and widens them to the whole church: I will be a father to you, and you shall be sons and daughters to me (2 Corinthians 6:18). What was sworn to David's son belongs, in Christ, to everyone joined to that Son. Many Christians have also seen a further mercy in the rod and the stripes: the punishment promised to David's sinful sons fell at last on the one Son who had no sin, and with his wounds we are healed (Isaiah 53:5; 1 Peter 2:24). That is how the love can stay while sin is still dealt with.

The words as I took it from Saul show why this promise is different in kind from anything before it.

My steadfast love is hesed, the loyal love that keeps covenant, and here it is God's. Will not depart from him.

Saul is named, and named as the contrast. Saul sinned and the kingdom was taken; the anointing was transferred; the Spirit departed; God would not answer him by dreams or Urim (the priest’s sacred lots) or prophets, and he died on a mountain, having been told the day before that he would. That is what removal looks like.

David's line will sin too (Solomon will go after other gods in his old age, and many of the kings after him will be idolaters and fools), and the discipline is promised in advance and it is not gentle. The rod of men, with the stripes of the sons of men. David will feel the first stroke of it in chapter 12, in his own household, and it will run through the rest of his life.

But the love does not go.

That is the difference between a relationship that lasts only while conditions are met and one that rests on God’s promise. Discipline is what happens to sons. Removal is what happened to Saul. And any Christian who has ever wondered whether a particular failure has finally put them outside God’s love is standing in front of this verse, because the New Testament makes exactly this argument: the Lord disciplines the one he loves... it is for discipline that you have to endure. God is treating you as sons (Heb. 12:6-7).

Verse 16 makes three things sure, David’s house, his kingdom and his throne, and says forever twice. Then verse 17 quietly adds something that matters.

Nathan delivers the whole thing, including the part that reverses what he himself said the day before, and including the sentence that tells the king he will not be building anything. He does not soften it, delay it, or shape it into something easier to receive.

That is what a prophet is for, and it is why this man can be trusted five chapters later when he walks in with a story about a lamb.

Is the eternal throne fulfilled now or in a future earthly kingdom? Dispensationalists look for Christ to reign from Jerusalem for a thousand years. But Peter says that God swore to seat a descendant of David on his throne and fulfilled it by raising Christ to his right hand (Acts 2:30–36). The line seemed to end at the exile, but the promise did not: it rests on the Son of David who reigns now and for ever (Luke 1:32–33). Premillennial and dispensational Christians also expect a future reign on earth, and they too confess Jesus as David's Son and King; faithful believers differ here. This commentary takes the amillennial view because Peter places David's throne in Christ's present reign at the Father's right hand.

How Jewish readers take it. Jewish readers take Nathan's oracle as the charter of the house of David, first fulfilled in Solomon, and as the root of the hope that God will restore David's throne under an anointed king; daily Jewish prayer still asks God to establish the throne of David. The father and son language is read as God's adoption of the king, not as a claim that he is divine. Here the two readings share a great deal. This commentary holds that the promise of a throne for ever is met only in Jesus, raised from the dead and enthroned as David's son (Luke 1:32–33; Acts 2:30–31).
verseByVerse.note: Psalms 89 and 132 sing this covenant back to God, and 1 Chronicles 17 gives a parallel account of the chapter.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 18–24 — Who Am I, O Lord GOD?
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: David sits before the LORD and asks who he is to be brought this far (vv. 18-20). He traces it all to God's promise and God's own heart, praises God as without equal, and turns to Israel, the nation God went to redeem (vv. 21-24).
verseByVerse.theology: David's posture says as much as his words: this is a man overwhelmed by grace, not a petitioner arriving with a list.
verseByVerse.examples: The prayer never asks for anything until verse 25. Its whole first half is about who God is and what God has done, and when David finally moves off himself he moves not to his dynasty but to the nation: who is like your people Israel.

verseByVerse.quote: Then King David went in and sat before the LORD and said, "Who am I, O Lord GOD, and what is my house, that you have brought me thus far? And yet this was a small thing in your eyes, O Lord GOD. You have spoken also of your servant's house for a great while to come, and this is instruction for mankind, O Lord GOD! And what more can David say to you? For you know your servant, O Lord GOD! Because of your promise, and according to your own heart, you have brought about all this greatness, to make your servant know it. Therefore you are great, O Lord GOD. For there is none like you, and there is no God besides you, according to all that we have heard with our ears. And who is like your people Israel, the one nation on earth whom God went to redeem to be his people, making himself a name and doing for them great and awesome things by driving out before your people, whom you redeemed for yourself from Egypt, a nation and its gods? And you established for yourself your people Israel to be your people forever. And you, O LORD, became their God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
He goes in and sits down.

The posture is unusual enough that commentators have been remarking on it for centuries. Israelites stood to pray, or knelt, or lay face down; Solomon knelt at the dedication of the temple, Ezra fell on his knees, Daniel knelt three times a day. Sitting is not the posture of petition and it is not the posture of ceremony.

It is what a man does when he has been handed something he cannot stand up under.

He has not come to ask for anything; he will not ask for a single thing until verse 25. He has come to be in the presence of what has just been said to him, and he sits down in front of the ark in the tent he pitched, and starts talking.

His question is not a set phrase, and it is not false modesty.

He has just been told his family will hold a throne forever, and the honest response to that from the eighth son of a Bethlehem farmer is who am I? He knows the answer. The last time anybody described him at length it was as a man with a sling standing in a valley, and before that as the one who was out with the sheep.

And what is my house uses the same word again, in a third sense: not a palace and not a dynasty but simply his family, which is nobody in particular. Jesse's people were farmers in a small town, and Jesse's grandmother Ruth had walked in from Moab with nothing.

The last clause of verse 19 is one of the harder pieces of Hebrew in the book, and it is better to say so than to pretend.

The words are literally something like "and this is the law of the man", torat ha'adam. Translators go different ways. Some read it as a statement: this is the charter, or the instruction, for humanity, meaning that what God has just promised David is his way of dealing with the whole human race, not merely one family's succession. Others read it as a question, as the older English versions did: "is this the manner of man?", meaning do human beings deal with each other like this? Both readings are defensible and the grammar does not decide between them.

What is not in doubt is the astonishment underneath, and the two readings are not far apart in effect. Either David is saying that this promise is about more than himself and reaches out to mankind, or he is saying that nobody has ever behaved like this. And in either case he has grasped that something has just happened which is out of proportion to the occasion.

You know your servant.

He gives up trying to respond adequately, and the reason he gives is the best one available. There is no point telling God what this means to him, because God already knows him, better than he knows himself, as chapters 11 and 12 will show with terrible thoroughness.

Verse 21 gives two reasons for everything that has happened, your promise and your own heart, and neither is anything in David.

That second phrase is the deeper of the two. God did this because of what he is like. Not because of anything found in David and not because of any need in himself; the reason for the covenant is in God's own character, which is the only place any covenant in Scripture is ever grounded.

The prayer turns into praise and the subject changes from what David has been given to who gave it.

Note the word therefore. He does not begin with God's greatness as a formality; he arrives at it, out of what has just been done to him. He knows God is great because of what God has just done for him.

Where he goes next is not where anybody would expect.

He has just been promised an eternal throne for his own family. He turns to the exodus and to the nation.

Who is like your people Israel uses the same form of words he used of God one verse earlier, now used of Israel: there is none like you, and there is no nation like this one. And the reason is entirely about God's action. The one nation on earth whom God went to redeem. God went. He came down to Egypt and got them out.

Note also making himself a name. Two verses about names, and the same point in both: God gave David a great name in verse 9, and God made a name for himself in the exodus. A great name is something God makes: he made David’s great, and by the exodus he made his own known. The exodus was as much about who God is as about who Israel is.

Verse 24 echoes the oldest summary of the covenant: you shall be my people and I will be your God.

The man with the newest and largest promise in Israel's history reaches back to the oldest one, and puts his own dynasty inside it. What he has been given is not a new arrangement running alongside what God did at Sinai. It is the same covenant, carried forward.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 25–29 — Do as You Have Spoken
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: David asks God to confirm his word and do as he has spoken, so that his name is magnified (vv. 25-26). He dares to pray because God revealed it first; God's words are true, and he asks for the blessing promised to his house (vv. 27-29).
verseByVerse.theology: He prays the promise back. Each request in this half of the prayer hands God's own words back to him with do as you have spoken attached, taking him at his word in his hearing.
verseByVerse.examples: Verse 27 says where the courage came from: not from David, who would never have dared ask for a dynasty, but from what God had said first.

verseByVerse.quote: And now, O LORD God, confirm forever the word that you have spoken concerning your servant and concerning his house, and do as you have spoken. And your name will be magnified forever, saying, 'The LORD of hosts is God over Israel,' and the house of your servant David will be established before you. For you, O LORD of hosts, the God of Israel, have made this revelation to your servant, saying, 'I will build you a house.' Therefore your servant has found courage to pray this prayer to you. And now, O Lord GOD, you are God, and your words are true, and you have promised this good thing to your servant. Now therefore may it please you to bless the house of your servant, so that it may continue forever before you. For you, O Lord GOD, have spoken, and with your blessing shall the house of your servant be blessed forever."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Here is the first request in the prayer, and it arrives seven verses in.

Do as you have spoken.

Read what he is actually doing, because it is the pattern of many of the great prayers in Scripture. He is not proposing anything. He is not telling God about a need. He takes the promise God has just made, and hands it back, and asks God to do it.

That is praying the promise. Abraham does it over Sodom, holding God to his own justice. Moses does it on the mountain after the golden calf, and the argument he uses is God's oath to Abraham (Ex. 32:13). Daniel does it with Jeremiah's seventy years open in front of him (Dan. 9:2). And the Lord Jesus taught his disciples to pray your kingdom come, which is asking God for the one thing he has already announced he will do.

There is nothing presumptuous in it, and it tells God nothing he does not know. God is not being reminded. He is being taken at his word in his own hearing, which is the sincerest thing a person can do with a promise.

Look at the order he puts things in when he asks.

God's name first, and David's house second, and the second clause is the consequence of the first. He is not asking for the dynasty for its own sake. He is asking for it because a permanent house of David will be a permanent advertisement that the LORD of hosts is God over Israel.

Whether he could have kept that order under pressure is another question, and chapter 11 is the answer. But he has it right here, and it is the same order as 5:12.

Verse 27 tells us where the boldness came from: your servant has found courage.

Literally, he found his heart. He would never have dared. Sitting down in front of God and asking him to establish your family on a throne forever is not a thing a man thinks up on his own, and the whole reason David can ask for it is that God said it first.

The promise is what makes the prayer possible. Take away verse 11 and verse 27 is presumption; with verse 11, it is obedience.

That is the answer to a question most Christians have felt at some point without putting it into words: what am I actually allowed to ask for? Here is one answer: you may ask for what he has said he will do. The size of the request is not the issue; what matters is whether God has promised it.

Verse 28 makes three statements, and they are the ground of everything he has said.

You are God. Your words are true. You have promised this good thing. Take any one of those away and the prayer collapses. Together they are the whole basis of confidence: the one who spoke is God, what he says is true, and this particular thing has actually been said.

He ends where the whole conversation began, on the word house, and by now it has travelled a long way.

He came in wanting to build one. He is going out having been given one, and asking that it may stand.

Now step back from the chapter, because it is the hinge of the Old Testament, and a great deal hangs on it.

Everything after this in Israel's story is read against this promise. The prophets appeal to it when the monarchy is collapsing: Isaiah's child who will sit on the throne of David and over his kingdom... from this time forth and forevermore (Isa. 9:7); Jeremiah's righteous Branch raised up for David when the dynasty is going down into exile (Jer. 23:5).

And when the line runs out, the promise does not. There is a period of centuries with no son of David on any throne anywhere, and then an angel stands in front of a girl in a village and announces it again (Luke 1:32-33).

A thousand years between the promise and the birth. God had taken fifteen years to give David a crown and had explained nothing; here he takes a millennium, and the promise holds the whole way.

And the last thing to say about the chapter is the simplest. David wanted to build God a house and was told no. What he got instead was a son who would build the house, and a Son whose house would never fall, and the discovery every believer eventually makes: the thing you wanted to give God turns out to be the occasion on which he gives you something you would never have dared to ask for.

7.theology:
Good counsel is not the word of God. Nathan's first answer (v. 3) was devout, wise and wrong, and God corrected it before morning. The difference between counsel and revelation is not the godliness of the counsellor but whether God has spoken, and Nathan's readiness to come back and reverse himself in front of the king (v. 17) is part of what made him trustworthy. It is possible to want something for God that he has not asked for, out of real love, and still be wrong.

God out-gives those who offer to give. David offered a building and was promised a house of another kind. In verses 8-11 God is the subject of nearly every verb, and the reason given for it all is your promise and your own heart (v. 21), not anything found in David. A great name is a thing men grasp at, as at Babel (Gen. 11:4), and a thing God gives, as to Abram (Gen. 12:2).

A promise that keeps travelling. The promise applies first to Solomon and the kings after him, sinners who were disciplined but never removed as Saul was, and then reaches past all of them to the Son whose throne truly is for ever. The prophets appealed to it as the monarchy collapsed (Isa. 9:7; Jer. 23:5), and it outlasted the line of kings itself.

Prayer that rests on a promise. David's prayer dwells first on who God is and what he has done, and only then asks, and asks only for what God has said: do as you have spoken. With verse 11 behind it, that is not presumption but obedience.
7.examples:
Then: A king in a cedar palace decided the tent God lived in was not good enough, was told that God had never asked for a building, and in the same breath was promised a throne for his family that would not end. Then he went in and sat down in front of a tent and asked for nothing for seven verses.

Now: Two things, and the first is uncomfortable because it concerns good advice. A proposal can be devout, sound, blessed by every visible circumstance and endorsed by someone genuinely spiritual, and still not be what God has asked for. The second is verse 27. Most people pray timidly because they are not sure what they are entitled to ask for. David asked for a dynasty forever because God had said it first. Find what he has actually promised, and ask for it plainly: do as you have spoken. The promise does not rest on how well we pray or serve; it rests on the Son of David who kept faith where David's sons failed, and whose Father is now ours.

8.title: David's Victories
8.text: <sup>1</sup>After this David defeated the Philistines and subdued them, and David took Metheg-ammah out of the hand of the Philistines.<sup>2</sup>And he defeated Moab and he measured them with a line, making them lie down on the ground. Two lines he measured to be put to death, and one full line to be spared. And the Moabites became servants to David and brought tribute.<sup>3</sup>David also defeated Hadadezer the son of Rehob, king of Zobah, as he went to restore his power at the river Euphrates.<sup>4</sup>And David took from him 1,700 horsemen, and 20,000 foot soldiers. And David hamstrung all the chariot horses but left enough for 100 chariots.<sup>5</sup>And when the Syrians of Damascus came to help Hadadezer king of Zobah, David struck down 22,000 men of the Syrians.<sup>6</sup>Then David put garrisons in Aram of Damascus, and the Syrians became servants to David and brought tribute. And Joram brought with him articles of silver, of gold, and of bronze.<sup>11</sup>These also King David dedicated to the LORD, together with the silver and gold that he dedicated from all the nations he subdued,<sup>12</sup>from Edom, Moab, the Ammonites, the Philistines, Amalek, and from the spoil of Hadadezer the son of Rehob, king of Zobah.<sup>13</sup>And David made a name for himself when he returned from striking down 18,000 Edomites in the Valley of Salt.<sup>14</sup>Then he put garrisons in Edom; throughout all Edom he put garrisons, and all the Edomites became David's servants. And David administered justice and equity to all his people.<sup>16</sup>Joab the son of Zeruiah was over the army, and Jehoshaphat the son of Ahilud was recorder,<sup>17</sup>and Zadok the son of Ahitub and Ahimelech the son of Abiathar were priests, and Seraiah was secretary,<sup>18</sup>and Benaiah the son of Jehoiada was over the Cherethites and the Pelethites, and David's sons were priests.
8.overview:
A chapter of campaign summaries, moving fast because it is meant to: perhaps twenty years compressed into eighteen verses. Chapter 7 promised that God would cut off David's enemies and give Israel rest, and here that promise is kept in campaign after campaign, with the same sentence said twice: the LORD gave victory to David wherever he went.

Two things stop a reader. One is a savage measuring of Moabite prisoners that the text records and does not explain; the other is the hamstringing of captured chariot horses, which is costly obedience to the law. Then comes the chapter's key word, dedicated: the man forbidden to build the temple gives all his plunder to the LORD. Last comes a single sentence on how David governed at home, which a rebellion will one day turn against him.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–8 — The LORD Gave Victory to David Wherever He Went
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: David subdues the Philistines and Moab, measuring the Moabite prisoners with a line (vv. 1-2). He defeats Hadadezer of Zobah, hamstrings the chariot horses, and garrisons Aram (vv. 3-6).
verseByVerse.theology: The Moab measurement is savage, and the text supplies no reason for it. It is all the harder to read because of David's own family ties to Moab, which the commentary below sets out.
verseByVerse.examples: The hamstrung horses are the opposite case: an act of obedience to the law about kings, and a costly one, which his son Solomon would not repeat.

verseByVerse.quote: After this David defeated the Philistines and subdued them, and David took Metheg-ammah out of the hand of the Philistines. And he defeated Moab and he measured them with a line, making them lie down on the ground. Two lines he measured to be put to death, and one full line to be spared. And the Moabites became servants to David and brought tribute. David also defeated Hadadezer the son of Rehob, king of Zobah, as he went to restore his power at the river Euphrates. And David took from him 1,700 horsemen, and 20,000 foot soldiers. And David hamstrung all the chariot horses but left enough for 100 chariots. And when the Syrians of Damascus came to help Hadadezer king of Zobah, David struck down 22,000 men of the Syrians. Then David put garrisons in Aram of Damascus, and the Syrians became servants to David and brought tribute. And the LORD gave victory to David wherever he went. And David took the shields of gold that were carried by the servants of Hadadezer and brought them to Jerusalem. And from Betah and from Berothai, cities of Hadadezer, King David took very much bronze.
verseByVerse.commentary:
After the summit of chapter 7, this is the same man doing his job for perhaps twenty years. The two belong together. The promise of chapter 7 said God would cut off all your enemies from before you and give Israel a place where they would be disturbed no more (7:9-10). Chapter 8 is that happening, and the writer is showing the promise being kept in the ordinary events of a reign.

Verse 2 is one of the ugliest verses in the book, and it will not be softened here.

Prisoners are made to lie down in a row on the ground. A measuring cord is stretched along them. Two cord-lengths of men are killed and one cord-length is allowed to live, and the selection is made by where a man happens to be lying.

The text offers no justification of any kind. There is no provocation described, no atrocity avenged, no command of God cited, and no comment from the narrator afterwards. He states what happened in one sentence and moves to the next campaign.

Two things a reader will feel should be named. The first is the irony. When David was a fugitive with a price on his head, the country he sent his father and mother to for safety was Moab: please let my father and my mother stay with you, till I know what God will do for me (1 Sam. 22:3-4). And he had family reasons for choosing it: his great-grandmother was Ruth, who came out of Moab to Bethlehem and would not go back. There is Moabite blood in the man measuring the cord.

Some have supposed that the Moabites betrayed or killed his parents, and that this is the answer to it. It is possible. The text does not say so, and inventing a reason the writer withheld is not a service to anybody.

The second is what the silence means. This narrator does not comment on much. He did not comment when David wiped out whole villages to protect a lie at Ziklag, or when Joab murdered Abner, or when David took more wives after learning the kingdom was for the people's sake. He records. And a reader who has learned how he works knows by now that when he says nothing he is not approving. He expects the reader to judge.

The Chronicler records Moab's defeat and tribute but leaves out the measuring line (1 Chron. 18:2).

Then, in the same report, an act of obedience that costs him a great deal.

He has just captured the finest cavalry force in the region. Chariot horses were the heavy armour of the ancient world, the thing Israel had never had and had been terrified of since the days of the judges. Any king in the region would have absorbed them into his own army immediately.

He hamstrings them. The tendon is cut, the animal can never pull a chariot again, and a fortune in military capability is deliberately destroyed on the field.

Why? Because of a sentence in the law about kings, in the same short passage that warned about wives: only he must not acquire many horses for himself or cause the people to return to Egypt in order to acquire many horses (Deut. 17:16).

The reason given in the law is about trust. A chariot corps is the thing a nation leans on instead of God, and the psalms say so directly: some trust in chariots and some in horses, but we trust in the name of the LORD our God (Ps. 20:7), which is very likely David's own line.

So he obeys a command that costs him a strategic advantage, on the day he wins it.

Set that beside his son. Solomon also had 40,000 stalls of horses for his chariots, and 12,000 horsemen (1 Kings 4:26), and he imported them from Egypt, which is the second thing the law forbade in the same breath. The father cut the tendons; the son built the stables. (Chronicles gives four thousand stalls, 2 Chron. 9:25, and many think the larger figure is a copying slip.)

And it is the same law, one verse further on, that David is breaking in his own household by taking wives. Nobody obeys the whole of it.

The LORD gave victory to David wherever he went (v. 6) is the sentence the chapter is built around, and it will come again in verse 14.

Everything between the two occurrences is enclosed by it. The tactics are real, the soldiering is real, the numbers are large and the men who fell were killed by other men. And the writer will not allow the account to be read as a list of David's achievements.

The LORD gave victory. It matches the answers David kept receiving when he inquired of the LORD: I will certainly give the Philistines into your hand. The king who asked before every battle is the king who is now being told, by the historian, whose the victories were.

Why do the numbers differ from the parallel account? Numbers in Hebrew manuscripts were easily miscopied, since they were often written with letters or abbreviations; and the two accounts sometimes count different things, such as chariots and charioteers, or a total and a part. Neither touches what the passage teaches. Here the Greek Old Testament reads 1,000 chariots and 7,000 horsemen in verse 4, as Chronicles does (1 Chron. 18:4), which suggests words dropped out of the Hebrew in copying. This commentary holds, with the historic confessions, that Scripture as God gave it is true in all it says; most differences of this kind are explained by copying, though not every one can now be settled with certainty.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 9–14 — These Also King David Dedicated to the LORD
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Toi of Hamath sends tribute, and David dedicates it to the LORD with the spoil of every nation he has subdued (vv. 9-12). Edom falls in the Valley of Salt and is garrisoned (vv. 13-14).
verseByVerse.theology: Everything goes to the LORD: the tribute of a friendly king and the plunder of every defeated nation.
verseByVerse.examples: The Chronicler makes plain what this treasure was for, and why it is the most moving thing in the chapter (1 Chron. 22:14; 29:2-5).

verseByVerse.quote: When Toi king of Hamath heard that David had defeated the whole army of Hadadezer, Toi sent his son Joram to King David, to ask about his health and to bless him because he had fought against Hadadezer and defeated him, for Hadadezer had often been at war with Toi. And Joram brought with him articles of silver, of gold, and of bronze. These also King David dedicated to the LORD, together with the silver and gold that he dedicated from all the nations he subdued, from Edom, Moab, the Ammonites, the Philistines, Amalek, and from the spoil of Hadadezer the son of Rehob, king of Zobah. And David made a name for himself when he returned from striking down 18,000 Edomites in the Valley of Salt. Then he put garrisons in Edom; throughout all Edom he put garrisons, and all the Edomites became David's servants. And the LORD gave victory to David wherever he went.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A king David has never met sends his son with congratulations, and the reason is entirely practical: David has just destroyed the man who had been fighting Toi for years.

Hamath is far to the north, up beyond Damascus. The whole region is adjusting to David’s new power.

The heart of the chapter is a single verb in verse 11: dedicated.

Not banked. Not distributed to the troops. Not spent on the palace, which he had every right to do and which every other king in the region did as a matter of course. Set apart for the LORD.

And it is not a share of it but all of it: the tribute of a friendly king in the north, the plunder of every nation he has defeated, and the spoil taken from Hadadezer’s Syrian kingdom.

Now put that next to what happened one chapter ago, because the two verses are inseparable.

David asked to build God a house and was told no. The reason, given elsewhere in his own words, was blood: you have shed much blood and have waged great wars. You shall not build a house to my name (1 Chron. 22:8).

So he cannot build it. And here is what he does about that, for the rest of his reign: he wins wars and gives every penny of the proceeds to the project he has been forbidden to work on.

The Chronicler is explicit that this is where the temple's funding came from. David tells Solomon what he has laid up, 100,000 talents of gold, a million talents of silver, and bronze and iron beyond weighing, and adds that he had provided it with great pains (1 Chron. 22:14). At the end of his life he addresses the assembly and says he is giving his own personal fortune to it as well, because of my devotion to the house of my God (1 Chron. 29:2-5).

He never saw a stone of it laid. The foundations went in after he was dead.

There is something in that worth carrying away by anybody who has been told no about the thing they most wanted to do for God. David was refused the work and did not sulk, did not lose interest, and did not decide that if he could not build it, it was not his concern. He funded it for years and handed his son a finished budget and a set of plans.

Wanting the work done matters more than being the one who does it, and that is a harder test than the refusal was.

David made a name for himself (v. 13): the name again, and it should be read alongside chapter 7, where God said I will make for you a great name (7:9). The name David made is the one God gave him. The traditional Hebrew text reads Syrians here, and the KJV follows it; in Hebrew the two names differ by one easily confused letter, and the ESV follows the Greek and Chronicles in reading Edomites (1 Chron. 18:12).

The sentence of verse 6 returns in verse 14 to close the list.

Edom deserves a note, because a promise made in a tent centuries earlier is being kept in it. Edom is Esau's country, and what was said to Rebekah before the twins were born was the older shall serve the younger (Gen. 25:23). Isaac said the same to Jacob. It takes the better part of a thousand years and a battle in the Valley of Salt, and here it is: all the Edomites became David's servants.

That is how God’s promises work in this book. God says a thing, and then history does it, slowly, by ordinary means, long after everybody who heard the promise is dead.

David, his commander Abishai (1 Chr 18:12), and Joab (Ps 60 title) are all credited with the Edomite victory, as a king is credited with his generals’ battles. The 12,000 of the psalm’s title may count one part of the campaign.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 15–18 — Justice and Equity to All His People
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: David reigns with justice and equity, and the officers of his court are listed (vv. 15-18).
verseByVerse.theology: One sentence covers the domestic government, and it is the right one: justice and equity to all his people, which is what a shepherd-king is for.
verseByVerse.examples: The cabinet list is brief, but nearly every name in it carries a history, and its last clause is a genuine puzzle.

verseByVerse.quote: So David reigned over all Israel. And David administered justice and equity to all his people. Joab the son of Zeruiah was over the army, and Jehoshaphat the son of Ahilud was recorder, and Zadok the son of Ahitub and Ahimelech the son of Abiathar were priests, and Seraiah was secretary, and Benaiah the son of Jehoiada was over the Cherethites and the Pelethites, and David's sons were priests.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Eighteen verses of conquest, and one sentence about how he governed.

The summary of the reign is not the size of the empire, the tribute, the garrisons from Damascus to the Valley of Salt, or the treasury. It is justice and equity to all his people.

The two words are the standard pair in the Old Testament for good government: mishpat, which is judgment given rightly in actual cases, and tsedaqah, which is righteousness: doing right by people, particularly people who cannot enforce their own claims. Together they are what a king exists for.

And to all his people. Not only to those with influence. That phrase is the test, and it is the reason the courts of the ancient world were judged by how they treated widows and foreigners and the poor, because those were the people in court whom nobody was forced to treat fairly.

This is the same principle as 5:12, the kingdom exalted for the sake of his people Israel, now seen in practice. He is the shepherd the elders called him at Hebron, and this is what shepherding a nation looks like on an ordinary day: hearing cases.

Hold on to this verse, because it is going to be used against him.

Seven chapters from now his son Absalom will get up early every morning and stand beside the road into the city gate, and stop every man coming in with a lawsuit, and say to him: see, your claims are good and right, but there is no man designated by the king to hear you, and then, oh that I were judge in the land! Then every man with a dispute or cause might come to me, and I would give him justice (15:2-4).

That is a rebellion built entirely on the claim that verse 15 has stopped being true. And it works: so Absalom stole the hearts of the men of Israel.

Whether the claim was fair is a question the text leaves open, and the honest answer is probably that a kingdom this size had outgrown one man hearing cases, and that David had not noticed. What is certain is that a son found the one place his father was no longer paying attention, and stood in it every morning for four years.

Joab is still there.

Five chapters ago he murdered the commander of the opposing army inside a city of refuge and was cursed for it in public. Here he is at the head of the cabinet list, running the army, and he will still be running it years from now when he kills the king's son against a direct order.

The writer does not remark on it. He simply puts the name at the top of the list, as he will again at 20:23, and lets the reader remember what David said: these men, the sons of Zeruiah, are more severe than I (3:39).

Two priests, and the second name carries a history.

Ahimelech is called the son of Abiathar, and Abiathar was the priest's son who escaped from Nob with the ephod (the priestly garment used for inquiring of God) in his hand when Doeg the Edomite killed eighty-five priests on Saul's order, and ran to David in the wilderness (1 Sam. 22:20-23). David said to him then: stay with me; do not be afraid... with me you shall be in safekeeping.

A generation later his family is in the king's cabinet. Elsewhere Abiathar is Ahimelech’s son (1 Sam 22:20), so either Abiathar named his own son Ahimelech after his father, or the names were reversed in copying.

Benaiah is the head of the royal bodyguard, and the Cherethites and Pelethites are foreign troops: Cretan and Philistine mercenaries, most probably, men David perhaps came to know during his sixteen months at Ziklag. The king's personal guard is not Israelite, which is a shrewd arrangement in a country that has recently had a civil war.

Benaiah himself is one of the mighty men, and the writer will come back to him: he struck down two ariels of Moab (the meaning of the word is uncertain), and a lion in a pit on a snowy day, and an Egyptian giant with the Egyptian's own spear (23:20-21). He ends up commanding Solomon's army after executing Joab.

The last clause is a puzzle and it should be admitted as one. David's sons were priests. They were not Levites, and the priesthood was closed to anyone outside Aaron's line. The word may be being used in a wider sense, for royal ministers or advisers; the Chronicler, listing the same cabinet, writes that David's sons were the chief officials in the service of the king (1 Chron. 18:17), which is probably the meaning.

Saying the term is uncertain is better than inventing a certainty about it.

8.theology:
The victories are the LORD's. The sentence repeated in verses 6 and 14 stands on either side of the list of victories, so that the list cannot be read as a list of David's achievements. The tactics and the soldiering were real, but the king who asked before every battle is told by the historian whose the victories were. Even the old word to Rebekah, the older shall serve the younger (Gen. 25:23), is kept here in a valley in Edom, slowly and by ordinary means.

Obedience is partial, and grace still works. David obeys the law about horses at real cost, trusting the LORD rather than chariots (Ps. 20:7), and in the same years breaks the law about wives at home. Moab's prisoners are measured with a cord and the narrator says nothing; silence here is not approval. Then a man who has been refused gives everything he has won to the house he may not build, and the giving is the finest thing in the chapter.

The king the psalms kept asking for. Justice and righteousness are what Israel prayed for in its kings (Psalm 72:1-2) and seldom received for long, and the prophets fastened the pair to a coming son of David: a throne upheld with justice and with righteousness from this time forth and forevermore (Isaiah 9:7), a Branch who shall execute justice and righteousness in the land (Jeremiah 23:5). David's justice in verse 15 was a first instalment of that, and it did not last. The empire it governed was won with the sword and, in Moab, measured with a cord. The King who fulfils it said his kingdom is not of this world, so his servants do not fight for it (John 18:36), and he gathers the nations not by tribute taken but by his own blood given (Revelation 5:9).
8.examples:
Then: A king captured the best chariot force in the region and had almost every horse hamstrung where it stood, destroying on the day he won it the advantage every kingdom around him was built on, because of one sentence about what a king must not acquire.

Now: The dedicated plunder is the thing to remember. David was told he could not build the temple, and spent the rest of his working life funding it. Being refused the work you wanted is not the same as being released from caring whether it gets done, and the temptation after a no is to lose interest and call it acceptance. He could give like that because everything he had won, the LORD had given; and the same Lord gives his Spirit to make our giving glad rather than grudging. And verse 15 says what all authority is for, and the telling word is all: justice for everyone, not only for those who matter.

9.title: Mephibosheth: Grace at the King's Table
9.text: <sup>1</sup>And David said, "Is there still anyone left of the house of Saul, that I may show him kindness for Jonathan's sake?"<sup>2</sup>Now there was a servant of the house of Saul whose name was Ziba, and they called him to David. And the king said to him, "Are you Ziba?" And he said, "I am your servant."<sup>3</sup>And the king said, "Is there not still someone of the house of Saul, that I may show the kindness of God to him?" Ziba said to the king, "There is still a son of Jonathan; he is crippled in his feet."<sup>4</sup>The king said to him, "Where is he?" And Ziba said to the king, "He is in the house of Machir the son of Ammiel, at Lo-debar."<sup>5</sup>Then King David sent and brought him from the house of Machir the son of Ammiel, at Lo-debar.<sup>6</sup>And Mephibosheth the son of Jonathan, son of Saul, came to David and fell on his face and paid homage. And David said, "Mephibosheth!" And he answered, "Behold, I am your servant."<sup>7</sup>And David said to him, "Do not fear, for I will show you kindness for the sake of your father Jonathan, and I will restore to you all the land of Saul your father, and you shall eat at my table always."<sup>8</sup>And he paid homage and said, "What is your servant, that you should show regard for a dead dog such as I?"<sup>9</sup>Then the king called Ziba, Saul's servant, and said to him, "All that belonged to Saul and to all his house I have given to your master's grandson.<sup>10</sup>And you and your sons and your servants shall till the land for him and shall bring in the produce, that your master's grandson may have bread to eat. But Mephibosheth your master's grandson shall always eat at my table." Now Ziba had fifteen sons and twenty servants.<sup>11</sup>Then Ziba said to the king, "According to all that my lord the king commands his servant, so will your servant do." So Mephibosheth ate at David's table, like one of the king's sons.<sup>12</sup>And Mephibosheth had a young son, whose name was Mica. And all who lived in Ziba's house became Mephibosheth's servants.<sup>13</sup>So Mephibosheth lived in Jerusalem, for he ate always at the king's table. Now he was lame in both his feet.
9.overview:
The kingdom is secure and the wars are won, and one day, unprompted, the king asks whether anybody is left of the family that hunted him. The reason he gives is a promise made years ago, in a field, to a man now dead. It had no witnesses and no legal force, and he remembers it.

The one left is Saul's grandson, a rival claimant, lame since childhood. He arrives on his face, expecting to be killed, as the heirs of a fallen house usually were, and is given his grandfather's estate and a permanent seat at the king's table.

The story follows the pattern of the gospel, and its honest last clause, lame in both his feet, makes it worth more than a tidier ending would be.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–5 — Is There Still Anyone Left?
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: David asks whether anyone is left of Saul's house to whom he may show kindness for Jonathan's sake (v. 1). Saul's servant Ziba tells him of Jonathan's lame son at Lo-debar, and David sends for him (vv. 2-5).
verseByVerse.theology: David initiates all of this, and the word he uses twice is hesed, the covenant love that keeps going after the reason for keeping it has gone. The second time he calls it the kindness of God, which is the standard he is measuring by.
verseByVerse.examples: He is keeping a promise made to Jonathan (1 Sam. 20:14-15), and Jonathan had named the exact moment it would be tested.

verseByVerse.quote: And David said, "Is there still anyone left of the house of Saul, that I may show him kindness for Jonathan's sake?" Now there was a servant of the house of Saul whose name was Ziba, and they called him to David. And the king said to him, "Are you Ziba?" And he said, "I am your servant." And the king said, "Is there not still someone of the house of Saul, that I may show the kindness of God to him?" Ziba said to the king, "There is still a son of Jonathan; he is crippled in his feet." The king said to him, "Where is he?" And Ziba said to the king, "He is in the house of Machir the son of Ammiel, at Lo-debar." Then King David sent and brought him from the house of Machir the son of Ammiel, at Lo-debar.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Nobody asked him.

There is no petition in front of him, no delegation, no political pressure. The kingdom is secure, the wars in chapter 8 are won, the treasury is full, and one day the king asks whether anybody is left from the family that tried to kill him for a decade.

And the question has a reason attached: for Jonathan's sake.

Years ago, in a field outside Gibeah, Jonathan said this: if I am still alive, show me the steadfast love of the LORD, that I may not die; and do not cut off your steadfast love from my house forever, when the LORD cuts off every one of the enemies of David from the face of the earth (1 Sam. 20:14-15).

Read what he actually asked for. Not protection while he lived; he adds that almost as an afterthought. What he asks for is kindness to his descendants at the precise moment David has no reason on earth to give it: when the LORD cuts off every one of the enemies of David.

Jonathan knew exactly what he was asking. When a new dynasty is secure, it removes the old one. That is not cynicism about ancient kings; it is simply what happened, every time, in every kingdom around them, and Jonathan was the crown prince of the house being replaced. He was asking David to break the rule.

Here is David, years later, with the man dead on a mountain and the house of Saul finished, raising the subject himself.
