Consider what that means about promises. This one was made to a man who has been dead for years, about a person David has never met, in a conversation that had no witnesses and no legal force, at a time when David was a fugitive with nothing. There is not one external reason to remember it.

He remembers it.

They have to go and find a former servant of Saul's household to answer the question, which tells you how completely that house has disappeared.

Watch Ziba through this chapter and remember him, because he comes back twice, and both times he seems to be seeking his own advantage (16:1-4; 19:24-30).

The king asks the same question again and raises the standard while doing it: the kindness of God.

That is what he is measuring by. Not ordinary generosity and not a ruler’s show of goodwill, but the sort of kindness God shows, which in the Old Testament means kindness to people who have no claim on it, faithfully kept when nothing compels it.

Ziba's answer is oddly put. Asked whether anyone is left, he says yes, there is a son of Jonathan, and then immediately volunteers the disability. He is not asked about it.

It may be an honest attempt to be helpful: you should know he cannot walk. It may be something less generous: a suggestion that this one is not worth troubling about, no threat, no use. The text does not say. But the writer records that the first fact anyone offers David about this man is what is wrong with him.

How he came to be crippled is told earlier, in one sentence, and it is a terrible one. When the news came from Gilboa that Saul and Jonathan were dead, the household panicked: his nurse took him up and fled, and as she fled in her haste, he fell and became lame. And his name was Mephibosheth (4:4). He was five years old. Somebody dropped him while running for their lives, and he never walked again.

Lo-debar is across the Jordan, out in Gilead, well away from anywhere that matters.

The name has been much preached on and a little care is in order. It is often explained as "no pasture," or simply "no thing," but no note in the text says so. It is a real village with a real man living in it, and the writer is not making a point about the name. But notice where the grandson of a king of Israel has been living: in somebody else's house, in a place on the far side of the river, for years.

Note also the man he is living with. Machir the son of Ammiel appears once more in this book, and it is the last place you would expect. When David is fleeing from Absalom, broken and hungry, three men bring food to him at Mahanaim, and Machir of Lo-debar is one of them (17:27-29). The man who sheltered Saul's grandson feeds David in his worst hour.

David sends. Mephibosheth does not come and ask.

State that plainly, because the whole chapter depends on it. This man has been keeping his head down in a village across the river for years, expecting nothing, asking for nothing, and almost certainly hoping the king had never heard of him. The king's men arrive at Machir's door with an order to bring him to Jerusalem.

Everything in this chapter is initiated by the king.
verseByVerse.note: Chronicles calls him Merib-baal (1 Chron. 8:34; 9:40).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 6–8 — A Dead Dog Such as I
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Mephibosheth falls on his face; David tells him not to fear, restores Saul's land to him, and gives him a place at his table, and he calls himself a dead dog (vv. 6-8).
verseByVerse.theology: He is Saul's grandson, a rival claimant with a better hereditary title than the man on the throne, summoned from the far side of the Jordan. There was one normal outcome to a journey like that.
verseByVerse.examples: A dead dog is not a phrase Mephibosheth invented, and where it came from is one of the quiet wonders of the chapter.

verseByVerse.quote: And Mephibosheth the son of Jonathan, son of Saul, came to David and fell on his face and paid homage. And David said, "Mephibosheth!" And he answered, "Behold, I am your servant." And David said to him, "Do not fear, for I will show you kindness for the sake of your father Jonathan, and I will restore to you all the land of Saul your father, and you shall eat at my table always." And he paid homage and said, "What is your servant, that you should show regard for a dead dog such as I?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Take in what this arrival looks like from his side of the room.

The writer gives his full pedigree in the verse, the son of Jonathan, son of Saul, and that is the whole problem. He is not a private citizen. He is the direct male descendant of the previous king, which makes him, in the eyes of anybody who cared about hereditary right, the rightful heir to the throne of the king he is being carried in to see.

He is at Jerusalem because the king's men came for him. He is on the floor, on his face, and getting up again will not be easy for him.

He has grown up hearing one version of David: the man who broke his grandfather, who took the kingdom, who fought a long war against his uncle's regime. Whatever else he expects from this interview, he does not expect to survive it.

The king says his name.

Mephibosheth. Not son of Saul, the kind of label the writer pinned on Michal three times in chapter 6. Not a title, not a charge. His name.

Do not fear. Which tells you how afraid he was.

Then three things, and each one is larger than the last.

The first is the reason: for the sake of your father Jonathan. Not for anything Mephibosheth is or has done or might be useful for. He is receiving all of this on account of somebody else, and he is told so to his face at the start, before anything is given.

The second is the land. All of Saul's estate is restored, which had presumably reverted to the crown, as a defeated dynasty's property does. That is a fortune, and it is also a statement: the house of Saul is not to be treated as forfeited.

The third is the table, and it is the one that costs David something and matters most. You shall eat at my table always.

Not a pension paid to a man in a distant village. Not permission to live quietly. A permanent seat in the king's own household, at the king's own meals, every day, for the rest of his life.

Now hold that against a proverb this same book gave us four chapters ago.

When David took Jerusalem, the Jebusites jeered that the blind and the lame could hold the place against him, and out of that day came a saying: the blind and the lame shall not come into the house (5:8).

And here, into the house, into the palace, to the king's own table, comes a man who is lame in both feet, and stays there.

His answer is the sentence everybody remembers, and the phrase in it has a history.

A dead dog.

Dogs in that world were not pets; they were scavengers on the edge of a village, and a dead one was refuse. It is about as low as a person can put himself in that language.

But those exact words have been spoken before in this story, and they were spoken by David.

Standing outside the cave at Engedi, holding a corner of Saul's robe, shouting down at the king who was hunting him: after whom has the king of Israel come out? After whom do you pursue? After a dead dog! After a flea! (1 Sam. 24:14).

David said it about himself, to Saul. Now Saul's grandson says it about himself, to David.

The wheel has come completely round, and the man on the throne is hearing his own words of self-abasement from the family that made him say them. If anybody in Israel understood what it felt like to speak that sentence, it was the man being spoken to.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 9–13 — He Ate Always at the King's Table
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Ziba's household is set to farm the estate, and Mephibosheth eats at David's table like one of the king's sons, though he is lame in both his feet (vv. 9-13).
verseByVerse.theology: The king's generosity is not a pension paid at a distance but a place in the household, and the writer says it four times in seven verses.
verseByVerse.examples: The writer ends on the disability rather than the honour, and the commentary below explains why that is the most hopeful thing he could have done.

verseByVerse.quote: Then the king called Ziba, Saul's servant, and said to him, "All that belonged to Saul and to all his house I have given to your master's grandson. And you and your sons and your servants shall till the land for him and shall bring in the produce, that your master's grandson may have bread to eat. But Mephibosheth your master's grandson shall always eat at my table." Now Ziba had fifteen sons and twenty servants. Then Ziba said to the king, "According to all that my lord the king commands his servant, so will your servant do." So Mephibosheth ate at David's table, like one of the king's sons. And Mephibosheth had a young son, whose name was Mica. And all who lived in Ziba's house became Mephibosheth's servants. So Mephibosheth lived in Jerusalem, for he ate always at the king's table. Now he was lame in both his feet.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Note the phrase David uses about Mephibosheth when speaking to Ziba: your master's grandson.

Ziba has just been re-assigned. He came in as a free agent, a man who used to serve a household that no longer exists, and he leaves as a steward with a master again.

The arrangement is complete and it is generous, and the last sentence of verse 10 shows how large it is.

Ziba is not a poor man. Fifteen sons and twenty servants is a considerable operation, and that whole establishment is now put to work farming Saul's estate on behalf of a man who cannot walk out to inspect it.

It should be said that this is a great deal to ask of Ziba, and the writer plants the detail on purpose. Seven chapters from now, when David is running from Absalom, Ziba meets him on the road with two hundred loaves and a story: Mephibosheth has stayed in Jerusalem hoping to get the kingdom back. David believes him on the spot and hands him the entire estate (16:1-4). And when David returns, Mephibosheth comes to meet him having not washed his feet or trimmed his beard since the day the king left, and says Ziba deceived him (19:24-30).

David never resolves it. He splits the land between them, and Mephibosheth says: oh, let him take it all, since my lord the king has come safely home.

Like one of the king's sons.

The phrase is the writer's own, not David's. Amnon and Absalom and Adonijah and Solomon sat at that table, and so did the grandson of the man who threw spears at their father.

He is not a pensioner and not a hostage. He is family.

Mephibosheth has a son, Mica. The line of Jonathan continues, and the Chronicler follows it down for generations (1 Chron. 8:34-40), which means Jonathan's request was answered further than he could have known. He asked for kindness to his house, and his house went on.

Four times in this chapter the writer says the man ate at the king's table, and then he ends the chapter on something else.

Lame in both his feet is the last clause, and it is deliberate, and it should not be tidied away into something more triumphant.

Nothing here is healed. Mephibosheth is fed, restored, honoured and given a permanent place among the king's sons, and he is still carried to the table. He will be lame at every meal for the rest of his life. The chapter that could have ended on like one of the king's sons ends on the disability instead.

Now, this story follows the pattern of the gospel, and it would be strange not to say so, provided it is said carefully. The passage is not an allegory, a story in which every detail stands for something else, and forcing it does it no favours.

What is genuinely there is this. A man who could not come is sent for. He is found in a place far from the king, expecting judgment and receiving the opposite. He is given everything on account of somebody else's covenant, and told so plainly at the start. He is seated at the king's table not as a guest but as a son. And he brings nothing to it except the admission that he is a dead dog.

Every one of those is in the text, and the likeness is not accidental: this is how God has always dealt with people, and the Old Testament keeps showing it.

The New Testament gives the words for it. For Jonathan's sake is how David's kindness reached a man with no claim of his own, and Paul tells believers to forgive as God in Christ forgave you (Ephesians 4:32): mercy given on account of another, on the ground of a covenant made before we came. The Son of David told of a great banquet where the servant is sent out to bring in the poor and crippled and blind and lame (Luke 14:21), and he ate with the people his world kept outside the house. This is not a hidden code in the chapter. It is the same God with the same heart, doing fully in Christ what David did in part in a palace.

Which brings us back to the last clause. Being brought to the table does not undo what happened to him when he was five years old. He eats as a son and he arrives carried, and both of those are true for the rest of his life.

Any Christian who has wondered why grace has not fixed the thing that is actually wrong with them (the illness, the memory, the temperament, the damage somebody else did in a moment of panic) is looking at the right verse. The table is real and the lameness is real, and the writer put them in the same sentence on purpose. The healing comes later, and it is not in this chapter, and Scripture never pretends the meantime is comfortable. But it does come: the Son of David made the lame walk as a sign of what his kingdom brings (Matthew 11:5), and on the day he raises his people the lame will leap like a deer (Isaiah 35:6).

9.theology:
Kindness that keeps a promise no one could enforce. David's hesed, his loyal covenant love, is kept to a dead man, about a person he had never met, when nobody would have known if it lapsed (v. 1). He calls it the kindness of God (v. 3) because that is what God's kindness is: given to people with no claim on it, and faithfully kept when nothing compels it.

Grace takes the first step. Mephibosheth does not come and ask; he is sent for from across the river (v. 5). The king says his name, tells him not to fear, and gives the reason before the gift, for the sake of your father Jonathan, so that he knows from the start that none of it is on his own account. The proverb that the lame shall not come into the house (5:8) is undone at the king's own table, and Jonathan's line goes on for generations (1 Chron. 8:34-40), further than he could have known to ask.

Received as a son, and still carried. Mephibosheth contributes nothing but the confession that he is a dead dog, the very words the hunted David once used of himself (1 Sam. 24:14). He is seated as one of the king's sons, and nothing in the chapter heals him. The grace is real and the lameness is real, and the writer will not let either cancel the other. Ziba, who will return twice seeking his own advantage (16:1-4; 19:24-30), is a reminder that even good arrangements are lived out among people with mixed motives.
9.examples:
Then: A king sent across the Jordan for the surviving heir of the dynasty he had replaced, gave him back his grandfather's entire estate, and sat him at the royal table with the princes for the rest of his life, because of a promise made in a field to that man's father years before.

Now: Two things. The first is about promises. Nothing enforced this one, and no one alive would have known if David had let it lapse. Most promises that get broken are broken exactly there, allowed to lapse once the reason for them is gone; that is precisely where hesed is tested. We keep faith like that badly, but we have been kept by a God who never lets his word to us lapse, and his Spirit makes us people who keep ours. The second is the last clause. Mephibosheth eats as a son and is still carried to the table. The seat does not depend on his legs being healed, and they are not healed.

10.title: War with Ammon and Aram
10.text: <sup>1</sup>After this the king of the Ammonites died, and Hanun his son reigned in his place.<sup>2</sup>And David said, "I will deal loyally with Hanun the son of Nahash, as his father dealt loyally with me." So David sent by his servants to console him concerning his father. And David's servants came into the land of the Ammonites.<sup>3</sup>But the princes of the Ammonites said to Hanun their lord, "Do you think, because David has sent comforters to you, that he is honoring your father? Has not David sent his servants to you to search the city and to spy it out and to overthrow it?"<sup>4</sup>So Hanun took David's servants and shaved off half the beard of each and cut off their garments in the middle, at their hips, and sent them away.<sup>5</sup>When it was told David, he sent to meet them, for the men were greatly ashamed. And the king said, "Remain at Jericho until your beards have grown and then return."<sup>6</sup>When the Ammonites saw that they had become a stench to David, the Ammonites sent and hired the Syrians of Beth-rehob, and the Syrians of Zobah, 20,000 foot soldiers, and the king of Maacah with 1,000 men, and the men of Tob, 12,000 men.<sup>7</sup>And when David heard of it, he sent Joab and all the host of the mighty men.<sup>8</sup>And the Ammonites came out and drew up in battle array at the entrance of the gate, and the Syrians of Zobah and of Rehob and the men of Tob and Maacah were by themselves in the open country.<sup>9</sup>When Joab saw that the battle was set against him both in front and in the rear, he chose some of the best men of Israel and arrayed them against the Syrians.<sup>10</sup>The rest of his men he put in the charge of Abishai his brother, and he arrayed them against the Ammonites.<sup>11</sup>And he said, "If the Syrians are too strong for me, then you shall help me, but if the Ammonites are too strong for you, then I will come and help you.<sup>12</sup>Be of good courage, and let us be courageous for our people, and for the cities of our God, and may the LORD do what seems good to him."<sup>13</sup>So Joab and the people who were with him drew near to battle against the Syrians, and they fled before him.<sup>14</sup>And when the Ammonites saw that the Syrians fled, they likewise fled before Abishai and entered the city. Then Joab returned from fighting against the Ammonites and came to Jerusalem.<sup>15</sup>But when the Syrians saw that they had been defeated by Israel, they gathered themselves together.<sup>16</sup>And Hadadezer sent and brought out the Syrians who were beyond the Euphrates. They came to Helam, with Shobach the commander of the army of Hadadezer at their head.<sup>17</sup>And when it was told David, he gathered all Israel together and crossed the Jordan and came to Helam. The Syrians arrayed themselves against David and fought with him.<sup>18</sup>And the Syrians fled before Israel, and David killed of the Syrians the men of 700 chariots, and 40,000 horsemen, and wounded Shobach the commander of their army, so that he died there.<sup>19</sup>And when all the kings who were servants of Hadadezer saw that they had been defeated by Israel, they made peace with Israel and became subject to them. So the Syrians were afraid to save the Ammonites anymore.
10.overview:
Chapter 9 began with David showing kindness for Jonathan's sake. This one begins with the same word, hesed, offered to the son of a dead Ammonite king: Nahash, the man who once offered Jabesh-gilead a treaty on condition of gouging out every right eye in the town.

Hanun's counsellors talk him out of accepting it on no evidence at all, and the envoys are shamed and sent home to be seen. David spares them, Joab answers a two-front trap with skill and a fine sentence about leaving the outcome with the LORD, and David himself crosses the Jordan and destroys the Syrian relief army. The Syrian allies give up, the Ammonites are left without help, and Rabbah is still standing.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–5 — As His Father Dealt Loyally with Me
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: David sends comfort to Hanun on his father's death; Hanun's princes call the envoys spies, and Hanun shames them and sends them away. David tells them to wait at Jericho until their beards have grown (vv. 1-5).
verseByVerse.theology: Two chapters running, David initiates hesed on account of somebody who is dead, and this time the dead man is a foreign king. When and how Nahash showed him kindness the text never says.
verseByVerse.examples: The insult is aimed past the envoys at the king who sent them. A leader insulted through his people is tempted to make their shame his own grievance and display it; David makes their shame his first care and hides it.

verseByVerse.quote: After this the king of the Ammonites died, and Hanun his son reigned in his place. And David said, "I will deal loyally with Hanun the son of Nahash, as his father dealt loyally with me." So David sent by his servants to console him concerning his father. And David's servants came into the land of the Ammonites. But the princes of the Ammonites said to Hanun their lord, "Do you think, because David has sent comforters to you, that he is honoring your father? Has not David sent his servants to you to search the city and to spy it out and to overthrow it?" So Hanun took David's servants and shaved off half the beard of each and cut off their garments in the middle, at their hips, and sent them away. When it was told David, he sent to meet them, for the men were greatly ashamed. And the king said, "Remain at Jericho until your beards have grown and then return."
verseByVerse.commentary:
It is the same word as in chapter 9: hesed, loyalty that outlasts the reason for it. And here David extends it to a foreigner.

Nahash the Ammonite is not a stranger to this book. He besieged Jabesh-gilead at the start of Saul's reign and offered terms: a treaty on condition that he gouge out every right eye in the place, and thus bring disgrace on all Israel (1 Sam. 11:2). That is the threat that brought the Spirit on Saul and made him king in fact as well as name.

And this man, at some point, showed David kindness. The text never says when or how. Perhaps during the fugitive years, when Ammon would gladly have helped any enemy of Saul. It is better to leave it unexplained than to invent something. What we are told is that David remembered it and intended to repay it to the man's son.

The counsellors talk him out of it in a sentence. There is no evidence for their charge that the envoys are spies: a delegation of condolence has arrived, exactly as such delegations do. The princes have no information, only a theory that sounds shrewd and the flattering assumption that they are too clever to be taken in.

And it is not entirely unreasonable, which is the point. David has spent two chapters subduing everybody within reach, Moab, Zobah, Damascus, Edom, and a young and untested king receiving his envoys might well be nervous. The trouble is what they do with the suspicion. Not investigate it, not watch the envoys, not politely hasten their departure: they act on it as a certainty.

What Hanun does is planned, not done in a moment of temper. He shaves half of each beard, not the whole. A fully shaved beard was a sign of mourning and could be borne; a half-shaved one makes every face a joke that cannot be explained. A beard in that world was a man's dignity; the law of Israel even regulated how it might be trimmed. And the robes cut off at the hips left them exposed on a public road all the way home.

In one respect it is worse than a beating: it is designed to be seen, carried home and displayed to the man who sent them. Hanun’s real target is not the envoys. He is using them to insult David in public.

David's response is the best thing in the chapter. He does not march them into Jerusalem in that state so the nation can see the outrage and be roused by it, which is precisely what a king interested in a war would do. He sends word to the first town on the road and tells them to stay there until they can face people again.

For the men were greatly ashamed. That is the narrator's whole explanation. The king's first thought is their humiliation, and his first act is to spare them the rest of it. How a man treats people who have been made ridiculous in his service is a real test, and it does not usually get recorded.
verseByVerse.note: The law's rule about trimming the beard is in Leviticus 19:27; shaving the whole beard was a sign of mourning (Isa. 15:2; Jer. 48:37).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 6–14 — Let Us Be Courageous for Our People
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Ammon hires thirty-three thousand Syrians, and Joab finds the enemy in front of him and behind. He splits the army with Abishai, agrees mutual help, and leaves the outcome with the LORD; the Syrians flee, and the Ammonites run into the city (vv. 6-14).
verseByVerse.theology: Joab is a professional and this is professional work: a two-front trap answered by splitting the force, keeping the elite for the harder enemy, and arranging mutual reinforcement before either engages.
verseByVerse.examples: Joab's sentence can be borrowed as a prayer by anyone who knows how far their own life falls short of their words. A true prayer does not become false because the one praying it has not yet lived up to it.

verseByVerse.quote: When the Ammonites saw that they had become a stench to David, the Ammonites sent and hired the Syrians of Beth-rehob, and the Syrians of Zobah, 20,000 foot soldiers, and the king of Maacah with 1,000 men, and the men of Tob, 12,000 men. And when David heard of it, he sent Joab and all the host of the mighty men. And the Ammonites came out and drew up in battle array at the entrance of the gate, and the Syrians of Zobah and of Rehob and the men of Tob and Maacah were by themselves in the open country. When Joab saw that the battle was set against him both in front and in the rear, he chose some of the best men of Israel and arrayed them against the Syrians. The rest of his men he put in the charge of Abishai his brother, and he arrayed them against the Ammonites. And he said, "If the Syrians are too strong for me, then you shall help me, but if the Ammonites are too strong for you, then I will come and help you. Be of good courage, and let us be courageous for our people, and for the cities of our God, and may the LORD do what seems good to him." So Joab and the people who were with him drew near to battle against the Syrians, and they fled before him. And when the Ammonites saw that the Syrians fled, they likewise fled before Abishai and entered the city. Then Joab returned from fighting against the Ammonites and came to Jerusalem.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Hanun knows what he has done, and buys an army: thirty-three thousand hired troops from four sources, an enormous outlay. The main supplier is the Syrians of Zobah, whose king Hadadezer David defeated two chapters ago, so this is the whole northern coalition getting a second attempt, paid for by Ammon.

The tactical situation is as bad as it can be. The Ammonites are drawn up in front of their own city gate, and the hired Syrians are out in the open country behind Joab. He has walked into the classic trap: an enemy in front and an enemy behind, able to close on him at a signal.

He splits the army, which takes nerve, and the allocation shows that he knows his trade. He takes the picked men himself and faces the Syrians, the professionals, in the harder fight on open ground. Abishai gets the remainder and the Ammonites, who are defending a gate and can retreat into it. Then, before either force engages, the agreement: whichever of us is losing, the other comes. That is a plan for the situation actually in front of them rather than the one they would prefer, and it removes from both commanders the temptation to look after their own front and let the other manage. Neither can win separately.

Then comes Joab's sentence, and it is a good deal better than Joab. It has two halves, and the balance between them is what makes it worth having.

The first half is duty. Let us be courageous for our people, and for the cities of our God. He names what they are fighting for, and it is not the king, the empire, plunder or their own reputations. It is the people, and the cities of our God: this is God's territory and these are God's people.

The second half is submission. May the LORD do what seems good to him. He does not promise victory, or claim God is on their side, or assert that the LORD will certainly give the enemy into their hand. He has done everything a competent general can do, splitting the force, putting his best men where the fight is hardest and arranging for each half to help the other, and then he hands the result over without a guarantee.

That is the right pattern for anybody's work, and it is genuinely hard to keep: do the thing as well as it can be done, fight as if it depends on you, and then leave the outcome with God, on the understanding that what seems good to him may not be what seems good to you.

And it comes out of the mouth of a murderer. This is the man who called Abner aside at the gate of Hebron as though to speak privately with him and put a knife in his stomach, in a city of refuge (a town where the law promised safety), in peacetime, and was cursed for it in public by his own king. He will kill Absalom against a direct royal order, and Amasa the same way he killed Abner, and he will die holding the horns of the altar.

The writer never reconciles the two. He does not explain how a man can speak like this and behave like that, or suggest the words are hypocrisy; he puts the speech in the record and moves on. It is a fair warning about how little a true sentence proves about the person saying it, and equally a reminder that a true sentence is still true. Joab was right about the people, about the cities of God and about leaving the outcome with the LORD, and he was a murderer, and both are true of the same man.

The hired men break first, which is what hired men do, and the Ammonites go back inside their walls the moment they see it. Joab does not besiege the city: he has beaten the field army, and he goes home. That matters, because the war is not over. Rabbah is still standing, and somebody will have to come back for it next spring.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 15–19 — Afraid to Save the Ammonites Anymore
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Hadadezer brings Syrians from beyond the Euphrates under Shobach. David crosses the Jordan himself and destroys them, Shobach dies, and the vassal kings make peace with Israel (vv. 15-19).
verseByVerse.theology: David goes out himself here, and wins. Remember it when the next chapter opens with him doing the opposite.
verseByVerse.examples: The vassal kings make peace, and one enemy is left behind its walls. Unfinished business often sets the scene for temptation: the next chapter's sin happens in the gap between a war begun and a war finished.

verseByVerse.quote: But when the Syrians saw that they had been defeated by Israel, they gathered themselves together. And Hadadezer sent and brought out the Syrians who were beyond the Euphrates. They came to Helam, with Shobach the commander of the army of Hadadezer at their head. And when it was told David, he gathered all Israel together and crossed the Jordan and came to Helam. The Syrians arrayed themselves against David and fought with him. And the Syrians fled before Israel, and David killed of the Syrians the men of 700 chariots, and 40,000 horsemen, and wounded Shobach the commander of their army, so that he died there. And when all the kings who were servants of Hadadezer saw that they had been defeated by Israel, they made peace with Israel and became subject to them. So the Syrians were afraid to save the Ammonites anymore.
verseByVerse.commentary:
This has now stopped being about Ammon. Hadadezer calls up troops from the far side of the Euphrates, which means the whole Aramean world is being mobilised, and his commander-in-chief takes the field in person. What began as a diplomatic insult in a small kingdom has become a war for control of the north.

David goes himself. Mark that sentence, because a few verses later the writer is going to say the opposite about him in words that shape the rest of the book. Here, when the enemy is a serious army under a serious commander, the king gathers all Israel, crosses the river and stands in the line. The Syrian army is destroyed and its commander killed on the field.

The coalition collapses, and the last clause, the Syrians were afraid to save the Ammonites anymore, is the one that matters for what comes next. Ammon is now alone. The hired army is gone, the great power that backed it has been beaten twice and has decided this is no longer its quarrel, and the men who shaved the beards of David's envoys are sitting inside the walls of Rabbah with nobody coming. And the city has not been taken.

That is the reason chapter 11 opens as it does. Campaigning stopped for the winter, as it usually did, and in the spring the army went back out under Joab to besiege Rabbah. Then come five words on which the whole book turns: But David remained at Jerusalem.

This chapter is why that sentence is an accusation. There is a war on, it is his war, it started because his own envoys were humiliated, he fought the northern half of it in person and won, and the army is now in the field finishing it without him.

Why do the numbers differ from the parallel account? Numbers in Hebrew manuscripts were easily miscopied, since they were often written with letters or abbreviations; and the two accounts sometimes count different things, such as chariots and charioteers, or a total and a part. Neither touches what the passage teaches. Here 2 Samuel has 700 chariots and 40,000 horsemen (v. 18) where Chronicles has 7,000 chariots and 40,000 foot soldiers (1 Chron. 19:18), the kind of difference that copying numbers easily produces. This commentary holds, with the historic confessions, that Scripture as God gave it is true in all it says; not every such difference can now be explained with certainty.
verseByVerse.note: “The Euphrates” is “the River” in Hebrew (ESV note).

10.theology:
Two chapters running, faith kept with the dead (v. 2). Jonathan in chapter 9, Nahash here, and the same word both times: hesed, loyalty that outlasts the reason for it. This time the beneficiary is a foreign dynasty, and the man being repaid is best known in Scripture for a threatened atrocity (1 Sam. 11:2). The writer does not explain the debt, and inventing one is not a service; what he shows is that David paid it.

How suspicion works (v. 3). The princes' theory was not absurd: a young, untested king had some reason to be nervous of David. The fault is not in having the thought. It is in acting on it as a certainty, rather than watching, testing, or simply hastening the envoys home. Suspicion that is never checked feels like shrewdness from the inside, and it flatters the people who hold it: they are too clever to be taken in. That is why it so rarely gets checked, and why it can start a war over a condolence visit.

An insult meant to be seen, and a king who would not use it (vv. 4-5). Hanun shamed the envoys in order to insult David, and the insult was meant to be carried home and displayed. David could have displayed it himself to rouse the nation, which is what a king who wanted a war would do. His first thought was for the men instead, and the narrator gives the reason in a single clause: for the men were greatly ashamed. A king who will protect people made ridiculous in his service, when their humiliation would be useful to him, is showing the kind of rule this book has been looking for since Saul.

Joab's speech, and Joab (v. 12). Duty done for the people and the cities of God, and the result left with the LORD without a guarantee: that is the right pattern for anybody's work. It comes from a man who murdered Abner and will murder Amasa, and the writer never reconciles the two. A true sentence proves little about the person saying it, and it is still true. Both halves are worth remembering when good words come from someone whose life does not match them, including when that someone is ourselves.

Kindness taken for a threat. A king sent comfort to a grieving house and was suspected of spying, and his envoys were shamed and sent away. Jesus told a parable with the same pattern about himself: a king sends servants to call people to his son's feast, and they treat them shamefully (Matthew 22:2-6). The Son of David came with comfort to a grieving world and met the same suspicion, the council fearing that if they let him go on, the Romans would come and take away their place (John 11:48). And Joab's fine sentence about leaving the outcome with the LORD came from a man whose life contradicted it. The same prayer in Gethsemane, not as I will, but as you will (Matthew 26:39), came from the one man whose whole life matched his words; and because he kept it for us, our own half-kept prayers of surrender are not the end of us.

Why this chapter exists (vv. 17-19). When the enemy is a serious army, the king crosses the Jordan and stands in the line. By the end of the chapter the coalition is broken and Ammon is alone, but Rabbah has not been taken. That unfinished war is the setting of 11:1, and it is why but David remained at Jerusalem is an accusation rather than a detail: it is his war, begun over his own envoys, and the army is finishing it without him.
10.examples:
Then: A king's counsellors decided, on no evidence whatever, that a delegation of condolence was a reconnaissance party, and their king shamed the envoys and turned them out to walk home. The war it started ran for two campaigning seasons and cost the lives of an entire allied army and its commander.

Now: Two things. The princes of Ammon show what a plausible suspicion costs when it is acted on as a certainty. Their theory was not absurd; they simply never checked it, and by the time anybody could have, there was no way back. And Joab's line is the one to carry into ordinary work: do the thing as well as it can be done, for the people it is actually for, and then leave the result with God, on the honest understanding that what seems good to him may not be what seems good to you. We can do that because he is already our God, as he was Israel's, and his Spirit gives the courage the work needs.

11.title: The Great Fall
11.text: <sup>1</sup>In the spring of the year, the time when kings go out to battle, David sent Joab, and his servants with him, and all Israel. And they ravaged the Ammonites and besieged Rabbah. But David remained at Jerusalem.<sup>2</sup>It happened, late one afternoon, when David arose from his couch and was walking on the roof of the king's house, that he saw from the roof a woman bathing; and the woman was very beautiful.<sup>3</sup>And David sent and inquired about the woman. And one said, "Is not this Bathsheba, the daughter of Eliam, the wife of Uriah the Hittite?"<sup>4</sup>So David sent messengers and took her, and she came to him, and he lay with her. (Now she had been purifying herself from her uncleanness.) Then she returned to her house.<sup>5</sup>And the woman conceived, and she sent and told David, "I am pregnant."<sup>6</sup>So David sent word to Joab, "Send me Uriah the Hittite." And Joab sent Uriah to David.<sup>7</sup>When Uriah came to him, David asked how Joab was doing and how the people were doing and how the war was going.<sup>8</sup>Then David said to Uriah, "Go down to your house and wash your feet." And Uriah went out of the king's house, and there followed him a present from the king.<sup>9</sup>But Uriah slept at the door of the king's house with all the servants of his lord, and did not go down to his house.<sup>10</sup>When they told David, "Uriah did not go down to his house," David said to Uriah, "Have you not come from a journey? Why did you not go down to your house?"<sup>11</sup>Uriah said to David, "The ark and Israel and Judah dwell in booths, and my lord Joab and the servants of my lord are camping in the open field. Shall I then go to my house, to eat and to drink and to lie with my wife? As you live, and as your soul lives, I will not do this thing."<sup>12</sup>Then David said to Uriah, "Remain here today also, and tomorrow I will send you back." So Uriah remained in Jerusalem that day and the next.<sup>13</sup>And David invited him, and he ate in his presence and drank, so that he made him drunk. And in the evening he went out to lie on his couch with the servants of his lord, but he did not go down to his house.<sup>14</sup>In the morning David wrote a letter to Joab and sent it by the hand of Uriah.<sup>15</sup>In the letter he wrote, "Set Uriah in the forefront of the hardest fighting, and then draw back from him, that he may be struck down, and die."<sup>16</sup>And as Joab was besieging the city, he assigned Uriah to the place where he knew there were valiant men.<sup>17</sup>And the men of the city came out and fought with Joab, and some of the servants of David among the people fell. Uriah the Hittite also died.<sup>18</sup>Then Joab sent and told David all the news about the fighting.<sup>19</sup>And he instructed the messenger, "When you have finished telling all the news about the fighting to the king,<sup>20</sup>then, if the king's anger rises, and if he says to you, 'Why did you go so near the city to fight? Did you not know that they would shoot from the wall?<sup>21</sup>Who killed Abimelech the son of Jerubbesheth? Did not a woman cast an upper millstone on him from the wall, so that he died at Thebez? Why did you go so near the wall?' then you shall say, 'Your servant Uriah the Hittite is dead also.'"<sup>22</sup>So the messenger went and came and told David all that Joab had sent him to tell.<sup>23</sup>The messenger said to David, "The men gained an advantage over us and came out against us in the field, but we drove them back to the entrance of the gate.<sup>24</sup>Then the archers shot at your servants from the wall. Some of the king's servants are dead, and your servant Uriah the Hittite is dead also."<sup>25</sup>David said to the messenger, "Thus shall you say to Joab, 'Do not let this matter displease you, for the sword devours now one and now another. Strengthen your attack against the city and overthrow it.' And encourage him."<sup>26</sup>When the wife of Uriah heard that Uriah her husband was dead, she lamented over her husband.<sup>27</sup>And when the mourning was over, David sent and brought her to his house, and she became his wife and bore him a son. But the thing that David had done displeased the LORD.
11.overview:
The key to the chapter is the last sentence of verse 1, and the previous chapter spent nineteen verses preparing for it. Joab, Uriah and all Israel are at Rabbah. But David remained at Jerusalem.

The turn comes not on the roof but in verse 3, when he is told whose daughter and whose wife she is, and goes ahead. The cover-up gets worse at every step: a loyal Hittite who will not go home, a death warrant carried by the man it condemns, and a general who makes the murder harder to detect at the cost of more lives. For twenty-six verses the narrator passes no judgment at all. Then, in one clause, he gives the LORD’s verdict.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–5 — But David Remained at Jerusalem
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: While the army besieges Rabbah, David stays in Jerusalem, sees a woman bathing, is told she is Bathsheba, the wife of Uriah, and sends for her and lies with her. She conceives (vv. 1-5).
verseByVerse.theology: Sin rarely needs a plan to begin; it needs an empty afternoon and a heart that has stopped asking. The man who enquired of the LORD before his battles (5:19, 23) is not recorded asking God anything in this chapter.
verseByVerse.examples: Notice how easily ordinary authority does the work. David does not argue or persuade; he sends, and people go. Anyone with power over others, in a home, a workplace or a church, should notice how little effort it takes to make other people serve our wishes, and how rarely anyone says no.

verseByVerse.quote: In the spring of the year, the time when kings go out to battle, David sent Joab, and his servants with him, and all Israel. And they ravaged the Ammonites and besieged Rabbah. But David remained at Jerusalem. It happened, late one afternoon, when David arose from his couch and was walking on the roof of the king's house, that he saw from the roof a woman bathing; and the woman was very beautiful. And David sent and inquired about the woman. And one said, "Is not this Bathsheba, the daughter of Eliam, the wife of Uriah the Hittite?" So David sent messengers and took her, and she came to him, and he lay with her. (Now she had been purifying herself from her uncleanness.) Then she returned to her house. And the woman conceived, and she sent and told David, "I am pregnant."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The time when kings go out to battle. Campaigning stopped over the winter, when the roads were mud and there was nothing in the fields to live on. In the spring, armies moved. That is simply how the year worked, and the phrase is not sarcasm; it is a calendar note that becomes an accusation because of what comes after it. (The written Hebrew actually has messengers, a word one letter away from kings; the scribes' own margin, the Greek and Chronicles, 1 Chron. 20:1, read kings, as the ESV does.)

And this is not some optional foreign adventure. It is the second season of the Ammonite war, which began when Hanun shaved the beards of David's own envoys and sent them home half-dressed. It is his war. Rabbah is unfinished business from chapter 10, and the coalition that was propping the Ammonites up has already quit. More than that, he fought the hard half of that war in person. When the Syrians brought up an army from beyond the Euphrates, he gathered all Israel together and crossed the Jordan (10:17) and destroyed them and killed their commander. He knows how to do this and he has just done it.

But David remained at Jerusalem. The whole army is in the field. Uriah is in the field. Joab is in the field. And the man who has been asking God before every battle since he came out of a cave is at home with nothing to do.

Nothing in the verse says he was wrong to delegate; kings did delegate. What the verse does is put him in the one place where the next verse can happen, at the one time of year when there is nobody around, with no responsibility on him for the first time in his adult life.

He is perhaps around fifty, and he has won everything. The writer, who has spent five chapters showing us a man who asks God about everything, now shows us a man with an afternoon free. He gets up from a nap in the late afternoon and walks about on his roof.

The palace was the highest building in a very small city built on a steep ridge, and the houses below were packed close. From that roof you could see into a good many courtyards. There is no indication anywhere in the text that she is doing anything improper. The bathing is most likely the purification the law required after a period, a detail the writer supplies in verse 4. It matters because it shows that the child cannot be her husband's.

The seeing is not the sin. It should be said plainly, because a great deal of preaching has made this chapter about a glance. He saw something from his own roof; what happens next is the sin, and verse 3, not verse 4, is the point of no return.

He asks. And the answer he gets back is not a name but a warning, and it is delivered in the form of a question, is not this...?, which is how a servant tells a king something he does not want to say. The answer contains three pieces of information, and every one of them should have stopped him.

She has a name: Bathsheba. She is not an anonymous body on a roof; she is a person, and people in this city know her.

She is the daughter of Eliam. And Eliam is on the list at the end of this book, one of the thirty, David's own elite (23:34). The same list makes an Eliam the son of Ahithophel the Gilonite. If it is the same man, as many think, Bathsheba was the granddaughter of David's greatest counsellor, and that would explain something that otherwise makes little sense: why, years later, Ahithophel abandons David for Absalom without a word of hesitation (15:31), and why his advice to Absalom is so ferocious. The wisest man in the kingdom may have had his own reason to turn on David: what was done to his granddaughter.

And she is the wife of Uriah the Hittite. Married. And the husband is also on the list at the end of the book, the very last name on it (23:39), which is the writer's own quiet memorial. He is not a stranger. He is one of the king's own thirty, and he is at this moment sleeping in a field outside Rabbah on David's orders.

David asked a question and was told, in one sentence, that the woman was somebody's daughter and somebody's wife, and given both men's names, and both men were his. He went ahead.

That is where this chapter turns: not on the roof, but in the half minute after the servant answered him, when he had every fact he needed and could still have stopped.

Read the verbs, because the writer has chosen them and they are all David's. He sent. He took. He lay. She came and she returned, and those are the only two things attributed to her in the entire verse, and both of them are responses to being summoned.

Took has appeared before, in a sentence the narrator laid down without a syllable of comment: David took more concubines and wives from Jerusalem (5:13), immediately after the finest thing ever said about him. And behind that stands the law about Israel's king, and its stated reason: he shall not acquire many wives for himself, lest his heart turn away (Deut. 17:17). A man who has spent twenty years taking women in marriage whenever he wanted them has practised something, and here it is.

Bathsheba needs care, because commentators have gone both ways for centuries and the text supports neither confidently. Some have made her a temptress who bathed where she could be seen. There is nothing whatever in the passage to support it; she is washing in her own courtyard, and the man looking is on the roof of the tallest building in the city. Others have written her a full interior life of terror or of complicity. The honest position is that the narrator does not tell us her mind at any point, and filling the silence in either direction is invention.

What the text does establish is the situation. She is the wife of a serving soldier, in a small city, summoned by the king of Israel, by messengers, to the palace. There is no version of that scene in which she is a free party to a negotiation. Whatever she felt, the power in that room was entirely on one side, and Scripture's own verdict, delivered by Nathan in the next chapter, assigns the guilt to one person and describes her as a lamb that was taken.

I am pregnant: two words in Hebrew, and they end the private phase of this. She sends, which is the one action she initiates in the chapter, and the message is three words long in English and unanswerable. The purification note in verse 4 has already told the reader what David is about to work out for himself: the child cannot be Uriah's, because Uriah has been at Rabbah, and the whole city will be able to count. Everything from here is a cover-up, and it gets worse at every step.

Was this rape or adultery? The king sent for her, and a subject could hardly refuse a king; the text puts the whole guilt on David (12:9), and Nathan’s parable makes her the lamb, not the thief. It was an abuse of power, whatever she felt she could do, and Scripture never blames Bathsheba.

What if something like this has happened to you? If you have been used by someone with power over you, at work, in a church or in a family, the first thing this chapter says is that the guilt was his. You are the lamb in Nathan's story, not the thief. The second is in verse 27: everyone saw what the powerful man arranged for them to see, and the LORD saw what was actually done, and called it evil. Nothing done to you was hidden from him. If you are still in danger, seek safety at once and tell someone who can act, including the police where a crime has been committed; no leader's position puts him beyond the law or beyond God's judgment. And God did not leave Bathsheba where this chapter leaves her. She became the mother of a king, and Matthew names her in the line of Jesus (Matthew 1:6): the Saviour came through the wound, not around it.
verseByVerse.note: Rabbah, the Ammonite capital, is modern Amman in Jordan.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 6–13 — Shall I Then Go to My House?
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: David recalls Uriah and sends him home, but Uriah sleeps at the palace door and refuses, by the king's life, to go to his house while the ark and the army are in the field. Even drunk he does not go (vv. 6-13).
verseByVerse.theology: A Hittite mercenary will not sleep under his own roof while the ark of God is in a field shelter. The king of Israel, who danced that ark into the city, is sleeping in a palace and has just taken this man's wife.
verseByVerse.examples: Some people are no different when their guard is down. Uriah drunk is more faithful than David sober. That is the integrity worth praying for: not a performance kept up while someone is watching, but a character that holds when no one is checking.

verseByVerse.quote: So David sent word to Joab, "Send me Uriah the Hittite." And Joab sent Uriah to David. When Uriah came to him, David asked how Joab was doing and how the people were doing and how the war was going. Then David said to Uriah, "Go down to your house and wash your feet." And Uriah went out of the king's house, and there followed him a present from the king. But Uriah slept at the door of the king's house with all the servants of his lord, and did not go down to his house. When they told David, "Uriah did not go down to his house," David said to Uriah, "Have you not come from a journey? Why did you not go down to your house?" Uriah said to David, "The ark and Israel and Judah dwell in booths, and my lord Joab and the servants of my lord are camping in the open field. Shall I then go to my house, to eat and to drink and to lie with my wife? As you live, and as your soul lives, I will not do this thing." Then David said to Uriah, "Remain here today also, and tomorrow I will send you back." So Uriah remained in Jerusalem that day and the next. And David invited him, and he ate in his presence and drank, so that he made him drunk. And in the evening he went out to lie on his couch with the servants of his lord, but he did not go down to his house.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The first plan is the obvious one, and if it had worked nobody would ever have known. Bring the husband home for a night; the dates will be close enough, the child will be assumed to be his, Uriah will go back to the siege, and the whole thing disappears. David has to pull a named officer out of an active siege to do it, which Joab will certainly have noticed.

Then comes the small talk (v. 7), and it is repulsive. Three questions: how is Joab, how are the men, how is the war. Every one of them the right question for a king to ask a soldier just in from the front, and every one of them a delay while the man stands there waiting to be told why he has been summoned all the way from a siege. He asks after the welfare of the army while planning to deceive one of its officers.

Go down to your house and wash your feet is an ordinary phrase for going home and resting, with a plain enough implication attached. And then the present, sent after him: food from the palace, most likely, for a homecoming meal. The king is setting up the evening.

Uriah sleeps on the doorstep with the palace staff. The plan has failed and David does not yet know why. Neither does the reader, until Uriah is asked.

Uriah's answer (v. 11) is the moral centre of the chapter, and it is spoken by a foreigner. The ark and Israel and Judah dwell in booths. He begins with the ark, not the army, his commander or his own comfort: the ark of God is out in a field shelter, and while it is there he will not sleep under a roof.

That is the same ark David danced into this city in a linen ephod, having spent three months learning how to carry it properly. The Hittite is more careful of it than the man who brought it home.

My lord Joab and the servants of my lord are camping in the open field. His officers and his mates are sleeping in the dirt outside Rabbah. He will not take a comfort they cannot have.

He swears it. And he swears it by the life of the king who is standing in front of him trying to arrange exactly that thing, which is the cruellest irony in the passage.

Now set the two men side by side, because the writer has arranged this and means it to be seen. Uriah is a Hittite, a foreigner from a people Israel was told to drive out, serving in Israel's army under an Israelite name usually taken to mean "the LORD is my light". He will not sleep in his own bed because the ark of God is in a tent.

David is the anointed king of Israel, the man after God's own heart, who wrote about the ark and danced in front of it. He has slept in a palace, taken this man's wife, and is now trying to get him drunk enough to go home so the dates will fit.

Neither man knows what the other knows. Uriah is being honourable in front of a king who is counting days, and every honourable thing he says makes his own death more certain.

There is a question worth asking here that the text leaves open: did Uriah suspect? Some have thought so: the palace was small and servants talk, and his refusal is very firm. It is possible, and the text gives no answer. What it gives is a soldier's principle stated twice and kept under pressure, and that is enough.

So David gets him drunk. Read that as what it is: the king of Israel sitting at a table with a loyal officer, filling his cup, working on him for an evening, in order to lower the man's guard enough to send him home to a wife the king has already slept with.

And it does not work. Drunk, at the end of a long evening, Uriah goes out and lies down with the servants.

The wine has loosened him, but it has not touched his loyalty, and the king can see it.

He has now tried decency, hospitality and alcohol, and the man will not be moved. There is one thing left, and he does it in the morning.
verseByVerse.note: The Hittites were counted among the peoples of Canaan (Gen. 10:15; 23:3). Uriah was not the only one in David's service: Ahimelech the Hittite was with him in the wilderness (1 Sam. 26:6).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 14–21 — Set Uriah in the Forefront
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: David sends Joab a letter by Uriah's own hand ordering his death. Joab puts him where the defenders are strongest, other men die with him, and Joab coaches the messenger to end his report with Uriah's name (vv. 14-21).
verseByVerse.theology: Sin that is hidden needs more sin to keep it hidden. In one morning David moves from covering a pregnancy to disposing of a witness, and the only thing that witness has done is behave well.
verseByVerse.examples: Count the people the cover-up has now drawn in: the servant who answered, the messengers, Bathsheba, Uriah, Joab, the soldiers at the wall and the runner with the report. One man's secret has become the business of an army.

verseByVerse.quote: In the morning David wrote a letter to Joab and sent it by the hand of Uriah. In the letter he wrote, "Set Uriah in the forefront of the hardest fighting, and then draw back from him, that he may be struck down, and die." And as Joab was besieging the city, he assigned Uriah to the place where he knew there were valiant men. And the men of the city came out and fought with Joab, and some of the servants of David among the people fell. Uriah the Hittite also died. Then Joab sent and told David all the news about the fighting. And he instructed the messenger, "When you have finished telling all the news about the fighting to the king, then, if the king's anger rises, and if he says to you, 'Why did you go so near the city to fight? Did you not know that they would shoot from the wall? Who killed Abimelech the son of Jerubbesheth? Did not a woman cast an upper millstone on him from the wall, so that he died at Thebez? Why did you go so near the wall?' then you shall say, 'Your servant Uriah the Hittite is dead also.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
He writes the order for the man's death, in his own hand, and gives it to the man to carry. Uriah walks the whole way back to Rabbah carrying his own execution, and delivers it to his commanding officer himself.

The reason he is chosen as courier is the reason he is being killed: he is the one man in the kingdom who is certain not to open it. David is using the man’s loyalty to kill him.

The instruction is precise and it is murder, and it is murder of a kind that leaves no body to explain and no blood on anybody's hands.

Note what David is willing to spend. A deliberate withdrawal from a man in contact with the enemy would be seen by every soldier in the line; it would need Joab to give an order that would be remembered. He does not care. He also does not seem to consider that the manoeuvre will cost other men, which it does.

Joab does it differently, and the difference tells you a great deal about Joab. He does not stage a withdrawal. He puts Uriah where he knows the defenders are strongest, and then sends the whole assault in against the wall.

Why? Because Joab is a professional and he can see what David, sitting in Jerusalem, has not thought about. A visible abandonment of one named officer would be talked about in the army for twenty years and would eventually reach somebody who would ask why. A costly assault on a fortified wall is a normal military disaster, and one dead officer in a casualty list is invisible. Joab's method is safer, and it kills more people.

Other men die. The writer does not say how many and does not name them, and their families were told they fell in an assault on Rabbah, and that was true, and it was not the reason.

Then, at the end of the verse, as though it were an afterthought: Uriah the Hittite also died. Which is the only part of the operation David was interested in.

Then comes the most chilling piece of stage management in the book, and it is entirely Joab's. He briefs the messenger on the king's likely reaction, anticipates the exact rebuke, including the historical example David will reach for (the death of Abimelech under a millstone thrown by a woman at Thebez, Judg. 9:53), and gives the man the sentence that will make the anger stop.

Joab has understood the letter completely. He knows that the casualties are irrelevant to the king and that one name will settle everything, and he has arranged for a junior messenger to say it out loud in the throne room without knowing what he is saying.

He is also, in the same breath, establishing something. He has the letter. He has done the thing. And he has now demonstrated to himself that the king will accept a report of unnecessary dead soldiers as long as the right man is among them. From this morning, Joab owns David.

Everything the man does for the rest of the reign rests on this. He kills Absalom against a direct, public, repeated royal order and suffers nothing. He murders Amasa in the road exactly as he murdered Abner and suffers nothing. He speaks to the king with a contempt no other subject would survive. And David, dying, has to ask Solomon to do what he could never do himself (1 Kings 2:5-6). A man who has helped you do something you cannot admit is not your servant afterwards.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 22–27 — The Sword Devours Now One and Now Another
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: David tells Joab not to be troubled, for the sword devours now one and now another. After Bathsheba's mourning he takes her as his wife, and she bears a son; but the thing displeased the LORD (vv. 22-27).
verseByVerse.theology: David uses a proverb about the chances of war to describe a death he arranged in writing. Familiar moral language can be put to work to quiet a conscience, and the more familiar the saying, the better it works.
verseByVerse.examples: The chapter's last clause is a comfort as well as a warning: nothing done in secret escapes the eyes of the LORD, and that includes every wrong done to people like Uriah and Bathsheba that no court ever heard.

verseByVerse.quote: So the messenger went and came and told David all that Joab had sent him to tell. The messenger said to David, "The men gained an advantage over us and came out against us in the field, but we drove them back to the entrance of the gate. Then the archers shot at your servants from the wall. Some of the king's servants are dead, and your servant Uriah the Hittite is dead also." David said to the messenger, "Thus shall you say to Joab, 'Do not let this matter displease you, for the sword devours now one and now another. Strengthen your attack against the city and overthrow it.' And encourage him." When the wife of Uriah heard that Uriah her husband was dead, she lamented over her husband. And when the mourning was over, David sent and brought her to his house, and she became his wife and bore him a son. But the thing that David had done displeased the LORD.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The messenger delivers the whole thing at once and never gets to find out whether the king would have been angry. Then comes the coldest sentence David ever speaks: the sword devours now one and now another.

On any other day that is a decent thing for a commander to say to a commander who has taken losses. War is like that; men die; do not blame yourself. It is the sort of thing that keeps an army functioning.

Said by this man, on this morning, it is obscene. He knows precisely which one the sword devoured and why, because he wrote the instruction. He is telling the executioner not to feel bad about the execution, using a proverb about the randomness of war to describe a death he arranged in advance, in writing. And note the last two words of the message: encourage him. Buck Joab up.

The phrase will come back. Abner shouted across a valley at this same Joab, years ago: shall the sword devour forever? Do you not know that the end will be bitter? (2:26). The sword does not stop, and it is bitter in the end, and Nathan is about to tell David that it will never leave his house.

She is not given her name in this verse. The writer has called her Bathsheba once, in verse 3, in the servant's warning. Here, and in the next verse, she is the wife of Uriah, and the New Testament does the same thing at the head of the Gospels, where Matthew declines to name her at all and writes that David was the father of Solomon by the wife of Uriah (Matt. 1:6). That is not an accident in either place. She is identified by the man who was killed, in the sentence recording that she mourned him.

And she lamented over her husband is all we are told about what this did to her. A time of mourning, for a man she was married to and who would not come home to her while the ark was in a field.

David sent: the verb that has driven the whole chapter. He sent Joab, sent to ask about the woman, sent for her, sent for Uriah, sent the letter, and sends now.

And from the outside it is a decent act. A king marries the widow of an officer killed at the siege of Rabbah, quickly, before anybody counts months. The child arrives inside a marriage. The dates are covered, the household is provided for, and the whole business is closed.

Twenty-six verses, and the narrator has not said a word of judgment. He has reported a walk on a roof, a question and its answer, a summons, a pregnancy, three failed attempts to make Uriah seem the father, a letter, a battle, a casualty list, a piece of coaching, a shrug, and a wedding. No comment at all.

And there it is, at the very end, in one clause: the thing that David had done displeased the LORD. The Hebrew is stronger than the English: the thing was "evil in the eyes of the LORD".

Everything in the chapter has been about eyes. David saw a woman from a roof. He arranged matters so that nobody else would see what had happened. The mathematics were made to look right, the marriage was made to look decent, the death was made to look like the ordinary attrition of a siege, and the messenger did not know what he was carrying and neither did Uriah.

It worked. Every person in Jerusalem who mattered saw exactly what David wanted them to see. One did not.

That single sentence is the writer's whole method. He has refused to comment for a full chapter, letting the reader watch it happen and feel the sickness of it without being told what to think, and then he puts the verdict down in one clause and stops.

There is no punishment in this verse, no lightning, no visible consequence. There is a year of silence coming, while the child is born, the household settles and the siege goes on, and Psalm 32 is probably David's own record of what that year was like from the inside: when I kept silent, my bones wasted away through my groaning all day long. For day and night your hand was heavy upon me (Ps. 32:3-4).

How could the man after God's own heart do this? That phrase (1 Samuel 13:14) describes God's choice of him, not a promise that he would never fall, and this chapter is Scripture's own refusal to make a saint out of a sinner. What marks David out is not that he did not sin but what he does when he is confronted, and the mercy he finds (12:13; Psalm 51).

And then a man walks into the room with a story about a lamb.

11.theology:
Why verse 1 is an accusation. Kings delegated; but this is his own unfinished war, and staying home leaves him idle at the one season when everyone else is away.

The point of no return is verse 3, not verse 4. A name, a father who is one of the thirty (23:34), and a husband who is another (23:39): David was told all of it and went ahead. Knowing the facts did not stop him; temptation is seldom overcome by information alone.

What can and cannot be said about Bathsheba. The narrator never reports her mind, and filling that silence in either direction is invention. What the text establishes is the situation, a serving soldier's wife summoned by the king, and Scripture's own verdict comes next chapter, in a parable where the lamb is not blamed.

A foreigner at the moral centre (v. 11). The Hittite is more careful of the ark than the king who danced it into the city, and every honourable sentence he speaks makes his death more certain.

An accomplice is a master (vv. 14-21). The cover-up needed Joab, and Joab now holds the letter. A man who has helped you do what you cannot admit is not your servant afterwards, and the rest of David's reign shows it.

A soldier's life spent to save a king. Uriah carries the letter, takes the front of the line, and dies so that David's sin can stay hidden. The gospel is this chapter turned inside out. Jesus said the rulers of the nations lord it over them, but the Son of Man came not to be served but to serve, and to give his life as a ransom for many (Mark 10:45). The Son of David did not take what belonged to another; he gave up what was his own. He did not send the innocent to die for a guilty king; he is the innocent King who died for guilty subjects, David among them. And the sin this chapter hides so carefully he bore in the open, before the whole city, on a hill outside its walls.

One clause, at the very end (v. 27). The whole chapter has been about eyes: David saw a woman from a roof, and then arranged matters so that nobody would see what followed. Everyone in Jerusalem saw what he meant them to see. The LORD saw what was done, and there is no lightning in the verse, only a year of silence and then a man who walks in with a story about a lamb.
11.examples:
Then: A king wrote out the order for a man's death in his own hand and gave it to that man to carry to the general who would carry it out, choosing him as the courier for the same reason he was killing him: he was the one officer in the kingdom certain not to open it.

Now: Two things. The first is where the chapter actually turns: not the roof but verse 3, the half minute after the servant answered, when David had every fact he needed and sent anyway. Almost nobody walks into a disaster without being told first; the warning comes and is overruled, and after that one step leads to the next. The second is Joab. The cover-up required an accomplice, and from the moment he had one, David was never free of him again. And where we have already gone past the warning, the next chapter shows the way back: not a better cover, but confession, and a mercy that does not wait for us to have stopped in time.

12.title: You Are the Man
12.text: <sup>1</sup>And the LORD sent Nathan to David. He came to him and said to him, "There were two men in a certain city, the one rich and the other poor.<sup>2</sup>The rich man had very many flocks and herds,<sup>3</sup>but the poor man had nothing but one little ewe lamb, which he had bought. And he brought it up, and it grew up with him and with his children. It used to eat of his morsel and drink from his cup and lie in his arms, and it was like a daughter to him.<sup>4</sup>Now there came a traveler to the rich man, and he was unwilling to take one of his own flock or herd to prepare for the guest who had come to him, but he took the poor man's lamb and prepared it for the man who had come to him."<sup>5</sup>Then David's anger was greatly kindled against the man, and he said to Nathan, "As the LORD lives, the man who has done this deserves to die,<sup>6</sup>and he shall restore the lamb fourfold, because he did this thing, and because he had no pity."<sup>7</sup>Nathan said to David, "You are the man! Thus says the LORD, the God of Israel, 'I anointed you king over Israel, and I delivered you out of the hand of Saul.<sup>8</sup>And I gave you your master's house and your master's wives into your arms and gave you the house of Israel and of Judah. And if this were too little, I would add to you as much more.<sup>9</sup>Why have you despised the word of the LORD, to do what is evil in his sight? You have struck down Uriah the Hittite with the sword and have taken his wife to be your wife and have killed him with the sword of the Ammonites.<sup>10</sup>Now therefore the sword shall never depart from your house, because you have despised me and have taken the wife of Uriah the Hittite to be your wife.'<sup>11</sup>Thus says the LORD, 'Behold, I will raise up evil against you out of your own house. And I will take your wives before your eyes and give them to your neighbor, and he shall lie with your wives in the sight of this sun.<sup>12</sup>For you did it secretly, but I will do this thing before all Israel and before the sun.'"<sup>13</sup>David said to Nathan, "I have sinned against the LORD." And Nathan said to David, "The LORD also has put away your sin; you shall not die.<sup>14</sup>Nevertheless, because by this deed you have utterly scorned the LORD, the child who is born to you shall die."<sup>15</sup>Then Nathan went to his house. And the LORD afflicted the child that Uriah's wife bore to David, and he became sick.<sup>16</sup>David therefore sought God on behalf of the child. And David fasted and went in and lay all night on the ground.<sup>17</sup>And the elders of his house stood beside him, to raise him from the ground, but he would not, nor did he eat food with them.<sup>18</sup>On the seventh day the child died. And the servants of David were afraid to tell him that the child was dead, for they said, "Behold, while the child was yet alive, we spoke to him, and he did not listen to us. How then can we say to him the child is dead? He may do himself some harm."<sup>19</sup>But when David saw that his servants were whispering together, David understood that the child was dead. And David said to his servants, "Is the child dead?" They said, "He is dead."<sup>20</sup>Then David arose from the earth and washed and anointed himself and changed his clothes. And he went into the house of the LORD and worshiped. He then went to his own house. And when he asked, they set food before him, and he ate.<sup>21</sup>Then his servants said to him, "What is this thing that you have done? You fasted and wept for the child while he was alive; but when the child died, you arose and ate food."<sup>22</sup>He said, "While the child was still alive, I fasted and wept, for I said, 'Who knows whether the LORD will be gracious to me, that the child may live?'<sup>23</sup>But now he is dead. Why should I fast? Can I bring him back again? I shall go to him, but he will not return to me."<sup>24</sup>Then David comforted his wife, Bathsheba, and went in to her and lay with her, and she bore a son, and he called his name Solomon. And the LORD loved him<sup>25</sup>and sent a message by Nathan the prophet. So he called his name Jedidiah, because of the LORD.<sup>26</sup>Now Joab fought against Rabbah of the Ammonites and took the royal city.<sup>27</sup>And Joab sent messengers to David and said, "I have fought against Rabbah; moreover, I have taken the city of waters.<sup>28</sup>Now then gather the rest of the people together and encamp against the city and take it, lest I take the city and it be called by my name."<sup>29</sup>So David gathered all the people together and went to Rabbah and fought against it and took it.<sup>30</sup>And he took the crown of their king from his head. The weight of it was a talent of gold, and in it was a precious stone, and it was placed on David's head. And he brought out the spoil of the city, a very great amount.<sup>31</sup>And he brought out the people who were in it and set them to labor with saws and iron picks and iron axes and made them toil at the brick kilns. And thus he did to all the cities of the Ammonites. Then David and all the people returned to Jerusalem.
12.overview:
About a year of silence, and nothing happened. Then the LORD sends Nathan, the prophet who brought the promise in chapter 7, and he does not accuse. He brings a case, and the king pronounces sentence under oath before he knows who the defendant is.

The indictment is built out of gifts, not laws, and God calls the killing David's own act, though an Ammonite arrow did it. David says one short sentence and is forgiven in the next, and is then told the sword will never leave his house. The pardon and the judgment both stand. The child dies, David prays and then worships, and at the end of the worst chapter of his life comes one clause about the next son: and the LORD loved him.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–6 — There Were Two Men in a Certain City
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Nathan tells the king of a rich man who took a poor man's one ewe lamb to feed a guest, and David, furious, swears the man deserves to die and must restore fourfold (vv. 1-6).
verseByVerse.theology: A conscience that has been silent for a year can still be reached, but not head-on. God's messenger comes round the side, through the king's own sense of justice, and lets David's verdict do what an accusation could not.
verseByVerse.examples: David's anger is right; it is simply aimed at the wrong man. Indignation at other people's sins is easy to feel, and it can sit comfortably beside the same sin unconfessed in ourselves (compare Romans 2:1).

verseByVerse.quote: And the LORD sent Nathan to David. He came to him and said to him, "There were two men in a certain city, the one rich and the other poor.
