The rich man had very many flocks and herds, but the poor man had nothing but one little ewe lamb, which he had bought. And he brought it up, and it grew up with him and with his children. It used to eat of his morsel and drink from his cup and lie in his arms, and it was like a daughter to him. Now there came a traveler to the rich man, and he was unwilling to take one of his own flock or herd to prepare for the guest who had come to him, but he took the poor man's lamb and prepared it for the man who had come to him." Then David's anger was greatly kindled against the man, and he said to Nathan, "As the LORD lives, the man who has done this deserves to die, and he shall restore the lamb fourfold, because he did this thing, and because he had no pity."
verseByVerse.commentary:
About a year has passed. The child in 11:27 has been born, which means roughly nine months of silence at least, and probably more. Nothing happened in that year. The marriage held, the household ran, the siege of Rabbah continued, and no one in Jerusalem said anything. David got away with it completely.

Psalm 32 very probably reports that year from within it: when I kept silent, my bones wasted away through my groaning all day long. For day and night your hand was heavy upon me; my strength was dried up as by the heat of summer (Ps. 32:3-4).

The LORD sent Nathan: not the court, not a rival, not a rumour. And it is the same prophet who brought the covenant promise in chapter 7; the man who told him his house would stand forever now walks in to tell him what is going to happen to it.

Nathan's method is as instructive as his message. He does not accuse; he brings a case. Every detail of the lamb (v. 3) adds to the picture, down to it was like a daughter to him. The Hebrew word for daughter is bat, and the woman's name is Bath-sheba. The echo may be deliberate, and even if it is not, the picture is exact: the lamb stands for Uriah's wife, who was not a possession but a member of the family, loved.

The occasion is trivial, and that is the point. It is not famine, not desperation, not a debt. A visitor arrives and a meal has to be made, and the rich man will not spend one animal out of many, so he takes the one animal a poor man owns. He needed so little and destroyed so much: that is the whole case.

Now the trap closes, and it closes because David does his job. This is not a king being taken in by a clever story. Nathan has brought him a legal matter, which is exactly what the king of Israel was for: David administered justice and equity to all his people (8:15). A man with no standing has been robbed and has no redress, and the case has come up to the supreme court, and David hears it and does what he is supposed to do. He gets angry, and he gives judgment.

That is why the parable works. It is not a moral tale that he happens to identify with; it is a verdict he pronounces in office, under oath (as the LORD lives), before he knows who the defendant is.

And note how far he goes. Nobody has died in the story; a sheep was taken. And the king's instant, furious sentence is capital. Then the restitution, and it is straight out of the law: if a man steals an ox or a sheep and kills it or sells it, he shall repay five oxen for an ox, and four sheep for a sheep (Ex. 22:1). David sets the figure himself: fourfold.

Many readers have seen that number paid in the rest of the story. Four of his sons die: the child in this chapter; Amnon, murdered by his brother at a sheepshearing; Absalom, killed in an oak tree against David's explicit order; and Adonijah, executed by Solomon. The man who set the figure was their father.

And listen to the last clause of his own verdict, because it is the sharpest thing in the chapter: because he had no pity. Not because he broke the law, but because there was nothing in him that stopped.
verseByVerse.note: “In his arms” is literally “in his bosom” (ESV note).

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: You are the man! Nathan sets out God's gifts, names the murder and the taking of Uriah's wife, and pronounces that the sword will not depart from David's house. David confesses, and Nathan tells him the LORD has put away his sin (vv. 7-15).
verseByVerse.theology: The charge is built from gifts, not laws. Before it is anything else, David's sin is a refusal to trust the Giver for what he wanted.
verseByVerse.examples: Distance does not dilute guilt. Whatever we arrange for other people to do on our behalf, God counts as our own act.

verseByVerse.quote: Nathan said to David, "You are the man! Thus says the LORD, the God of Israel, 'I anointed you king over Israel, and I delivered you out of the hand of Saul. And I gave you your master's house and your master's wives into your arms and gave you the house of Israel and of Judah. And if this were too little, I would add to you as much more. Why have you despised the word of the LORD, to do what is evil in his sight? You have struck down Uriah the Hittite with the sword and have taken his wife to be your wife and have killed him with the sword of the Ammonites. Now therefore the sword shall never depart from your house, because you have despised me and have taken the wife of Uriah the Hittite to be your wife.' Thus says the LORD, 'Behold, I will raise up evil against you out of your own house. And I will take your wives before your eyes and give them to your neighbor, and he shall lie with your wives in the sight of this sun. For you did it secretly, but I will do this thing before all Israel and before the sun.'" David said to Nathan, "I have sinned against the LORD." And Nathan said to David, "The LORD also has put away your sin; you shall not die. Nevertheless, because by this deed you have utterly scorned the LORD, the child who is born to you shall die." Then Nathan went to his house. And the LORD afflicted the child that Uriah's wife bore to David, and he became sick.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Two words in Hebrew: Attah ha-ish. Few sentences in Scripture are so compressed. No preamble, no softening, no appeal to the king's better nature. The judge has passed sentence and the prophet identifies the defendant.

Consider what Nathan is risking. He is standing alone in front of a man who has, within the last year, arranged the death of one of his own mighty men and several other soldiers to conceal a pregnancy, and got away with it. Nathan knows this, because God has just told him. And he says it anyway.

Read the indictment carefully, because of what it is made of. It is not a list of laws; it is a list of gifts. I anointed you: at Bethlehem, when he was the eighth son, out with the sheep. I delivered you out of the hand of Saul: from the spears, through the window, in the caves, and twice from the three thousand men. I gave you your master's house, and Israel, and Judah. Every clause begins with God as the giver, exactly as chapter 7 did.

And then the line that is worse than any accusation: if this were too little, I would add to you as much more.

There was more available. If the man had needed something, or wanted something, or found himself in middle age with an empty afternoon and an appetite he could not manage, he could have asked. The giver was generous and had never once refused him. He did not ask. He went and took.

That is what kind of sin this was, and it should be stated exactly. Not a starving man stealing bread. A man with everything, who had never been refused anything, helping himself to the one thing that was not on offer, from a household that had nothing else.

Now God's account of the killing, and every word of it should be felt. David never touched him. He was in Jerusalem. An Ammonite archer on a wall at Rabbah killed Uriah, in an assault ordered by Joab, and David's only involvement was a sentence in a letter. God says: You have struck down Uriah the Hittite with the sword.

And then, so that nobody can miss what is being said: you have killed him with the sword of the Ammonites. The instrument is named. The arrangement is named. And the killer is named, and it is not the archer and it is not Joab.

Every layer David built into that operation, the distance, the deniability, the fact that the actual weapon belonged to an enemy of Israel in the middle of a legitimate siege, is simply set aside. It kept the truth from his neighbours for a year. It hid nothing from God.

He used a sword to solve a problem, and the sword is going to live in his family. Amnon killed at a feast, Absalom run through in a tree, Adonijah executed, and a rebellion in between that costs twenty thousand men in one day. And the correspondence is exact, which is how the judgments in this book generally work. He took a wife in secret; wives will be taken from him in public. He worked in the dark from a roof; this will happen before the sun. And it does, on that same roof, when Absalom pitches a tent on it in front of the whole city (16:22), on the advice of Ahithophel, who may well have been Bathsheba’s grandfather.

Out of your own house. That is the hardest clause in the sentence. The judgment is not an invasion or a plague; it is his own sons.

I have sinned against the LORD. Six words in English, two in Hebrew, and that is the whole of it. No excuse. No explanation of the pressures. No mention of Bathsheba, or Joab, or the difficulty of the situation, or what the alternatives would have cost. No attempt to distinguish what he did from what the man in the story did. No request for time.

And the direction is right: against the LORD. He has wronged Uriah beyond repair, and Bathsheba, and the other men who died on that wall, and he will say so; but he names first the one against whom the offence is finally committed.

That is exactly what the psalm says. Psalm 51 is headed as David's, when Nathan the prophet went to him, after he had gone in to Bathsheba, and it contains the same sentence at greater length: against you, you only, have I sinned and done what is evil in your sight (Ps. 51:4).

The whole psalm belongs here. Have mercy on me, O God, according to your steadfast love... blot out my transgressions... create in me a clean heart, O God, and renew a right spirit within me... cast me not away from your presence, and take not your Holy Spirit from me (Ps. 51:1-11). That last line is not a formula; he had watched the Spirit leave Saul.

And the psalm knows what the man cannot bring: for you will not delight in sacrifice, or I would give it; you will not be pleased with a burnt offering. The sacrifices of God are a broken spirit; a broken and contrite heart, O God, you will not despise (Ps. 51:16-17). He had good reason to know that. There was no sacrifice in the law for premeditated murder or adultery. Those carried the death penalty and no offering covered them. The man had nothing to bring.

The answer comes in the same breath as the confession. There is no interval: no period of proving it, no probation, no series of works to be completed first. He says I have sinned and is told, in the next sentence, that it is dealt with.

Put away is the language of removal: the sin taken off him and carried elsewhere.

And you shall not die is a direct reversal of the verdict David gave in verse 5. He said the man deserved to die. He was right; the law agreed with him twice over. And he does not die. Somebody else does, and the whole Bible is about how that comes to be just.

Paul answers it with this very year of David's life. He quotes Psalm 32, David's own account of that silence and its ending, as the description of every believer's pardon: blessed is the man against whom the Lord will not count his sin (Romans 4:6-8). And he explains how a holy God could do that: God had passed over former sins, and at the cross he put Christ forward as a propitiation (a sacrifice that turns away his just anger), to show that he is both just and the one who justifies whoever has faith in Jesus (Romans 3:25-26). David's pardon was real the moment Nathan spoke it; it was paid for centuries later, when Christ died outside the walls of the same city.

In verse 14 the Hebrew literally says David scorned the enemies of the LORD, probably a scribe's reverent way of avoiding writing that a man scorned God; the KJV reads given great occasion to the enemies of the LORD to blaspheme, and either way the point is that his sin brought God's name into contempt.

And then, immediately after the pardon, the consequence. The two must be held together, because this verse is where a great deal of shallow teaching about forgiveness breaks. The sin is put away and the sword still comes. Both are said by the same prophet in the same conversation, and neither cancels the other.

Forgiveness does not remove the consequences. It removes the sin. David is not going to be cut off as Saul was, not going to lose the covenant, not going to be abandoned; and his family is going to be torn apart for the rest of his life, and it starts with a baby.

Anybody who has come to God with something genuinely destructive and been genuinely forgiven, and then found that the wreckage was still there in the morning, is standing in this verse. The relationship is restored. The consequences run their course.

The prophet goes home, and the writer calls her Uriah's wife one last time.

Did God approve polygamy by giving David Saul’s wives? In that world a new king took over the old king’s household; God is saying that he had given David everything Saul had. It describes what God allowed in his providence, not what he commanded; the law still warned against many wives (Deut 17:17).

Is God the author of Absalom’s evil? God foretold the judgment and gave David over to it, but Absalom chose his own sin and was guilty of it (16:22). God rules even the wicked deeds of men without being the author of their sin (Acts 2:23).

Was it fair for the child to die for David’s sin? Each person answers for his own guilt (Ezek 18:20), and the child was not punished for David’s guilt. The death was God’s judgment on David, who had treated life lightly, and God as Giver of life may take it when he wills. The child was not lost: David says I shall go to him (v. 23).
verseByVerse.note: Chronicles, which follows this war closely (1 Chron. 20:1-3), leaves out the whole Bathsheba episode.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 16–23 — I Shall Go to Him
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The child falls ill; David fasts and lies on the ground for seven days. When the child dies he gets up, washes, worships, and eats, and explains himself to his bewildered servants (vv. 16-23).
verseByVerse.theology: Seven days on the ground while there was any possibility, and not one day after. He is not callous and he is not resigned; he prayed as long as praying could change anything, and when it could not, he got up and went to worship.
verseByVerse.examples: For those who grieve: David's servants were afraid to tell him, and then bewildered by how he took it. People in grief rarely behave as others expect, and they need presence more than explanations.

verseByVerse.quote: David therefore sought God on behalf of the child. And David fasted and went in and lay all night on the ground. And the elders of his house stood beside him, to raise him from the ground, but he would not, nor did he eat food with them. On the seventh day the child died. And the servants of David were afraid to tell him that the child was dead, for they said, "Behold, while the child was yet alive, we spoke to him, and he did not listen to us. How then can we say to him the child is dead? He may do himself some harm." But when David saw that his servants were whispering together, David understood that the child was dead. And David said to his servants, "Is the child dead?" They said, "He is dead." Then David arose from the earth and washed and anointed himself and changed his clothes. And he went into the house of the LORD and worshiped. He then went to his own house. And when he asked, they set food before him, and he ate. Then his servants said to him, "What is this thing that you have done? You fasted and wept for the child while he was alive; but when the child died, you arose and ate food." He said, "While the child was still alive, I fasted and wept, for I said, 'Who knows whether the LORD will be gracious to me, that the child may live?' But now he is dead. Why should I fast? Can I bring him back again? I shall go to him, but he will not return to me."
verseByVerse.commentary:
He has been told what will happen, by a prophet, plainly, and he prays anyway. That is unusual, and it is not disobedience. He does not argue with Nathan or deny the word. He goes into a room and lies on the floor and asks God to change his mind, on the basis he states himself two verses further on: who knows whether the LORD will be gracious to me? He is not claiming a promise. He is appealing to what God is like.

Seven days of this. His household cannot get him off the floor and cannot get him to eat, and when the child dies his own staff are frightened of what the news will do to him. They have watched a man lie on the ground for a week refusing food, and they conclude, reasonably, that the death will break him completely. They stand in the corridor whispering and cannot make themselves go in.

He gets up. Read the order of what he does, because it is deliberate and it is not what anybody expected. He washes. He anoints himself. He changes his clothes. He goes into the house of the LORD and worships. Then he goes home and asks for food and eats it.

Worship comes before the meal. The first place he goes after seven days on the floor and the death of his son is into God's presence, to worship the God who had told him this would happen.

They ask, and it is a fair question. Here is his account of the seven days, and it is the honest one.

Who knows? He never had a promise. He had a word of judgment and a knowledge of God's character, and on the strength of the second he spent a week begging against the first. There was always a possibility, and while there was a possibility he prayed with everything he had.

I shall go to him, but he will not return to me is the sentence people come to this chapter for, and it should be handled slowly and without a trace of glibness, because the people who need it are usually holding something unbearable.

Take the first half first: can I bring him back again? What David is refusing is the thing grief most wants to do, which is to keep going with the protest after the outcome is settled. He is not being cold; he wept on a floor for a week. He is saying that the fasting had a purpose, the purpose is finished, and continuing it would be doing something to himself rather than for the child.

There is a hard-won wisdom in that and it belongs to people who have prayed properly. He gave everything he had while it could matter. He is not going to punish himself now that it cannot.

Look at what the sentence says, and what it does not. It does not say the child will be restored to him in this life; that is the clause he explicitly denies. What he says is that he is going where the child is. The movement is one way, and it is David who is travelling.

How much weight will that sentence bear? Some read it as no more than a statement about death: I shall die as he has died, and go to the grave where he is. That reading is possible and it should be admitted. But it is difficult to account for the effect it has on the man. He has been on the ground for a week; this sentence is what gets him up, washed and into the house of God to worship. A remark that everybody dies eventually is not a comfort, and it does not explain the change in him.

What is certain is this. David, who knew as much about God as anybody in the Old Testament, faced with the death of an infant, and an infant who died under a stated judgment on his own sin, looked forward and not back, and expected to be with him, and got up and worshipped. That is what the passage gives, and it is a great deal.

Two things stand beside it. The first is that David's whole hope in this chapter rests on the character of God rather than on the child's record, which is the only ground anybody has ever had. His question was who knows whether the LORD will be gracious?, and the answer he received about himself was that the LORD had put away his sin. The God who does that is the God he expects to find the child with.

And the second is the Lord Jesus, who said let the children come to me; do not hinder them, for to such belongs the kingdom of God (Mark 10:14), and who was indignant with the disciples for getting in the way.

Pretending Scripture says more than it does is not kindness. Anybody standing where David stood should be given what it does give, the settled conviction of a grieving father who knew God well and the character of the God who put away his sin the moment he named it, and no less, and nothing invented.

Do infants who die go to heaven? David expected to be with his son: I shall go to him, but he will not return to me. Scripture does not set out a full doctrine, and Christians have answered differently. But God is merciful, infants have not rejected him, and Jesus welcomed little children, for to such belongs the kingdom of heaven (Matt 19:14). Many in the Reformed tradition have held that God saves those who die in infancy, by his grace in Christ. Grieving parents may rest their little ones in God’s hands with real hope. This commentary holds, with the 1689 London Baptist Confession and the Westminster Confession (both at 10.3), that elect infants dying in infancy are regenerated and saved by Christ through the Spirit, who works when and where and how he pleases; and many believers, with good reason, hope that God's mercy embraces every child who dies so young, though Scripture does not say so in so many words.

One more word to a bereaved mother or father. David got up on the seventh day, but this passage is not a timetable for grief. The same man wept for Absalom with a cry the whole army heard (18:33), and Jesus wept at a friend's grave though he was about to raise him (John 11:35). Tears that go on are not unbelief. What David shows is where to carry them: to the God who is gracious, in the hope of going where the child has gone.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 24–31 — And the LORD Loved Him
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Solomon is born, and the LORD loves him and names him Jedidiah through Nathan. Joab, at Rabbah, summons the king to take the city, and David does (vv. 24-31).
verseByVerse.theology: Grace has the last word in the chapter, but it does not erase what went before: the child of this marriage is loved by God, and the house is still under judgment.
verseByVerse.examples: Finishing a job someone else neglected and then handing them the credit can be generosity or it can be leverage. With Joab it is hard to tell which, and probably it is both.

verseByVerse.quote: Then David comforted his wife, Bathsheba, and went in to her and lay with her, and she bore a son, and he called his name Solomon. And the LORD loved him and sent a message by Nathan the prophet. So he called his name Jedidiah, because of the LORD. Now Joab fought against Rabbah of the Ammonites and took the royal city. And Joab sent messengers to David and said, "I have fought against Rabbah; moreover, I have taken the city of waters. Now then gather the rest of the people together and encamp against the city and take it, lest I take the city and it be called by my name." So David gathered all the people together and went to Rabbah and fought against it and took it. And he took the crown of their king from his head. The weight of it was a talent of gold, and in it was a precious stone, and it was placed on David's head. And he brought out the spoil of the city, a very great amount. And he brought out the people who were in it and set them to labor with saws and iron picks and iron axes and made them toil at the brick kilns. And thus he did to all the cities of the Ammonites. Then David and all the people returned to Jerusalem.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Two things in this verse, and both of them are grace.

The first is small and easy to miss: David comforted his wife, Bathsheba.

It is the first time since she was introduced in 11:3 that she is called by her name and not the wife of Uriah. And it is the first indication anywhere in the account that anybody thought about what this had been like for her. She has been summoned by a king, made pregnant, widowed, married as soon as the mourning was over, and has now buried a baby, and until this moment everything in her story has been done to her by somebody else.

He comforts her. It does not repair anything, but it matters.

The second is five words at the end of the worst chapter in the man's life: And the LORD loved him. This is the child of this marriage, a marriage that began in adultery and a murder, in a household under an announced judgment, born to the woman whose first husband David killed. And God loves him: not tolerates, not permits, but loves, and the writer says it flatly, without explanation, in the same sentence that gives his name.

Solomon will inherit the throne. He will build the house David was not allowed to build. He will be the son through whom the covenant of chapter 7 runs. And Matthew, opening the New Testament with the genealogy of Jesus Christ, writes it into the line with the fact still attached: and David was the father of Solomon by the wife of Uriah (Matt. 1:6).

The New Testament refuses to tidy this up; it puts the murdered man's name in the family tree of the Messiah.

God sends the prophet back with a name. Nathan's last visit was you are the man and a sentence of judgment. He comes this time carrying a name for the baby, and the name is Jedidiah, which means "beloved of the LORD". The same prophet, the same house, the same God: that is the shape of the chapter in two visits.

Meanwhile the war has been going on the whole time. Joab has taken the water supply, which means the city cannot hold out, and he sends word, and his message can be read in two ways.

On the surface it is loyalty: come and finish it, so the credit is yours and not mine. Kings were touchy about this and generals were wise to be careful.

Underneath it is something else, and the sentence is a small masterpiece. Lest I take the city and it be called by my name. He is telling the king, in writing, that he could take the city himself and let everyone know who did it, and that he is choosing not to.

Remember what has passed between these two men since the last time we saw them corresponding. David sent Joab a letter ordering Uriah's death. Joab carried it out in his own way and coached a messenger on how to manage the king's anger. Nothing was ever said about it afterwards.

This message is from a man who knows the king’s secret, telling his king to come out to the war he should have gone to in the first place.

He goes. The chapter that began with a prophet and a lamb ends with the king finally doing what the first verse of chapter 11 said kings do in the spring: go out to battle.

The crown's talent of gold is something like seventy-five pounds, which is not a weight a man wears; it was presumably held above him, or the figure refers to the value of it.

The last verse is genuinely disputed, and it is better to say so than to choose confidently.

The Hebrew can be read as forced labour, the population put to work with saws and picks and axes and at the brick kilns, which is how the ESV and most modern versions take it. The Hebrew of the Chronicler's parallel (1 Chronicles 20:3) has a verb that normally means sawed, though many think a one-letter copying slip has turned set into sawed. The verse in Samuel can also be read as the population being killed with those implements, which is how the older English versions took it, and which would make this an atrocity.

The difference turns on a preposition and a single letter in one verb, and honest scholars have divided on it for a long time. The same writer reported the killing of two-thirds of the Moabite prisoners without flinching (8:2), so he would have said plainly if this were a massacre. And forced labour is what conquerors normally did, so that reading is at least as likely. It is not possible to be certain, and pretending to be would be worse than the difficulty.

What can be said is that the chapter ends with the war finished, the crown on the right head, and the king back in Jerusalem, and with everything Nathan said still ahead of him.
verseByVerse.note: The “royal city” and “city of waters” that Joab took (vv. 26-27) were probably the lower town and its water supply; the citadel still had to fall when David came.

12.theology:
Nathan brings a case, not an accusation (vv. 1-6). David hears it in office, as the judge 8:15 says he was, and gives judgment under oath. Nobody in the story has died, yet his instant sentence is death, with repayment at the law's fourfold rate for a stolen sheep (Ex. 22:1). His own last clause is the sharpest sentence in the chapter: because he had no pity.

An indictment made of gifts (vv. 7-9). God's charge reminds David of all he has been given and offers more, and then names the murder as David's own, though an Ammonite arrow did it. God would have given him more; he did not ask; he took. And the distance he put between himself and the killing counted for nothing before God.

The judgments match the crime (vv. 10-12). He used a sword to solve a problem, and the sword will live in his family. He took a wife in secret, and wives will be taken from him before the sun. And the hardest clause is out of your own house: the judgment is his sons.

One sentence, and the pardon in the same breath (v. 13). No excuse and no request for time, and the direction is right: against the LORD, which Psalm 51 sets out at greater length. The law provided no sacrifice for premeditated murder or adultery, and David had nothing to bring. You shall not die reverses the verdict he gave in verse 5, which was correct. He does not die. Somebody else does: the Son of David, on whom the LORD laid the iniquity of us all (Isaiah 53:6), so that God is just in pardoning (Romans 3:25-26).

Forgiveness and consequence (vv. 13-14). The same prophet says both in the same conversation, and neither cancels the other. David keeps the covenant and the relationship is restored; the consequences run their course.

Prayer against a word already given (vv. 16-23). David appeals not to a promise but to God's character, prays while it could matter, and goes first to worship when it no longer can. His hope for the child rests on that same character, the God who put away his sin the moment he named it; and beside it stands the Lord Jesus saying let the children come to me (Mark 10:14).

And the LORD loved him (vv. 24-25). Bathsheba is called by her name and comforted, and the child of that marriage, born in a house under an announced judgment, is loved by God. Nathan, whose last visit was you are the man, comes back carrying Jedidiah, and Matthew writes the whole history into the Messiah's line: David was the father of Solomon by the wife of Uriah (Matt. 1:6). The grace of God reaches into the very marriage that began in sin.

An unfinished war finished (vv. 26-31). Joab's message is loyal on the surface, and underneath it reminds the king what Joab knows about him, and the king at last goes out to the war he should have fought from the start. How he treated the conquered city (v. 31) is disputed; this commentary takes the forced-labour reading as at least as likely, without claiming certainty.
12.examples:
Then: A prophet walked into a throne room with a lawsuit about a stolen lamb, and the king, doing his job, in office, under oath, lost his temper and sentenced the defendant to death and fourfold repayment before he was told the defendant's name. In the years that followed, four of his own sons died.

Now: Three things. Nathan's method is the first: he did not accuse a man who had already killed to protect this secret. He got him to pronounce his own verdict, on a case he could judge clearly because he did not yet see that it was about himself. Anybody who has to tell someone something true and unwelcome should study that. The second is verse 13 and verse 14 held together: the sin was put away in the same breath as the confession, with no probation and nothing to complete first, and the sword still came. Forgiveness does not remove the consequences, and anyone who has been genuinely pardoned and then found the wreckage still there in the morning is reading the right chapter. And the third is verse 23, for anybody carrying a grief like his: he prayed with everything he had while it could still matter, and he stopped when it could not, and what got him off the floor was not resignation but the expectation that he was going where the child had gone.

13.title: Amnon, Tamar, Absalom
13.text: <sup>1</sup>Now Absalom, David's son, had a beautiful sister, whose name was Tamar. And after a time Amnon, David's son, loved her.<sup>2</sup>And Amnon was so tormented that he made himself ill because of his sister Tamar, for she was a virgin, and it seemed impossible to Amnon to do anything to her.<sup>3</sup>But Amnon had a friend, whose name was Jonadab, the son of Shimeah, David's brother. And Jonadab was a very crafty man.<sup>4</sup>And he said to him, "O son of the king, why are you so haggard morning after morning? Will you not tell me?" Amnon said to him, "I love Tamar, my brother Absalom's sister."<sup>5</sup>Jonadab said to him, "Lie down on your bed and pretend to be ill. And when your father comes to see you, say to him, 'Let my sister Tamar come and give me bread to eat, and prepare the food in my sight, that I may see it and eat it from her hand.'"<sup>6</sup>So Amnon lay down and pretended to be ill. And when the king came to see him, Amnon said to the king, "Please let my sister Tamar come and make a couple of cakes in my sight, that I may eat from her hand."<sup>7</sup>Then David sent home to Tamar, saying, "Go to your brother Amnon's house and prepare food for him."<sup>8</sup>So Tamar went to her brother Amnon's house, where he was lying down. And she took dough and kneaded it and made cakes in his sight and baked the cakes.<sup>9</sup>And she took the pan and emptied it out before him, but he refused to eat. And Amnon said, "Send out everyone from me." So everyone went out from him.<sup>10</sup>Then Amnon said to Tamar, "Bring the food into the chamber, that I may eat from your hand." And Tamar took the cakes she had made and brought them into the chamber to Amnon her brother.<sup>11</sup>But when she brought them near him to eat, he took hold of her and said to her, "Come, lie with me, my sister."<sup>12</sup>She answered him, "No, my brother, do not violate me, for such a thing is not done in Israel; do not do this outrageous thing.<sup>13</sup>As for me, where could I carry my shame? And as for you, you would be as one of the outrageous fools in Israel. Now therefore, please speak to the king, for he will not withhold me from you."<sup>14</sup>But he would not listen to her, and being stronger than she, he violated her and lay with her.<sup>15</sup>Then Amnon hated her with very great hatred, so that the hatred with which he hated her was greater than the love with which he had loved her. And Amnon said to her, "Get up! Go!"<sup>16</sup>But she said to him, "No, my brother, for this wrong in sending me away is greater than the other that you did to me." But he would not listen to her.<sup>17</sup>He called the young man who served him and said, "Put this woman out of my presence and bolt the door after her."<sup>18</sup>Now she was wearing a long robe with sleeves, for thus were the virgin daughters of the king dressed. So his servant put her out and bolted the door after her.<sup>19</sup>And Tamar put ashes on her head and tore the long robe that she wore. And she laid her hand on her head and went away, crying aloud as she went.<sup>20</sup>And her brother Absalom said to her, "Has Amnon your brother been with you? Now hold your peace, my sister. He is your brother; do not take this to heart." So Tamar lived, a desolate woman, in her brother Absalom's house.<sup>21</sup>When King David heard of all these things, he was very angry.<sup>22</sup>But Absalom spoke to Amnon neither good nor bad, for Absalom hated Amnon, because he had violated his sister Tamar.<sup>23</sup>After two full years Absalom had sheepshearers at Baal-hazor, which is near Ephraim, and Absalom invited all the king's sons.<sup>24</sup>And Absalom came to the king and said, "Behold, your servant has sheepshearers. Please let the king and his servants go with your servant."<sup>25</sup>But the king said to Absalom, "No, my son, let us not all go, lest we be burdensome to you." He pressed him, but he would not go but gave him his blessing.<sup>26</sup>Then Absalom said, "If not, please let my brother Amnon go with us." And the king said to him, "Why should he go with you?"<sup>27</sup>But Absalom pressed him until he let Amnon and all the king's sons go with him.<sup>28</sup>Then Absalom commanded his servants, "Mark when Amnon's heart is merry with wine, and when I say to you, 'Strike Amnon,' then kill him. Do not fear; have I not commanded you? Be courageous and be valiant."<sup>29</sup>So the servants of Absalom did to Amnon as Absalom had commanded. Then all the king's sons arose, and each mounted his mule and fled.<sup>30</sup>While they were on the way, news came to David, "Absalom has struck down all the king's sons, and not one of them is left."<sup>31</sup>Then the king arose and tore his garments and lay on the earth. And all his servants who were standing by tore their garments.<sup>32</sup>But Jonadab the son of Shimeah, David's brother, said, "Let not my lord suppose that they have killed all the young men, the king's sons, for Amnon alone is dead. For by the command of Absalom this has been determined from the day he violated his sister Tamar.<sup>33</sup>Now therefore let not my lord the king so take it to heart as to suppose that all the king's sons are dead, for Amnon alone is dead."<sup>34</sup>But Absalom fled. And the young man who kept the watch lifted up his eyes and looked, and behold, many people were coming from the road behind him by the side of the mountain.<sup>35</sup>And Jonadab said to the king, "Behold, the king's sons have come; as your servant said, so it has come about."<sup>36</sup>And as soon as he had finished speaking, behold, the king's sons came and lifted up their voice and wept. And the king also and all his servants wept very bitterly.<sup>37</sup>But Absalom fled and went to Talmai the son of Ammihud, king of Geshur. And David mourned for his son day after day.<sup>38</sup>So Absalom fled and went to Geshur, and was there three years.<sup>39</sup>And the spirit of the king longed to go out to Absalom, because he was comforted about Amnon, since he was dead.
13.overview:
Nathan said evil would rise out of your own house, and it begins here, and the sons’ sins match the father’s exactly. David saw a woman who was not his and took her; his firstborn does the same. David arranged a killing to cover it; his third son arranges one too.

Before Amnon acts, the writer shows that his "love" is only appetite, and Jonadab supplies the method. Tamar argues for her life in a locked room and is not heard; afterwards she refuses to let it be hidden. Her brother tells her to be quiet, her father is very angry and does nothing, and Absalom says nothing to Amnon, good or bad, for two years while he plans a murder. The chapter ends with a father who has stopped grieving the murdered son and aches for the murderer.
13.theology:
The judgment of chapter 12, arriving (vv. 1-2). This is the household of many wives (3:2-5; 5:13) producing what such a household produces, in a kingdom whose law had warned its king in advance. The sons' sins match David's own exactly, and this is the first part of out of your own house to come true.

What the chapter teaches about desire (vv. 2, 15). A man who is troubled only because he cannot get at a woman, and not because it is wrong to want her, is not in love. And appetite satisfied does not become affection; it becomes disgust, and he turns it not on himself, who is responsible, but on her, because the sight of her reminds him of what he did.

Tamar's dignity (vv. 12-19). She argues from the law, from what it will do to her and to him, and offers a way out; she is not heard, twice; and then she refuses to let the deed be hidden. The book records her arguments in full, calls the deed nebalah, a disgraceful outrage, and calls her desolate, a word used of ruined cities. The story moves on without her, but the book does not treat her as unimportant.

Very angry, and nothing else (v. 21). Every sentence David could have spoken to Amnon had already been spoken to him by a prophet. He is silent because he has disqualified himself, and his sons know it. That is what chapter 12's judgment actually looks like: not God striking David, but David unable to act.

The King Tamar needed. Israel's king was meant to be the protector of those with no one else, and the royal psalm prays for a son of David who delivers the needy when he calls, the poor and him who has no helper, and in whose sight their blood is precious (Psalm 72:12-14). Every man in Tamar's house failed her, the king most of all. The promise of chapter 7 never rested on that house's goodness; it waited for the Son of David who would judge the poor with righteousness (Isaiah 11:4), who did not look away from the shamed or hush them up, and who will one day judge the world in justice (Acts 17:31), so that nothing done in a locked room goes unanswered.

Commands others carry out (vv. 22-29). Absalom waits two years in civil silence, then dresses a murder in the language of the battlefield and lets his servants do it, as David wrote a letter and Joab did it. Sin is learned in families, and the method as well as the appetite is passing from father to sons.

Jonadab, and the last verse (vv. 32-39). The man who devised the plan against Tamar saw the murder coming for two years and said nothing. And the chapter ends with no justice anywhere: a daughter desolate, a firstborn dead, and a father whose grief fades into longing for the murderer. The next chapter is Joab noticing that longing.
13.examples:
Then: A young woman argued for her life in a locked room, from the law, from what it would cost her, from what it would make of the man holding her, and finally by offering to marry him if he would only ask her father first; and when he had finished she tore the robe that marked her as a king's daughter and walked through the capital crying aloud so that nobody could pretend it had not happened. Her father was very angry and did nothing.

Now: Three things. Verse 15 is the one to remember: hatred follows the act at once, because appetite satisfied turns to disgust, and the man turns that disgust on his victim, never on himself. Anyone tempted to believe that getting the thing will settle it should notice how fast it turns. Second, Jonadab, who never lifts a hand and is on hand at both disasters with a clever word. Some people do all their damage by supplying a method to someone who had only an appetite. And third, David's silence. He lost the standing to say "this is wrong" and be heard, and he lost it years earlier, in a different room, over a different woman. Even so, the way back was the one he had already been shown: not silence, but owning his own sin before his sons and trusting the mercy that had put it away (12:13).

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Amnon, David's firstborn, is tormented with desire for his half-sister Tamar, and his friend Jonadab, a very crafty man, gives him a plan: feign illness and ask the king to send her to feed him (vv. 1-6).
verseByVerse.theology: The narrator diagnoses it before Amnon acts. What he calls love in verse 1 he calls torment in verse 2, and the obstacle named is not that she is his sister but that she is guarded.
verseByVerse.examples: A friend who hears that we want something wrong and helps us plan it is no friend. The kindest thing Jonadab could have said was no.

verseByVerse.quote: Now Absalom, David's son, had a beautiful sister, whose name was Tamar. And after a time Amnon, David's son, loved her. And Amnon was so tormented that he made himself ill because of his sister Tamar, for she was a virgin, and it seemed impossible to Amnon to do anything to her. But Amnon had a friend, whose name was Jonadab, the son of Shimeah, David's brother. And Jonadab was a very crafty man. And he said to him, "O son of the king, why are you so haggard morning after morning? Will you not tell me?" Amnon said to him, "I love Tamar, my brother Absalom's sister." Jonadab said to him, "Lie down on your bed and pretend to be ill. And when your father comes to see you, say to him, 'Let my sister Tamar come and give me bread to eat, and prepare the food in my sight, that I may see it and eat it from her hand.'" So Amnon lay down and pretended to be ill. And when the king came to see him, Amnon said to the king, "Please let my sister Tamar come and make a couple of cakes in my sight, that I may eat from her hand."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Three of David's children in one verse, and the writer names the relationship each time: Absalom, David's son; Amnon, David's son. They are half-brothers and half-sister, sons and daughter of the same father by different mothers.

This is what the household described at 3:2-5 and 5:13 actually produced. Six sons at Hebron by six women, eleven more at Jerusalem, and a law that had warned Israel's king in advance not to multiply wives.

Nathan said the sword would not depart from this house and that evil would be raised up out of your own house (12:10-11). It begins here, and the reader should see how closely the sons’ sins match the father’s. David saw a woman who was not his and took her. His firstborn is about to do exactly that. David arranged a killing to cover it. His third son will do exactly that.

The narrator has already told us what this is. Verse 1 called it love, which is what Amnon would have called it. Verse 2 calls it torment, and then names the obstacle, and note carefully what the obstacle is not. It is not that she is his sister. It is that she is a virgin daughter of the king, which means she is guarded. As Amnon sees it, the only problem is how to get to her.

A man who is frustrated by the difficulty of getting at a person rather than by the wrongness of wanting to is not in love, and the writer establishes it before anything happens.

Jonadab (v. 3) is the man who makes this happen. He is David's nephew, a cousin of the princes, and the word used of him is not wicked but wise in its shrewd sense: clever, sharp, able to see how a thing can be arranged. The translation crafty is well judged. Keep him in view; he is going to reappear at the end of the chapter knowing more than anybody else in the room.

Hear Amnon's own description: my brother Absalom's sister, not my sister. He describes her by her brother, which is either an attempt to put a little distance between himself and the relationship, or simply how the household worked: full siblings by the same mother, half-siblings otherwise.

Then there is the plan, worked out in a sentence, and the craft in it. A sick prince is visited by the king. A sick man's request for particular food from a particular hand is exactly the sort of thing an ill man asks and a father grants without thinking. It works on David's affection for his son, it requires Tamar to come unaccompanied because she is being sent by the king himself, and it puts her in a private room with a plausible reason. Nobody has to be lied to except David, and he will not question it.

It is also worth being clear about what Jonadab has done. He has been told by a prince that the man is consumed with wanting his own half-sister, and his response is not to talk him out of it, or to warn anybody, or to walk away. He immediately supplies a method. He does not lay a hand on her; he does not have to.

The plan is executed word for word, and the king walks straight into it.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 7–19 — He Would Not Listen to Her
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Tamar comes to cook for him; he sends everyone out and seizes her. She pleads and reasons with him, but he will not listen, and violates her. Then he hates her more than he had loved her, has her thrown out, and she goes away tearing her robe and crying aloud (vv. 7-19).
verseByVerse.theology: Her speech is the most intelligent thing anybody says in this chapter. She argues from the law, from what it will do to her, from what it will do to him, and then offers him a way out that costs her everything and saves them both: ask the king.
verseByVerse.examples: What it does not mean: the silence later forced on Tamar by others is neither consent nor peace. She protested in words, and then in the street, and Scripture keeps both protests on record.

verseByVerse.quote: Then David sent home to Tamar, saying, "Go to your brother Amnon's house and prepare food for him." So Tamar went to her brother Amnon's house, where he was lying down. And she took dough and kneaded it and made cakes in his sight and baked the cakes. And she took the pan and emptied it out before him, but he refused to eat. And Amnon said, "Send out everyone from me." So everyone went out from him. Then Amnon said to Tamar, "Bring the food into the chamber, that I may eat from your hand." And Tamar took the cakes she had made and brought them into the chamber to Amnon her brother. But when she brought them near him to eat, he took hold of her and said to her, "Come, lie with me, my sister." She answered him, "No, my brother, do not violate me, for such a thing is not done in Israel; do not do this outrageous thing. As for me, where could I carry my shame? And as for you, you would be as one of the outrageous fools in Israel. Now therefore, please speak to the king, for he will not withhold me from you." But he would not listen to her, and being stronger than she, he violated her and lay with her. Then Amnon hated her with very great hatred, so that the hatred with which he hated her was greater than the love with which he had loved her. And Amnon said to her, "Get up! Go!" But she said to him, "No, my brother, for this wrong in sending me away is greater than the other that you did to me." But he would not listen to her. He called the young man who served him and said, "Put this woman out of my presence and bolt the door after her." Now she was wearing a long robe with sleeves, for thus were the virgin daughters of the king dressed. So his servant put her out and bolted the door after her. And Tamar put ashes on her head and tore the long robe that she wore. And she laid her hand on her head and went away, crying aloud as she went.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The father sends her. He suspects nothing, which is not much of a defence, because the whole scheme depended on his not asking a single question about why an adult prince needed his half-sister to come and cook in his bedroom. He has never had to think hard about Amnon.

She goes because the king sent her and does what she was told to do. Amnon refuses the food, which was never the point, and clears the room. There were other people present until this moment, servants at least, and a prince ordering a room emptied is not questioned. Every stage of this has used ordinary authority to arrange something nobody would have allowed if they had seen what it was.

My sister: he uses the word while he is doing it. Her answer (vv. 12-13) is the best speech in the chapter, made by somebody with a hand already on her. He called her my sister; she answers my brother, reminding him what they are to each other.

Her first argument is not personal. Such a thing is not done in Israel. She appeals to what the nation is. The word translated outrageous thing is nebalah, the strong term used of the worst offences in Israel, the same word used of the atrocity at Gibeah in Judges 19 and of Achan's sin. She is telling him what kind of sin this would be.

Three more arguments follow, and the order matters. First herself: where could I carry my shame? A woman in her position, in that society, had no future after this. It is not a figure of speech; she is describing the rest of her life, and she is right, as verse 20 will confirm.

Then him: you would be as one of the outrageous fools in Israel. She is arguing for his good. Standing in a locked room with a man twice her strength, she takes the trouble to tell him what this will make of him. The word is nabal, the same word that was Nabal's name, the fool of 1 Samuel 25, and it does not mean a silly man; it means a man with no moral sense at all.

Speak to the king is the remarkable one: she offers to marry him. Leviticus forbids a man to marry his half-sister (Lev. 18:9, 11; 20:17), so this is most likely not a legal proposal but a desperate plea, anything that might stop him (see the question at the end of this section). Some have suggested royal practice differed from the law, but the text does not say so. What is not in doubt is what it costs her to say it. She is offering to spend her life married to the man currently holding her down, if only he will not do it this way.

She has appealed to the law, to what it will cost her, to his own reputation, and to another way of getting what he says he wants. There is nothing left to say.

And none of it reaches him, because appetite that has already decided does not hear counsel. Proverbs has a whole chapter on a young man walking a road he has been warned about, deaf the entire way, as an ox goes to the slaughter (Prov. 7:22). It could have been written about this room.

In verse 14 the Hebrew is literally "he would not listen to her voice", and it is the first of two refusals. The rest of the verse is three facts in the order the writer chose: he was stronger, he violated her, he lay with her. There is no description and no lingering. It is stated the way a report is stated, and the brevity is a kind of respect.

Verse 15 is easy to read as mere brutality, but it sees much further than that. The hatred comes immediately, not later or after reflection: the sentence puts it straight after the act.

Why? Because what he had was never love, and the writer told us so in verse 2. It was appetite, and appetite that has been satisfied does not become affection; it becomes disgust, and the disgust has to be aimed at someone. He will not aim it at himself, so he aims it at her.

She is now the evidence. Every time he looks at her he sees what he did, and he hates the sight of it, and he calls that hating her.

This is a permanent feature of that kind of sin and Scripture states it here once, exactly. A man will wreck a family to get a thing and find it has turned to ash moments after he has it, and he cannot bear the person he took, precisely because she is the proof of what he did.

Get up! Go! Two words in Hebrew, barked at her. And she speaks again, and his second refusal to listen is recorded in the same words as the first.

Her argument is legal and it is correct. The law of Israel required a man who violated an unbetrothed virgin to marry her and never divorce her (Deut. 22:28-29), and harsh as that provision sounds to modern ears, its purpose was to protect the woman, to give her a household and a standing rather than leave her discarded. A parallel law lets her father refuse the marriage (Exodus 22:16-17), so it was, most think, a protection she could claim, not a sentence laid on her. Being put out of the door is a second destruction on top of the first, and she says so.

But he would not listen to her. Twice in three verses. The writer will not let it be missed.

This woman. He will not use her name and does not speak to her directly; he gives an order about an object to a servant, in her hearing, and the door is bolted behind her.

The writer stops the narrative to tell us what she is wearing, which means it matters.

It is a distinctive garment, described with the same phrase as Joseph's coat, and it is a uniform: this is what the unmarried daughters of the king wore, and everyone in Jerusalem would have recognised it at a distance.

And she goes public. Everything she does here is a formal act of mourning, performed in the street: ashes on the head, the garment torn, the hand laid on the head, and the loud crying that was the recognised sound of grief.

She tears the robe that says she is a virgin daughter of the king, because she is not one any more, and she walks through the city letting everybody see it.

She had every reason to go home quietly. Instead she made it impossible for the household to pretend: whatever was going to be done about this, it was not going to be done in the dark. That is a brave thing, and it is the last free act she performs in the book.

Could Tamar have married Amnon? The law forbade marriage to a half-sister (Lev 18:9), but in her terror she said whatever might stop him. Most likely it was a desperate plea, not a legal proposal.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 20–29 — Absalom Spoke to Amnon Neither Good Nor Bad
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Absalom tells Tamar to keep quiet, and she lives desolate in his house. David is very angry and does nothing. Absalom says nothing to Amnon for two years, then has him killed at a sheepshearing feast (vv. 20-29).
verseByVerse.theology: Two silences sit side by side: a father's, who has lost the standing to speak, and a brother's, who is waiting. Neither of them is peace.
verseByVerse.examples: Anger that does nothing is not justice. David felt the right thing and did nothing with it, and the cost of his inaction fell on the one person in the story who had done no wrong.

verseByVerse.quote: And her brother Absalom said to her, "Has Amnon your brother been with you? Now hold your peace, my sister. He is your brother; do not take this to heart." So Tamar lived, a desolate woman, in her brother Absalom's house. When King David heard of all these things, he was very angry. But Absalom spoke to Amnon neither good nor bad, for Absalom hated Amnon, because he had violated his sister Tamar. After two full years Absalom had sheepshearers at Baal-hazor, which is near Ephraim, and Absalom invited all the king's sons. And Absalom came to the king and said, "Behold, your servant has sheepshearers. Please let the king and his servants go with your servant." But the king said to Absalom, "No, my son, let us not all go, lest we be burdensome to you." He pressed him, but he would not go but gave him his blessing. Then Absalom said, "If not, please let my brother Amnon go with us." And the king said to him, "Why should he go with you?" But Absalom pressed him until he let Amnon and all the king's sons go with him. Then Absalom commanded his servants, "Mark when Amnon's heart is merry with wine, and when I say to you, 'Strike Amnon,' then kill him. Do not fear; have I not commanded you? Be courageous and be valiant." So the servants of Absalom did to Amnon as Absalom had commanded. Then all the king's sons arose, and each mounted his mule and fled.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Her brother's first response is to tell her to be quiet. Read the sentence carefully, because it is doing several things at once and only one of them is kind.

He already knows. The question has Amnon your brother been with you? is not really a question; the torn robe and the ashes have told him, and the fact that he names Amnon without being told suggests he had some idea this was coming.

He takes her in, and that is real. She lives in his house from this day.

And then: hold your peace... do not take this to heart. He has just watched his sister walk through the city tearing her clothes, and his instruction is silence: not "I will get justice for you", not "we are going to the king", but be quiet.

Two things are probably true of that at once. Part of it is a brother trying to spare her more public exposure. And part of it is a man who has already decided what he is going to do and needs the matter to go quiet so that he can do it in two years' time. Either way, she is silenced by the person protecting her.

A desolate woman. That is the writer's own word for her, and it is the last thing said about her own life. The Hebrew is shomemah, and it is not a word about feelings. It is used of ruined cities and of land laid waste after an army has been through it. Tamar is the town Amnon sacked, and she stays that way. Her name appears once more: Absalom calls his daughter Tamar, and of that daughter it is said, she was a beautiful woman (14:27). Nothing else. No marriage, no children, no restoration.

She is the only person in this chapter who behaves well throughout, arguing rightly, warning the offender for his own sake, offering a way out, protesting the second wrong as well as the first and refusing to let it be hidden, and she is the one whose life is over.

The narrative moves on to what her brothers do, because the narrative is about the house of David and the judgment on it. That is the writer's subject. But she should not be left behind without saying plainly that the book knows what was done to her, records her arguments in full, calls it nebalah, and calls her desolate. The story moves on without her, but the book does not treat her as unimportant.

If you have suffered what Tamar suffered, hear what this chapter says. The shame is Amnon's, not hers: Scripture calls the deed nebalah and calls him the fool, and never hints that she was to blame. She said no, and it is recorded. Her brother told her to keep quiet and her father did nothing, and the book sets both down as failures, not as wisdom. Abuse is never to be tolerated, and never hushed up for the sake of a family's name, a church's reputation or anyone's comfort. If you are in danger, seek safety at once, and tell someone who can act: the police, a doctor, a trusted pastor or elder. And the Son of David is not like David here. He sees what was done, he does not look away, and he himself endured the cross, despising the shame (Hebrews 12:2), so that shame would not have the last word over anyone who trusts him.

He was very angry, and that is the whole of the father's response: anger, and nothing after it. No summons, no judgment, no protection ordered for Tamar, no punishment, not even a recorded conversation with Amnon. The king who administered justice and equity to all his people (8:15) hears that his firstborn has raped his daughter, becomes very angry, and does nothing.

The Hebrew text stops there. The Greek Septuagint and a manuscript of Samuel found at Qumran both carry an additional clause at this point, and it supplies the reason: "But he would not punish his son Amnon, because he loved him, since he was his firstborn."

Whether or not that sentence belongs in the text, it describes what happened. And beneath the favouritism lay a deeper reason, which everybody in that palace knew.

What exactly was David going to say to Amnon? That a son of the king may not take a woman he has decided he wants? That a man in power may not use that power to get a woman into a private room? That a man must answer for taking whatever he thinks he can get away with?

Every sentence available to him had already been spoken to him, by a prophet, in this same palace, about a woman called Bathsheba. He is not silent because he does not care. He is silent because he has disqualified himself, and his son knows it, and his other sons know it. The judgment of chapter 12 is not that God struck David; it is that David can no longer act.

That is what a father loses. Not the love of his children and not their obedience, necessarily, but the standing to say "this is wrong" and be heard saying it.

Then there is the other silence, and it is worse. Neither good nor bad: not a word, in either direction, for two full years. He does not accuse him, or quarrel with him, or avoid him conspicuously. He is civil. He behaves, at every family occasion, exactly as a brother behaves. The writer explains it in the same sentence: for Absalom hated Amnon.

That is not restraint and it is not forgiveness. It is a man who has decided on murder and understands that the way to arrange one is to give nobody the slightest reason to remember that you had a grievance. Two years of speaking neither good nor bad is a colder thing than a rage.

Sheepshearing was the great festival of the pastoral year, a harvest feast, with a great deal to eat and more to drink. Nabal was holding one when David's men came for provisions.

Absalom invites the king first, and it is debated whether he meant the invitation. What is certain is that he needed a refusal, because David's presence would have made the thing impossible, and he needed the refusal to look like reluctance on the king's side.

And David asks the right question.

Why should he go with you? Somewhere in the man there is still an instinct that this is odd, that of all the sons, this is the one Absalom has singled out, and that there is a reason these two should not be alone together in the country.

He asks the question and then does not press it; he gives way, as he gave way when Amnon asked for Tamar to bake for him. Twice in this chapter David has been asked for something that should have made him uneasy, and twice he has handed over a child to a request he did not examine.

Now hear the language of the order. The plan itself is squalid: wait until the man is drunk, and stab him at the table. And Absalom dresses it in the vocabulary of the battlefield. Do not fear. Have I not commanded you? Be courageous and be valiant. Those are the words spoken to soldiers before an engagement, the words Joshua was given and Joab used before battle with the Ammonites (10:12), and they are being used here to steady a group of servants for the murder of an unarmed man at a party.

He is giving them, and himself, an excuse: this is not an assassination but a brave deed done under orders. And note who takes the risk. He commands, and they do it, exactly as David wrote a letter and Joab did it.

The other princes get on their mules and ride, and they are right to. They have just watched their brother stab their brother, and none of them knows where it stops.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 30–39 — The Spirit of the King Longed to Go Out
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: David hears that all his sons are dead; Jonadab tells him only Amnon is, by Absalom's long-settled intent. Absalom flees to Geshur for three years, and the king's heart longs for him (vv. 30-39).
verseByVerse.theology: The house of David weeps together for the first time in the chapter, over a death that every one of its failures helped to cause.
verseByVerse.examples: The chapter ends with a father grieving a murdered son and longing for the murderer, and the next four chapters grow out of that longing.

verseByVerse.quote: While they were on the way, news came to David, "Absalom has struck down all the king's sons, and not one of them is left." Then the king arose and tore his garments and lay on the earth. And all his servants who were standing by tore their garments. But Jonadab the son of Shimeah, David's brother, said, "Let not my lord suppose that they have killed all the young men, the king's sons, for Amnon alone is dead. For by the command of Absalom this has been determined from the day he violated his sister Tamar. Now therefore let not my lord the king so take it to heart as to suppose that all the king's sons are dead, for Amnon alone is dead." But Absalom fled. And the young man who kept the watch lifted up his eyes and looked, and behold, many people were coming from the road behind him by the side of the mountain. And Jonadab said to the king, "Behold, the king's sons have come; as your servant said, so it has come about." And as soon as he had finished speaking, behold, the king's sons came and lifted up their voice and wept. And the king also and all his servants wept very bitterly. But Absalom fled and went to Talmai the son of Ammihud, king of Geshur. And David mourned for his son day after day. So Absalom fled and went to Geshur, and was there three years. And the spirit of the king longed to go out to Absalom, because he was comforted about Amnon, since he was dead.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The report arrives before the survivors do, and it is wrong. David tears his clothes and lies on the ground, the posture from chapter 12, when the baby was dying. He has spent a night on the floor before, over a child, and the writer is not likely to have chosen the detail by accident.

Then Jonadab walks back into the story, and what he says is chilling. He knows the true casualty figure before any survivor has arrived. He knows the number is one. He knows the name. He knows whose command it was. And he knows the motive, and dates it exactly: from the day he violated his sister Tamar. This is the man who wrote the plan that put Tamar in that bedroom.

So he has spent two years watching Absalom say neither good nor bad, understanding perfectly well what the silence meant, and he said nothing: not to David, and not to Amnon, who was his friend and whom he could have warned.

And now he steps forward with the correct information at the moment when producing it makes him look indispensable to a grieving king.

The writer calls him crafty in verse 3 and then shows us what the word means over a span of two years. He never once acts. He arranges, he observes, and he is present with the right sentence at the right moment. He is one of the most quietly frightening figures in the book, and he never touches anybody.

He says Amnon alone is dead twice, which is the only kindness he offers, and as your servant said, so it has come about: he cannot help pointing out that he was right. Then the house of David weeps together, which is the only thing in this chapter they do together.

Talmai of Geshur is Absalom's grandfather; his mother Maacah was Talmai's daughter (3:3). So the murderer goes to his mother's father, a foreign king, beyond David's reach. He has a place to go because his father married a foreign princess years earlier, probably for political reasons.

The last verse of the chapter is one of the saddest sentences about David anywhere. Three years pass. The grief for Amnon fades (the writer says so flatly, and it is simply what grief does), and as it fades, what is left is longing for the son who is alive. He wants Absalom back.

Now set that beside what he did about Tamar, because the two belong together. He was very angry about his daughter and did nothing. He mourned his firstborn and then stopped. And what remains, three years on, is a father's ache for the son who murdered the other one.

There is no justice anywhere in this. Amnon was never punished and is now beyond punishment. Absalom has not been tried, charged, pardoned or condemned; he is simply out of the country. Tamar is in a house, desolate, and nobody has mentioned her since verse 20.

And the king of Israel, whose task was justice for all his people, cannot bring himself to do anything at all about a rape and a murder in his own family, and misses the murderer. The next chapter is Joab noticing that longing and deciding to use it.
verseByVerse.note: Geshur was a small kingdom north-east of the Sea of Galilee, home of Absalom’s mother.

14.title: Joab's Stratagem; Absalom's Return
14.text: <sup>1</sup>Now Joab the son of Zeruiah knew that the king's heart went out to Absalom.<sup>2</sup>And Joab sent to Tekoa and brought from there a wise woman and said to her, "Pretend to be a mourner and put on mourning garments. Do not anoint yourself with oil, but behave like a woman who has been mourning many days for the dead.<sup>3</sup>Go to the king and speak thus to him." So Joab put the words in her mouth.<sup>4</sup>When the woman of Tekoa came to the king, she fell on her face to the ground and paid homage and said, "Save me, O king."<sup>5</sup>And the king said to her, "What is your trouble?" She answered, "Alas, I am a widow; my husband is dead.<sup>6</sup>And your servant had two sons, and they quarreled with one another in the field. There was no one to separate them, and one struck the other and killed him.<sup>7</sup>And now the whole clan has risen against your servant, and they say, 'Give up the man who struck his brother, that we may put him to death for the life of his brother whom he killed.' And so they would destroy the heir also. Thus they would quench my coal that is left and leave to my husband neither name nor remnant on the face of the earth."<sup>8</sup>Then the king said to the woman, "Go to your house, and I will give orders concerning you."<sup>9</sup>And the woman of Tekoa said to the king, "On me be the guilt, my lord the king, and on my father's house; let the king and his throne be guiltless."<sup>10</sup>The king said, "If anyone says anything to you, bring him to me, and he shall never touch you again."<sup>11</sup>Then she said, "Please let the king invoke the LORD your God, that the avenger of blood kill no more, and my son be not destroyed." He said, "As the LORD lives, not one hair of your son shall fall to the ground."<sup>12</sup>Then the woman said, "Please let your servant speak a word to my lord the king." He said, "Speak."<sup>13</sup>And the woman said, "Why then have you planned such a thing against the people of God? For in giving this decision the king convicts himself, inasmuch as the king does not bring his banished one home again.<sup>14</sup>We must all die; we are like water spilled on the ground, which cannot be gathered up again. But God will not take away life, and he devises means so that the banished one will not remain an outcast.<sup>15</sup>Now I have come to say this to my lord the king because the people have made me afraid, and your servant thought, 'I will speak to the king; it may be that the king will perform the request of his servant.<sup>16</sup>For the king will hear and deliver his servant from the hand of the man who would destroy me and my son together from the heritage of God.'<sup>17</sup>And your servant thought, 'The word of my lord the king will set me at rest,' for my lord the king is like the angel of God to discern good and evil. The LORD your God be with you!"<sup>18</sup>Then the king answered the woman, "Do not hide from me anything I ask you." And the woman said, "Let my lord the king speak."<sup>19</sup>The king said, "Is the hand of Joab with you in all this?" The woman answered and said, "As surely as you live, my lord the king, one cannot turn to the right hand or to the left from anything that my lord the king has said. It was your servant Joab who commanded me; it was he who put all these words in the mouth of your servant.<sup>20</sup>In order to change the course of things your servant Joab did this. But my lord has wisdom like the wisdom of the angel of God to know all things that are on the earth."<sup>21</sup>Then the king said to Joab, "Behold now, I grant this; go, bring back the young man Absalom."<sup>22</sup>And Joab fell on his face to the ground and paid homage and blessed the king. And Joab said, "Today your servant knows that I have found favor in your sight, my lord the king, in that the king has granted the request of his servant."<sup>23</sup>So Joab arose and went to Geshur and brought Absalom to Jerusalem.<sup>24</sup>And the king said, "Let him dwell apart in his own house; he is not to come into my presence." So Absalom lived apart in his own house and did not come into the king's presence.<sup>25</sup>Now in all Israel there was no one so much to be praised for his handsome appearance as Absalom. From the sole of his foot to the crown of his head there was no blemish in him.<sup>26</sup>And when he cut the hair of his head (for at the end of every year he used to cut it; when it was heavy on him, he cut it), he weighed the hair of his head, two hundred shekels by the king's weight.<sup>27</sup>There were born to Absalom three sons, and one daughter whose name was Tamar. She was a beautiful woman.<sup>28</sup>So Absalom lived two full years in Jerusalem, without coming into the king's presence.<sup>29</sup>Then Absalom sent for Joab, to send him to the king, but Joab would not come to him. And he sent a second time, but Joab would not come.<sup>30</sup>Then he said to his servants, "See, Joab's field is next to mine, and he has barley there; go and set it on fire." So Absalom's servants set the field on fire.<sup>31</sup>Then Joab arose and went to Absalom at his house and said to him, "Why have your servants set my field on fire?"<sup>32</sup>Absalom answered Joab, "Behold, I sent word to you, 'Come here, that I may send you to the king, to ask, "Why have I come from Geshur? It would be better for me to be there still." Now therefore let me go into the presence of the king, and if there is guilt in me, let him put me to death.'"<sup>33</sup>Then Joab went to the king and told him, and he summoned Absalom. So he came to the king and bowed himself on his face to the ground before the king, and the king kissed Absalom.
14.overview:
Joab notices that the king's heart has gone out to Absalom, and acts on it. He hires a wise woman from Tekoa, dresses her as a mourner and scripts her, and what she brings the king is a case that turns out to apply to himself. It is Nathan's method exactly; the difference is the sender. Nathan came because the LORD sent him; this woman comes because Joab put the words in her mouth.

She says a sentence that holds the gospel in miniature, God... devises means so that the banished one will not remain an outcast, and uses it to bring home a man who is never once recorded as sorry. Then David does the one thing worse than either punishing or forgiving: he lets Absalom come home but refuses to see him. Two years of that end in a kiss with not one word spoken by either man.
14.theology:
Nathan's method, Joab's purpose (vv. 1-20). A petitioner, a case that is not what it appears, a king who gives judgment and finds it applies to him: it is chapter 12 repeated deliberately, and the only difference is who sent her. Nathan told David what he did not want to hear, and he submitted; Joab told him what he did want to hear, and he went along. The first produced repentance; the second will produce a rebellion. The test of a word that reaches us is not how skilfully it is put, or even whether it moves us, but whether it comes from God and leads us towards him. A word we are glad to hear deserves at least as much scrutiny as one we resent.

Water spilled on the ground (v. 14). Death is beyond human recovery, and much of human religion is an attempt to gather up the water. God did not accept the loss and did not leave it to us: he devised a means, and it cost him his Son (Col. 1:21-22). The woman meant only that the dead stay dead, so the living should be spared. The verse means far more than she did: the God who will not let the banished remain outcasts is the God of the whole Bible's story, from the garden of Eden to the heavenly city.

What her argument leaves out. The means God devises deal with sin; they involve a price paid and, on our side, repentance, as David's own restoration in chapter 12 shows. Absalom never repents, here or anywhere. A true sentence about God's mercy can be quoted accurately in the service of an outcome God has not authorised, and that is far more common than open error.
