Neither justice nor mercy (v. 24). No trial, no verdict, and no welcome either: a house in Jerusalem and a closed door. Mephibosheth was received at the king's table for nothing more than being Jonathan's son; Absalom is kept outside it, and the in-between that looks like restraint is the one course that guarantees disaster. It is easy to understand. David could not execute his son and could not bear to sit across a table from him, and many parents, friends and churches have made the same choice for the same reasons. But distance that is never discussed is not peace, and it does not heal.

Looks and memory (vv. 25-27). The narrator places Absalom's beauty directly after the closed door, because the country is about to choose this man, and the reader has learned from Saul and Eliab what outward appearance is worth (1 Sam. 16:7). Yet he also named his daughter Tamar: whatever else is true of him, he did not forget what was done to his sister.

Arson, a challenge, and a kiss (vv. 28-33). Absalom learns that destruction gets results, and that others will carry the risk for him. His if there is guilt in me is a challenge, not a confession. And the kiss makes things look right and settles nothing; the very next verse is after this Absalom got himself a chariot and horses, and fifty men to run before him. Set it beside the father in Jesus' parable who runs and kisses his son (Luke 15:20-21): there the son has come home saying I have sinned, and the kiss seals a real return. Here no one has said anything at all.
14.examples:
Then: A general hired an actress, dressed her as a widow and wrote her a speech, and she manoeuvred the king of Israel into swearing a public oath about an imaginary son, and in the middle of the performance said one of the truest sentences in the Old Testament about the mercy of God, in order to get a murderer home without a trial.

Now: Two things, and both are uncomfortable. The first is that a true statement about God can be used for a purpose God has not approved, and the more true it is the better it works. He devises means so that the banished one will not remain an outcast is the gospel, and the means he devises deal with the sin rather than waving it through, which is the part the speech omits. Test not only whether a thing is true, but what it is being used for. And the second is verse 24: David could not bring himself to punish and could not bring himself to forgive, so he chose the middle course, and it looked like restraint and was the only option that could not work. Distance maintained and never discussed is not peace. It is a wound with a lid on it, and the lid comes off. The God who devised means for our own return, at such cost, is the one who gives us the courage, by his Spirit, to have the conversation David never had.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Joab sends a wise woman from Tekoa to the king with a scripted case: a widow whose one son killed the other, and whose clan now demands the survivor's life. She presses David until he swears an oath to protect him (vv. 1-11).
verseByVerse.theology: The same technique can carry the word of God or a general's scheme. What made Nathan's parable a word from God was not its craft but its sender.
verseByVerse.examples: In everyday life, a promise drawn out under pressure still binds the one who gave it, which is why people who want something from us press for one. David would have done well to stop at his first answer.

verseByVerse.quote: Now Joab the son of Zeruiah knew that the king's heart went out to Absalom. And Joab sent to Tekoa and brought from there a wise woman and said to her, "Pretend to be a mourner and put on mourning garments. Do not anoint yourself with oil, but behave like a woman who has been mourning many days for the dead. Go to the king and speak thus to him." So Joab put the words in her mouth. When the woman of Tekoa came to the king, she fell on her face to the ground and paid homage and said, "Save me, O king." And the king said to her, "What is your trouble?" She answered, "Alas, I am a widow; my husband is dead. And your servant had two sons, and they quarreled with one another in the field. There was no one to separate them, and one struck the other and killed him. And now the whole clan has risen against your servant, and they say, 'Give up the man who struck his brother, that we may put him to death for the life of his brother whom he killed.' And so they would destroy the heir also. Thus they would quench my coal that is left and leave to my husband neither name nor remnant on the face of the earth." Then the king said to the woman, "Go to your house, and I will give orders concerning you." And the woman of Tekoa said to the king, "On me be the guilt, my lord the king, and on my father's house; let the king and his throne be guiltless." The king said, "If anyone says anything to you, bring him to me, and he shall never touch you again." Then she said, "Please let the king invoke the LORD your God, that the avenger of blood kill no more, and my son be not destroyed." He said, "As the LORD lives, not one hair of your son shall fall to the ground."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Joab notices, and that is how the chapter starts. The last verse of chapter 13 said the spirit of the king longed to go out to Absalom. Joab has worked it out, and Joab is a man who acts on what he works out.

Why he wants Absalom back is not stated, and the honest answer is that we do not know. It may be simple concern for a grieving king he has served for decades. It is more likely political: with Amnon dead, Absalom is the likely heir, and while he is in exile nobody knows who will be the next king. A general has an interest in knowing that. Chapter 18 will show what Joab thinks of Absalom when the man becomes inconvenient, and it does not suggest affection.

Tekoa is a village about ten miles south of Jerusalem, the same place Amos came from more than two centuries later.

She is a wise woman, which in that world was something like a recognised office; there is another at Abel of Beth-maacah in chapter 20 who talks Joab out of destroying a town. These were women known locally for judgment and for the ability to speak well. And Joab hires her, dresses her for the part, and tells her what to say.

Before she speaks, a reader who has been paying attention will recognise what is being set up. A petitioner comes to the king with a case that is not what it appears to be. The king hears it, gives judgment, and the judgment turns out to apply to himself. That is exactly chapter 12: Nathan did this two chapters ago, and it broke David open. The difference is the sender. Nathan came because the LORD sent Nathan to David (12:1). This woman comes because Joab put the words in her mouth. Hold that distinction through the whole chapter. The method is identical and the results could hardly be more different, and the reason is not the method but who sent the messenger.

The story is constructed with great care, and every element is chosen. She is a widow, so there is no man to protect her interest. There were two sons and now there is one. The killing happened in a field with nobody present, which makes it ambiguous: a quarrel that went wrong rather than a planned murder, and no witnesses to establish which.

Every one of those details makes her son easier to excuse than Absalom. Absalom planned his brother's death for two years, gave the order to servants, and did it at a feast in front of the whole family.

The clan is invoking blood vengeance, the custom by which a murdered man’s nearest relative put the killer to death. It was real, and the law of Israel regulated it rather than abolished it. There were cities of refuge precisely for the case she describes, a death without premeditation, and the clan is refusing to allow the distinction.

Then there is the picture that does the work: my coal that is left. A household kept a fire going and banked the coals overnight, and if the last coal went out there was no fire in the morning. One surviving son is the last live coal in a dead man's house. Put that out and the family is finished: no name, no inheritance, nothing on the earth to show that the man ever lived.

It is an argument about the dead husband as much as the living son, and it is beautifully judged.

David gives a vague answer, a promise to consider, and she does not accept it. The second is better, a promise to intervene, and still not enough. So she presses a third time, and there it is: an oath in the name of the LORD, covering every hair of the son's head, that cannot be taken back. She would not leave without it.

He does not yet know what he has done. It took Nathan six verses; it has taken her eight, and she has been more thorough, because she needed an oath and Nathan only needed a verdict.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: She turns the case on the king's own banished son, speaks of water spilled on the ground and the God who devises means to bring the banished home, and, asked directly, admits Joab sent her (vv. 12-20).
verseByVerse.theology: Whatever use the woman made of it, verse 14 is one of the great sentences of the Old Testament, and it is entirely true. God does not leave the banished where they are; he plans their way home.
verseByVerse.examples: She is challenged only at the end, and then tells the truth at once. A moving story and a little flattery had carried a king a long way before anyone asked who sent them.

verseByVerse.quote: Then the woman said, "Please let your servant speak a word to my lord the king." He said, "Speak." And the woman said, "Why then have you planned such a thing against the people of God? For in giving this decision the king convicts himself, inasmuch as the king does not bring his banished one home again. We must all die; we are like water spilled on the ground, which cannot be gathered up again. But God will not take away life, and he devises means so that the banished one will not remain an outcast. Now I have come to say this to my lord the king because the people have made me afraid, and your servant thought, 'I will speak to the king; it may be that the king will perform the request of his servant. For the king will hear and deliver his servant from the hand of the man who would destroy me and my son together from the heritage of God.' And your servant thought, 'The word of my lord the king will set me at rest,' for my lord the king is like the angel of God to discern good and evil. The LORD your God be with you!" Then the king answered the woman, "Do not hide from me anything I ask you." And the woman said, "Let my lord the king speak." The king said, "Is the hand of Joab with you in all this?" The woman answered and said, "As surely as you live, my lord the king, one cannot turn to the right hand or to the left from anything that my lord the king has said. It was your servant Joab who commanded me; it was he who put all these words in the mouth of your servant. In order to change the course of things your servant Joab did this. But my lord has wisdom like the wisdom of the angel of God to know all things that are on the earth."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Having got what she came for, she asks permission to say one thing more, and the trap closes. It is a good one. The argument is that David has just sworn to protect a man he has never met, who killed his own brother, in a village he has never visited, on the ground that a family should not lose its heir, while his own heir sits in a foreign country under no sentence at all.

By his own judgment, in his own mouth, under oath, the king is inconsistent. That is what convicts himself means.

And she widens it: against the people of God. It is not a private family matter. The succession of the house of David is a national question, and everybody in Israel knows there is now one obvious heir and he is in Geshur.

Verse 14 deserves to be read slowly, and it is spoken by a hired actress in the middle of a manipulation. She is arguing that Amnon cannot be brought back, so killing Absalom achieves nothing. But the image is bigger than her argument. Pour a jug of water onto dry ground and try to collect it: you cannot. Not most of it, not some of it. It is gone into the dust and there is no method by which a human being can retrieve it. That is what death is like, and the picture is exact. Everybody knows it and everybody spends their life not thinking about it.

Then the second half of the verse turns to hope. The Hebrew is difficult in places and translations vary a little (the KJV has neither doth God respect any person where the ESV has God will not take away life), but the heart of it is not in doubt. God devises means. He plans, he contrives, he engineers: the verb is about working something out deliberately, and what he works out is a way to get the banished one home. That sentence is the gospel in Old Testament words, and it should be said plainly.

The whole human problem is in the first half of the verse: the water is spilled, the loss is irreversible, and nobody can gather it up. Much of human religion is an attempt to gather up the water. And the second half says that God did not accept the loss and did not leave it to us; he set about devising a means.

He devised one. It took most of the length of the Bible to arrive, and it cost him his Son, and Paul describes it in exactly these terms: we were alienated and hostile in mind and have been reconciled, brought back, by the death of Christ (Col. 1:21-22). The banished one does not remain an outcast, because God took the trouble to arrange it. Every word of that is true.

And it is being said, at this moment, by a woman in borrowed mourning clothes, reciting a speech written by Joab, in order to procure the unconditional return of a man who murdered his brother and has never once been recorded as sorry.

Both of those things are the case, and holding them together is the whole lesson of the chapter.

Here is what her argument leaves out. God devises means so that the banished one need not remain an outcast, and the means he devises do not simply overlook the sin. They involve a price paid and a sin dealt with, and on the human side they involve repentance. David himself is the proof: he was restored in chapter 12, and the restoration came by way of I have sinned against the LORD.

Absalom has not said anything of the kind, and he does not say it in this chapter either. When he finally speaks, in verse 32, what he offers is not repentance but a challenge.

So the theology is right and the application is wrong, and a reader should take the warning seriously, because this is a great deal more common than open error. True things about God's mercy can be quoted accurately in the service of an outcome God has not authorised. The sentence is genuine. The use of it is not.

Then the flattery, laid on thickly: like the angel of God to discern good and evil. She says it here and says it again in verse 20. It is the kind of thing a king hears often enough to stop noticing, and she is using it to close the deal.

There is a bleak joke in it that she cannot have intended. The man being told he is like an angel of God at discerning good and evil has been sitting there for ten verses failing to discern that the woman in front of him is an actress.

He works it out, and asks straight, and she admits it straight. Give her that: challenged, she does not keep up the pretence, and names Joab immediately.

And notice how little David's discovery changes. He knows now that the whole thing was staged, that the widow is not a widow, that the two sons never existed, and that his general has manoeuvred him into an oath. Nathan's parable ended with I have sinned. This one ends with David simply telling Joab to fetch Absalom. He has been manipulated, and he lets it stand, because he wanted the outcome anyway.

That is the real difference between the two parables. Nathan told David something he did not want to hear, and David submitted to it. Joab told him something he wanted to hear, and David went along with it. The first produced repentance. The second is going to produce a rebellion.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 21–27 — Let Him Not Come Into My Presence
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Joab brings Absalom back, but David will not see him. The narrator pauses on Absalom's beauty and his heavy hair, and names his daughter Tamar (vv. 21-27).
verseByVerse.theology: Justice was what the case required, and if mercy was to be shown it had to be real: received, restored, welcome at the table. David chooses neither, and the arrangement he does choose is the one guaranteed to feed a proud man's grievance for two years.
verseByVerse.examples: The hair is weighed and recorded without comment. In chapter 18 his head is caught in an oak, very likely by this hair, and he dies there.

verseByVerse.quote: Then the king said to Joab, "Behold now, I grant this; go, bring back the young man Absalom." And Joab fell on his face to the ground and paid homage and blessed the king. And Joab said, "Today your servant knows that I have found favor in your sight, my lord the king, in that the king has granted the request of his servant." So Joab arose and went to Geshur and brought Absalom to Jerusalem. And the king said, "Let him dwell apart in his own house; he is not to come into my presence." So Absalom lived apart in his own house and did not come into the king's presence. Now in all Israel there was no one so much to be praised for his handsome appearance as Absalom. From the sole of his foot to the crown of his head there was no blemish in him. And when he cut the hair of his head (for at the end of every year he used to cut it; when it was heavy on him, he cut it), he weighed the hair of his head, two hundred shekels by the king's weight. There were born to Absalom three sons, and one daughter whose name was Tamar. She was a beautiful woman.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The young man Absalom. He is a grown man with a murder behind him, and his father still speaks of him as a youth.

Joab thanks the king at length, and it costs him nothing.

He is not to come into my presence (v. 24) is the decision that shapes everything that follows. Look at what David has actually done. He has brought home a man who arranged the murder of the crown prince, and has neither tried him nor pardoned him. There is no charge and no acquittal. There is a house in Jerusalem and a closed door. Consider the two things he did not do.

He did not exercise justice. Absalom killed Amnon and there was never a trial, never a hearing, never a verdict. Tamar has never been mentioned again by anybody. A king whose one recorded qualification was that he administered justice and equity to all his people (8:15) has now failed to administer any at all, twice, in his own family.

And he did not extend mercy. If the man was to be forgiven, forgive him: receive him, restore him, eat with him. That is what forgiveness is, and Mephibosheth got it from this same king for nothing more than being Jonathan's son.

Instead there is a third thing, which is the worst available. The man is home, at liberty, in the capital, with a household and time on his hands and a grievance that grows every single day, and no way to resolve anything because he cannot get into the room.

Two years of that are coming. David's instinct here is not hard to understand. He cannot execute his son and he cannot bring himself to sit across a table from the man who killed his other son. So he does something in between, which feels like a reasonable compromise and is in fact the only option that guarantees disaster.

Anybody who has ever managed a broken relationship by keeping the person at arm's length, not confronting, not restoring, just maintaining a distance that never gets discussed, can see here where that leads. An arrangement that looks peaceful while the wrong is left unsettled holds for a while and then comes apart, and the result is worse than the original problem.

The narrator stops and describes him, which he rarely does. No blemish in him uses the word applied to sacrificial animals, and it means physically perfect. There is nobody in the country better looking.

And the reader has been here before. Saul was a handsome young man. There was not a man among the people of Israel more handsome than he. From his shoulders upward he was taller than any of the people (1 Sam. 9:2). And when Samuel came to Bethlehem he looked at Eliab and thought, surely this is the one, and was told the LORD sees not as man sees: man looks on the outward appearance, but the LORD looks on the heart (1 Sam. 16:7).

The writer puts the description here, immediately after the sentence about the closed door, because the country is about to choose this man.

Then the hair, and the writer weighs it. It is a great deal of hair, and the note that he cut it only when it became too heavy to carry is not admiration. A man who weighs his own hair annually and lets people know the figure is telling you something about himself.

He named his daughter after his sister. Nothing else is said. The three sons are not named, and a later verse implies they died (18:18), but the daughter has a name, and it is Tamar, and she is beautiful.

That is the only memorial his sister gets in this book, and her brother gave it to her. Whatever else is true of Absalom, and a great deal is, he did not forget what was done to her.
verseByVerse.note: Absalom’s yearly haircut weighed 200 shekels, about 5 pounds.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 28–33 — So He Set the Field on Fire
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: After two years, Absalom burns Joab's barley to make him come, demands to see the king, and is received with a kiss (vv. 28-33).
verseByVerse.theology: Five years after the murder, father and son have still not spoken about it. A silence managed that long does not become peace; it becomes a grievance.
verseByVerse.examples: Real reconciliation names the wrong. David's kiss names nothing, and within a chapter the peace it made has unravelled. The welcome home the gospel offers does name the wrong, and pays for it at the cost of a cross, and that is why it holds.

verseByVerse.quote: So Absalom lived two full years in Jerusalem, without coming into the king's presence. Then Absalom sent for Joab, to send him to the king, but Joab would not come to him. And he sent a second time, but Joab would not come. Then he said to his servants, "See, Joab's field is next to mine, and he has barley there; go and set it on fire." So Absalom's servants set the field on fire. Then Joab arose and went to Absalom at his house and said to him, "Why have your servants set my field on fire?" Absalom answered Joab, "Behold, I sent word to you, 'Come here, that I may send you to the king, to ask, "Why have I come from Geshur? It would be better for me to be there still." Now therefore let me go into the presence of the king, and if there is guilt in me, let him put me to death.'" Then Joab went to the king and told him, and he summoned Absalom. So he came to the king and bowed himself on his face to the ground before the king, and the king kissed Absalom.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Two years, in the same city. Add it up. Three years in Geshur, two years in Jerusalem behind a closed door: five years since he killed Amnon, and in all that time not one conversation with his father about any of it.

Nobody has ever told him he is forgiven. Nobody has told him he is condemned. There has been no hearing, no sentence, no reconciliation, no explanation. He has simply been managed, and what that does to a proud man over two years is the whole of the next chapter.

Joab, who went to Geshur to fetch him, will not now cross the city to see him. He wanted the heir back in the country; having achieved it, he has no further use for the man and twice leaves his messages unanswered.

So he burns the barley. Take it in: he is a prince of Israel who cannot get a meeting, and his solution is arson against the commander of the army, destroying a standing crop belonging to a man who has just done him a considerable favour.

And note the pattern, because it is the second time. Amnon was killed by Absalom's servants on Absalom's order. The field is burned by Absalom's servants on Absalom's order. Absalom gives instructions and other people carry the risk.

Joab comes immediately, and Absalom has learned something. Two polite requests were ignored; destroying something valuable produced the commander of the army on his doorstep at once. A man who discovers that so young is dangerous.

And his complaint, that he was better off in Geshur, is on its own terms entirely fair. In exile he at least knew where he stood; here he does not. He was better off in a foreign country than in his father's capital with the door shut. David created this. Absalom is describing accurately what the half-measure feels like from inside.

If there is guilt in me, let him put me to death is often read as courage or even repentance, and it is neither.

There is guilt in him. He arranged a murder in front of witnesses and fled the country for three years, and no one has ever disputed it. So the offer is not an offer. It is a challenge, made by a man who knows exactly what his father will do, which is nothing. He has watched David fail to act about Tamar and fail to act about Amnon, and he is forcing the choice: put me on trial, or receive me.

He is not saying "I did wrong". He is saying "either kill me or stop pretending." Nowhere in this chapter, or anywhere else in the book, is Absalom recorded as being sorry for anything.

And the chapter ends with a kiss, the most ambiguous gesture in the book. Look at what does not happen. Nothing is said. There is no recorded word from either man: not a question, not an accusation, not a confession, not a condition. Absalom comes in, goes down on the floor, and is kissed.

The kiss looks like everything a reader wants. It is what the father does in Jesus’ parable, running down the road to his returning son (Luke 15:20). But there is no repentance behind it and justice has not been done, and both men know it.

All that has been achieved is that things now look right. The prince is received at court. The awkwardness is over. Nobody has to explain anything to anybody, and Tamar is still in a house somewhere, and Amnon is still dead, and nothing whatever has been dealt with.

The very next verse begins: after this Absalom got himself a chariot and horses, and fifty men to run before him.

A surface peace laid over a wound that was never cleaned does not hold. It holds long enough for everyone to relax, and then it comes apart, and it takes the kingdom with it.

15.title: Absalom's Rebellion and David's Flight
15.text: <sup>1</sup>After this Absalom got himself a chariot and horses, and fifty men to run before him.<sup>2</sup>And Absalom used to rise early and stand beside the way of the gate. And when any man had a dispute to come before the king for judgment, Absalom would call to him and say, "From what city are you?" And when he said, "Your servant is of such and such a tribe in Israel,"<sup>3</sup>Absalom would say to him, "See, your claims are good and right, but there is no man designated by the king to hear you."<sup>4</sup>Then Absalom would say, "Oh that I were judge in the land! Then every man with a dispute or cause might come to me, and I would give him justice."<sup>5</sup>And whenever a man came near to pay homage to him, he would put out his hand and take hold of him and kiss him.<sup>6</sup>Thus Absalom did to all of Israel who came to the king for judgment. So Absalom stole the hearts of the men of Israel.<sup>7</sup>And at the end of four years Absalom said to the king, "Please let me go and pay my vow, which I have vowed to the LORD, in Hebron.<sup>8</sup>For your servant vowed a vow while I lived at Geshur in Aram, saying, 'If the LORD will indeed bring me back to Jerusalem, then I will offer worship to the LORD.'"<sup>9</sup>The king said to him, "Go in peace." So he arose and went to Hebron.<sup>10</sup>But Absalom sent secret messengers throughout all the tribes of Israel, saying, "As soon as you hear the sound of the trumpet, then say, 'Absalom is king at Hebron!'"<sup>11</sup>With Absalom went two hundred men from Jerusalem who were invited guests, and they went in their innocence and knew nothing.<sup>12</sup>And while Absalom was offering the sacrifices, he sent for Ahithophel the Gilonite, David's counselor, from his city Giloh. And the conspiracy grew strong, and the people with Absalom kept increasing.<sup>13</sup>And a messenger came to David, saying, "The hearts of the men of Israel have gone after Absalom."<sup>14</sup>Then David said to all his servants who were with him at Jerusalem, "Arise, and let us flee, or else there will be no escape for us from Absalom. Go quickly, lest he overtake us quickly and bring down ruin on us and strike the city with the edge of the sword."<sup>15</sup>And the king's servants said to the king, "Behold, your servants are ready to do whatever my lord the king decides."<sup>16</sup>So the king went out, and all his household after him. And the king left ten concubines to keep the house.<sup>17</sup>And the king went out, and all the people after him. And they halted at the last house.<sup>18</sup>And all his servants passed by him, and all the Cherethites, and all the Pelethites, and all the six hundred Gittites who had followed him from Gath, passed on before the king.<sup>19</sup>Then the king said to Ittai the Gittite, "Why do you also go with us? Go back and stay with the king, for you are a foreigner and also an exile from your home.<sup>20</sup>You came only yesterday, and shall I today make you wander about with us, since I go I know not where? Go back and take your brothers with you, and may the LORD show steadfast love and faithfulness to you."<sup>21</sup>But Ittai answered the king, "As the LORD lives, and as my lord the king lives, wherever my lord the king shall be, whether for death or for life, there also will your servant be."<sup>22</sup>And David said to Ittai, "Go then, pass on." So Ittai the Gittite passed on with all his men and all the little ones who were with him.<sup>23</sup>And all the land wept aloud as all the people passed by, and the king crossed the brook Kidron, and all the people passed on toward the wilderness.<sup>24</sup>And Abiathar came up, and behold, Zadok came also with all the Levites, bearing the ark of the covenant of God. And they set down the ark of God until the people had all passed out of the city.<sup>25</sup>Then the king said to Zadok, "Carry the ark of God back into the city. If I find favor in the eyes of the LORD, he will bring me back and let me see both it and his dwelling place.<sup>26</sup>But if he says, 'I have no pleasure in you,' behold, here I am, let him do to me what seems good to him."<sup>27</sup>The king also said to Zadok the priest, "Are you not a seer? Go back to the city in peace, with your two sons, Ahimaaz your son, and Jonathan the son of Abiathar.<sup>28</sup>See, I will wait at the fords of the wilderness until word comes from you to inform me."<sup>29</sup>So Zadok and Abiathar carried the ark of God back to Jerusalem, and they remained there.<sup>30</sup>But David went up the ascent of the Mount of Olives, weeping as he went, barefoot and with his head covered. And all the people who were with him covered their heads, and they went up, weeping as they went.<sup>31</sup>And it was told David, "Ahithophel is among the conspirators with Absalom." And David said, "O LORD, please turn the counsel of Ahithophel into foolishness."<sup>32</sup>While David was coming to the summit, where God was worshiped, behold, Hushai the Archite came to meet him with his coat torn and dirt on his head.<sup>33</sup>David said to him, "If you go on with me, you will be a burden to me.<sup>34</sup>But if you return to the city and say to Absalom, 'I will be your servant, O king; as I have been your father's servant in time past, so now I will be your servant,' then you will defeat for me the counsel of Ahithophel.<sup>35</sup>Are not Zadok and Abiathar the priests with you there? So whatever you hear from the king's house, tell it to Zadok and Abiathar the priests.<sup>36</sup>Behold, their two sons are with them there, Ahimaaz, Zadok's son, and Jonathan, Abiathar's son, and by them you shall send to me everything you hear."<sup>37</sup>So Hushai, David's friend, came into the city, just as Absalom was entering Jerusalem.
15.overview:
After the kiss, Absalom buys the equipment of a king and stands at the gate every day for four years, with a message that has almost nothing false in it: he takes a real grievance and turns it against his father. He steals the hearts of Israel, uses a vow as cover, and is proclaimed at Hebron, and Ahithophel, perhaps Bathsheba's grandfather, goes over to him. Nothing in chapter 11 was ever really over.

David walks out of a defensible city rather than have Israelites fight over its walls. Ittai the Gittite, who arrived yesterday, answers as Ruth answered Naomi, in a soldier's words. The ark is sent back, because David will not use God as a lucky charm even to save a throne. Then a barefoot king goes up the Mount of Olives weeping, prays one short sentence about the one thing that will decide the war, and the next verse begins behold.
15.theology:
A true grievance, aimed (vv. 1-6). Absalom never calls the king unjust, which would be a lie anyone could refute. He names a genuine failure, a kingdom with more cases than one man can hear, and lets every litigant draw the conclusion himself. In four years the writer never shows him judging one case: he promises what nobody could deliver to all of them, and is never tested. The writer's verdict is one word, stole.

Religion as cover, and a father who does not ask (vv. 7-9). He picks the one request his father cannot examine without looking impious, and for the third time in three chapters David hands over something precious to a request he does not look at.

Why Ahithophel went (v. 12). The book never says, but it lays the pieces where a careful reader will find them (23:34; 11:3): he may well have been Bathsheba’s grandfather. Nothing in chapter 11 was ever really over.

A king who gives a city away (vv. 14-23). He will not have Israelites killed over walls he built, and what follows is not panic but a sequence of clear decisions. And the foreigners keep faith: Uriah the Hittite, Obed-edom the Gittite, Ittai the Gittite, each set beside an Israelite who failed at the same point.

The ark goes back (vv. 25-26). Israel once carried the ark into battle as a charm and lost it (1 Sam. 4), and David learned in chapter 6 that it is not equipment. He will not claim to know the outcome either: let him do to me what seems good to him echoes Joab's words before battle with the Ammonites (10:12). Yet in the same breath he sets up his network of priests and runners. Neither cancels the other, and the chapter will not let a reader choose between them.

The road the Son of David would take (v. 30). He crossed the Kidron and went up the Mount of Olives, betrayed by a man who ate at his table, and a psalm of David about betrayal says it: even my close friend in whom I trusted, who ate my bread, has lifted his heel against me (Ps. 41:9), which the Lord Jesus quoted in the upper room about Judas (John 13:18). Jesus went out over the Kidron (John 18:1) and up the Mount of Olives (Luke 22:39). And Ahithophel set his house in order and hanged himself (17:23), the only person in Scripture to die that way apart from the man who betrayed Christ (Matt. 27:5). David went up the hill under the consequences of his own sin; the greater Son of David went up it without sin, to bear the sins of others.

One sentence, aimed where it will be decided (vv. 31-32). David prays about the counsel, not the army, and the next verse begins behold. The prayer is answered not by lightning but by a friend in a torn coat who agrees to walk into a captured city, and the kingdom turns on him.
15.examples:
Then: A king who could have defended the strongest city in the country walked out of it barefoot with his head covered, weeping, and when the priests brought the ark of God out to go with him he sent it back inside, into the hands of the son who wanted him dead, because he would not carry God about as a lucky charm even to keep his throne.

Now: Two things. Recognise Absalom's method, because it is still how such men work: find a real failure, tell everyone their complaint is justified without ever examining it, promise what you will never be required to deliver, and behave as though you were one of the crowd. The test of the man offering to fix it is whether he has ever decided anything that cost him a supporter. And verse 31 is the practical one: when everything is going wrong at once, most people pray about the whole of it, which is another way of praying about none of it. David worked out where the thing would actually be decided, prayed for that single point, and then walked up the hill and met the answer coming down. He could pray like that on the worst day of his life, under consequences he had brought on himself, because the LORD had already put away his sin and was still his God; and believers who do not know how to pray have the Spirit's own help in it (Romans 8:26).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–12 — So Absalom Stole the Hearts of the Men of Israel
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Absalom takes a chariot and runners, and for four years stands at the gate telling every litigant his claim is good and that he would give him justice, and so steals the hearts of Israel. He goes to Hebron under cover of a vow, sends word through the tribes, and summons Ahithophel (vv. 1-12).
verseByVerse.theology: Absalom's appeal works because it is built on something true. A real grievance is the most persuasive tool a demagogue has, and the hardest to answer, because the honest reply has to begin by admitting it.
verseByVerse.examples: Be wary of anyone who uses a religious reason to avoid questions. A vow, a prayer meeting or a sense of calling can be entirely genuine, and it can also be the one errand nobody dares to examine.

verseByVerse.quote: After this Absalom got himself a chariot and horses, and fifty men to run before him. And Absalom used to rise early and stand beside the way of the gate. And when any man had a dispute to come before the king for judgment, Absalom would call to him and say, "From what city are you?" And when he said, "Your servant is of such and such a tribe in Israel," Absalom would say to him, "See, your claims are good and right, but there is no man designated by the king to hear you." Then Absalom would say, "Oh that I were judge in the land! Then every man with a dispute or cause might come to me, and I would give him justice." And whenever a man came near to pay homage to him, he would put out his hand and take hold of him and kiss him. Thus Absalom did to all of Israel who came to the king for judgment. So Absalom stole the hearts of the men of Israel. And at the end of four years Absalom said to the king, "Please let me go and pay my vow, which I have vowed to the LORD, in Hebron. For your servant vowed a vow while I lived at Geshur in Aram, saying, 'If the LORD will indeed bring me back to Jerusalem, then I will offer worship to the LORD.'" The king said to him, "Go in peace." So he arose and went to Hebron. But Absalom sent secret messengers throughout all the tribes of Israel, saying, "As soon as you hear the sound of the trumpet, then say, 'Absalom is king at Hebron!'" With Absalom went two hundred men from Jerusalem who were invited guests, and they went in their innocence and knew nothing. And while Absalom was offering the sacrifices, he sent for Ahithophel the Gilonite, David's counselor, from his city Giloh. And the conspiracy grew strong, and the people with Absalom kept increasing.
verseByVerse.commentary:
After this: after the kiss. The reconciliation of the last verse of chapter 14 is followed immediately by a man buying the equipment of a king. A chariot, horses, and fifty runners going ahead of him through the streets is not transport; it is a king’s procession, and everyone who saw it understood what it meant.

The writer has recorded exactly this before. When Samuel told Israel what a king would do to them, the first thing on the list was: he will take your sons and appoint them to his chariots and to be his horsemen and to run before his chariots (1 Sam. 8:11).

He gets up early, every day, and stands by the road. That is the detail to hold on to, because whatever else Absalom is, he is not lazy. The gate of the city was where cases were heard and business was done, and he is there before anyone else, intercepting people on their way in.

And his opening question is personal. From what city are you? He asks a man where he is from before he asks what he wants, which is the oldest technique there is and it works every time.

Look carefully at what he says, because almost nothing in it is a lie. First: your claims are good and right. He tells every man who comes that his case is a winner, without having heard the other side, without evidence, and without the slightest intention of deciding anything. Every litigant in Israel walks away from that gate having been told by a prince that he was in the right.

And his claim that nobody has been appointed to hear them is probably true. Here is the sentence that made David's reign: so David reigned over all Israel. And David administered justice and equity to all his people (8:15). That was the summary of the whole kingdom: not the conquests, not the tribute, but that people could get a hearing.

By now the kingdom stretches from Egypt to the Euphrates, and one man cannot hear its cases. The system has not kept up. There are almost certainly people at that gate who have walked three days and will go home unheard, and their complaint is real, and Absalom has found it.

That is the craft of it. He does not accuse his father of injustice, which would be a lie anybody could dispute. He points at a genuine administrative failure and lets each man draw the conclusion that the king does not care about him personally. He takes a true grievance and aims it at his father.

Oh that I were judge in the land! The offer costs him nothing, because it is entirely hypothetical. Read the whole passage again and see what is missing. In four years standing at that gate, Absalom is never shown judging a single case. He never hears both parties, never weighs evidence, never gives a ruling that disappoints anybody, never does the actual work. He tells every man his claim is good and says how much better things would be if he were in charge.

It is the permanent advantage of the man who is not responsible for anything: he can promise everyone what nobody could deliver to all of them, and never be tested. The moment he has to actually judge, half the people at that gate become his enemies, because in every dispute somebody loses.

And the physical touch, every time. A man bows to a prince, as he should, and the prince catches him before he gets down, takes him by the hand, and kisses him. It says: do not bow to me, we are equals. It is the gesture of a man refusing the distance his position gives him, and it is completely calculated. There is another kiss behind it, his father’s, a few verses back (14:33), and Absalom has learned exactly what a kiss can be made to do.

Stole is the writer's own verdict, in one word: not won, not earned, but taken from somebody it belonged to.

Four years of standing at a gate. The Hebrew as it stands says forty, which cannot be right in this reign; the Greek, the Syriac and Josephus all read four, and most modern versions, including the ESV, follow them.

And the cover story is a vow, an invented piece of piety. It is well chosen, because a vow is the one errand nobody questions. It is between a man and God; it is unverifiable; and refusing it would be an act of irreligion by the king. Absalom has picked the only request his father cannot examine without looking impious.

Go in peace. And that is the third time. He sent Tamar to Amnon's house without a question. He let Amnon go to the sheepshearing after asking one question and not pressing it. And now he sends the son who has been holding court at his own city gate for four years off to his own first capital, with a blessing, having asked nothing.

The years at the gate now pay: he knows men in every tribe and can reach them all at once. And the choice of Hebron shows what he intends. It is where David was anointed king of Judah, and then king over all Israel; it is the ancient covenant town where Abraham is buried; and it is where Absalom himself was born (3:2-3). Proclaiming a king there says: the throne has moved back to where it started.

Two hundred men from the capital were invited to a religious observance and found out what they were part of when the trumpet sounded. The writer says it twice in one clause: in their innocence, and knew nothing. They are hostages of a kind, two hundred prominent men of Jerusalem publicly at Absalom's side, whose presence tells the country that the capital has gone over.

Ahithophel comes. This is the worst news in the chapter, and chapter 16 will say why: the counsel that Ahithophel gave was as if one consulted the word of God (16:23). He is the finest political mind in Israel and he has been David's for years.

Why does he go? The book never says, but it lays out the pieces and leaves them where a careful reader will find them. Ahithophel is from Giloh. One of David's mighty men is Eliam the son of Ahithophel the Gilonite (23:34). And the woman on the roof was Bathsheba, the daughter of Eliam, the wife of Uriah the Hittite (11:3).

If it is the same Eliam, as many think, that makes Ahithophel her grandfather, and Uriah, who is also on that list of the thirty, the grandson-in-law he lost. He has sat in that council chamber giving faultless advice, for years, to the man who took his granddaughter and killed her husband, and said nothing. And the moment there is an alternative king, he is gone before he is asked twice.

Nothing in chapter 11 was ever really over.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 13–23 — Wherever My Lord the King Shall Be
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Told that Israel has gone after Absalom, David leaves Jerusalem at once. Ittai the Gittite refuses to turn back, and the whole land weeps as the king crosses the Kidron (vv. 13-23).
verseByVerse.theology: He leaves rather than let Jerusalem be fought over. Whatever else is true of these chapters, that decision costs him a kingdom and saves a city.
verseByVerse.examples: Faithfulness is often found where it is least expected. The newcomer from Gath keeps faith when the king's own son and counsellor do not, and the book wants its Israelite readers to notice.

verseByVerse.quote: And a messenger came to David, saying, "The hearts of the men of Israel have gone after Absalom." Then David said to all his servants who were with him at Jerusalem, "Arise, and let us flee, or else there will be no escape for us from Absalom. Go quickly, lest he overtake us quickly and bring down ruin on us and strike the city with the edge of the sword." And the king's servants said to the king, "Behold, your servants are ready to do whatever my lord the king decides." So the king went out, and all his household after him. And the king left ten concubines to keep the house. And the king went out, and all the people after him. And they halted at the last house. And all his servants passed by him, and all the Cherethites, and all the Pelethites, and all the six hundred Gittites who had followed him from Gath, passed on before the king. Then the king said to Ittai the Gittite, "Why do you also go with us? Go back and stay with the king, for you are a foreigner and also an exile from your home. You came only yesterday, and shall I today make you wander about with us, since I go I know not where? Go back and take your brothers with you, and may the LORD show steadfast love and faithfulness to you." But Ittai answered the king, "As the LORD lives, and as my lord the king lives, wherever my lord the king shall be, whether for death or for life, there also will your servant be." And David said to Ittai, "Go then, pass on." So Ittai the Gittite passed on with all his men and all the little ones who were with him. And all the land wept aloud as all the people passed by, and the king crossed the brook Kidron, and all the people passed on toward the wilderness.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The hearts of the men of Israel (v. 13): the same phrase the writer used in verse 6. What Absalom stole, David has now lost.

He decides in a sentence, and the reason he gives is the city. Jerusalem is defensible. He took it himself against a garrison that thought it could hold out with the blind and the lame, and he has fortified it since. He has the Cherethites and the Pelethites, he has six hundred professional soldiers from Gath, and he has Joab.

He could fight for it, and he says why he will not: lest he... strike the city with the edge of the sword. A siege of Jerusalem would be Israelites killing Israelites over a wall David built, and the people inside it would pay for it.

So he walks out of his own capital and gives it away rather than have it fought over. That decision has been read as panic. Look at what he does in the next twenty verses: he sends the ark back with a reasoned speech, posts two priests in the city to send him news, identifies Ahithophel as the decisive threat, prays about it, and sends a friend back to work against Absalom from inside. A panicking man does not do those things in that order.

Ten women are left behind to keep the palace, in a sentence that reads like housekeeping. Remember them. They have done nothing and chosen nothing, and in chapter 16 Absalom will do to them exactly what Nathan said would be done, in public, on the roof; and 20:3 records what became of them afterwards, which is that they lived shut up until the day they died.

The finest thing in the chapter is a conversation with a foreigner. Ittai is a Gittite, from Gath, Goliath's city, the town David hid in twice. He commands six hundred men, which is exactly the number David had in the wilderness, and he has been in the country for a matter of days.

David tries to send him home. Read what he says: go back and stay with the king. He means Absalom. He is telling this man to go and serve the winner, and he is not being bitter about it; he is releasing a foreign officer from a quarrel that is not his.

He is being honest about what he is offering: no destination, no plan, no prospect. And he sends him off with a blessing that uses the covenant words, steadfast love and faithfulness, the same pair he sent to Jabesh-gilead when he first became king at Hebron.

Wherever my lord the king shall be: any reader of the Old Testament will hear the echo. A Moabite woman said something very like it on a road out of Moab: where you go I will go, and where you lodge I will lodge. Your people shall be my people, and your God my God. Where you die I will die, and there will I be buried (Ruth 1:16-17).

Ittai says the same thing in a soldier's words. He swears by the LORD, the God of a country he has lived in for hardly any time, and by the king, and he names the two possibilities in the order that matters: whether for death or for life. He puts death first.

Now set him against the men who are not there. Ahithophel, the wisest man in Israel, has gone. Absalom, the king's son, is leading the rebellion. Two hundred prominent men of Jerusalem are at Hebron. Amasa, David's nephew, will command Absalom's army. And a Philistine mercenary who arrived yesterday will not leave.

The book keeps doing this and it is not accidental. Uriah the Hittite would not sleep in his own bed while the ark was in a field. Obed-edom the Gittite took the ark into his house when Israel was afraid of it. Ittai the Gittite goes into exile with a king he has barely known. Three foreigners, and each of them is put beside an Israelite who failed at the same point.

And all the little ones. He has brought his family. He is not a mercenary taking a contract; he has moved his household into the losing side of a civil war.

The whole countryside is standing along the road crying while the king walks out, and he crosses the Kidron. A thousand years later another son of David went out of that city at night, over that same brook, with a small group of followers, on his way to be betrayed, and John records the crossing specifically: Jesus went out with his disciples across the brook Kidron (John 18:1). The likeness is going to get closer before this chapter ends.
verseByVerse.note: The brook Kidron runs east of Jerusalem, between the city and the Mount of Olives.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 24–31 — Let Him Do to Me What Seems Good to Him
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: David sends the ark back with Zadok and Abiathar, leaving the outcome with the LORD and posting the priests as his eyes. He goes up the Mount of Olives barefoot and weeping, and, told of Ahithophel, prays that his counsel be turned to foolishness (vv. 24-31).
verseByVerse.theology: Trust in God is not the same as holding on to the signs of his presence. David lets the ark go and keeps hold of God.
verseByVerse.examples: Let him do to me what seems good to him is a prayer for the worst day of a life, and here it is prayed by a man suffering for his own sin. Submission to God is not only for the innocent, and he does not refuse it from the guilty.

verseByVerse.quote: And Abiathar came up, and behold, Zadok came also with all the Levites, bearing the ark of the covenant of God. And they set down the ark of God until the people had all passed out of the city. Then the king said to Zadok, "Carry the ark of God back into the city. If I find favor in the eyes of the LORD, he will bring me back and let me see both it and his dwelling place. But if he says, 'I have no pleasure in you,' behold, here I am, let him do to me what seems good to him." The king also said to Zadok the priest, "Are you not a seer? Go back to the city in peace, with your two sons, Ahimaaz your son, and Jonathan the son of Abiathar. See, I will wait at the fords of the wilderness until word comes from you to inform me." So Zadok and Abiathar carried the ark of God back to Jerusalem, and they remained there. But David went up the ascent of the Mount of Olives, weeping as he went, barefoot and with his head covered. And all the people who were with him covered their heads, and they went up, weeping as they went. And it was told David, "Ahithophel is among the conspirators with Absalom." And David said, "O LORD, please turn the counsel of Ahithophel into foolishness."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Bringing the ark out with the king is the obvious thing to do, and it is meant kindly, and every instinct in the nation is behind it. The presence of God should go with the true king.

He sends it back. Understand what this costs and what it proves. Israel had done the other thing once, and the writer of this book told the story at length. At Aphek the army was beaten, and the elders said, let us bring the ark of the covenant of the LORD here from Shiloh, that it may come among us and save us, and the whole camp shouted when it arrived, and they lost thirty thousand men and the ark itself in a single day (1 Sam. 4).

David knows that story better than anybody. He also knows chapter 6 of this book, where he learned in the hardest possible way that the ark is not a piece of equipment to be moved about at convenience.

So here, running for his life, with a rebel army behind him and no idea where he is going, the one thing that would look most like divine endorsement is offered to him and he sends it home, to stay in Jerusalem in Absalom's hands. He will not use God as a lucky charm even when it might save his throne, and he says the reason: if God intends to bring him back, God will bring him back, and the box is not what does it.

There is the other half, which is harder: let him do to me what seems good to him. He does not claim to know how it will end. He would like to come back (he says so in the previous verse), and he will not pretend to know that he will, and he will not arrange matters to force it.

That exact sentence has been said once before in this book, by Joab, drawn up between two armies before the Ammonite city: may the LORD do what seems good to him (10:12). Do everything a man can do, and then leave the result where it belongs.

David is a fugitive from his own son, walking barefoot out of the city he captured, and he is not bargaining. He is not reminding God of the promise in chapter 7, and he could. He is saying: I want to come back, I have no claim, and whatever he decides is right.

That is one of the high points of the man's life, and it happens on the worst day of it.

In the same breath he sets up an intelligence network. The two priests go back with the ark, which is legitimate and expected, and their two sons will carry messages out to the fords. Nobody will question priests staying in the city with the ark, and nobody watches the sons of priests.

Both things are David at once: he refuses to manipulate God and he makes every arrangement a competent man would make. Neither cancels the other, and the chapter will not let a reader choose between them.

Now the picture, and it should be allowed to stand for a moment before anything is said about it. The king of Israel is walking up a hill outside his own capital. He has no shoes on. His head is covered, which is a sign of mourning and of shame. He is crying, out loud, where everyone can see him. And the entire column behind him has covered their heads and is crying too.

He is probably about sixty. He captured that city. He built the walls he has just walked out of. And he is going up a hill in his bare feet because his son wants him dead and the country agreed.

Now the likeness to Christ, which lies in the events themselves and is not a decoration added to them. David crossed the Kidron. He is going up the Mount of Olives. He has been betrayed by his closest counsellor, a man who ate at his table, and a psalm of David, which many think has Ahithophel in mind, speaks of exactly that: even my close friend in whom I trusted, who ate my bread, has lifted his heel against me (Ps. 41:9). The Lord Jesus quoted that verse in the upper room, about Judas, on the night he was betrayed (John 13:18).

Jesus went out over the Kidron (John 18:1). He went up the Mount of Olives (Luke 22:39). And two chapters from now, Ahithophel set his house in order and hanged himself (17:23). Only one other person in Scripture dies that way: the man who betrayed Christ (Matt. 27:5).

The greater Son of David went up that same slope, in anguish, with a small group of loyal and bewildered followers, and prayed not my will, but yours, be done, which is what David has just said to Zadok in different words.

The likeness has a limit, and the limit is the gospel. David climbed that hill under the consequences of his own sin, as Nathan had said he would (12:10-11). The Son of David climbed it without sin, betrayed for no wrong of his own, to bear the sins of others in his body on the tree (1 Peter 2:22-24). David came back to his throne by way of a battle in which his son died; Christ came back from the dead to his throne by way of a cross on which he died himself, for those who had rebelled against him.

One sentence of prayer, on a hillside, and it is exactly right. It is short. It is specific. It does not inform God of the situation, rehearse the injustice, or ask for the rebellion generally to fail. It identifies the single thing that will decide the war and asks for that one thing.

David can count. Absalom has the numbers, the capital, the ark and the momentum. What he does not yet have is a good decision, and the man who can give him one has just arrived. If Ahithophel's advice is taken, David is dead within a day; chapter 17 shows the advice, and it is lethal, and it would have worked.

So he prays about the counsel, not the army. Anybody who has prayed vaguely in a crisis because the crisis was too big to think about should look at that sentence.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 32–37 — And Behold, Hushai Came to Meet Him
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: At the summit Hushai meets him in mourning, and David sends him back to defeat Ahithophel's counsel from inside. Hushai enters the city just as Absalom does (vv. 32-37).
verseByVerse.theology: God's answers to prayer usually come through people. Hushai is the answer to verse 31, and he arrives with dirt on his head, not yet knowing it.
verseByVerse.examples: And David does both things at once. He prays a specific prayer and then uses every means available (a friend inside the palace, two priests, two runners) without treating the second as a substitute for the first.

verseByVerse.quote: While David was coming to the summit, where God was worshiped, behold, Hushai the Archite came to meet him with his coat torn and dirt on his head. David said to him, "If you go on with me, you will be a burden to me. But if you return to the city and say to Absalom, 'I will be your servant, O king; as I have been your father's servant in time past, so now I will be your servant,' then you will defeat for me the counsel of Ahithophel. Are not Zadok and Abiathar the priests with you there? So whatever you hear from the king's house, tell it to Zadok and Abiathar the priests. Behold, their two sons are with them there, Ahimaaz, Zadok's son, and Jonathan, Abiathar's son, and by them you shall send to me everything you hear." So Hushai, David's friend, came into the city, just as Absalom was entering Jerusalem.
verseByVerse.commentary:
He prayed in verse 31; verse 32 begins behold. The writer puts the two sentences side by side and says nothing at all, which is how he does his most serious work. David asks God to turn Ahithophel's counsel into foolishness, and before he reaches the top of the hill a man is walking up it who is the only person in Israel capable of doing that.

Hushai comes in mourning, coat torn and dirt on his head, which tells you he has come to grieve with his friend and not to be useful. He has no idea what he is walking into.

David tells him, kindly enough, that on the road he would only be a burden. Then he sees that this man is the answer to his prayer. He is asking Hushai to go back into a captured city, lie to a usurper's face, take an oath of loyalty he does not mean, and sit in a council chamber where one wrong word means execution, perhaps at an age when he could not keep up with an army on the march.

Then you will defeat for me the counsel of Ahithophel. David has already seen exactly how his own prayer is going to be answered, and it is going to be answered through a frightened friend saying the right thing at the right moment in an enemy's council.

That is normally how God answers: not by lightning, but by a friend being asked to do something extremely dangerous, and agreeing.

The network is complete: a counsellor in the council, two priests to receive his reports, two runners to carry them, and a king waiting at the fords. Every piece of it will be used in chapter 17, and the two runners will end up hiding in a well with a woman spreading grain over the mouth of it.

The timing of the last verse is the writer's, and it is exact. Two men walk into Jerusalem at the same moment from opposite directions. One is a prince arriving to take a throne with an army behind him and the wisest counsellor in Israel at his side. The other is a man with a torn coat, alone, who has agreed to risk his life as a spy. The kingdom turns on the second one.

And the phrase the writer chooses for him is David's friend. It is used of him twice in these chapters, and it may well be a court title; the King's Friend was a recognised office in some ancient courts. It is also simply true, and it is the reason he goes.

16.title: Shimei's Curse and Absalom in Jerusalem
16.text: <sup>1</sup>When David had passed a little beyond the summit, Ziba the servant of Mephibosheth met him, with a couple of donkeys saddled, bearing two hundred loaves of bread, a hundred bunches of raisins, a hundred of summer fruits, and a skin of wine.<sup>2</sup>And the king said to Ziba, "Why have you brought these?" Ziba answered, "The donkeys are for the king's household to ride on, the bread and summer fruit for the young men to eat, and the wine for those who faint in the wilderness to drink."<sup>3</sup>And the king said, "And where is your master's son?" Ziba said to the king, "Behold, he remains in Jerusalem, for he said, 'Today the house of Israel will give me back the kingdom of my father.'"<sup>4</sup>Then the king said to Ziba, "Behold, all that belonged to Mephibosheth is now yours." And Ziba said, "I pay homage; let me ever find favor in your sight, my lord the king."<sup>5</sup>When King David came to Bahurim, there came out a man of the family of the house of Saul, whose name was Shimei, the son of Gera, and as he came he cursed continually.<sup>6</sup>And he threw stones at David and at all the servants of King David, and all the people and all the mighty men were on his right hand and on his left.<sup>7</sup>And Shimei said as he cursed, "Get out, get out, you man of blood, you worthless man!<sup>8</sup>The LORD has avenged on you all the blood of the house of Saul, in whose place you have reigned, and the LORD has given the kingdom into the hand of your son Absalom. See, your evil is on you, for you are a man of blood."<sup>9</sup>Then Abishai the son of Zeruiah said to the king, "Why should this dead dog curse my lord the king? Let me go over and take off his head."<sup>10</sup>But the king said, "What have I to do with you, you sons of Zeruiah? If he is cursing because the LORD has said to him, 'Curse David,' who then shall say, 'Why have you done so?'"<sup>11</sup>And David said to Abishai and to all his servants, "Behold, my own son seeks my life; how much more now may this Benjaminite! Leave him alone, and let him curse, for the LORD has told him to.<sup>12</sup>It may be that the LORD will look on the wrong done to me, and that the LORD will repay me with good for his cursing today."<sup>13</sup>So David and his men went on the road, while Shimei went along on the hillside opposite him and cursed as he went and threw stones at him and flung dust.<sup>14</sup>And the king, and all the people who were with him, arrived weary at the Jordan. And there he refreshed himself.<sup>15</sup>Now Absalom and all the people, the men of Israel, came to Jerusalem, and Ahithophel with him.<sup>16</sup>And when Hushai the Archite, David's friend, came to Absalom, Hushai said to Absalom, "Long live the king! Long live the king!"<sup>17</sup>And Absalom said to Hushai, "Is this your loyalty to your friend? Why did you not go with your friend?"<sup>18</sup>And Hushai said to Absalom, "No, for whom the LORD and this people and all the men of Israel have chosen, his I will be, and with him I will remain.<sup>19</sup>And again, whom should I serve? Should it not be his son? As I have served your father, so I will serve you."<sup>20</sup>Then Absalom said to Ahithophel, "Give your counsel. What shall we do?"<sup>21</sup>Ahithophel said to Absalom, "Go in to your father's concubines, whom he has left to keep the house, and all Israel will hear that you have made yourself a stench to your father, and the hands of all who are with you will be strengthened."<sup>22</sup>So they pitched a tent for Absalom on the roof. And Absalom went in to his father's concubines in the sight of all Israel.<sup>23</sup>Now in those days the counsel that Ahithophel gave was as if one consulted the word of God; so was all the counsel of Ahithophel esteemed, both by David and by Absalom.
16.overview: David's flight continues down the far side of the Mount of Olives, and three meetings fill the day. Ziba is waiting past the summit with exactly what an exhausted column needs, and attached to the generosity is a story: Mephibosheth has stayed behind, expecting the tribes to give him back Saul's kingdom. The story is a lie, as chapter 19 will show, but David, exhausted, betrayed and hearing only one side, hands Ziba the whole estate in a single sentence. At Bahurim, Shimei of Saul's house curses the king and throws stones, and David gives one of the great answers in Scripture, hedged with an honest it may be. In Jerusalem, Absalom takes the palace, Hushai talks his way into the rebel court, and on Ahithophel's advice the judgment Nathan announced (12:11-12) is carried out in public, on the same palace roof from which David first saw Bathsheba. The chapter is quiet about all of these connections; it leaves them where an attentive reader will find them.
16.theology:
Judging on the worst day (vv. 3-4). Ziba's lie worked because of its timing. He produced generosity at the exact moment a betrayed man was least able to weigh a story, and David, deceived that week by his son and his counsellor, was ready to believe he had been deceived by everyone. Chapter 19 settles the facts: Mephibosheth was in mourning the whole time and says Ziba slandered him (19:24-26). Yet even then David never decides who lied. He splits the land, and the man who had received his greatest act of kindness loses half of it and answers only oh, let him take it all, since my lord the king has come safely home (19:30). Justice given in haste is very hard to undo.

A false charge and a true word (vv. 7-8). Shimei accuses David of shedding the blood of Saul’s house. David is innocent of that, but it is the charge a Benjaminite would believe without evidence. But man of blood is true: not about Saul, but about a Hittite officer at the wall of Rabbah. A bitter partisan shouting out of tribal spite has landed on exactly the right word, and he does not know it. The writer gives him no credit for insight; he is a man kicking somebody who is finally down. God can let a malicious man speak a word that finds its mark without making the malice any less his own.

The word if, and what it does not say (v. 10). If the LORD has said to him, curse David. He does not say Shimei is right, or that the accusation is fair, or that God approves; Shimei will answer for this, and David raises it on his deathbed. He says only that he will not get rid of a trouble until he knows whether God sent it.

Perspective and hope (vv. 11-12). A man who has taken the measure of the real disaster, a son who seeks his life, is not much moved by an insult from a stranger. And his hope is hedged: perhaps God will look on what is done today and repay it with good. He does not announce that God will vindicate him, quote the promise of chapter 7 at anybody, or promise himself an outcome. That is faith with no guarantee attached, and it is the more honest for it. His circumstances are at their lowest and his trust in God is at its clearest, and the two are connected.

The Son of David did it perfectly. When Christ was reviled he did not revile in return, but entrusted himself to the Judge; that is not passivity and not agreement, but handing the case to a judge who cannot be corrupted. David bore curses he had partly earned. Christ, who had earned none, became a curse for us, and that is what frees his people to bear slander without answering it in kind.

Hushai's answers (vv. 18-19). Not a false word in either, and every sentence means the opposite of what Absalom takes it to mean. It is deception, and the book does not pretend otherwise; the question it raises is taken up at the end of the notes on vv. 15-23.

Nathan's word kept (vv. 21-22). Ahithophel's counsel is shrewd politics. Half the country is waiting to see whether this is a real revolt or a family quarrel, and a public act that makes reconciliation impossible tells every waverer that Absalom cannot climb down, so it is safe to join him. But the writer sees more. Every clause of Nathan's sentence (12:11-12) is fulfilled, in the very place where David's sin began. David had been forgiven and his life spared (12:13), yet the consequences God had announced still came. Forgiveness removes the guilt; it does not always remove the consequences.

The cost falls on people who did nothing. The ten concubines chose none of it, were not consulted about the arrangement that made them royal property, and are not consulted now; what happens on that roof happens because two men are using them to make a political point. The book does not forget them (20:3). Sin rarely confines its damage to the people who committed it, and those who pay most are frequently those with the least say. Uriah did not choose it. Tamar did not choose it. These ten women did not choose it.

What David was up against (v. 23). As if one consulted the word of God is an extraordinary estimate of a man's political judgment, and the writer says both David and Absalom rated him so. That is why the prayer on the hillside was aimed where it was: not that the army would fail or that Absalom would repent, but that this man's advice would be turned into foolishness, because nothing else in the rebellion was going to beat him.
16.examples:
Then: One man walked along a hillside throwing stones and dirt at the king of Israel and his bodyguard, shouting that God was paying him back, and the king forbade his officers to touch him, because he could not be certain God had not sent him.

Now: Two things sit oddly together here. Ziba is the warning about judging: David heard one side, from the party who stood to gain, at the moment he was least able to weigh anything. Grief, exhaustion and a recent betrayal are the conditions in which most unjust snap decisions get made, and the wise course is to refuse to decide anything then. And Shimei is the model for being slandered. David neither agreed with the man nor silenced him; he refused to defend himself, and said it may be. What freed him was that he had already faced the real wound, and had already put himself in God's hands. The believer has firmer ground still: Christ took the curse we earned, and his Spirit gives the patience to leave our case with the Judge. And where we have judged as hastily as David did for Ziba, the way back is the same mercy David himself needed.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–4 — All That Belonged to Mephibosheth Is Now Yours
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Ziba meets David past the summit with loaded donkeys and a story about his master (vv. 1-3), and David gives him Mephibosheth's whole estate on the spot (v. 4).
verseByVerse.theology: Ziba's gift is real and his story is false. The section shows how a good king came to believe it.
verseByVerse.examples: David hands over the whole estate in one sentence, without hearing the other side, and it concerns the man who had received his own greatest act of grace. When you are tired, grieved and grateful to the person in front of you, that is the moment to send for the other side before you decide anything.

verseByVerse.quote: When David had passed a little beyond the summit, Ziba the servant of Mephibosheth met him, with a couple of donkeys saddled, bearing two hundred loaves of bread, a hundred bunches of raisins, a hundred of summer fruits, and a skin of wine. And the king said to Ziba, "Why have you brought these?" Ziba answered, "The donkeys are for the king's household to ride on, the bread and summer fruit for the young men to eat, and the wine for those who faint in the wilderness to drink." And the king said, "And where is your master's son?" Ziba said to the king, "Behold, he remains in Jerusalem, for he said, 'Today the house of Israel will give me back the kingdom of my father.'" Then the king said to Ziba, "Behold, all that belonged to Mephibosheth is now yours." And Ziba said, "I pay homage; let me ever find favor in your sight, my lord the king."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Ziba is waiting past the top of the hill with supplies for a fleeing king. The timing is not accidental. He has worked out which road David will take and got there first, with exactly what a column of exhausted people needs. Two hundred loaves is the same figure Abigail brought down the mountain to stop a massacre (1 Sam. 25:18), and Ziba may well have the precedent in mind.

His answer to why have you brought these? is excellent: itemised, thoughtful, and precisely matched to the need. Then comes what he really came to deliver, and it is a lie.

We know because the book tells us. When David comes back, Mephibosheth comes down to meet him, and he had neither taken care of his feet nor trimmed his beard nor washed his clothes, from the day the king departed until the day he came back in safety (19:24). He had been in mourning the entire time. His account is that he asked Ziba to saddle a donkey so that he could go with the king, and he has slandered your servant, and that he could not go himself because he is lame (19:26).

It is also absurd if anybody stops to think. The rebellion in progress is Absalom's. Nobody is proposing to restore the house of Saul, and the candidate Ziba describes is a man crippled in both feet who has spent years at David's table as a pensioner, with no faction, no army and no following of any kind. The idea that the tribes would hand him a kingdom in the middle of a coup by David's own son is not plausible for a moment.

David gives him everything, in one sentence, without asking a single question. No summons, no hearing. The other party is a short walk behind them and is not sent for, and the estate of Saul changes hands on the word of the man who benefits from it.

This is the king who administered justice and equity to all his people (8:15), on the worst day of his life: probably about sixty, barefoot, just told his most trusted counsellor has defected, and handed food by the first person all morning to show him any loyalty. Ziba has attached his accusation to his generosity at the exact moment a betrayed man is least able to weigh a story.

That does not excuse him, but it explains him: the fault lies less in his character than in the state he was in. A man who has just been deceived by his son and his counsellor is ready to believe he has been deceived by everybody else.

The wrong is never properly put right. When David hears the other side he does not apologise, does not restore the estate, and does not decide who was lying. He splits the land, and Mephibosheth answers, oh, let him take it all, since my lord the king has come safely home (19:30). The man given everything for Jonathan's sake loses half of it to a lie, and does not complain.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 5–14 — Let Him Alone, and Let Him Curse
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: At Bahurim, Shimei of the house of Saul curses David and throws stones (vv. 5-8). Abishai offers to take his head off, and David refuses, leaving the matter with the LORD (vv. 9-12). Shimei keeps pace along the hillside until the column reaches the Jordan, weary (vv. 13-14).
verseByVerse.theology: Shimei's charge is false, but one word in it is true, and David has the humility to hear it.
verseByVerse.examples: Here David’s circumstances are at their lowest and his trust in God is at its clearest. He will not silence the man, and he will not pretend to know what God is doing with him: it may be is as far as he will go.
