verseByVerse.quote: When King David came to Bahurim, there came out a man of the family of the house of Saul, whose name was Shimei, the son of Gera, and as he came he cursed continually. And he threw stones at David and at all the servants of King David, and all the people and all the mighty men were on his right hand and on his left. And Shimei said as he cursed, "Get out, get out, you man of blood, you worthless man! The LORD has avenged on you all the blood of the house of Saul, in whose place you have reigned, and the LORD has given the kingdom into the hand of your son Absalom. See, your evil is on you, for you are a man of blood." Then Abishai the son of Zeruiah said to the king, "Why should this dead dog curse my lord the king? Let me go over and take off his head." But the king said, "What have I to do with you, you sons of Zeruiah? If he is cursing because the LORD has said to him, 'Curse David,' who then shall say, 'Why have you done so?'" And David said to Abishai and to all his servants, "Behold, my own son seeks my life; how much more now may this Benjaminite! Leave him alone, and let him curse, for the LORD has told him to. It may be that the LORD will look on the wrong done to me, and that the LORD will repay me with good for his cursing today." So David and his men went on the road, while Shimei went along on the hillside opposite him and cursed as he went and threw stones at him and flung dust. And the king, and all the people who were with him, arrived weary at the Jordan. And there he refreshed himself.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Bahurim is a village on the road down to the Jordan, in Benjaminite country, Saul's tribe. It is also where Paltiel stood weeping when Michal was taken back from him (3:16).

The picture is grimly funny as well as awful. A man is throwing rocks at a column that contains the professional army of Israel: the Cherethites, the Pelethites, the six hundred Gittites, and the mighty men of chapter 23 who killed lions in pits and held fields alone. They walk on either side of the king, and they let him do it.

Shimei is wrong and right in the same speech, and it matters which is which. The charge is false. All the blood of the house of Saul: David never shed it. He had Saul at his mercy in a cave and cut a corner off his robe and was troubled about that much. He stood over him asleep with a spear in the ground beside his head and would not let Abishai use it. He executed the Amalekite who claimed to have finished Saul off and the two men who murdered Ish-bosheth, and buried the head in Abner's tomb. He sought out Jonathan's surviving son and fed him at his own table for years. Shimei has picked the charge a Benjaminite would believe without evidence (though he may have in mind the Gibeonite executions of 21:1-9).

And man of blood is true. Not about Saul. About a Hittite officer at the wall of Rabbah, and the unnamed soldiers who died in the same assault so that the death would not stand out, and a letter carried by the man it killed. So a bitter partisan, shouting a false accusation out of tribal spite, has accidentally hit the one word that is exactly right. Shimei does not know that. He is not a prophet and not being noble; he is kicking somebody who is finally down. But the word lands.

Abishai is entirely in character. He offered the same service over Saul asleep at Hachilah, let me pin him to the earth with one stroke of the spear, and I will not strike him twice (1 Sam. 26:8). He is a brave man who solves every problem the same way, and it is his brother Joab who does such things when David says no (3:27; 18:14). This dead dog is the phrase Mephibosheth and David both used of themselves in humility, here turned to pure contempt.

David's answer is easy to make either more or less than it is. He does not say Shimei is right or the accusation fair. If the LORD has said to him, curse David: he entertains the possibility that a man throwing stones at him is part of something God is doing. He is not saying God approves of Shimei, who will be judged for this, as David himself says on his deathbed. He will not get rid of a trouble until he knows whether God sent it.

Then the argument, devastating in its simplicity: my own son seeks my life. Given what my child is doing to me today, why would I be surprised or offended by a stranger from Saul's tribe throwing rocks? Compared with the actual wound, this is nothing. A man who has taken the measure of the real disaster is not much moved by an insult, and one reason people are so easily wounded by small slights is that they have not honestly faced the large things.

And three words keep the whole speech honest: it may be. He does not announce vindication or promise himself an outcome. That is faith with no guarantee attached, from a man walking downhill barefoot with dirt flying at him, and it is exactly what he said to Zadok earlier that day about the ark: if I find favor... but if he says, "I have no pleasure in you," behold, here I am.

The New Testament shows the same thing done perfectly, without mentioning David. Christ when he was reviled, he did not revile in return; when he suffered, he did not threaten, but continued entrusting himself to him who judges justly (1 Pet. 2:23): not passivity, but handing the case to a judge who cannot be corrupted. And the Son of David, arrested on the Mount of Olives, told a man with a sword to put it away, and said he could have twelve legions of angels for the asking, and would not ask (Matt. 26:53). David had Abishai, and refused his sword. It is the same refusal on a smaller scale, with one difference that is the whole gospel: David bore curses he had partly earned, and Christ, who had earned none, became a curse for us to redeem us from the curse of the law (Galatians 3:13).

Shimei keeps it up along the slope for what must have been a long way, and they arrive worn out at the river. The writer lets that be the end of the day.

Did God send Shimei to curse? David accepts that God may be humbling him through it; God rules even a sinner’s words to chasten his servant. But Shimei chose his malice and was guilty of it, as David later recognised (1 Kgs 2:8–9).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 15–23 — In the Sight of All Israel
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Absalom enters Jerusalem with Ahithophel; Hushai talks his way into the rebel court (vv. 15-19). Ahithophel counsels Absalom to take his father's concubines publicly, and he does, on the roof (vv. 20-22). The section closes on how Ahithophel's counsel was valued (v. 23).
verseByVerse.theology: What happens on the roof fulfils Nathan's sentence of 12:11-12 in public, and in the very place where David's sin began.
verseByVerse.examples: Hushai's double answer is a small masterpiece: every clause is technically about whoever God has chosen, and Absalom hears what he wants to hear. The last verse then measures exactly what David prayed against on the hillside.

verseByVerse.quote: Now Absalom and all the people, the men of Israel, came to Jerusalem, and Ahithophel with him. And when Hushai the Archite, David's friend, came to Absalom, Hushai said to Absalom, "Long live the king! Long live the king!" And Absalom said to Hushai, "Is this your loyalty to your friend? Why did you not go with your friend?" And Hushai said to Absalom, "No, for whom the LORD and this people and all the men of Israel have chosen, his I will be, and with him I will remain. And again, whom should I serve? Should it not be his son? As I have served your father, so I will serve you." Then Absalom said to Ahithophel, "Give your counsel. What shall we do?" Ahithophel said to Absalom, "Go in to your father's concubines, whom he has left to keep the house, and all Israel will hear that you have made yourself a stench to your father, and the hands of all who are with you will be strengthened." So they pitched a tent for Absalom on the roof. And Absalom went in to his father's concubines in the sight of all Israel. Now in those days the counsel that Ahithophel gave was as if one consulted the word of God; so was all the counsel of Ahithophel esteemed, both by David and by Absalom.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The rebellion enters the capital without a fight, as David intended when he left it. Hushai, the friend with the torn coat, does what he agreed on the hillside to do. He shouts the acclamation twice, louder than anybody else in the room, and does not say which king. That will be his whole technique.

Absalom is nobody's fool, and his question has a barb: friend twice, Hushai's own title at court.

There is not a false word in either answer. Whom the LORD and this people and all the men of Israel have chosen, and the LORD chose David; Absalom hears an endorsement because the people have just acclaimed him.

Should it not be his son? sounds like an argument that the son has the right to the throne, and is in fact only a question. As I have served your father, so I will serve you: Absalom takes that as a transfer of loyalty, but Hushai has always served David’s interests, and in Absalom’s court he will go on doing exactly that.

Every sentence is technically true and means the opposite of what the hearer takes it to mean.

It should be said plainly that this is deception, and the book does not pretend otherwise. Hushai is a spy in a rebel court, and there is a real question about it that Scripture does not stop to answer here. What can be said is that he is in a war, that Absalom would kill him on the spot for an honest answer, and he belongs with the midwives in Egypt and Rahab at Jericho rather than with Ziba, who lied for an estate.

Ahithophel's advice is why David prayed on the hillside. It is cold, brilliant, and correct on its own terms. Absalom's problem is not military. Half the country is waiting to see whether this is a real revolt or a family quarrel, and nobody wants to have committed to the son and then face the father. Taking the royal harem was the recognised act of a successor. Doing it publicly makes peace with his father impossible, so every waverer in Israel now knows that Absalom cannot back down, which means it is safe to join him. It is a plan for burning a bridge, and it works.

On the roof. Match it with Nathan clause by clause: Behold, I will raise up evil against you out of your own house. And I will take your wives before your eyes and give them to your neighbor, and he shall lie with your wives in the sight of this sun. For you did it secretly, but I will do this thing before all Israel and before the sun (12:11-12). Out of his own house: his son. Before all Israel: a tent the whole city can see. Before the sun: in daylight, nothing hidden.

And on a roof. There is only one palace roof in this book: he saw from the roof a woman bathing (11:2). The place where a man looked down and saw something he wanted is where the judgment is carried out, by his own son, on the advice of the man who was probably her grandfather (Bathsheba was the daughter of Eliam, and an Eliam son of Ahithophel is listed among the mighty men; 11:3; 23:34). Nothing in that arrangement is coincidental, and none of it is stated; it is put where an attentive reader will find it.

And there is a cost here that falls on people who did nothing. The ten concubines (secondary wives, lawfully bound to the king but of lower standing) were left to keep the house in a sentence that read like a housekeeping detail (15:16). They were not consulted about being made royal property, and are not consulted now; two men are using them to make a political point. The book does not forget them. When David comes back he provides for them, but did not go in to them. So they were shut up until the day of their death, living as if in widowhood (20:3). Provided for, but with no life of their own left, perhaps while still young. Sin does that. It rarely confines its damage to the people who committed it, and the ones who pay the most are frequently the ones with the least say in any of it.

The chapter ends by telling us what David is up against. As if one consulted the word of God: when Ahithophel spoke, both kings did what he said, as they would an oracle. That is why David prayed not that the army would fail or Absalom repent, but that this man's advice would be turned into foolishness. The next chapter is that prayer being answered, in a council chamber, by a friend in a torn coat.

Was this deception right? Scripture records it without approving every detail. Many hold that deceiving those bent on murder, in war, is not the false witness the ninth commandment forbids, as with Rahab and the midwives; others hold that every untruth is sin, which God may overrule. Either way it is no licence for ordinary lying (Col 3:9).

17.title: Ahithophel's Counsel Overthrown
17.text: <sup>1</sup>Moreover, Ahithophel said to Absalom, "Let me choose twelve thousand men, and I will arise and pursue David tonight.<sup>2</sup>I will come upon him while he is weary and discouraged and throw him into a panic, and all the people who are with him will flee. I will strike down only the king,<sup>3</sup>and I will bring all the people back to you as a bride comes home to her husband. You seek the life of only one man, and all the people will be at peace."<sup>4</sup>And the advice seemed right in the eyes of Absalom and all the elders of Israel.<sup>5</sup>Then Absalom said, "Call Hushai the Archite also, and let us hear what he has to say."<sup>6</sup>And when Hushai came to Absalom, Absalom said to him, "Thus has Ahithophel spoken; shall we do as he says? If not, you speak."<sup>7</sup>Then Hushai said to Absalom, "This time the counsel that Ahithophel has given is not good."<sup>8</sup>Hushai said, "You know that your father and his men are mighty men, and that they are enraged, like a bear robbed of her cubs in the field. Besides, your father is expert in war; he will not spend the night with the people.<sup>9</sup>Behold, even now he has hidden himself in one of the pits or in some other place. And as soon as some of the people fall at the first attack, whoever hears it will say, 'There has been a slaughter among the people who follow Absalom.'<sup>10</sup>Then even the valiant man, whose heart is like the heart of a lion, will utterly melt with fear, for all Israel knows that your father is a mighty man, and that those who are with him are valiant men.<sup>11</sup>But my counsel is that all Israel be gathered to you, from Dan to Beersheba, as the sand by the sea for multitude, and that you go to battle in person.<sup>12</sup>So we shall come upon him in some place where he is to be found, and we shall light upon him as the dew falls on the ground, and of him and all the men with him not one will be left.<sup>13</sup>If he withdraws into a city, then all Israel will bring ropes to that city, and we shall drag it into the valley, until not even a pebble is to be found there."<sup>14</sup>And Absalom and all the men of Israel said, "The counsel of Hushai the Archite is better than the counsel of Ahithophel." For the LORD had ordained to defeat the good counsel of Ahithophel, so that the LORD might bring harm upon Absalom.<sup>15</sup>Then Hushai said to Zadok and Abiathar the priests, "Thus and so did Ahithophel counsel Absalom and the elders of Israel, and thus and so have I counseled.<sup>16</sup>Now therefore send quickly and tell David, 'Do not stay tonight at the fords of the wilderness, but by all means pass over, lest the king and all the people who are with him be swallowed up.'"<sup>17</sup>Now Jonathan and Ahimaaz were waiting at En-rogel. A female servant was to go and tell them, and they were to go and tell King David, for they were not to be seen entering the city.<sup>18</sup>But a young man saw them and told Absalom. So both of them went away quickly and came to the house of a man at Bahurim, who had a well in his courtyard. And they went down into it.<sup>19</sup>And the woman took and spread a covering over the well's mouth and scattered grain on it, and nothing was known of it.<sup>20</sup>When Absalom's servants came to the woman at the house, they said, "Where are Ahimaaz and Jonathan?" And the woman said to them, "They have gone over the brook of water." And when they had sought and could not find them, they returned to Jerusalem.<sup>21</sup>After they had gone, the men came up out of the well, and went and told King David. They said to David, "Arise, and go quickly over the water, for thus and so has Ahithophel counseled against you."<sup>22</sup>Then David arose, and all the people who were with him, and they crossed the Jordan. By daybreak not one was left who had not crossed the Jordan.<sup>23</sup>When Ahithophel saw that his counsel was not followed, he saddled his donkey and went off home to his own city. He set his house in order and hanged himself, and he died and was buried in the tomb of his father.<sup>24</sup>Then David came to Mahanaim. And Absalom crossed the Jordan with all the men of Israel.<sup>25</sup>Now Absalom had set Amasa over the army instead of Joab. Amasa was the son of a man named Ithra the Ishmaelite, who had married Abigal the daughter of Nahash, sister of Zeruiah, Joab's mother.<sup>26</sup>And Israel and Absalom encamped in the land of Gilead.<sup>27</sup>When David came to Mahanaim, Shobi the son of Nahash from Rabbah of the Ammonites, and Machir the son of Ammiel from Lo-debar, and Barzillai the Gileadite from Rogelim,<sup>28</sup>brought beds, basins, and earthen vessels, wheat, barley, flour, parched grain, beans and lentils,<sup>29</sup>honey and curds and sheep and cheese from the herd, for David and the people with him to eat, for they said, "The people are hungry and weary and thirsty in the wilderness."
17.overview:
The chapter turns on a council meeting. Ahithophel proposes to strike that night with a small force and kill only the king, and it is the right plan. Hushai answers with a speech in which every fact is true and every conclusion is wrong, and Absalom, flattered by the picture of himself at the head of all Israel, chooses it. The writer then stops the story for the only time in the whole rebellion to say why: the LORD had ordained it, in answer to the prayer David prayed on the Mount of Olives (15:31).

The rest of the chapter shows what that answer looked like on the ground: a servant girl carrying a message, two young men hidden in a well by a woman with a handful of grain, Ahithophel riding home to take his own life, and three unlikely men bringing beds and food to a tired king at Mahanaim.
17.theology:
The plan that would have worked (vv. 1-3). Speed, surprise, one target, minimum bloodshed, and the army brought home intact. Kill David and there is no rebellion left to fight, because the Gittites and the mighty men are not fighting for a cause; they are fighting for him. The narrator himself calls it the good counsel, and the chapter cannot be understood unless the reader grants that.

How the worse plan won (vv. 7-13). Hushai grants that Ahithophel's advice is normally right and disputes only this time, because attacking him directly would be fatal. He finds Absalom's weak point within a sentence or two: not tactics but reputation, the fear that a single reverse would empty his support overnight. Then he offers him what Ahithophel's plan withheld, the glory of winning the kingdom in person. Militarily it is a disaster: surprise surrendered, weeks instead of hours, a muster that cannot be hidden, everything staked on one pitched battle. But Absalom is not weighing tactics; he is choosing the plan that puts him at the head of the army. The elders were not stupid; they had simply heard the better speech, and the better speech is what carries a room.

Verse 14: good counsel, God's purpose, and a prayer answered. Three things are packed into the sentence. First, God's own historian calls the plan God overthrew good. Second, the LORD had ordained: not merely permitted or foresaw, but ordained, while every person in the room did exactly what he thought best. Nobody was coerced. Ahithophel gave honest professional judgment, Hushai used his own courage and wit, Absalom exercised a vanity he had cultivated for years, and the elders preferred a better speech. Every human factor is fully accounted for, and still the writer says God ordained the result. Scripture holds these together everywhere without explaining how: Joseph's brothers meant evil and God meant good by the same act (Gen. 50:20), and at the cross men did what God's hand and plan had predestined (Acts 4:28) and were held responsible as lawless men (Acts 2:23). Any account of God’s rule that drops either half, his ordaining or their responsibility, is not what this verse teaches.

Third, this is 15:31 answered, and the way it was answered matters. There was no voice and no sign, and nothing David could have seen; anyone in that council would have seen only politics. David never learns it. He is told only to cross the river at once. He does not get verse 14; we do. That is the honest position of everyone who prays: the answer normally looks exactly like other people making their own decisions for their own reasons, and the sentence explaining what was really happening is not available at the time.

Hushai does not trust his own success (v. 16). He has just won the argument and gained David weeks, yet his message is to cross tonight, in case Absalom changes his mind. Only the river makes the delay safe. Confidence in God's providence did not make him careless; it made him diligent.

Providence through ordinary courage (vv. 17-20). The ordaining of verse 14 was carried out by people who never knew they were part of it. A servant girl walked out of the city with the most dangerous information in Israel, because nobody notices a maid going to the spring. A woman at Bahurim, the same village where Shimei threw stones that morning, thought on the spot of scattering grain over a well. She has no name and gets two verses, and a kingdom depended on her nerve.

Ahithophel calculates one last time (v. 23). This is not despair over a professional slight. He can see the end from where he stands: Absalom will muster, David will have time, there will be a pitched battle and David will win it, and the counsellor who left the king's table will be the first called to account. So he rides home, sets his house in order, and takes his own life, with no rage and no impulse. Scripture records it as the end of a man who put great gifts to the service of betrayal, not as a model. Anyone who has lost someone this way should read the question answered at the end of the notes on vv. 23-26.

The other man who died that way. Ahithophel is the only man in the Old Testament to hang himself. The next in Scripture is the one who sat at the table of the Son of David, ate his bread, took silver, and went and hanged himself (Matt. 27:5). Psalm 41:9 speaks of the close friend who ate David's bread and lifted his heel against him, and Jesus applied that verse to Judas in the upper room (John 13:18). Betrayal by a trusted counsellor, over the Kidron, on the Mount of Olives, ending in a rope: the pattern was written into this book a thousand years before the night it happened again.

Two sons of two sisters (v. 25). Amasa is Joab's cousin and both are David's nephews, so the two armies about to meet are commanded by members of the same family. The name matters later: David confirms Amasa in command in chapter 19 as a peace offering to the rebels, and Joab kills him for it in chapter 20 with the same feigned friendliness and the same wound he used on Abner.

Help from the edges (vv. 27-29). An Ammonite prince, a provincial from Lo-debar, and an old man from across the river come out with beds, basins, wheat, beans, honey and cheese, with no weapons and no money among them, and nobody wins a war with lentils. They come at the very moment the whole country from Dan to Beersheba is mustering behind the king's son. The book has done this from the beginning: Obed-edom, Uriah and Ittai were all outsiders who proved more faithful than insiders. The people who show up are from the edges, and they come not to back a winner but because the people are hungry and weary and thirsty.
17.examples:
Then: The best political mind in Israel proposed a plan that would have ended the war that night with a single death, and the council agreed. Then a young man who liked being consulted asked for one more opinion, and David's friend talked them out of it. And somewhere in a village, a woman put a cloth over a well and scattered grain on it.

Now: Verse 14 is the one to think over slowly, and it is not a comfortable verse. It insists that God ordained the outcome of a meeting in which everyone freely did what he thought best, and it does not explain how. What is practically useful is that David got his answer and never knew it. He prayed ten specific words, and the answer looked like nothing more than a committee preferring a better speech. Most answered prayer is like that. If you are waiting to see God's hand before you believe he has moved, you will usually be waiting for something that only shows up in the account written afterwards; meanwhile you may keep praying, and keep doing the next faithful thing. The woman at Bahurim is what verse 14 looks like from ground level: no name, two verses, an idea she had on the spot, and a kingdom depending on it.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–14 — The LORD Had Ordained to Defeat the Good Counsel
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Ahithophel proposes to strike David that night and kill the king alone (vv. 1-3), and Absalom and the elders agree (v. 4). Hushai is called in and argues for a national muster led by Absalom in person (vv. 5-13). The council prefers Hushai's counsel, and the writer says why (v. 14).
verseByVerse.theology: The text itself calls Ahithophel's plan the good counsel. Hushai's is worse in every military respect, and it wins because it flatters.
verseByVerse.examples: Here, for one sentence, the only such sentence in the whole rebellion, the writer lifts the curtain on what God was doing, and it answers a prayer prayed barefoot on a hillside two chapters ago.

verseByVerse.quote: Moreover, Ahithophel said to Absalom, "Let me choose twelve thousand men, and I will arise and pursue David tonight. I will come upon him while he is weary and discouraged and throw him into a panic, and all the people who are with him will flee. I will strike down only the king, and I will bring all the people back to you as a bride comes home to her husband. You seek the life of only one man, and all the people will be at peace." And the advice seemed right in the eyes of Absalom and all the elders of Israel. Then Absalom said, "Call Hushai the Archite also, and let us hear what he has to say." And when Hushai came to Absalom, Absalom said to him, "Thus has Ahithophel spoken; shall we do as he says? If not, you speak." Then Hushai said to Absalom, "This time the counsel that Ahithophel has given is not good." Hushai said, "You know that your father and his men are mighty men, and that they are enraged, like a bear robbed of her cubs in the field. Besides, your father is expert in war; he will not spend the night with the people. Behold, even now he has hidden himself in one of the pits or in some other place. And as soon as some of the people fall at the first attack, whoever hears it will say, 'There has been a slaughter among the people who follow Absalom.' Then even the valiant man, whose heart is like the heart of a lion, will utterly melt with fear, for all Israel knows that your father is a mighty man, and that those who are with him are valiant men. But my counsel is that all Israel be gathered to you, from Dan to Beersheba, as the sand by the sea for multitude, and that you go to battle in person. So we shall come upon him in some place where he is to be found, and we shall light upon him as the dew falls on the ground, and of him and all the men with him not one will be left. If he withdraws into a city, then all Israel will bring ropes to that city, and we shall drag it into the valley, until not even a pebble is to be found there." And Absalom and all the men of Israel said, "The counsel of Hushai the Archite is better than the counsel of Ahithophel." For the LORD had ordained to defeat the good counsel of Ahithophel, so that the LORD might bring harm upon Absalom.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The whole chapter depends on understanding that this plan is a very good one.

Twelve thousand is a strike force and not an army: enough to overwhelm a column of refugees and small enough to move fast. And tonight is the heart of the plan. David crossed the Kidron this morning. He is somewhere short of the Jordan, on foot, with women and children and a weeping crowd.

Weary and discouraged. Ahithophel knows exactly what condition David is in, because he has sat in his council for years. And then the surgical part: I will strike down only the king. He has grasped what Absalom has not, that this is not a war between two armies but a question about one man.

The plan is not only effective, it is humane, which is the last thing anybody expects. One death instead of a battle. The army comes home intact and changes sides without a fight. No Israelite kills another. He even puts an image to it: the nation returning like a bride coming home. Ahithophel is proposing an assassination to prevent a civil war, he is right on the facts and the timing, and it would have worked.

Everybody agrees. It is settled. And then comes the sentence on which the kingdom turns, and it looks like nothing at all. Absalom, who has been in the room for about a day, says: let us also hear from the other one. He is not suspicious of Ahithophel. He is a man who likes to be consulted and cannot quite bring himself to act on a decision that is finished. Why he says it, the writer does not tell us. Verse 14 tells us who was behind it.

Hushai has to answer fast and with total confidence, and he does. Note the two words he adds: this time. He does not attack Ahithophel, which would be fatal, since the man's advice is treated like the word of God (16:23). He concedes everything about the counsellor and disputes only this one occasion.

The technique repays study. Every single thing he says is true, and every conclusion he draws from it is wrong. David's men are mighty men; the writer will list them in chapter 23. David is expert in war. A bear robbed of her cubs is an exact picture of those six hundred men at this moment. All of which is precisely why Ahithophel wanted to hit them tonight, before they have slept or crossed the river. Hushai takes the same facts and turns them into a reason to wait.

Then the hook, aimed straight at what Absalom cares about: if the first attack goes even slightly wrong, the news will spread that his men are being slaughtered, and his support will evaporate overnight. That is a fear about reputation, not tactics, and Absalom has spent four years at a gate building a reputation one handshake at a time.

Now the flattery, and it is enormous. All Israel, from Dan to Beersheba, the formula for the entire nation. As the sand by the sea for multitude, Abraham's promise (Gen. 22:17) applied to Absalom's army. And that you go to battle in person.

There it is. In Ahithophel's version, Ahithophel goes and Absalom stays home, and somebody else kills the king and hands him a kingdom. In Hushai's version, Absalom rides at the head of the largest army ever assembled in Israel and wins it himself. Militarily it is a disaster: it surrenders surprise, gives David weeks instead of hours, requires a muster that cannot be hidden, and commits the whole rebellion to a single pitched battle. But Absalom is not asking which plan is sounder. He is choosing the one in which he leads the army himself.

And the last two verses are not a plan at all. They are poetry. Nobody drags a city into a valley with ropes. It is a picture of total, effortless victory, exactly what a proud man wants to hear about himself. Ahithophel gave a plan. Hushai gave a vision.

They vote for the worse plan unanimously, and they are not stupid. These are the elders of Israel, and they have just heard a better speech. The man with the correct answer spoke in numbers and hours; the man with the wrong answer spoke about the sand by the sea and the king at the head of the nation. The better argument lost to the more flattering one, and that does not happen only in ancient councils.

Here the writer stops the narrative and tells us what has actually been happening, and there are three things in it.

First: the good counsel of Ahithophel. God's own historian, in the sentence in which he describes God overthrowing it, calls the plan good. It was the right plan, competently argued, by the best mind in Israel.

Second: the LORD had ordained to defeat it. Not permitted. Not foresaw. Ordained. The outcome of that council was settled before anybody spoke, and nobody in it was coerced. Ahithophel gave his honest judgment, Hushai used his own intelligence and courage, Absalom exercised his vanity freely, the elders were persuaded by a better speech. Every human factor is accounted for, and God still ordained the result. Scripture holds those together everywhere and never explains how. Joseph's brothers meant evil and God meant good, and both are said of the same act (Gen. 50:20). So it was at the cross: men did whatever God's hand and plan had predestined to take place (Acts 4:28), and they were still lawless men, held responsible for it (Acts 2:23).

Third: two chapters ago, a barefoot man going up the Mount of Olives with dirt on his head prayed ten words. O LORD, please turn the counsel of Ahithophel into foolishness (15:31). This verse is that prayer being answered, and the writer wants us to see it.

And look at how it was answered. Not by a voice, not by a sign, and not by any event David could have seen. It was answered through a friend's courage, a young man's vanity, a room full of elders who liked one speech better than another, and a decision that took perhaps a minute. If you had been in that council you would have seen politics. There is no moment in the whole sequence where God is visible.

David never learns this. He is told, later that night, only that he must cross the river at once. He does not get verse 14; we do. Which is the honest situation of anybody who prays: the answer, if it comes, will normally look like other people making their own decisions for their own reasons.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 15–22 — A Woman Spread a Covering Over the Well
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Hushai sends word through the priests that David must cross the Jordan tonight (vv. 15-16). The runners are seen, and a woman at Bahurim hides them in a well and sends the pursuers away (vv. 17-21). By daybreak David's whole company is across the river (v. 22).
verseByVerse.theology: Everything now depends on ordinary people doing something dangerous: a servant girl carrying messages, two young men in a hole in the ground, and a woman with a handful of grain.
verseByVerse.examples: Courage here does not look heroic. It looks like a woman in her own courtyard keeping her voice steady while soldiers ask questions, because she has decided whose side she is on.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Hushai said to Zadok and Abiathar the priests, "Thus and so did Ahithophel counsel Absalom and the elders of Israel, and thus and so have I counseled. Now therefore send quickly and tell David, 'Do not stay tonight at the fords of the wilderness, but by all means pass over, lest the king and all the people who are with him be swallowed up.'" Now Jonathan and Ahimaaz were waiting at En-rogel. A female servant was to go and tell them, and they were to go and tell King David, for they were not to be seen entering the city. But a young man saw them and told Absalom. So both of them went away quickly and came to the house of a man at Bahurim, who had a well in his courtyard. And they went down into it. And the woman took and spread a covering over the well's mouth and scattered grain on it, and nothing was known of it. When Absalom's servants came to the woman at the house, they said, "Where are Ahimaaz and Jonathan?" And the woman said to them, "They have gone over the brook of water." And when they had sought and could not find them, they returned to Jerusalem. After they had gone, the men came up out of the well, and went and told King David. They said to David, "Arise, and go quickly over the water, for thus and so has Ahithophel counseled against you." Then David arose, and all the people who were with him, and they crossed the Jordan. By daybreak not one was left who had not crossed the Jordan.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Hushai gets the message out immediately, and he reports both plans. David needs to know what was proposed as well as what was decided.

And note the caution. Hushai's counsel won, and he has every reason to think he has bought David several weeks. He does not trust his own success for one night: by all means pass over, tonight, in case Absalom changes his mind. He is right to. Ahithophel's plan was better and Absalom could still take it.

The network from chapter 15 is now working as designed, and its first link is a servant girl. She walks out of the city with the most dangerous information in Israel in her head. Nobody notices a maid going to the spring, which is precisely why she is doing it.

And then it goes wrong: a boy sees them and reports it. They run into a courtyard at Bahurim, the village where Shimei came out throwing stones earlier that day, and climb down a well.

One verse, and the kingdom hangs on it. Two strangers drop into her husband's well with pursuit behind them. She covers the mouth of it, and then, and this shows what kind of person she is, she scatters grain across the covering, so that any soldier walking into that yard sees an ordinary courtyard with grain spread out to dry. That detail was not part of any plan. She thought of it while it was happening.

She lies to armed men on her own doorstep, calmly, and sends them off in a believable direction. If her voice shakes, or one of them decides to look under the grain, two young men die in a well, David is not warned, and Absalom takes Ahithophel's advice after all. Her name is not recorded, and few in Israel can ever have known what she did. Here is what the ordaining of verse 14 looked like on the ground: a woman with a handful of grain, thinking fast, in a village.

By dawn the river is behind them, and the writer counts: not one was left. The women, the children, the Gittites with their little ones, the priests' households, a night crossing by a whole community, and nobody is left on the wrong bank.

Was the woman wrong to lie to the soldiers? Scripture records her words without comment. She was hiding men from armed pursuers who meant to kill the king, much as Rahab hid the spies (Joshua 2:4-6) and is commended for her faith (Hebrews 11:31). Many hold that misleading those bent on murder is not the false witness the ninth commandment forbids; others hold that every untruth is sin, which God may forgive and overrule. Faithful Christians differ here, and neither view is a licence for ordinary lying (Col 3:9).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 23–26 — He Set His House in Order and Hanged Himself
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Ahithophel goes home and takes his own life (v. 23). David reaches Mahanaim; Absalom crosses the Jordan with Amasa in command of the army in place of Joab, and encamps in Gilead (vv. 24-26).
verseByVerse.theology: Ahithophel is not despairing at a setback. He has just watched the council choose the losing plan, and he can see how it will end, both for Absalom and for a man who has publicly betrayed David.
verseByVerse.examples: One chapter ago his advice was reckoned as the word of God. Great ability is no protection against a life that ends in ruin when it has been put to the service of betrayal.

verseByVerse.quote: When Ahithophel saw that his counsel was not followed, he saddled his donkey and went off home to his own city. He set his house in order and hanged himself, and he died and was buried in the tomb of his father. Then David came to Mahanaim. And Absalom crossed the Jordan with all the men of Israel. Now Absalom had set Amasa over the army instead of Joab. Amasa was the son of a man named Ithra the Ishmaelite, who had married Abigal the daughter of Nahash, sister of Zeruiah, Joab's mother. And Israel and Absalom encamped in the land of Gilead.
verseByVerse.commentary:
One verse, and it is one of the coldest in Scripture.

This is not a man in despair over a professional slight. Ahithophel can see the whole thing to the end: Absalom will muster, David will have time to organise across the Jordan, there will be a pitched battle, and David will win it. And when David wins, the first man called to account will be the counsellor who left the king's own table for the son's. So he calculates, as he has calculated everything else. He is a dead man either way, and he prefers to arrange it himself.

The sequence of verbs is what makes it terrible. He saddled his donkey. He went home to Giloh, a day's ride. He set his house in order: settled his affairs and provided for his family. And then he took his own life. There is no rage in any of that and no impulse. He is buried in his father's tomb, which suggests his family did not treat him as disgraced.

One chapter ago his counsel was as if one consulted the word of God (16:23). All that ability, and he is dead in a house at Giloh because a vain young man liked a better speech.

And the writer has been preparing one more likeness since chapter 15. Ahithophel is the only man in the Old Testament who dies by hanging himself. The only other in Scripture is in the New Testament: the man who sat at the table of the Son of David, ate his bread, took silver to betray him, and went and hanged himself (Matt. 27:5). A psalm of David, very possibly with Ahithophel in mind, says even my close friend in whom I trusted, who ate my bread, has lifted his heel against me (Ps. 41:9), and Jesus quoted it in the upper room about Judas (John 13:18). The likeness is deliberate.

Mahanaim is across the Jordan in Gilead, a name with a history. Jacob met the angels of God there and called the place Two Camps (Gen. 32:2), shortly before he faced Esau. It was also a defensible town (see the note below).

Amasa’s parentage is given because it matters. Amasa is Joab's cousin, and both are David's nephews: the two armies about to fight are commanded by the sons of two sisters.

There are two puzzles in verse 25. This Nahash is almost certainly not the Ammonite king; 1 Chronicles 2:16 names Zeruiah and Abigail as David's sisters, so Nahash may have been their mother, or their mother's first husband. And the Hebrew here calls Ithra the Israelite (as the KJV has it), while 1 Chronicles 2:17 calls him an Ishmaelite, which the ESV follows, probably rightly, since an ordinary Israelite father would hardly need his nation named.

Remember the name Amasa. David will confirm Amasa's appointment in chapter 19 as a peace offering to the rebels, and Joab will kill him for it in chapter 20.

Is suicide a sin, and is it unforgivable? Taking one’s own life breaks the sixth commandment, a grave sin against the God who gives life (Exod 20:13). But it is not the unforgivable sin; that is the settled rejection of Christ (Mark 3:28–29). A true believer who dies this way, in despair or illness of mind, is not cut off from the grace that saves sinners, for salvation rests on Christ’s work, not on the state of our last moment (Rom 8:38–39). Anyone thinking of it should speak to someone today: a pastor, a friend, a doctor; and anyone in immediate danger should call the local emergency number now.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 27–29 — Three Men Brought Beds and Bowls
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: At Mahanaim three men come out to David with bedding, vessels and food (vv. 27-28), because the people are hungry and weary in the wilderness (v. 29).
verseByVerse.theology: Each of these men has a history with David, and chapter 9 and chapter 10 lie behind two of them. Kindness shown years before is being repaid at the lowest point of the reign.
verseByVerse.examples: What they bring is domestic rather than military, and they bring it because the people are hungry. Practical care for the weary is never a small thing in this book.

verseByVerse.quote: When David came to Mahanaim, Shobi the son of Nahash from Rabbah of the Ammonites, and Machir the son of Ammiel from Lo-debar, and Barzillai the Gileadite from Rogelim, brought beds, basins, and earthen vessels, wheat, barley, flour, parched grain, beans and lentils, honey and curds and sheep and cheese from the herd, for David and the people with him to eat, for they said, "The people are hungry and weary and thirsty in the wilderness."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Three men come out to meet a defeated king, and behind at least two of them lies an old kindness now being repaid.

The first is a son of Nahash, the Ammonite king whose death set off chapter 10. His son Hanun shaved David's envoys and started a war. Shobi comes from Rabbah, the city Joab was besieging when David was on the roof, at whose wall Uriah was killed. Shobi is Hanun's brother, from the house David tried to show kindness to and was insulted for, from the city where David committed his worst act, and he has come out with food.

The second, Machir of Lo-debar, was last seen in chapter 9. Mephibosheth lived in his house for all the years nobody in Jerusalem thought about him. The man who took in the last of the old dynasty when the new king might have wanted him dead now supplies the new king when his own son has driven him out. Whatever Machir is, he is consistent: he looks after whoever has been driven out.

The third is Barzillai, a very old and very rich man from Gilead, and chapter 19 will give him one of the finest speeches in the book.

Now read the list, because it is not a military supply column. There are no weapons on it and no money. What these men send is what you send to people who have walked a long way and are sleeping outdoors: something to lie on, something to cook in, and enough food for a few thousand exhausted people. And the writer gives their reason in their own words: not "the king's cause is just", but the people are hungry and weary and thirsty in the wilderness.

Israel has just thrown David out. The whole country is mustering behind his son, and his nephew commands the rebel army. And what arrives at Mahanaim is a foreigner, a provincial, and an old man from across the river, with bedding. The book has been doing this from the beginning. Obed-edom the Gittite took the ark when Israel was afraid of it. Uriah the Hittite would not sleep in his own bed while the ark was in a field. Ittai the Gittite went into exile with a king he had barely known. At the lowest point of the reign, the people who show up are again from the edges.
verseByVerse.note: Mahanaim, east of the Jordan, had been Ish-bosheth’s capital, which made it a natural refuge for a government in exile.

18.title: The Death of Absalom
18.text: <sup>1</sup>Then David mustered the men who were with him and set over them commanders of thousands and commanders of hundreds.<sup>2</sup>And David sent out the army, one third under the command of Joab, one third under the command of Abishai the son of Zeruiah, Joab's brother, and one third under the command of Ittai the Gittite. And the king said to the men, "I myself will also go out with you."<sup>3</sup>But the men said, "You shall not go out. For if we flee, they will not care about us. If half of us die, they will not care about us. But you are worth ten thousand of us. Therefore it is better that you send us help from the city."<sup>4</sup>The king said to them, "Whatever seems best to you I will do." So the king stood at the side of the gate, while all the army marched out by hundreds and by thousands.<sup>5</sup>And the king ordered Joab and Abishai and Ittai, "Deal gently for my sake with the young man Absalom." And all the people heard when the king gave orders to all the commanders about Absalom.<sup>6</sup>So the army went out into the field against Israel, and the battle was fought in the forest of Ephraim.<sup>7</sup>And the men of Israel were defeated there by the servants of David, and the loss there was great on that day, twenty thousand men.<sup>8</sup>The battle spread over the face of all the country, and the forest devoured more people that day than the sword.<sup>9</sup>And Absalom happened to meet the servants of David. Absalom was riding on his mule, and the mule went under the thick branches of a great oak, and his head caught fast in the oak, and he was suspended between heaven and earth, while the mule that was under him went on.<sup>10</sup>And a certain man saw it and told Joab, "Behold, I saw Absalom hanging in an oak."<sup>11</sup>Joab said to the man who told him, "What, you saw him! Why then did you not strike him there to the ground? I would have been glad to give you ten pieces of silver and a belt."<sup>12</sup>But the man said to Joab, "Even if I felt in my hand the weight of a thousand pieces of silver, I would not reach out my hand against the king's son, for in our hearing the king commanded you and Abishai and Ittai, 'For my sake protect the young man Absalom.'<sup>13</sup>On the other hand, if I had dealt treacherously against his life (and there is nothing hidden from the king), then you yourself would have stood aloof."<sup>14</sup>Joab said, "I will not waste time like this with you." And he took three javelins in his hand and thrust them into the heart of Absalom while he was still alive in the oak.<sup>15</sup>And ten young men, Joab's armor-bearers, surrounded Absalom and struck him and killed him.<sup>16</sup>Then Joab blew the trumpet, and the troops came back from pursuing Israel, for Joab restrained them.<sup>17</sup>And they took Absalom and threw him into a great pit in the forest and raised over him a very great heap of stones. Then Ahimaaz ran by the way of the plain, and outran the Cushite.<sup>24</sup>Now David was sitting between the two gates, and the watchman went up to the roof of the gate by the wall, and when he lifted up his eyes and looked, he saw a man running alone.<sup>25</sup>The watchman called out and told the king. And as he went, he said, "O my son Absalom, my son, my son Absalom! Would I had died instead of you, O Absalom, my son, my son!"
18.overview: The battle that ends the rebellion. David, who walked barefoot out of Jerusalem three chapters ago, has used the time Hushai bought him to turn a column of refugees into an army, and his men will not let him fight. At the gate he gives an order that runs through the whole chapter: deal gently with the young man Absalom. The forest of Ephraim swallows twenty thousand men, Absalom is caught by the head in an oak, and Joab, refusing to hear a soldier who quotes the king's order back at him, kills him himself. Then two runners come to a king waiting between two gates with one question, and the chapter ends on a father's lament on the stairs: my son, five times in one verse.
18.theology:
An order that could not be obeyed (v. 5). David gives his command aloud, at the gate, to all three commanders, with the whole army filing past, because he knows what Joab does with an inconvenient man. It works, in a way: an ordinary infantryman can quote it back to the commander-in-chief. Yet the order is also indefensible. Absalom is a grown man who murdered his brother, stole a kingdom and shamed his father before the nation, and an army cannot be sent to win a battle against an enemy it has been told not to hurt. For my sake does not claim the order is right; it asks a favour. Love for a child can be real and still be no guide to justice.

The bitter end (v. 8). Twenty thousand dead in a forest. Ahithophel’s plan would have cost one life, David’s (17:2). Abner had asked across a valley years before, shall the sword devour forever? The rejection of the king God chose ends, as such rebellion does, in waste.

The writer plants a detail and does not point to it (v. 9). The text says Absalom's head was caught, not his hair. But four chapters earlier the writer stopped to weigh that hair (14:25-26), and now its owner hangs between heaven and earth, belonging to neither, while the royal mule walks out from under him. Every reader makes the connection; the text never asserts it. Judgment in this book often comes through the very things a man was proudest of.

The case for Joab, and what is left of it (vv. 10-15). Absalom alive would have been a permanent rallying point, and Joab is not wrong about the politics. But he had a direct, public order from his king, and he set it aside, as he did with Abner and will do with Amasa. Each time there is a real political argument, and each time Joab decides that his judgment outranks the king's. David never punishes him; he cannot, and says so at 3:39 and again on his deathbed (1 Kings 2:5-6). The clearest conscience in the chapter belongs to a man with no name. Joab offers ten pieces of silver; the soldier says not for a thousand. He is not haggling; he means that no sum would make him do it. He quotes the king's order back with the names in it, and then tells his commander to his face that when the reckoning came, you yourself would have stood aloof. He is right: Joab has spent a career giving orders and letting other men carry the risk. Joab's reply, I will not waste time like this with you, is not an argument. He does not dispute the order or claim he did not hear it. He puts three javelins into a helpless man and has ten armour-bearers finish the body, spreading the act across eleven men so that no one of them can be held responsible. And the other side of Joab belongs in the record too: the moment Absalom is dead he sounds the recall, and thousands go home alive.

Two monuments (vv. 17-18). A pit under a heap of stones is the marker of a man who died under judgment, as with Achan and the king of Ai. Beside it stands the pillar Absalom raised to his own name because he had no son to remember him. He spent his life on being seen, and the last thing recorded of him is a stone with his name on it. If his sons had died young, as most readers take it, he was also a man who had buried his children, and that should temper any verdict passed on him.

Kindness, and the courage to say it (vv. 19-32). Joab, who has just killed the king's son, will not let young Ahimaaz carry the news, in one of his few kind acts in this book. He has seen what happens to the man who brings David such news: the Amalekite who came to Ziklag with Saul's crown was executed. So he sends a Cushite, a foreigner and probably a slave, who goes without being asked whether he wants to. Ahimaaz runs anyway, arrives first, and cannot say it. He knows exactly what happened, and he says he saw a commotion and does not know what it was. Wanting to be the one who arrives is not the same as being ready to speak. And David's single question shows where his heart is. Twenty thousand dead, the kingdom his again, and he does not ask about the battle or whether Ittai survived. He has been sitting between two gates all day, ready to read good news into the way a man runs. Ahimaaz shouts shalom, all is well, and David asks whether there is shalom for Absalom. The answer is no.

The lament (v. 33). Grief speaks like this. It circles, it does not develop, it says the one true thing again. The word is not “the rebel”; it is my son. Every reason to hate him is true, and not one of them weighs with David now.

Would I had died instead of you. The oldest wish of love, and in David's mouth it is useless: had he died in that forest, nothing in Absalom's heart would have changed, and the exchange would have purchased nothing. A father can want to take his son's place; he cannot do it, and he cannot make it mean anything if he does. Here the verse points beyond David to Christ, and it helps us only if we keep the difference between the two clear.

A thousand years later another Son of David, in David's own city, went out to die for rebels who had stolen the hearts of a kingdom from its rightful King and wanted a throne that was not theirs. He did not merely wish to die in their place; he did it. And the difference is not only that it happened but that it worked: while we were enemies we were reconciled to God by the death of his Son (Rom. 5:10). David on that staircase is not a picture of the cross. He is a picture of the longing the cross answers, and the one thing he wanted most was impossible for him and was not impossible for God.

For parents of a wayward child. Many who read this verse are mothers and fathers with a son or daughter who has turned against them or against God, and some have stood at a grave like this one. Scripture does not tell David to stop loving the boy, and it does not call his grief weakness. Nor does it pretend he had been a faultless father: he had indulged and neglected by turns, and Absalom's choices were still Absalom's own. Both are usually true, and neither guilt nor excuse is the place to stay. While the child lives, keep praying and keep the door open; the father in Jesus' parable was watching the road and ran when he saw his son (Luke 15:20). And where a child has died far off, the grieving may leave the question with the Judge of all the earth, who will do what is just (Genesis 18:25), and who did not spare his own Son but gave him up for us all (Romans 8:32).
18.examples:
Then: A king told his commanders, in front of his whole army, to deal gently with the man who had taken his throne, and when a soldier found that man hanging helpless in a tree and refused a thousand pieces of silver to touch him, the commander-in-chief killed him himself.

Now: The nameless soldier is the model, and what makes him one is not courage in the abstract. He had a clear word from his king, quoted accurately, and he could see exactly what the man pressuring him was like. You yourself would have stood aloof is the line to remember the next time somebody powerful asks you to do what they will not put their own name to. The Christian stands on a clearer word from a better King, who did not stand aloof but bore the reckoning himself, and whose Spirit gives the steadiness to say no. Ahimaaz, who ran faster than the man with the real message and then could not open his mouth, is the gentler warning: wanting to carry the news is not the same as being willing to say it. And the lament does not need improving. Scripture records five my sons in one verse without tidying any of them away. A parent who still loves a child who has broken their heart is not being foolish; David was that parent on those stairs.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–8 — The Forest Devoured More People
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: David divides the army in three and is persuaded not to go out himself (vv. 1-4). At the gate he orders the commanders, in everyone's hearing, to deal gently with Absalom (v. 5). The battle in the forest of Ephraim costs twenty thousand lives (vv. 6-8).
verseByVerse.theology: He gives the order publicly and to all three commanders at once, because he knows perfectly well that one of them will kill his son if he can. He is trying to make it impossible.
verseByVerse.examples: The terrain does most of the killing. Broken ground turns a hurried national muster into a rout, which is exactly what Hushai's plan exposed Absalom's army to and Ahithophel's would have avoided.

verseByVerse.quote: Then David mustered the men who were with him and set over them commanders of thousands and commanders of hundreds. And David sent out the army, one third under the command of Joab, one third under the command of Abishai the son of Zeruiah, Joab's brother, and one third under the command of Ittai the Gittite. And the king said to the men, "I myself will also go out with you." But the men said, "You shall not go out. For if we flee, they will not care about us. If half of us die, they will not care about us. But you are worth ten thousand of us. Therefore it is better that you send us help from the city." The king said to them, "Whatever seems best to you I will do." So the king stood at the side of the gate, while all the army marched out by hundreds and by thousands. And the king ordered Joab and Abishai and Ittai, "Deal gently for my sake with the young man Absalom." And all the people heard when the king gave orders to all the commanders about Absalom. So the army went out into the field against Israel, and the battle was fought in the forest of Ephraim. And the men of Israel were defeated there by the servants of David, and the loss there was great on that day, twenty thousand men. The battle spread over the face of all the country, and the forest devoured more people that day than the sword.
verseByVerse.commentary:
David the professional soldier is back. Three chapters ago he was walking barefoot out of Jerusalem in tears. He has now had the time that Hushai bought him, and he uses every hour of it: the refugees who crossed the Jordan in the dark have been organised into an army with a command structure.

Three divisions, and the third is commanded by the Philistine who arrived only days ago. Ittai said wherever my lord the king shall be, whether for death or for life, and David has given him a third of the army. That is what David thought of the speech.

He offers to fight and his men refuse to let him. Their argument is cold and correct. This war is about one man, exactly as Ahithophel said. If half the army dies it changes nothing; if David dies it is over. He is the objective, so he must not be on the field.

Set that against 11:1: the time when kings go out to battle... but David remained at Jerusalem. He stayed home then and should have gone. He offers to go now and is told to stay. All the trouble since then has come from that first decision to stay at home.

Then the order, and everything in the chapter runs into it. He names all three commanders. He gives it out loud, at the gate, while the whole army is marching past, and the writer makes sure we understand: all the people heard.

That is not carelessness. David has known Joab for decades, and knows exactly what Joab will do with a rebel prince, because he watched him do the same thing to Abner at the gate of Hebron. So he makes the order public, in front of thousands of witnesses, so that it cannot be denied or quietly not heard.

And the order is also a serious failure; both things are true. The young man Absalom is what he called him when he brought him back from Geshur. Absalom is a grown man, probably in his thirties, who has murdered his brother, stolen a kingdom, driven his father out, and lain with his father's concubines on a roof in front of the nation. And the king is sending an army out to fight a battle and telling it to be gentle with him. There is no way to obey both halves of that. Somebody has to win this battle, and every soldier on that road understands the arithmetic even if David will not. For my sake: he is not even claiming it is right. He is asking for a personal favour.

Against Israel. The writer will not soften it: this is civil war, David’s men against their own nation.

Twenty thousand dead. Recall what Ahithophel offered: twelve thousand men, one night, one death, and the nation brought home like a bride. This is the alternative that was chosen instead.

The forest devoured more people that day than the sword is one of the strangest sentences in the book. The country east of the Jordan is broken ground: ravines, gullies, thick scrub, rocks and trees. It is the worst terrain for a large army that does not know it, and Absalom's national muster is exactly that: farmers and townsmen called up in a hurry, fighting professionals on ground the professionals chose. Once a line like that breaks, men run into a forest in panic, fall into ravines, are lost, and are hunted down in ones and twos.

And “devoured” is a word for eating. It is the picture Abner used when he called across a valley years ago, shall the sword devour forever? Do you not know that the end will be bitter? (2:26). The bitter end is a wood full of dead Israelites.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 9–18 — The King's Command Concerning You
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Absalom is caught by the head in an oak (v. 9). A soldier refuses Joab's reward to kill him, quoting the king's order (vv. 10-13). Joab kills him himself, recalls the army, and has the body thrown into a pit under a heap of stones (vv. 14-17). The section closes on the pillar Absalom had raised to his own name (v. 18).
verseByVerse.theology: The writer records Absalom's end without a word of comment, and lets what he said four chapters earlier about Absalom's hair do its own work.
verseByVerse.examples: A man who refuses to do wrong for a thousand pieces of silver, and says why to his commander's face, needs no name to be remembered.

verseByVerse.quote: And Absalom happened to meet the servants of David. Absalom was riding on his mule, and the mule went under the thick branches of a great oak, and his head caught fast in the oak, and he was suspended between heaven and earth, while the mule that was under him went on. And a certain man saw it and told Joab, "Behold, I saw Absalom hanging in an oak." Joab said to the man who told him, "What, you saw him! Why then did you not strike him there to the ground? I would have been glad to give you ten pieces of silver and a belt." But the man said to Joab, "Even if I felt in my hand the weight of a thousand pieces of silver, I would not reach out my hand against the king's son, for in our hearing the king commanded you and Abishai and Ittai, 'For my sake protect the young man Absalom.' On the other hand, if I had dealt treacherously against his life (and there is nothing hidden from the king), then you yourself would have stood aloof." Joab said, "I will not waste time like this with you." And he took three javelins in his hand and thrust them into the heart of Absalom while he was still alive in the oak. And ten young men, Joab's armor-bearers, surrounded Absalom and struck him and killed him. Then Joab blew the trumpet, and the troops came back from pursuing Israel, for Joab restrained them. And they took Absalom and threw him into a great pit in the forest and raised over him a very great heap of stones. And all Israel fled every one to his own home. Now Absalom in his lifetime had taken and set up for himself the pillar that is in the King's Valley, for he said, "I have no son to keep my name in remembrance." He called the pillar after his own name, and it is called Absalom's monument to this day.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Say what the text says, and then say what the writer did with it.

The text says his head caught fast in the oak, not his hair: a man riding a mule at speed under low branches was caught by the head, and the animal kept going, and he was left hanging. And four chapters ago the writer stopped the narrative to describe Absalom's beauty and his hair, how he cut it once a year, only when it grew too heavy to carry, and weighed it (14:25-26). He recorded it and made no point of it whatever. Now a man is hanging by the head in a tree.

The writer does not join them up. He plants things and waits. Every reader makes the connection, and it is almost certainly intended, and the text still does not assert it.

Suspended between heaven and earth is exact in more than one way: between the two, belonging to neither, held by nothing he chose. And the mule is the royal mount; Solomon will be put on David's own mule to be proclaimed king (1 Kings 1:33). Absalom is riding the animal of a king, and it walks out from under him.

Joab's reaction is instant, and it tells you he had already decided. He does not ask whether the man is sure, or what the king's order was. He asks why the soldier did not kill him, and names a price on the spot: ten shekels and a belt, a mark of honour.

Here is the best speech in the chapter, made by a man with no name. Joab offers ten pieces of silver; the man says he would not do it for a thousand. He is not haggling and not being pious. There is no sum which turns this into a thing he would do. And his reason is the king's order, quoted back at Joab with the names in it.

In our hearing. That is why David gave the order at the gate in front of the whole army. An ordinary soldier can now quote it, accurately, to the commander-in-chief.

And the second half is devastating. The king finds out everything, there is nothing hidden from the king, and when there was a reckoning for the death of his son, Joab would have stood aloof. He would have let the soldier hang for it alone and said nothing about the ten pieces of silver. The man has taken his commander's measure precisely and says so to his face, and he is right. Joab has spent his career giving orders and letting other people carry the risk.

I will not waste time like this with you is his entire answer, and it is not an argument. He says he has no time for the conversation, and walks off to do it: three javelins into the heart of a man hanging helpless in a tree.

Then ten more. He was already dead, or dying. Joab has his armour-bearers finish the body, which spreads the act across eleven men, so that no single one can be held responsible and Joab himself is only one among many.

The case for Joab has to be put, because it is not nothing. Absalom alive is a permanent rallying point; there would be another rebellion inside five years; David is a father who cannot see it. Joab is thinking about the kingdom, and he is not wrong about the politics. But he had a direct order from his king, given publicly, which he heard, and he disobeyed it and killed the king’s son.

This is the third time. Abner at the gate of Hebron, in peacetime, in a city of refuge. Absalom here. Amasa in two chapters. Each time Joab is the one who decides that his judgment outranks the king's. David never punishes him. He cannot: he needs him, and says so at 3:39, these men, the sons of Zeruiah, are more severe than I, and he is still saying it on his deathbed when he tells Solomon to deal with what he could not (1 Kings 2:5-6).

And having killed him, Joab immediately stops the battle. That is the other side of the man. The moment Absalom is dead he sounds the recall, and thousands of Israelites who would have been hunted through that forest go home. He did the same at Gibeon when Abner called across the valley.

A pit in a wood and a pile of rocks is not a burial; it is a disposal, and Israel knew what it meant. Over Achan they raised over him a great heap of stones (Josh. 7:26), and over the king of Ai likewise (Josh. 8:29). The heap is the marker of a man who died under judgment. He is not carried back to Jerusalem or put in a tomb. His father is waiting at Mahanaim and is not asked.

And then, having told how Absalom was buried under a heap of stones, the writer tells us about the monument Absalom had built for himself. The placing is deliberate and merciless: two memorials in consecutive verses, the one he raised and the one the army raised. He commissioned his own, in the King's Valley, near the capital, while he was alive, and he named it Absalom.

The reason is strange to read, because four chapters ago the writer told us he had three sons and a daughter (14:27). The sons are not named and never mentioned again, and the plain sense of this verse is probably that they died young. If so, three sons were buried and one daughter was left, and here is a man building a stone with his own name on it because there will be nobody after him. Pause there before passing any verdict on him.

And the pillar still sums the man up. He spent his life on being seen: the chariot and the fifty runners, the hair, the kisses at the gate, the tent on the roof. The last thing recorded about him is a stone with his name on it so that people would keep saying it. His sister's memorial was a daughter he named after her. His own was a rock.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 19–32 — Is It Well with the Young Man Absalom?
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Joab keeps Ahimaaz from carrying the news and sends a Cushite, but Ahimaaz insists and outruns him (vv. 19-23). David waits between the gates as the watchman calls the runners in (vv. 24-27). Ahimaaz cannot answer the king's one question (vv. 28-30); the Cushite answers it (vv. 31-32).
verseByVerse.theology: The king asks one question, and asks it twice, and it is not about the battle. Twenty thousand men are dead in a forest, and he wants to know about one of them.
verseByVerse.examples: Joab, who is not a sentimental man, twice tried to stop Ahimaaz for the young man’s own sake. Ahimaaz arrived first, and when the king’s question came he could not bring himself to answer it.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Ahimaaz the son of Zadok said, "Let me run and carry news to the king that the LORD has delivered him from the hand of his enemies." And Joab said to him, "You are not to carry news today. You may carry news another day, but today you shall carry no news, because the king's son is dead." Then Joab said to the Cushite, "Go, tell the king what you have seen." The Cushite bowed before Joab, and ran. Then Ahimaaz the son of Zadok said again to Joab, "Come what may, let me also run after the Cushite." And Joab said, "Why will you run, my son, seeing that you will have no reward for the news?" "Come what may," he said, "I will run." So he said to him, "Run." Then Ahimaaz ran by the way of the plain, and outran the Cushite. Now David was sitting between the two gates, and the watchman went up to the roof of the gate by the wall, and when he lifted up his eyes and looked, he saw a man running alone. The watchman called out and told the king. And the king said, "If he is alone, there is news in his mouth." And he drew nearer and nearer. The watchman saw another man running. And the watchman called to the gate and said, "See, another man running alone!" The king said, "He also brings news." The watchman said, "I think the running of the first is like the running of Ahimaaz the son of Zadok." And the king said, "He is a good man and comes with good news." Then Ahimaaz cried out to the king, "All is well." And he bowed before the king with his face to the earth and said, "Blessed be the LORD your God, who has delivered up the men who raised their hand against my lord the king." And the king said, "Is it well with the young man Absalom?" Ahimaaz answered, "When Joab sent the king's servant, your servant, I saw a great commotion, but I do not know what it was." And the king said, "Turn aside and stand here." So he turned aside and stood still. And behold, the Cushite came, and the Cushite said, "Good news for my lord the king! For the LORD has delivered you this day from the hand of all who rose up against you." The king said to the Cushite, "Is it well with the young man Absalom?" And the Cushite answered, "May the enemies of my lord the king and all who rise up against you for evil be like that young man."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Ahimaaz wants to run. This is the young man who hid in a well at Bahurim under a covering of grain, and he has earned the right to ask. His message, the LORD has delivered him from the hand of his enemies, is a true sentence and a victory report, and it says nothing about a body in a pit.

And Joab, who has just put three javelins into the king’s son, will not let this young man be the one to report his death. It is one of the few kind things Joab does in this book, and it is clear-eyed. He knows what happens to the man who brings David that news: the Amalekite who came to Ziklag with Saul's crown, expecting a reward, was executed on the spot. The king's son is dead: Joab names it plainly, the only time he says it.

So he sends a foreigner instead. A Cushite is a man from south of Egypt, probably a slave or a mercenary, expendable in a way the son of the high priest is not. He bows and goes without a word. He was not asked whether he wanted to.

Ahimaaz asks a second time, and Joab tries again to talk him out of it, calling him my son. You will have no reward for the news: there is nothing in this for you. Whatever you think you are running towards, it is not there.

He goes anyway, takes the flat route by the Jordan valley, longer and quicker, and overtakes the man who left first. He wants to be the one who arrives. It has been his war too, and the thought of somebody else running up to the gate is more than he can bear. He has not thought about what he will say when he gets there.

The king is sitting in the gateway, between the inner and outer gates, where he cannot see anything himself. He has been there all day. He reads the runner as any commander would: a man alone is a messenger; men in numbers would be a rout. But the battle is not what he is thinking about.

And the next line is heartbreaking. He recognises a man by the way he runs, off a watchman's description, and immediately draws the conclusion he wants: he is a good man and comes with good news. He has been sitting between two gates all day with one question in his head, looking for any reason to believe the answer will be the one he wants.

Ahimaaz shouts it before he arrives: all is well. Shalom. And then the formal report, which is genuinely good theology: he gives the credit to God and does not say a word that is untrue.

Then the only question David has. The rebellion is over, the kingdom is his again, and he does not ask about the battle, or Joab, or whether Ittai survived, or how many of the twenty thousand were his own. He asks about one man, and calls him what he has always called him. And there is a terrible pun in the Hebrew: Ahimaaz shouted shalom, and David asks whether there is shalom for Absalom. The same word, and the answer is no.

Ahimaaz cannot say it. This young man, who knows exactly what happened, who was told plainly that the king's son is dead, says he saw a commotion and does not know what it was. It is a lie, and entirely understandable, and anybody who has ever had to tell somebody something like that will recognise the moment. Joab knew he could not do it. That is why he tried to stop him. One curt order from the king, and Ahimaaz is put to one side to wait.

The Cushite arrives second and opens the same way, and when the question comes he says it. Not he is dead, because that is not how such news was delivered; he uses the accepted formula, a wish rather than a report: may all the king’s enemies end as that young man has. It is meant kindly, in its way, and it is the plainest possible answer, and that young man gives David back his own words. The Cushite thinks he is bringing good news. He was sent by a commander who did not explain, to a king he does not know, and he says the correct thing in the correct form and expects to be thanked.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: David goes up to the chamber over the gate, weeping for his son.
verseByVerse.theology: My son, five times in one verse. It is not rhetoric; it is the way grief actually speaks.
verseByVerse.examples: Anyone who has wept like this over a child, or over anyone loved and lost, will find nothing here that tells them to stop. God gave this verse room in Scripture, and he gives grief room still.
