verseByVerse.quote: And the king was deeply moved and went up to the chamber over the gate and wept. And as he went, he said, "O my son Absalom, my son, my son Absalom! Would I had died instead of you, O Absalom, my son, my son!"
verseByVerse.commentary:
He goes up the stairs. The chamber over the gate is a small room above the gateway, the nearest thing to privacy in a fortified town. He walks away from the messenger without a word, climbs the stairs, and breaks.

As he went. He is saying it on the stairs, out loud, where the guards at the gate can hear every word. That detail matters, and Joab is going to throw it at him in the next chapter.

Now count. My son five times in one verse, Absalom three times, and in the next chapter, still going (19:4): eight times in two verses he says my son. This is not the lament for Saul and Jonathan, which was a poem written down and taught to the people of Judah. This is a man on a staircase saying the same two words over and over because there is nowhere else for them to go. Grief speaks like this. It circles. It does not develop or move on to a second point. It says the one true thing again.

Not "the rebel". Not Absalom the son of Maacah, as the book introduced him. Not the man who murdered Amnon, or drove his father out of Jerusalem, or would have killed him yesterday if the battle had gone the other way. My son. Every reason to hate him is true, and David is thinking of none of them. That is what a father is.

Would I had died instead of you is the oldest wish of love. Let it have been me. And in David's mouth it is useless, and he must have known it while he said it. If he had died in that forest, Absalom would have been a rebel king with his brother's blood on him and nothing changed in his heart, and the exchange would have purchased nothing at all.

Here the verse opens onto something larger, and it should be said carefully, because it helps only if the difference between David and Christ is kept clear. A thousand years later another Son of David, in David's own city, went out to die for rebels who had stolen the hearts of a kingdom away from its rightful King, who were his enemies by their own choice. He did not merely wish to die for them. He did it.

And the difference is not only that his death happened; it is that it worked. David's substitution would have been a gesture that saved nobody. Christ’s death actually achieved what it was for: while we were enemies we were reconciled to God by the death of his Son (Rom. 5:10). The rebels came home.

So David on that staircase is not a picture of the cross. He is a picture of the longing the cross answers: a father who wanted to die in his son's place and could not, crying out over a kingdom he had won and a boy he had lost. The one thing he wanted most in the world was impossible for him. It was not impossible for God.

19.title: The Return of the King
19.text: <sup>1</sup>It was told Joab, "Behold, the king is weeping and mourning for Absalom."<sup>2</sup>So the victory that day was turned into mourning for all the people, for the people heard that day, "The king is grieving for his son."<sup>3</sup>And the people stole into the city that day as people steal in who are ashamed when they flee in battle.<sup>4</sup>The king covered his face, and the king cried with a loud voice, "O my son Absalom, O Absalom, my son, my son!"<sup>5</sup>Then Joab came into the house to the king and said, "You have today covered with shame the faces of all your servants, who have this day saved your life and the lives of your sons and your daughters and the lives of your wives and your concubines,<sup>6</sup>because you love those who hate you and hate those who love you. For you have made it clear today that commanders and servants are nothing to you, for today I know that if Absalom were alive and all of us were dead today, then you would be pleased.<sup>7</sup>Now therefore arise, go out and speak kindly to your servants, for I swear by the LORD, if you do not go, not a man will stay with you this night, and this will be worse for you than all the evil that has come upon you from your youth until now."<sup>8</sup>Then the king arose and took his seat in the gate. And the people were all told, "Behold, the king is sitting in the gate." And all the people came before the king. Now Israel had fled every man to his own home.<sup>9</sup>And all the people were arguing throughout all the tribes of Israel, saying, "The king delivered us from the hand of our enemies and saved us from the hand of the Philistines, and now he has fled out of the land from Absalom.<sup>10</sup>But Absalom, whom we anointed over us, is dead in battle. Now therefore why do you say nothing about bringing the king back?"<sup>11</sup>And King David sent this message to Zadok and Abiathar the priests: "Say to the elders of Judah, 'Why should you be the last to bring the king back to his house, when the word of all Israel has come to the king?<sup>12</sup>You are my brothers; you are my bone and my flesh. Why then should you be the last to bring back the king?'<sup>13</sup>And say to Amasa, 'Are you not my bone and my flesh? God do so to me and more also, if you are not commander of my army from now on in place of Joab.'"<sup>14</sup>And he swayed the heart of all the men of Judah as one man, so that they sent word to the king, "Return, both you and all your servants."<sup>15</sup>So the king came back to the Jordan, and Judah came to Gilgal to meet the king and to bring the king over the Jordan.<sup>16</sup>And Shimei the son of Gera, the Benjaminite, from Bahurim, hurried to come down with the men of Judah to meet King David.<sup>17</sup>And with him were a thousand men from Benjamin. And Ziba the servant of the house of Saul, with his fifteen sons and his twenty servants, rushed down to the Jordan before the king,<sup>18</sup>and they crossed the ford to bring over the king's household and to do his pleasure. And Shimei the son of Gera fell down before the king, as he was about to cross the Jordan,<sup>19</sup>and said to the king, "Let not my lord hold me guilty or remember how your servant did wrong on the day my lord the king left Jerusalem. Do not let the king take it to heart.<sup>20</sup>For your servant knows that I have sinned. Therefore, behold, I have come this day, the first of all the house of Joseph to come down to meet my lord the king."<sup>21</sup>Abishai the son of Zeruiah answered, "Shall not Shimei be put to death for this, because he cursed the LORD's anointed?"<sup>22</sup>But David said, "What have I to do with you, you sons of Zeruiah, that you should this day be as an adversary to me? Shall anyone be put to death in Israel this day? For do I not know that I am this day king over Israel?"<sup>23</sup>And the king said to Shimei, "You shall not die." And the king gave him his oath.<sup>24</sup>And Mephibosheth the son of Saul came down to meet the king. He had neither taken care of his feet nor trimmed his beard nor washed his clothes, from the day the king departed until the day he came back in safety.<sup>25</sup>And when he came to Jerusalem to meet the king, the king said to him, "Why did you not go with me, Mephibosheth?"<sup>26</sup>He answered, "My lord, O king, my servant deceived me, for your servant said to him, 'I will saddle a donkey for myself, that I may ride on it and go with the king.' For your servant is lame.<sup>27</sup>He has slandered your servant to my lord the king. But my lord the king is like the angel of God; do therefore what seems good to you.<sup>28</sup>For all my father's house were but men doomed to death before my lord the king, but you set your servant among those who eat at your table. What further right have I, then, to cry to the king?"<sup>29</sup>And the king said to him, "Why speak any more of your affairs? I have decided: you and Ziba shall divide the land."<sup>30</sup>And Mephibosheth said to the king, "Oh, let him take it all, since my lord the king has come safely home."<sup>31</sup>Now Barzillai the Gileadite had come down from Rogelim, and he went on with the king to the Jordan, to escort him over the Jordan.<sup>32</sup>Barzillai was a very aged man, eighty years old. He had provided the king with food while he stayed at Mahanaim, for he was a very wealthy man.<sup>33</sup>And the king said to Barzillai, "Come over with me, and I will provide for you with me in Jerusalem."<sup>34</sup>But Barzillai said to the king, "How many years have I still to live, that I should go up with the king to Jerusalem?<sup>35</sup>I am this day eighty years old. Can I discern what is pleasant and what is not? Can your servant taste what he eats or what he drinks? Can I still listen to the voice of singing men and singing women? Why then should your servant be an added burden to my lord the king?<sup>36</sup>Your servant will go a little way over the Jordan with the king. Why should the king repay me with such a reward?<sup>37</sup>Please let your servant return, that I may die in my own city near the grave of my father and my mother. But here is your servant Chimham. Let him go over with my lord the king, and do for him whatever seems good to you."<sup>38</sup>And the king answered, "Chimham shall go over with me, and I will do for him whatever seems good to you, and all that you desire of me I will do for you."<sup>39</sup>Then all the people went over the Jordan, and the king went over. And the king kissed Barzillai and blessed him, and he returned to his own home.<sup>40</sup>The king went on to Gilgal, and Chimham went on with him. All the people of Judah, and also half the people of Israel, brought the king on his way.<sup>41</sup>Then all the men of Israel came to the king and said to the king, "Why have our brothers the men of Judah stolen you away and brought the king and his household over the Jordan, and all David's men with him?"<sup>42</sup>All the men of Judah answered the men of Israel, "Because the king is our close relative. Why then are you angry over this matter? Have we eaten at all at the king's expense? Or has he given us any gift?"<sup>43</sup>And the men of Israel answered the men of Judah, "We have ten shares in the king, and in David also we have more than you. Why then did you despise us? Were we not the first to speak of bringing back our king?" But the words of the men of Judah were fiercer than the words of the men of Israel.
19.overview:
The rebellion is over, and the king has to come home. First his own army has to be rescued from his grief: the men who saved his throne are creeping back into the city like a beaten army, and Joab, the man who killed Absalom, tells David the hardest truth anyone tells him in the whole book. David gets up and sits in the gate.

Then three men meet him on the road back. Shimei, who cursed him, arrives first with a thousand Benjaminites and is pardoned under oath. Mephibosheth, unwashed since the day the king left, shows Ziba's story to have been a lie, and David splits the estate rather than admit he judged carelessly. Barzillai, eighty years old, declines a place at court with a rare and honest speech about age, and sends his son instead. The chapter ends with Israel and Judah quarrelling over who escorted the king across the river, and the writer notes only which side shouted louder.
19.theology:
Stealing into the city (vv. 1-4). David’s men fought a hastily called-up national army in broken country and beat it, and saved the throne, and they come home in ones and twos, not meeting anyone's eye, because the lament was said aloud over the gate and the whole army heard it. Nobody said a word to them; no word was needed. A leader's private grief, however right, is never wholly private.

Joab is right, and Joab is the reason (vv. 5-7). The man who killed Absalom against a public order now orders the king to stop grieving, and every clause is true. His list of the household that would have died is accurate, since Absalom had already taken ten of the concubines on a roof. You love those who hate you is unfair as a statement about David's heart and exact as a description of what his behaviour has told everyone outside the room, and Joab is careful to claim only the second. The ultimatum is insolence, and it is also true: if the army walks out tonight, David has won a battle and lost a kingdom in the same week. This is the pattern of Joab throughout: he says the right thing, and he is the reason it needs saying.

And the king gets up (v. 8). Spoken to like that by the man who killed his son, he does not answer back or have him removed. Nothing here says the grief is over; it will not be over for the rest of his life. A duty owed to other people has been put in front of what he wants to do, which is what the office requires and what grief makes nearly impossible. The New Testament never asks anybody to stop grieving; it asks them not to grieve as others do who have no hope (1 Thess. 4:13). The grief stays. It does not get to run the household.

Amasa, and what it costs (v. 13). Offering the rebel general the royal command is a political masterstroke, since nothing reassures defeated rebels faster than seeing their own commander promoted rather than hanged. It is also personal, the one thing David can do about Joab. And it is Amasa's death warrant, because Joab does not give up a post; he kills the man who is given it.

Shimei, and the oath David did not keep (vv. 18-23). Shimei’s confession uses the right words, no one can tell whether he means them, and he is already bargaining with it. David's answer is magnificent: a secure man does not need to make an example of anybody, and a reign that resumes with a hanging at the river has told the whole country what to expect. But years later, dying, David names this very day to Solomon and tells him to bring Shimei's grey head down with blood (1 Kings 2:8-9). The book records both scenes and reconciles neither, and the notes on vv. 16-30 weigh the defences offered for David’s last instruction.

A pardon that holds. A king comes home across a river and decides what to do with those who rebelled, and the reader of the whole Bible cannot help setting the scene beside another King. David's word to Shimei was real and did not last; his son was told to undo it. Christ's pardon is spoken by a King who does not die and leave instructions, and it rests not on his mood on a day of celebration but on his own blood: no one will snatch them out of my hand (John 10:28), and there is therefore now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus (Romans 8:1). And Mephibosheth, who would rather have the king than the land, is a fair picture of what that pardon does to a heart; Paul counted everything loss because of the surpassing worth of knowing Christ Jesus my Lord (Philippians 3:8).

Half-justice (vv. 24-30). Mephibosheth's weeks of unwashed mourning, kept alone in a city under Absalom's control, and the plain fact that he cannot walk, settle the question. Yet the king who administered justice and equity to all his people (8:15) splits the land between the liar and the man he lied about, and does not want to hear more, because revisiting the judgment would mean admitting he made it carelessly. This is the second time in the book that David has fallen short of that description; the first was with Tamar. Mephibosheth's answer, let him take it all, is the last thing he says in Scripture, and nobody is obliged to believe he meant it. But he kept mourning when nobody was watching, walked in with no accusation prepared, and said his family deserved death and had been given a table instead. He never asked for the land in chapter 9 either.

Barzillai and honest old age (vv. 31-39). The power of his speech is its honesty. He does not pretend to be too humble for a court or make a show of declining an honour; he gives a plain account of what age has taken, judgment, taste and music, and concludes the offer would be wasted on him. He earned the place, and he can see that in Jerusalem he would be an old man who needs looking after. So he asks for a grave beside his parents, and then, having asked nothing for himself, asks for his son. Old age in Scripture is not a time to pretend, but neither is it a time when a person stops giving: he cannot use the offer, so he hands it to the next generation. David never forgot it (1 Kings 2:7).

The first crack (vv. 41-43). Both sides have a real point. Judah is the king's own tribe; Israel is ten-elevenths of the nation and raised the question first (vv. 9-10). Neither is lying and neither is listening, and David says nothing at all. Out of this quarrel comes Sheba's revolt in the very next verse, and two generations later the same words split the kingdom for good (1 Kings 12:16). A squabble at a river crossing about who escorted the king is the first visible crack in the thing that finally breaks Israel in half. Every large division starts somewhere this size.
19.examples:
Then: An eighty-year-old man who had fed a king's starving army at the risk of everything he owned was offered a permanent place at the royal table. He turned it down because he could no longer taste food or enjoy music, asked only to be buried near his parents, and sent his son in his place.

Now: Joab is the study in receiving a true rebuke from somebody with no right to give it. He had disobeyed a public order and killed the king's son, and he was still correct, and David got up and did what he said. Whether the person telling you is entitled to is a separate question from whether they are right, and most of us answer the first to avoid the second. Someone who knows he lives by a pardon he did not earn can afford to hear the truth from anybody. Barzillai is the study in knowing what you can no longer use: not false modesty but an honest inventory, and then asking for the next generation instead of yourself. And the quarrel at the end is the warning. Nobody in it was lying. It was about precedence and who was asked first, and the sentence shouted in it split the kingdom two generations later.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–15 — You Have Today Covered with Shame the Faces of All Your Servants
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The army steals back into the city ashamed while the king mourns (vv. 1-4). Joab rebukes David and warns that the army will leave him by nightfall (vv. 5-7), and the king takes his seat in the gate (v. 8). Then he works to bring Judah back, offering Amasa the command in place of Joab (vv. 9-15).
verseByVerse.theology: Joab’s rebuke is brutal, every word of it is true, and it comes from the man who caused the grief he is ordering the king to stop. Both facts stand.
verseByVerse.examples: David does what Joab says. He gets up and goes to sit where the army can see him, because the men who saved his kingdom deserve to see their king.

verseByVerse.quote: It was told Joab, "Behold, the king is weeping and mourning for Absalom." So the victory that day was turned into mourning for all the people, for the people heard that day, "The king is grieving for his son." And the people stole into the city that day as people steal in who are ashamed when they flee in battle. The king covered his face, and the king cried with a loud voice, "O my son Absalom, O Absalom, my son, my son!" Then Joab came into the house to the king and said, "You have today covered with shame the faces of all your servants, who have this day saved your life and the lives of your sons and your daughters and the lives of your wives and your concubines, because you love those who hate you and hate those who love you. For you have made it clear today that commanders and servants are nothing to you, for today I know that if Absalom were alive and all of us were dead today, then you would be pleased. Now therefore arise, go out and speak kindly to your servants, for I swear by the LORD, if you do not go, not a man will stay with you this night, and this will be worse for you than all the evil that has come upon you from your youth until now." Then the king arose and took his seat in the gate. And the people were all told, "Behold, the king is sitting in the gate." And all the people came before the king. Now Israel had fled every man to his own home. And all the people were arguing throughout all the tribes of Israel, saying, "The king delivered us from the hand of our enemies and saved us from the hand of the Philistines, and now he has fled out of the land from Absalom. But Absalom, whom we anointed over us, is dead in battle. Now therefore why do you say nothing about bringing the king back?" And King David sent this message to Zadok and Abiathar the priests: "Say to the elders of Judah, 'Why should you be the last to bring the king back to his house, when the word of all Israel has come to the king? You are my brothers; you are my bone and my flesh. Why then should you be the last to bring back the king?' And say to Amasa, 'Are you not my bone and my flesh? God do so to me and more also, if you are not commander of my army from now on in place of Joab.'" And he swayed the heart of all the men of Judah as one man, so that they sent word to the king, "Return, both you and all your servants." So the king came back to the Jordan, and Judah came to Gilgal to meet the king and to bring the king over the Jordan.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The lament over the gate was said out loud, and now the whole army knows.

The sentence about the army stealing in is terrible, and exact. These men won. They fought a hastily called-up national army in broken country and beat it, and twenty thousand of the enemy are dead. And they are coming back through the gate the way a beaten army comes home, quietly, in ones and twos, not meeting anybody's eye, because the king they did it for is upstairs crying over the man they killed. Nobody has said a word to them. That is the whole problem: no word was needed.

David is still saying my son: five times in the last verse of chapter 18 and three more here.

Joab walks in and says the hardest thing anybody says to David in the whole book. Before hearing it out, note who is speaking: the man told publicly to deal gently with Absalom, who put three javelins into him and had ten armour-bearers finish the body. Joab caused this grief. He is now ordering the king to stop it. And every word he says is true.

The list he begins with names what would have happened if the battle had gone the other way, and he is right. Absalom had already taken ten of those concubines on a roof; he was not going to spare the rest of the household.

You love those who hate you and hate those who love you cuts deepest. It is unfair as a statement about David's heart, and entirely fair as a description of what his behaviour has communicated. That distinction is the whole of Joab's argument. He is not claiming to know what the king feels. He is telling him what everyone outside that room has been given to understand.

And then the knife: the claim that the king would be pleased if Absalom lived and they had all died. Every man in that army has worked out the same arithmetic and none of them would ever have said it. Joab says it.

Then an ultimatum, sworn in the name of God, delivered by a general to his king. It is insolence, and it is also true. An army that believes its king despises it does not stay, and if those men walk out tonight, David has won a battle and lost a kingdom in the same week.

The king gets up and does it. That is remarkable. He does not answer back, does not defend himself, and does not have Joab removed. He walks down and sits in the gate where every man coming in can see him.

It is not a change of feeling; the grief will not be over for the rest of his life. He has put the duty he owes to other people in front of what he wants to do, which is what the office requires and what grief makes nearly impossible.

Meanwhile the country is embarrassed, and the tribes argue while nobody acts. They anointed Absalom, and he is dead in a pit under a heap of stones, and nobody wants to be the first to propose fetching David, because everyone backed the other side so recently.

He uses the priests again, the same two men who ran his intelligence during the flight. And he uses the phrase the elders of Israel used to him at Hebron when they made him king: we are your bone and flesh (5:1), the country's own words quoted back to his own tribe. Judah is the awkward case. Absalom launched the revolt from Hebron, Judah's own town, and the tribe is now the most compromised in Israel and the most nervous.

Here is David finally moving against Joab, and it is a considerable moment. Amasa led the force that fought in the forest of Ephraim, and David is offering him the royal command, permanently, sworn with an oath.

Two things are going on at once. It is a political masterstroke: nothing would reassure the defeated rebels faster than seeing their own general promoted rather than executed. And it is personal. Joab killed his son against a direct order and then humiliated him in his own room, and David cannot punish him, and this is the one thing he can do.

He is also, though he does not know it, signing Amasa's death warrant. Joab does not give up a post; he kills the man who is given it, and the reader who remembers Abner at the gate of Hebron knows how chapter 20 ends.

Behind the oath to Amasa lies a familiar formula, “God do so to me and more also”: may God punish me if I do not keep my word.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 16–30 — Shall Anyone Be Put to Death in Israel This Day?
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Shimei comes down with a thousand Benjaminites and confesses (vv. 16-20); Abishai wants his head, and David swears that Shimei will not die (vv. 21-23). Then Mephibosheth, in mourning since the day the king left, explains that Ziba deceived him (vv. 24-28). David divides the land between them, and Mephibosheth gives up his share (vv. 29-30).
verseByVerse.theology: The pardon at the Jordan is genuine in the moment, and it does not hold. The book records both the oath and the deathbed instruction, and leaves the tension standing.
verseByVerse.examples: Mephibosheth's appearance makes his account far more credible than Ziba's, yet David will not reverse his judgment. The man who was wronged does not argue; what matters to him is that the king is home.

verseByVerse.quote: And Shimei the son of Gera, the Benjaminite, from Bahurim, hurried to come down with the men of Judah to meet King David. And with him were a thousand men from Benjamin. And Ziba the servant of the house of Saul, with his fifteen sons and his twenty servants, rushed down to the Jordan before the king, and they crossed the ford to bring over the king's household and to do his pleasure. And Shimei the son of Gera fell down before the king, as he was about to cross the Jordan, and said to the king, "Let not my lord hold me guilty or remember how your servant did wrong on the day my lord the king left Jerusalem. Do not let the king take it to heart. For your servant knows that I have sinned. Therefore, behold, I have come this day, the first of all the house of Joseph to come down to meet my lord the king." Abishai the son of Zeruiah answered, "Shall not Shimei be put to death for this, because he cursed the LORD's anointed?" But David said, "What have I to do with you, you sons of Zeruiah, that you should this day be as an adversary to me? Shall anyone be put to death in Israel this day? For do I not know that I am this day king over Israel?" And the king said to Shimei, "You shall not die." And the king gave him his oath. And Mephibosheth the son of Saul came down to meet the king. He had neither taken care of his feet nor trimmed his beard nor washed his clothes, from the day the king departed until the day he came back in safety. And when he came to Jerusalem to meet the king, the king said to him, "Why did you not go with me, Mephibosheth?" He answered, "My lord, O king, my servant deceived me, for your servant said to him, 'I will saddle a donkey for myself, that I may ride on it and go with the king.' For your servant is lame. He has slandered your servant to my lord the king. But my lord the king is like the angel of God; do therefore what seems good to you. For all my father's house were but men doomed to death before my lord the king, but you set your servant among those who eat at your table. What further right have I, then, to cry to the king?" And the king said to him, "Why speak any more of your affairs? I have decided: you and Ziba shall divide the land." And Mephibosheth said to the king, "Oh, let him take it all, since my lord the king has come safely home."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The man who threw stones is at the river first. He hurried, and the reason is arithmetic. He cursed the LORD's anointed in public at a moment when he was sure David was finished, and David is not finished, and he has perhaps a day to get in front of him before somebody else raises the subject.

He brings a thousand men of Saul's own tribe, which is not repentance; it is a delegation. A king does not execute a man standing in front of a thousand of his own tribesmen on the first day of a reconciliation. And Ziba is there too, with his whole household, having done extremely well out of the rebellion.

He says the right words and he says them first, and both are the point. Your servant knows that I have sinned is a proper confession, and there is no way to tell from outside whether he means it. What can be observed is the sentence he attaches to it: the first of all the house of Joseph to come down. He is already bargaining: I got here before the northern tribes, so remember it in my favour.

Abishai, for the third time in these books, offers to kill somebody: Saul asleep at Hachilah, Shimei on the hillside, Shimei at the Jordan. He is a brave and useful man with exactly one idea, and this time he is quoting the law: cursing the LORD's anointed was a capital matter. He has a case.

David’s answer is magnificent, and he will not hold to it to the end of his life. This is the day the kingdom came back, and executions do not belong in it. A reign that resumes with a hanging at the river has told the whole country what to expect, and David will not start that way.

Do I not know that I am this day king over Israel? A secure man does not need to make an example of anybody. It is the same instinct that spared Saul twice.

He swears it, the strongest undertaking available to him. And now the honest difficulty, which should not be smoothed over. Some years later, dying, David gives Solomon his final instructions, and Shimei is on the list: and there is also with you Shimei the son of Gera... who cursed me with a grievous curse on the day when I went to Mahanaim. But when he came down to meet me at the Jordan, I swore to him by the LORD, saying, "I will not put you to death with the sword." Now therefore do not hold him guiltless... bring his gray head down with blood to Sheol (1 Kings 2:8-9). He remembers the oath and this exact day, and tells his son to do what he promised not to do himself.

There is no reading of that which makes it admirable. Some argue that Shimei's later conduct forfeited the protection, that the oath bound David personally and not the crown, and that a king has a duty to justice as well as to his word. Those arguments are not worthless. They also amount to keeping the letter of an oath while arranging for its substance to be broken by somebody else. The book records both scenes and does not reconcile them. The mercy at the Jordan is real. The deathbed instruction is real. He was capable of both.

Then the man Ziba lied about, and he does not have to say a word. He has not washed, not trimmed his beard, not changed his clothes, since the morning David walked out. Those are the signs of mourning, kept for weeks, alone, in a city under Absalom's control, visible to anybody who cared to look. The man Ziba described was waiting to be given his grandfather's kingdom. This man has been in mourning for the king since the day he left.

The king's question has an edge on it. The answer is complete, and turns on the one fact everybody knew. He cannot walk. He asked Ziba to saddle a donkey so that he could follow, and Ziba took the donkeys, two of them, loaded with food, and went alone, and got there first, and told a story. The lameness that made him harmless in chapter 9 is what made him helpless here.

And the argument he makes is not a demand for justice. His whole family should have been executed as a matter of course when David took the throne, and instead he was given a seat at the king's table. Against that, what claim could he press?

The king's ruling is a bad one, and it should be said plainly. Mephibosheth's account explains everything and Ziba's does not. Ziba's story required a crippled pensioner with no faction and no army to be expecting the tribes to crown him during a coup by David's own son, and David gave Ziba the estate for that story in one sentence. Now comes the proper hearing, and the verdict is to split the land between the liar and the man he lied about.

Why speak any more of your affairs? He does not want to hear it. He is tired, and he has a kingdom to reassemble, and revisiting the judgment means admitting he made it carelessly in the first place.

This is the king who administered justice and equity to all his people (8:15), and this is the second time in this book that he has fallen short of that description: first with Tamar, now here.

And the last thing Mephibosheth ever says in Scripture is the best line in the chapter. He has been slandered, robbed of his inheritance, and half-vindicated by a king who will not look properly at the evidence, and his answer is that Ziba can have the whole estate, because the king is home.

Nobody is obliged to believe he meant it. But look at the man who says it. He kept mourning when nobody was watching and there was no advantage in it. He walked in without a single accusation prepared. He said his family deserved death and had been given a table instead. And when he was half-robbed, he gave up the other half. He asked for nothing in chapter 9 either.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 31–40 — How Many Years Have I Still to Live?
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Barzillai, eighty years old and very wealthy, escorts the king to the Jordan, and David invites him to Jerusalem (vv. 31-33). He declines because of his age, asks to die near his parents' grave, and offers Chimham in his place (vv. 34-38). The king kisses him and blesses him, and he goes home (vv. 39-40).
verseByVerse.theology: This is one of the finest passages on old age in Scripture, and its power is the honesty with which an old man counts what has gone.
verseByVerse.examples: He asks nothing for himself except a grave near his parents, and the son he sends in his place is remembered in a place name four hundred years later.

verseByVerse.quote: Now Barzillai the Gileadite had come down from Rogelim, and he went on with the king to the Jordan, to escort him over the Jordan. Barzillai was a very aged man, eighty years old. He had provided the king with food while he stayed at Mahanaim, for he was a very wealthy man. And the king said to Barzillai, "Come over with me, and I will provide for you with me in Jerusalem." But Barzillai said to the king, "How many years have I still to live, that I should go up with the king to Jerusalem? I am this day eighty years old. Can I discern what is pleasant and what is not? Can your servant taste what he eats or what he drinks? Can I still listen to the voice of singing men and singing women? Why then should your servant be an added burden to my lord the king? Your servant will go a little way over the Jordan with the king. Why should the king repay me with such a reward? Please let your servant return, that I may die in my own city near the grave of my father and my mother. But here is your servant Chimham. Let him go over with my lord the king, and do for him whatever seems good to you." And the king answered, "Chimham shall go over with me, and I will do for him whatever seems good to you, and all that you desire of me I will do for you." Then all the people went over the Jordan, and the king went over. And the king kissed Barzillai and blessed him, and he returned to his own home. The king went on to Gilgal, and Chimham went on with him. All the people of Judah, and also half the people of Israel, brought the king on his way.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Barzillai is one of the three men who brought bedding and cheese to Mahanaim when David arrived with nothing (17:27-29).

Eighty years old and very rich, and he fed an army. The writer puts the two facts together, and there is a third implied. This man backed the losing side of a civil war at his own expense, at an age when nobody would have blamed him for staying out of it. If Absalom had won, an old landowner in Gilead who had provisioned David's army would not have kept his estate or his life.

David offers him a place at court, the highest thing he has to give, exactly what he gave Mephibosheth.

Now one of the finest speeches in the Old Testament, and it is entirely about being old. How many years have I still to live? He is not being morbid; he is doing arithmetic. What would be the point of uprooting himself now?

Then the inventory, and its power is that he is honest about it. Three questions, and each names something that has gone.

Can I discern what is pleasant and what is not? Judgment, in the ordinary sense of appreciating things properly.

Can your servant taste what he eats or what he drinks? His palate has gone. A court is a place of feasts, and food is wasted on him.

Can I still listen to the voice of singing men and singing women? His hearing, or his appetite for music, or both. And this one is the saddest, because David is a musician, and what Barzillai is saying is that the best thing about the king's table is a thing he can no longer enjoy.

He does not pretend to be too humble for a court, or claim he is more useful at home. He gives a plain and rather bleak account of what age has taken from him and concludes that the offer would be wasted on him. That is a rare kind of honesty. Most of us would take the seat and pretend to enjoy the singing.

And then the sentence a great many people cannot say: why then should your servant be an added burden? He has earned the place. He fed the king's army when it was starving and risked everything to do it. And he can see that what he would actually be, in Jerusalem, is an old man who needs looking after. He would rather not be that.

He will walk him across the river and no further. Even the escort is measured out.

The one thing he asks for is a grave: to die in his own city, near where his parents are buried. Not a title, not land, not a position. And then, having asked nothing for himself, he asks for somebody else. Here is your servant Chimham, probably his son (1 Kings 2:7 speaks of the sons of Barzillai). That is what an old man's request looks like when he has understood his own position. He cannot use the offer; the next generation can.

And it was not a small thing. Four hundred years later, when Jerusalem has fallen and the last Judeans are fleeing to Egypt, Jeremiah notes where they stopped: they went and stayed at Geruth Chimham near Bethlehem (Jer. 41:17). The name probably means "the lodging-place of Chimham". David probably gave that family land near Bethlehem, his own town, and the name outlasted the kingdom.

A kiss at a river, and an old man walks back up into Gilead to die at home. It is the last we hear of him, except that on his deathbed, giving Solomon the list of people to deal with, David includes one instruction that is not about revenge: but deal loyally with the sons of Barzillai the Gileadite, and let them be among those who eat at your table, for with such loyalty they met me when I fled from Absalom your brother (1 Kings 2:7). He never forgot the cheese and the bedding.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 41–43 — The Words of the Men of Judah Were Fiercer
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The men of Israel complain that Judah has taken the king over the Jordan without them (v. 41); Judah answers that he is their kinsman (v. 42); Israel claims ten shares in the king, and Judah answers more fiercely still (v. 43).
verseByVerse.theology: The rebellion is over, and the argument that starts here is worse, because it is not about Absalom. It is ten tribes against one, over precedence, and both sides are partly right.
verseByVerse.examples: The chapter ends by telling us how heated the exchange was, not how it was settled, because it was not settled, and the very next verse is a rebel’s trumpet. Quarrels about who was honoured first rarely stay small.

verseByVerse.quote: Then all the men of Israel came to the king and said to the king, "Why have our brothers the men of Judah stolen you away and brought the king and his household over the Jordan, and all David's men with him?" All the men of Judah answered the men of Israel, "Because the king is our close relative. Why then are you angry over this matter? Have we eaten at all at the king's expense? Or has he given us any gift?" And the men of Israel answered the men of Judah, "We have ten shares in the king, and in David also we have more than you. Why then did you despise us? Were we not the first to speak of bringing back our king?" But the words of the men of Judah were fiercer than the words of the men of Israel.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The war is over and the argument begins immediately. The complaint is about precedence: Judah escorted the king across the river and the other ten tribes were not invited. That is the entire subject.

And the word they use is stolen, the same verb the writer used of Absalom stealing the hearts of the men of Israel (15:6). They are accusing Judah of doing to the king what Absalom did to them.

Judah's answer has two parts. The first is honest and unhelpful: the king is our close relative. Of course we brought him home. The second is defensive: we have taken nothing and had no favours. That is true, but it does not answer the complaint.

Israel's reply is arithmetic: ten shares, ten tribes to your one. And their last question is fair: they were the first to speak of bringing back the king. Verses 9 and 10 recorded the northern tribes arguing about it while Judah said nothing, and David had to send the priests to prod Judah into moving.

So both sides have a real point. Judah is the king's tribe. Israel is ten-elevenths of the nation and raised the question first. Neither is lying, and neither is listening.

And the chapter ends by telling us only how heated the argument was, because it had no outcome. It does not say who was right, or what the king decided: David says nothing at all in this exchange. It says only that Judah shouted louder.

The first sentence of the next chapter is a man from Benjamin blowing a trumpet: we have no portion in David, and we have no inheritance in the son of Jesse; every man to his tents, O Israel! (20:1). Sheba's rebellion comes directly out of this quarrel, and it is over in a chapter. The quarrel is not.

Two generations later, when Rehoboam has answered the north with a threat about scorpions, the ten tribes walk out of the assembly saying this: what portion do we have in David? We have no inheritance in the son of Jesse. To your tents, O Israel! (1 Kings 12:16). The same words. The kingdom splits at that sentence and never comes back together.

So this small squabble at a river crossing is the first visible crack in the thing that finally breaks Israel in half. It is about who was asked first, and whose relative he is, and who felt slighted, and it is louder on one side than the other. Every large division starts somewhere this size.

20.title: Sheba's Revolt and the Wise Woman of Abel
20.text: <sup>1</sup>Now there happened to be there a worthless man, whose name was Sheba, the son of Bichri, a Benjaminite. And he blew the trumpet and said, "We have no portion in David, and we have no inheritance in the son of Jesse; every man to his tents, O Israel!"<sup>2</sup>So all the men of Israel withdrew from David and followed Sheba the son of Bichri. But the men of Judah followed their king steadfastly from the Jordan to Jerusalem.<sup>3</sup>And David came to his house at Jerusalem. And the king took the ten concubines whom he had left to care for the house and put them in a house under guard and provided for them, but did not go in to them. So they were shut up until the day of their death, living as if in widowhood.<sup>4</sup>Then the king said to Amasa, "Call the men of Judah together to me within three days, and be here yourself."<sup>5</sup>So Amasa went to summon Judah, but he delayed beyond the set time that had been appointed him.<sup>6</sup>And David said to Abishai, "Now Sheba the son of Bichri will do us more harm than Absalom. Take your lord's servants and pursue him, lest he get himself to fortified cities and escape from us."<sup>7</sup>And there went out after him Joab's men and the Cherethites and the Pelethites, and all the mighty men. They went out from Jerusalem to pursue Sheba the son of Bichri.<sup>8</sup>When they were at the great stone that is in Gibeon, Amasa came to meet them. Now Joab was wearing a soldier's garment, and over it was a belt with a sword in its sheath fastened on his thigh, and as he went forward it fell out.<sup>9</sup>And Joab said to Amasa, "Is it well with you, my brother?" And Joab took Amasa by the beard with his right hand to kiss him.<sup>10</sup>But Amasa did not observe the sword that was in Joab's hand. So Joab struck him with it in the stomach and spilled his entrails to the ground without striking a second blow, and he died. Then Joab and Abishai his brother pursued Sheba the son of Bichri.<sup>11</sup>And one of Joab's young men took his stand by Amasa and said, "Whoever favors Joab, and whoever is for David, let him follow Joab."<sup>12</sup>And Amasa lay wallowing in his blood in the highway. And anyone who came by, seeing him, stopped. And when the man saw that all the people stopped, he carried Amasa out of the highway into the field and threw a garment over him.<sup>13</sup>When he was taken out of the highway, all the people went on after Joab to pursue Sheba the son of Bichri.<sup>14</sup>And Sheba passed through all the tribes of Israel to Abel of Beth-maacah, and all the Bichrites assembled and followed him in.<sup>15</sup>And all the men who were with Joab came and besieged him in Abel of Beth-maacah. They cast up a mound against the city, and it stood against the rampart, and they were battering the wall to throw it down.<sup>16</sup>Then a wise woman called from the city, "Listen! Listen! Tell Joab, 'Come here, that I may speak to you.'"<sup>17</sup>And he came near her, and the woman said, "Are you Joab?" He answered, "I am." Then she said to him, "Listen to the words of your servant." And he answered, "I am listening."<sup>18</sup>Then she said, "They used to say in former times, 'Let them but ask counsel at Abel,' and so they settled a matter.<sup>19</sup>I am one of those who are peaceable and faithful in Israel. You seek to destroy a city that is a mother in Israel. Why will you swallow up the heritage of the LORD?"<sup>20</sup>Joab answered, "Far be it from me, far be it, that I should swallow up or destroy!<sup>21</sup>That is not true. But a man of the hill country of Ephraim, called Sheba the son of Bichri, has lifted up his hand against King David. Give up him alone, and I will withdraw from the city." And the woman said to Joab, "Behold, his head shall be thrown to you over the wall."<sup>22</sup>Then the woman went to all the people in her wisdom. And they cut off the head of Sheba the son of Bichri and threw it out to Joab. So he blew the trumpet, and they dispersed from the city, every man to his home. And Joab returned to Jerusalem to the king.<sup>23</sup>Now Joab was in command of all the army of Israel; and Benaiah the son of Jehoiada was in command of the Cherethites and the Pelethites;<sup>24</sup>and Adoram was in charge of the forced labor; and Jehoshaphat the son of Ahilud was the recorder;<sup>25</sup>and Sheva was secretary; and Zadok and Abiathar were priests;<sup>26</sup>and Ira the Jairite was also David's priest.
20.overview: Out of the quarrel at the Jordan comes a new revolt. Sheba, a man of no standing, blows a trumpet and gives the angry northern tribes a slogan, and the north walks out. His revolt is over in twenty verses, but his slogan will outlive him and, two generations later, divide the kingdom for good. Meanwhile the ten concubines bear the cost of what Absalom did in chapter 16; Joab murders Amasa, the commander David appointed in his place, exactly as he murdered Abner; and a wise woman of Abel, with no office and no name recorded, stops a siege with three sentences from a wall. The chapter closes with David's list of officials, and the first name on it is Joab's.
20.theology:
The slogan that outlives the man (v. 1). Sheba did not create the grievance. He found ten tribes freshly humiliated at the river and handed them words for what they already felt, which is all such men ever do. He loses within the chapter; his slogan wins two generations later.

The King who mends the split. Sheba’s slogan names a division that is never healed within the Old Testament. The prophets saw the cure in a coming son of David: one king shall be king over them all, and they shall be no longer two nations, with my servant David as their one shepherd (Ezekiel 37:22, 24). The New Testament finds that King in Jesus, who died to gather into one the children of God who are scattered abroad (John 11:52) and broke down the wall between Jew and Gentile (Ephesians 2:14). In him nobody need shout that they have no portion in David: every believer has an inheritance kept in heaven (1 Peter 1:4), and quarrels over precedence, as old as that river crossing, meet a Son of David who washed his disciples' feet.

Why a king had concubines at all (v. 3). A reader will ask it. A concubine was a wife of lower rank, without the full standing of a wife. Scripture records the practice without approving it: the law forbade Israel's king to multiply wives (Deuteronomy 17:17), the pattern from creation is one man and one woman (Genesis 2:24), and Jesus returns to that beginning (Matthew 19:4-6). Nearly every polygamous household in the Old Testament breeds rivalry and grief, and David's is the plainest case. The ten women shut in a house for life, living as if in widowhood, are its saddest result.

David still will not use Joab (v. 6). He gives the order to Abishai and goes round Joab through his brother, which is a weak arrangement, since Abishai has spent his life doing what Joab does, and the troops who march out are called Joab's men. David's assessment of the danger is right, though: Absalom wanted the throne, but Sheba wants the country in two pieces.

Worse than Abner (vv. 8-10). The method is the same: the greeting, the hand on the beard, the single blow to the stomach. But Abner was an enemy commander who had killed Joab's brother; Amasa is the commander of the royal army, appointed by David under oath only days before. This is a serving officer murdering the man the king set over him, in front of the troops, to get his job back, and verse 23 records that he got it. David's one attempt to discipline Joab was to give his post to someone else, and Joab answered it with a sword.

The body in the road (vv. 12-13). The army stops dead at the sight of the king's commander lying in his own blood, until someone drags him into a field and throws a cloak over him, and then the column moves on. The writer makes no comment of his own, and needs none: for the army the problem was never the death, but that it could be seen. Covering a wrong is not the same as dealing with it, and David, years later and dying, still cannot deal with it himself (1 Kings 2:5).

The wise woman of Abel (vv. 16-22). Unlike the woman of Tekoa, who was found, dressed and scripted by Joab, this woman has no employer and no script. She tells Joab what the town is, a place of counsel; establishes that she and it are loyal; and then names what he is about to do: destroy a mother in Israel and swallow up the heritage of the LORD. The land is not his to destroy, because every town is part of an inheritance God gave. Joab, who has just killed a man in a road, backs down at once. She is the third woman in this history, after Abigail and the woman of Tekoa, to turn events with nothing but words, and she asks nothing for herself.

A new office, and what it becomes (v. 24). Adoram over the forced labour is not in the chapter 8 list; the kingdom has acquired conscripted labour and a minister to run it. Under Solomon it becomes vast, and when he dies the northern tribes ask Rehoboam to lighten the hard service of your father and his heavy yoke (1 Kings 12:4). He refuses, and they stone Adoram (1 Kings 12:18). So both halves of the final split are already in this chapter: the slogan in verse 1 and the grievance in verse 24.

The list is a mercy and an indictment (vv. 23-26). It mirrors the one at the end of chapter 8, which came after the conquests. This one comes after Bathsheba, Amnon, Tamar, Absalom, the flight, the forest and Sheba, and says the same thing in the same form. The government works, and the ordinary business of governing goes on, which is how God generally keeps the world running after a catastrophe. Yet the two things that will destroy the kingdom are already inside the administration and drawing a salary: Joab at the top, unpunished, and Adoram over the forced labour, unnoticed.
20.examples:
Then: A woman with no office, no name recorded, and no one who sent her leaned over a city wall while the army of Israel was battering it down, called the commander-in-chief to come and talk, and stopped the siege. Then she went inside and persuaded the whole city to do the hard thing she had promised on their behalf.

Now: Sheba is the study in how a fracture happens. He had no case and no following, and it did not matter, because the grievance was already there and all he supplied was a sentence for it. Watch who hands people words for what they are already feeling, and remember that in the Son of David nobody is without a portion. The body in the road is a warning of another kind: once it was covered nobody had to decide anything, which is exactly how institutions, churches included, handle a thing they have no intention of dealing with. And the woman of Abel is the best example of the three. She did not plead, and asked nothing for herself. She told a violent man what his action really was, and then she went and did the part that cost something. Courage of that kind does not need a title.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–3 — We Have No Portion in David
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Sheba the son of Bichri blows a trumpet and calls Israel away from David (v. 1). The north follows him; Judah stays with the king (v. 2). David returns to Jerusalem and shuts the ten concubines in a guarded house for life (v. 3).
verseByVerse.theology: The last sentence of the previous chapter was that Judah shouted louder than Israel. This is what happens next: one man with a trumpet finds ten tribes already angry and gives them a slogan.
verseByVerse.examples: Words matter. A slogan shouted by a nobody in a moment of wounded pride outlived him and, two generations later, broke the kingdom in two.

verseByVerse.quote: Now there happened to be there a worthless man, whose name was Sheba, the son of Bichri, a Benjaminite. And he blew the trumpet and said, "We have no portion in David, and we have no inheritance in the son of Jesse; every man to his tents, O Israel!" So all the men of Israel withdrew from David and followed Sheba the son of Bichri. But the men of Judah followed their king steadfastly from the Jordan to Jerusalem. And David came to his house at Jerusalem. And the king took the ten concubines whom he had left to care for the house and put them in a house under guard and provided for them, but did not go in to them. So they were shut up until the day of their death, living as if in widowhood.
verseByVerse.commentary:
There happened to be there. The writer's phrasing is almost dismissive, and it is the point. Sheba is nobody. He has no army, no standing, no faction and no case; the word used of him, worthless, is the one Nabal’s servants used of Nabal and Shimei used of David. What he has is a trumpet and a sentence, and he is standing in the middle of an argument that was already burning.

Twelve words in Hebrew, and they will eventually break the kingdom. No portion and no inheritance are land words, the vocabulary of tribal allotment: the house of David is Judah's business and the north has no stake in it. The son of Jesse is a sneer with a history, what Saul called David when he would not use his name (1 Sam. 20:27; 22:7). Every man to his tents is the formula for breaking up a national muster: go home, this is not our war.

Now recall the last sentence of the previous chapter: Judah's words were fiercer (19:43). Ten tribes have just been shouted down in a quarrel over precedence at a river crossing, and a man with a trumpet gives them a slogan. He did not create the grievance. He found it fully formed and put words to it, which is all such men ever do.

The whole north walks out. The rebellion is over in twenty verses and it does not matter. What matters is that the country divided along the exact line it will divide along permanently: ten tribes on one side, Judah on the other.

Two generations from now Rehoboam will answer a northern delegation with a threat about scorpions, and this is what they say as they go: what portion do we have in David? We have no inheritance in the son of Jesse. To your tents, O Israel! (1 Kings 12:16). Close enough to be an echo, and the kingdom never comes back together. This chapter is showing us not so much a rebellion as the line along which the kingdom will break. Sheba loses; the slogan wins.

Then the cost of chapter 16, borne by ten women who had done nothing wrong. They appear first in a sentence that reads like a housekeeping note: David left them to keep the house when he fled (15:16). Then Ahithophel advised Absalom to take them publicly, and it was done in the sight of all Israel (16:22), on the roof, which is where the whole business began (11:2).

Now David comes home and has to decide what to do with them, and there is no good answer. He cannot take them back; the custom of the time, and probably the principle of Deuteronomy 24:4, made that impossible. He does not send them away either. He provides for them: a house, a guard, food, for the rest of their lives. And the writer records the result in one clause. They will not marry, will not have children, will not leave that house, and will be fed and housed and forgotten.

They chose none of it: not to be royal concubines, not to be left behind, and certainly not the roof. Two men conducted a political argument through their bodies, and the cost is paid entirely by them. Uriah did not choose it. Tamar did not choose it. Twenty thousand men in a forest did not choose it. Sin does not confine its damage to the people who commit it.

David has his throne again. Absalom is dead. These ten are alive, and shut in a house, and that is the last we hear of them.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 4–13 — Is It Well with You, My Brother?
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Amasa is slow to muster Judah, so David sends Abishai after Sheba, and Joab's men go with him (vv. 4-7). At the great stone in Gibeon, Joab greets Amasa as a brother and kills him with one blow (vv. 8-10). The army halts at the body until it is dragged from the road and covered, and the pursuit goes on under Joab (vv. 11-13).
verseByVerse.theology: Every element of this repeats Abner's murder: the affectionate greeting, the hand, the stomach, the one blow. Amasa's mistake is Abner's too: he did not look for a weapon in the hand of a man calling him brother.
verseByVerse.examples: The difference is that Amasa is the king's own appointed commander. The army halts at the body because it does not know what has just happened to the chain of command.

verseByVerse.quote: Then the king said to Amasa, "Call the men of Judah together to me within three days, and be here yourself." So Amasa went to summon Judah, but he delayed beyond the set time that had been appointed him. And David said to Abishai, "Now Sheba the son of Bichri will do us more harm than Absalom. Take your lord's servants and pursue him, lest he get himself to fortified cities and escape from us." And there went out after him Joab's men and the Cherethites and the Pelethites, and all the mighty men. They went out from Jerusalem to pursue Sheba the son of Bichri. When they were at the great stone that is in Gibeon, Amasa came to meet them. Now Joab was wearing a soldier's garment, and over it was a belt with a sword in its sheath fastened on his thigh, and as he went forward it fell out. And Joab said to Amasa, "Is it well with you, my brother?" And Joab took Amasa by the beard with his right hand to kiss him. But Amasa did not observe the sword that was in Joab's hand. So Joab struck him with it in the stomach and spilled his entrails to the ground without striking a second blow, and he died. Then Joab and Abishai his brother pursued Sheba the son of Bichri. And one of Joab's young men took his stand by Amasa and said, "Whoever favors Joab, and whoever is for David, let him follow Joab." And Amasa lay wallowing in his blood in the highway. And anyone who came by, seeing him, stopped. And when the man saw that all the people stopped, he carried Amasa out of the highway into the field and threw a garment over him. When he was taken out of the highway, all the people went on after Joab to pursue Sheba the son of Bichri.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Amasa's first task in his new job, and he is late. The writer does not say why. He was Absalom's general only weeks ago and may have found Judah unwilling to muster for him; he may simply have been slow. What matters is that the delay gives Joab a reason to be in the road at Gibeon.

Note who David speaks to: Abishai, not Joab. He is still refusing to give Joab a command, and going round him through his brother, a thin arrangement, since Abishai has spent his whole life doing what Joab does. And his assessment is right: Absalom wanted the throne; Sheba wants the country in two pieces.

Joab’s men. Joab holds no command, and the army is still his.

The sword falls out of the sheath as Joab walks. The Hebrew is awkward and has been argued over for centuries. It may mean that the sword genuinely worked loose and he picked it up, so that Amasa sees him bend down and stand up with a blade in his hand and thinks nothing of it. Or the whole arrangement was contrived so that the weapon would be in his left hand while his right was empty and reaching out. Either way the writer tells us before the greeting, so that we watch the greeting knowing what is in the hand.

Is it well with you, my brother? They are cousins; their mothers were sisters. Brother is not much of an exaggeration. Taking a man by the beard with the right hand to kiss him is the most intimate greeting available between men in that culture. It requires him to stand still and put his face forward. It only works if you are trusted, it occupies the right hand, and it puts the other man's stomach eighteen inches from your left.

Now go back seventeen chapters: And when Abner returned to Hebron, Joab took him aside into the midst of the gate to speak with him privately, and there he struck him in the stomach, so that he died (3:27). The same man. The same wound, in the same place. The same method. And here the writer adds that he needed no second blow. He knows exactly where to put it.

Amasa's mistake is Abner's. Neither saw the weapon, and neither was looking for one, because a man who takes you by the beard and calls you brother is not a man you are watching.

What Joab has done here is worse than the murder of Abner. Abner was the enemy commander and there was a blood feud: Abner had killed Asahel. Amasa is the commander of the royal army, appointed by David personally, under oath, only days ago. This is not private vengeance; it is a serving officer murdering the man the king put over him, in front of the troops, to get his job back. And he gets it; verse 23 says so.

This is what happens when a king cannot discipline his general. David's one attempt to act against Joab was to give the command to somebody else, and Joab answered it with a sword, and by the end of the chapter he is back at the head of the list.

He steps over the body and carries on with the campaign. A soldier stands beside the corpse shouting a loyalty formula, and the order of the names is whoever favors Joab, and whoever is for David. Joab first. That is either a slip or it is not, and either way it is an accurate description of who is running this army.

Here is the writer's comment on the whole business, made without a word of his own. The army will not walk past. Every man who comes up the road sees the king's commander lying in his own blood and stops dead, and the column jams. They know what they are looking at: not a battle casualty, but the man the king put in charge, killed by the man he replaced. So the young man drags him into a field and puts a cloak over him, and the moment he is covered the army moves again.

That is the point to keep. The problem was never the death; the problem was that it could be seen. Get it out of the road and throw something over it and the campaign proceeds and nobody has to decide anything.

Nothing more is said about Amasa until David is dying and tells Solomon: you also know what Joab the son of Zeruiah did to me, how he dealt with the two commanders of the armies of Israel, Abner the son of Ner, and Amasa the son of Jether, whom he killed, avenging in time of peace for blood that had been shed in war (1 Kings 2:5). Even then he cannot punish Joab himself. He asks his son to.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 14–22 — A City and a Mother in Israel
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Sheba is besieged in Abel of Beth-maacah (vv. 14-15). A wise woman calls Joab to the wall and argues for the city (vv. 16-19). Joab asks only for Sheba; she persuades the city, Sheba's head is thrown over the wall, and the army disperses (vv. 20-22).
verseByVerse.theology: She is hired by nobody and scripted by nobody. The woman of Tekoa came with Joab's words in her mouth; this one calls him to the wall on her own authority and argues with him.
verseByVerse.examples: Her argument is not a plea. She tells him what the place is, and then names what he is about to do in words he cannot answer.

verseByVerse.quote: And Sheba passed through all the tribes of Israel to Abel of Beth-maacah, and all the Bichrites assembled and followed him in. And all the men who were with Joab came and besieged him in Abel of Beth-maacah. They cast up a mound against the city, and it stood against the rampart, and they were battering the wall to throw it down. Then a wise woman called from the city, "Listen! Listen! Tell Joab, 'Come here, that I may speak to you.'" And he came near her, and the woman said, "Are you Joab?" He answered, "I am." Then she said to him, "Listen to the words of your servant." And he answered, "I am listening." Then she said, "They used to say in former times, 'Let them but ask counsel at Abel,' and so they settled a matter. I am one of those who are peaceable and faithful in Israel. You seek to destroy a city that is a mother in Israel. Why will you swallow up the heritage of the LORD?" Joab answered, "Far be it from me, far be it, that I should swallow up or destroy! That is not true. But a man of the hill country of Ephraim, called Sheba the son of Bichri, has lifted up his hand against King David. Give up him alone, and I will withdraw from the city." And the woman said to Joab, "Behold, his head shall be thrown to you over the wall." Then the woman went to all the people in her wisdom. And they cut off the head of Sheba the son of Bichri and threw it out to Joab. So he blew the trumpet, and they dispersed from the city, every man to his home. And Joab returned to Jerusalem to the king.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Sheba runs the length of the country to the far north, near the sources of the Jordan, about as far from Jerusalem as it is possible to get and still be in Israel. And note what following he has left: all the Bichrites, his own clan. The ten tribes who followed him out of the argument in chapter 19 went home.

They build a siege ramp against an Israelite town and start knocking the wall in. And a woman shouts down off the wall and summons the commander-in-chief of Israel to come and talk to her.

She is called a wise woman, the same phrase used of the woman of Tekoa, and the difference between them is the whole point. The woman of Tekoa was found by Joab, dressed by Joab, and given a speech to recite; the writer says so twice. This one has no employer. Nobody sent her or scripted her. She has looked over a wall at a siege ramp and decided to negotiate.

The exchange is short and businesslike, and Joab stops the assault to have it.

She opens by telling him what the town is. Abel had a reputation as a place people came to for a ruling, a town of counsel, and there was evidently a proverb about it. So her first move is not a plea for mercy. It is information: you are battering the wall of the place people come to when they want a matter resolved, and you did not think to ask anybody anything before you started.

Then three sentences, each putting a name on what he is doing.

I am one of those who are peaceable and faithful in Israel. She establishes her right to be heard. She is not a rebel and neither is the town.

A city that is a mother in Israel is how an important town with dependent villages was spoken of, a place that has daughters. Knock it down and you are not taking a fortress; you are killing a mother and orphaning everything around her.

Why will you swallow up the heritage of the LORD? And there is the theological argument, and it is the one that settles the matter. The land is not Joab's to destroy. Every town in Israel is part of an inheritance God distributed, and a general who flattens one is not conducting an operation; he is consuming what belongs to God.

The picture is close to Abner's at Gibeon: shall the sword devour forever? (2:26).

He backs down instantly, and even repeats her verb. This is Joab, who killed Abner at a gate and Absalom in a tree and Amasa in a road on the way here. He does not argue with her or threaten her. He answers the argument on its own terms, and states his actual objective, which is one man, and she agrees to it before consulting anybody.

The woman went to all the people in her wisdom. She has no office and no authority. She tells the town the terms and persuades them, and a whole city does what she says. The result is brutal and it is arithmetic: one head over a wall instead of a town under it.

She is the third such woman in this history, and the pattern is worth noticing. Abigail came down a mountain track with two hundred loaves and stopped David from slaughtering every male in Nabal's household, with a theological argument about bloodguilt (1 Sam. 25). The woman of Tekoa changed the succession of Israel with a story. This woman stops the army of Israel from destroying a city, with three sentences, from a wall. None of them holds any office at all.

And she never asks for anything for herself. She does not negotiate terms for her own household or trade information for a reward. She argues about what the town is and what the land is, and then she goes and does the hard part. We never learn her name.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 23–26 — Now Joab Was in Command
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The chapter closes with the list of David's officials, headed by Joab over the army (vv. 23-26).
verseByVerse.theology: The list mirrors the one at the end of chapter 8 and does the same work: the crisis is over, and the kingdom is in ordered operation again.
verseByVerse.examples: The first name on it is Joab, back at the head of the army days after murdering the king's appointed commander. Order has returned, but not justice. And a new post appears, Adoram over the forced labour, the grievance on which the north will one day secede.

verseByVerse.quote: Now Joab was in command of all the army of Israel; and Benaiah the son of Jehoiada was in command of the Cherethites and the Pelethites; and Adoram was in charge of the forced labor; and Jehoshaphat the son of Ahilud was the recorder; and Sheva was secretary; and Zadok and Abiathar were priests; and Ira the Jairite was also David's priest.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Joab's name comes in the first clause. Only days ago the king appointed Amasa to that post, personally, with an oath, from now on in place of Joab (19:13). Joab met Amasa in a road, called him brother, took him by the beard, and killed him. And the first name on the list of officials is Joab’s.

Not a word of censure. No inquiry, no charge, no demotion. The murder of the king's own commander in front of the army is followed, thirteen verses later, by an administrative note recording that the murderer has the job.

That is the verdict on the chapter and on the whole reign. David could not touch him. He said so at 3:39 after Abner, these men, the sons of Zeruiah, are more severe than I, and he is still saying it as a dying man, handing the problem to a son who will finally do what he never could (1 Kings 2:5-6).

Then a name that was not on the list in chapter 8. Adoram's office over the forced labour is new; there was no such post when the earlier cabinet was recorded (8:16-18). Somewhere in the intervening years the kingdom has acquired conscripted labour and a minister to run it. Remember that name.

Under Solomon the forced labour becomes vast, and when he dies the northern tribes come to Rehoboam with one request: your father made our yoke heavy. Now therefore lighten the hard service of your father and his heavy yoke on us, and we will serve you (1 Kings 12:4). He refuses, with the line about scorpions. Then King Rehoboam sent Adoram, who was taskmaster over the forced labor, and all Israel stoned him to death with stones (1 Kings 12:18).

The same office and, if the years allow it, very possibly the same man. The tribes stone the labour minister and go home with Sheba's sentence from verse 1 in their mouths. So both halves of the final split are already in this one chapter: the slogan in verse 1 and the grievance in verse 24.

The list closes the way the list in chapter 8 closed, and the parallel is deliberate. That one came after the conquests: here is the kingdom, ordered, at its height. This one comes after Bathsheba, Amnon, Tamar, Absalom, the flight, the forest, and Sheba, and says the same thing in the same form. The offices are filled. The government works.

That is a real mercy and should be seen as one. A kingdom that has been through all this still has a cabinet, and the ordinary business of governing goes on, which is how God generally keeps the world running after a catastrophe.

The list is also an indictment, because of the first name on it and the third. Joab at the top, unpunished. Adoram over the forced labour, unnoticed. The reign is restored, and the two things that will destroy the kingdom are already inside the administration, drawing a salary.

The Cherethites and Pelethites were David’s foreign bodyguard, probably from Crete and Philistia. Ira the “priest” was most likely a royal official or chaplain; the word was also used of David’s sons (8:18) for chief ministers.

21.title: The Gibeonites' Vengeance; War with Philistines
21.text: <sup>1</sup>Now there was a famine in the days of David for three years, year after year. And David sought the face of the LORD. And the LORD said, "There is bloodguilt on Saul and on his house, because he put the Gibeonites to death."<sup>2</sup>So the king called the Gibeonites and spoke to them. Now the Gibeonites were not of the people of Israel but of the remnant of the Amorites. Although the people of Israel had sworn to spare them, Saul had sought to strike them down in his zeal for the people of Israel and Judah.<sup>3</sup>And David said to the Gibeonites, "What shall I do for you? And how shall I make atonement, that you may bless the heritage of the LORD?"<sup>4</sup>The Gibeonites said to him, "It is not a matter of silver or gold between us and Saul or his house; neither is it for us to put any man to death in Israel." And he said, "What do you say that I shall do for you?"<sup>5</sup>They said to the king, "The man who consumed us and planned to destroy us, so that we should have no place in all the territory of Israel,<sup>6</sup>let seven of his sons be given to us, so that we may hang them before the LORD at Gibeah of Saul, the chosen of the LORD." And the king said, "I will give them."<sup>7</sup>But the king spared Mephibosheth, the son of Saul's son Jonathan, because of the oath of the LORD that was between them, between David and Jonathan the son of Saul.<sup>8</sup>The king took the two sons of Rizpah the daughter of Aiah, whom she bore to Saul, Armoni and Mephibosheth; and the five sons of Merab the daughter of Saul, whom she bore to Adriel the son of Barzillai the Meholathite;<sup>9</sup>and he gave them into the hands of the Gibeonites, and they hanged them on the mountain before the LORD, and the seven of them perished together. They were put to death in the first days of harvest, at the beginning of barley harvest.<sup>10</sup>Then Rizpah the daughter of Aiah took sackcloth and spread it for herself on the rock, from the beginning of harvest until rain fell upon them from the heavens. And she did not allow the birds of the air to come upon them by day, or the beasts of the field by night.<sup>11</sup>When David was told what Rizpah the daughter of Aiah, the concubine of Saul, had done,<sup>12</sup>David went and took the bones of Saul and the bones of his son Jonathan from the men of Jabesh-gilead, who had stolen them from the public square of Beth-shan, where the Philistines had hanged them, on the day the Philistines killed Saul on Gilboa.<sup>13</sup>And he brought up from there the bones of Saul and the bones of his son Jonathan; and they gathered the bones of those who were hanged.<sup>14</sup>And they buried the bones of Saul and his son Jonathan in the land of Benjamin in Zela, in the tomb of Kish his father. And they did all that the king commanded. And after that God responded to the plea for the land.<sup>15</sup>There was war again between the Philistines and Israel, and David went down together with his servants, and they fought against the Philistines. And David grew weary.<sup>16</sup>And Ishbi-benob, one of the descendants of the giants, whose spear weighed three hundred shekels of bronze, and who was armed with a new sword, thought to kill David.<sup>17</sup>But Abishai the son of Zeruiah came to his aid and attacked the Philistine and killed him. Then David's men swore to him, "You shall no longer go out with us to battle, lest you quench the lamp of Israel."<sup>18</sup>After this there was again war with the Philistines at Gob.
