Then Sibbecai the Hushathite struck down Saph, who was one of the descendants of the giants.<sup>19</sup>And there was again war with the Philistines at Gob, and Elhanan the son of Jaare-oregim, the Bethlehemite, struck down Goliath the Gittite, the shaft of whose spear was like a weaver's beam.<sup>20</sup>And there was again war at Gath, where there was a man of great stature, who had six fingers on each hand, and six toes on each foot, twenty-four in number, and he also was descended from the giants.<sup>21</sup>And when he taunted Israel, Jonathan the son of Shimei, David's brother, struck him down.<sup>22</sup>These four were descended from the giants in Gath, and they fell by the hand of David and by the hand of his servants.
21.overview:
Chapters 21 to 24 are an appendix to the book, arranged by theme rather than date: the famine probably came earlier in the reign, after Mephibosheth was brought to court (chapter 9), and the battles with giants come from various years.

The chapter opens with a hard story. A three-year famine is traced to Saul's breaking of Israel's ancient oath to the Gibeonites, and seven of Saul's descendants are handed over and put to death, while Mephibosheth is spared because David keeps his own oath to Jonathan. Then Rizpah, the mother of two of the seven, keeps watch over the bodies for months until the king hears of it and gives them, with Saul and Jonathan, a proper grave; only then does the writer say that God answered the plea for the land. The chapter closes with four battles against giants, in which an old and weary David is nearly killed and his men resolve that the lamp of Israel must not be put out.
21.theology:
The oath that held for centuries (v. 2). In Joshua 9 Israel was tricked into a treaty by the Gibeonites, discovered the fraud within three days, and kept the oath anyway because it had been sworn by the LORD (Josh. 9:19). It held through the whole period of the judges. Saul broke it in a fit of national zeal, and nothing in 1 Samuel records the act; we hear of it only here. Why should a whole nation suffer for it? Because the oath was Israel's, sworn by its leaders in God's name, and Saul broke it as Israel's king; Scripture holds a people answerable for what is done in its name until it is put right.

What the text asserts, and what it does not (vv. 3-6). It asserts bloodguilt, the guilt of shedding innocent blood, and God names it: blood shed on the land defiles the land (Num. 35:33), and Saul is beyond execution. It does not assert that God commanded the remedy. There is no oracle; David asks the injured party what they want and agrees in four words, though Israel's law says children are not to be put to death for their fathers (Deut. 24:16). The notes on vv. 1-9 set out what has been said to ease the difficulty. Some of it is probably right, none of it makes the scene comfortable, and the narrator does not try to make it comfortable either. He reports what was asked and done, and then spends five verses on a woman sitting on a rock.

One oath avenged and one oath kept (v. 7). Seven men die because Saul broke a promise sworn in the LORD's name; one crippled man lives, and keeps his place at the king's table, because David keeps one. That is the chapter's real subject: the weight of a promise with God's name on it.

Rizpah (vv. 10-11). A woman with no husband, no standing and no protector, whose family has been destroyed twice, at Gilboa and now at Gibeah, plants herself in public beside the evidence of a royal decision and stays until the rains come. She had been in this book once before, as the woman Ish-bosheth and Abner quarrelled over for political reasons (3:7), and she said nothing then either. Keeping the animals from her sons' bodies is the only thing left she can give them, and she gives it. And something happens because of her: the king hears, and gives the dead the burial the chapter had so far denied them. The writer sets her beside the men of Jabesh-gilead, who walked all night to take Saul's body off a Philistine wall (1 Sam. 31:11-13). Both acted for people who could do nothing for them, and both because the bodies of the dead matter to God.

Where the writer puts God's answer (v. 14). And after that God responded to the plea for the land. After what? The executions were in April; if they had settled it, the rain should have come then. The answer is recorded after Rizpah, after the bones were fetched, after a burial. The writer draws no conclusion, as he never does, but a reader may notice it.

So was it right, and where does it lead? The bloodguilt was real and God named it; the remedy was the Gibeonites' demand and David's decision, and the text never praises it. Many careful readers think David should have asked the LORD before agreeing, as he had asked about the cause, though the narrator does not say so. What no Christian may take from it is that God makes children pay for their parents' sins: the son shall not suffer for the iniquity of the father (Ezekiel 18:20). And the chapter's darkest image is one the gospel answers. The law it strains against says a hanged man is cursed (Deuteronomy 21:23), and Paul applies that very law to the cross: Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law by becoming a curse for us (Galatians 3:13). The seven were handed over against their will for another man's sin. He gave himself, the righteous for the unrighteous (1 Peter 3:18), and his blood does what theirs could not: it takes guilt away, so that the blessing promised to Abraham reaches the nations (Galatians 3:14).

And David grew weary (v. 15). The boy who ran at a giant with a sling is an old man on a battlefield who cannot keep going, and Abishai, the man who wanted to spear Saul in his sleep and behead Shimei, saves him. The sons of Zeruiah were more severe than David, and they also kept him alive.

The lamp of Israel (v. 17). His men swear that he will never go into battle again, out of love and out of plain calculation, and being told by the people who love you that you can no longer do the thing that defined you is a real grief of old age. The phrase they reach for becomes a word for God’s covenant promise to David: God keeps a tribe for Solomon's son that David my servant may always have a lamp before me in Jerusalem (1 Kings 11:36), and says it again at 1 Kings 15:4 and 2 Kings 8:19. Soldiers used it about a tired man on a battlefield, and Scripture carried it for centuries, until the promise was kept in the Son of David.

The Elhanan difficulty (v. 19). Here Elhanan kills Goliath, where 1 Chronicles 20:5 says he killed Goliath's brother. The likeliest explanation is a copyist's slip in Samuel, discussed in the notes on vv. 15-22; it costs nothing to admit, and the narrative of 1 Samuel 17 stands on its own.

By the hand of David and by the hand of his servants (v. 22). David killed none of the four giants, and the credit is given to David and his servants together. That is what a reign looks like at the end: the work goes on, other men do it, and the man who cannot go out any more is still named in the account, because he is why they are there.
21.examples:
Then: A woman whose two sons had been handed over by the king and hanged on a hill spread sackcloth on the rock beside their bodies and stayed there from April until the autumn rains, so that nothing would eat her children. The king heard what she had done, and went and gave them a grave.

Now: Rizpah is the study in doing the only thing left. She could not undo the sentence, appeal it, or bury them, but there was one thing she could do, and she did it for half a year without a word, and it moved a king. Most people faced with a wrong they cannot fix do nothing at all, on the grounds that what they could do would not be enough. Grieving people, too, may find in her that faithful love for the dead is not wasted. The chapter's other subject is the weight of a promise with God's name on it: a treaty extracted by fraud that Israel kept for centuries, and one man's life spared because David remembered what he had sworn to a friend dead for decades. We keep our word because the God whose name is on it keeps his, and every promise he made us is Yes in Christ (2 Corinthians 1:20); where we have broken ours, the way back is to own it and make it right, as this chapter does, at cost.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–9 — There Is Bloodguilt on Saul
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: A three-year famine is traced to Saul's bloodguilt against the Gibeonites, whom Israel had sworn to spare (vv. 1-2). David asks what will make it right, and they demand seven of Saul's sons (vv. 3-6). Mephibosheth is spared because of David's oath to Jonathan, and the seven are put to death at the beginning of barley harvest (vv. 7-9).
verseByVerse.theology: The oath Saul broke was the one Israel swore to the Gibeonites in Joshua 9 and kept for centuries, even though it had been obtained by fraud. The bloodguilt is real.
verseByVerse.examples: Keep the distinction the text keeps: David asked the Gibeonites what they wanted and did it. The text does not say God commanded it, and it records God answering the plea for the land only after a burial (v. 14).

verseByVerse.quote: Now there was a famine in the days of David for three years, year after year. And David sought the face of the LORD. And the LORD said, "There is bloodguilt on Saul and on his house, because he put the Gibeonites to death." So the king called the Gibeonites and spoke to them. Now the Gibeonites were not of the people of Israel but of the remnant of the Amorites. Although the people of Israel had sworn to spare them, Saul had sought to strike them down in his zeal for the people of Israel and Judah. And David said to the Gibeonites, "What shall I do for you? And how shall I make atonement, that you may bless the heritage of the LORD?" The Gibeonites said to him, "It is not a matter of silver or gold between us and Saul or his house; neither is it for us to put any man to death in Israel." And he said, "What do you say that I shall do for you?" They said to the king, "The man who consumed us and planned to destroy us, so that we should have no place in all the territory of Israel, let seven of his sons be given to us, so that we may hang them before the LORD at Gibeah of Saul, the chosen of the LORD." And the king said, "I will give them." But the king spared Mephibosheth, the son of Saul's son Jonathan, because of the oath of the LORD that was between them, between David and Jonathan the son of Saul. The king took the two sons of Rizpah the daughter of Aiah, whom she bore to Saul, Armoni and Mephibosheth; and the five sons of Merab the daughter of Saul, whom she bore to Adriel the son of Barzillai the Meholathite; and he gave them into the hands of the Gibeonites, and they hanged them on the mountain before the LORD, and the seven of them perished together. They were put to death in the first days of harvest, at the beginning of barley harvest.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Three years of failed harvests, and then David asks the LORD. The writer does not say what took him three years, and it is a fair question. A famine in Israel was understood to be a covenant matter, since the blessings and curses of Deuteronomy tie rain to obedience, and a king might have been expected to enquire in the first bad year rather than the third. When he does ask, the answer is about something that happened before he was king.

To understand it you have to go back to Joshua 9. When Israel came into the land, the Gibeonites saw what had happened to Jericho and Ai and decided to survive by fraud. They sent an embassy in worn-out sandals, carrying mouldy bread, claiming to be from a distant country, and asked for a treaty. Joshua and the elders did not enquire of the LORD, the text says so explicitly, and made the treaty and swore to it.

Three days later the fraud came out. They were neighbours. The congregation wanted to kill them, and the leaders refused, and the reason they gave is the whole point: they had sworn by the LORD (Josh. 9:19). They had been tricked into an oath, and they kept it, because it had God's name on it. The Gibeonites became woodcutters and water-carriers for the sanctuary and lived among Israel unharmed for centuries.

Then Saul broke it. Nothing in 1 Samuel records this, and the writer gives one clause about the motive: in his zeal for the people of Israel and Judah. That is the man who would not carry out the ban on Amalek (God's command to destroy it completely) when God commanded it, and did carry it out on Nob, a town of Israel's own priests, when nobody commanded it (1 Sam. 22:19). Zeal for Israel, applied to the wrong people, twice.

David asks the Gibeonites what they want. Hold on to that verb, because the moral question of the chapter turns on it. He does not enquire of the LORD what should be done. He was told what the problem was; he now asks the injured party to name the price. They refuse money and disclaim the right to execute anybody, and he presses them again. They name seven of Saul's sons, and David agrees in four words.

Honesty here means being exact about what the text says and what it does not. What it says: there was bloodguilt, and God named it. Blood shed on the land was understood to defile the land itself, and Numbers is explicit that no atonement can be made for the land for the blood that is shed in it, except by the blood of the one who shed it (Num. 35:33). Saul is dead and beyond execution. The Gibeonites ask for his house instead.

What it does not say: that God commanded this. There is no oracle here. God told David what the famine was about; the remedy is the Gibeonites' proposal and David's decision. When the writer finally records God acting, it is at the end of verse 14, after a burial.

And there is a further difficulty, because Israel's own law raises it: fathers shall not be put to death because of their children, nor shall children be put to death because of their fathers. Each one shall be put to death for his own sin (Deut. 24:16). Seven men die here for what their father did.

Various things have been said to ease this difficulty. That the ancient world reckoned bloodguilt to a household, and that Deuteronomy 24 governs the ordinary courts rather than a covenant breach at national level. That these sons may have shared in the killing; the text does not say. That an oath sworn in God's name and publicly broken is a different order of thing from a private crime. Some of that is probably right. None of it makes the scene comfortable, and the narrator does not try to.

In the middle of it, one man is spared, and the reason is an oath. Seven men die because Saul broke an oath sworn in the LORD's name. One man lives because David keeps an oath sworn in the LORD's name. Break one and the land does not yield for three years. Keep one and a crippled man eats at the king's table while his cousins are executed.

Two of the seven belong to Rizpah, and the writer names them. She has been in this book before: the concubine of Saul over whom Ish-bosheth accused Abner, in the quarrel that lost the house of Saul its kingdom (3:7). She was a political question then, argued over by men, and she said nothing.

The last clause is a date, and it is about to matter. Barley harvest is April.

Was the execution of Saul’s sons just, given that children must not die for their fathers (Deut 24:16)? Saul had broken Israel’s oath to the Gibeonites and slaughtered them (v. 1), and the famine showed God’s anger. Many think Saul’s house shared in the massacre (v. 1, There is bloodguilt on Saul and on his house), though the text does not say these seven did. Was it human sacrifice? Not in the sense of an offering to God: it was an execution, demanded by the injured party as justice for Saul’s bloodguilt and granted by David. God sent rain only after David also buried Saul’s and Jonathan’s bones (v. 14); Scripture records the event without making it a pattern. The five sons were Merab’s; most Hebrew manuscripts read “Michal”, an early copying slip, since Merab married Adriel (1 Sam 18:19).
verseByVerse.note: Gibeon lay a few miles north-west of Jerusalem, in the territory of Benjamin, Saul's own tribe (Josh. 18:25).

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Rizpah keeps watch over the bodies from harvest until the rains (v. 10). David is told, and brings the bones of Saul and Jonathan from Jabesh-gilead (vv. 11-12). All are buried in the tomb of Kish, and then God responds to the plea for the land (vv. 13-14).
verseByVerse.theology: Barley harvest is April, and the rains come in the autumn. For five or six months a mother sat beside seven bodies, two of them her sons, so that they would not be eaten.
verseByVerse.examples: It is Rizpah's doing that ends the chapter properly. Only when the king is told what she has done does he fetch Saul's bones and give them all a grave. A concubine with no power sat on a rock until the king of Israel did the right thing.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Rizpah the daughter of Aiah took sackcloth and spread it for herself on the rock, from the beginning of harvest until rain fell upon them from the heavens. And she did not allow the birds of the air to come upon them by day, or the beasts of the field by night. When David was told what Rizpah the daughter of Aiah, the concubine of Saul, had done, David went and took the bones of Saul and the bones of his son Jonathan from the men of Jabesh-gilead, who had stolen them from the public square of Beth-shan, where the Philistines had hanged them, on the day the Philistines killed Saul on Gilboa. And he brought up from there the bones of Saul and the bones of his son Jonathan; and they gathered the bones of those who were hanged. And they buried the bones of Saul and his son Jonathan in the land of Benjamin in Zela, in the tomb of Kish his father. And they did all that the king commanded. And after that God responded to the plea for the land.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Here is the heart of the chapter, and it is one woman doing something nobody asked her to do.

Take the timing first, because everything depends on it. Barley harvest is around April. The autumn rains usually come in October or November. That is perhaps five or six months. She spreads sackcloth, the coarse cloth of mourning, on the rock where the bodies are, and she stays there through a summer with no shelter, into the autumn. She does not go home at night. There is nobody to take turns with.

The bodies were left exposed, which was the point of the execution, though the law required even a criminal to be taken down and buried the same day "so that you do not defile your land" (Deut. 21:23). So the vultures come in daylight, and she drives them off. At night the jackals and hyenas come, and she drives them off too, alone, in the dark, beside seven decomposing bodies, two of which are her children. Every day for perhaps a hundred and eighty days.

She cannot bring them back and she cannot bury them; nobody has given her permission. What she can do is stop the animals eating them, and so she does that, for half a year, the only thing left that she can give them.

There is no speech from her. She does not accuse David, or curse the Gibeonites, or appeal to anybody. The book does not record a single word from Rizpah in her whole life. She sits on a rock.

And it should be said what she is up against. She is a woman with no husband, no standing, no protector and no legal claim, whose family has been destroyed twice over and whose sons were handed over by the reigning king. Nothing prevents anyone doing as they like to her, and she plants herself in public beside the evidence of a royal decision and stays there until the rains come.

This is the verse that turns the chapter. Something happens because of her. Word gets back, as it would; a woman on a rock for five months is not a private act. And what David does next is the thing the chapter had left undone until now: he buries the dead.

He goes across the Jordan for Saul's bones, and the writer takes a whole verse to remind us how those bones got to Jabesh-gilead. When Saul died on Gilboa the Philistines nailed his body and his sons' bodies to the wall at Beth-shan, and the men of Jabesh-gilead walked all night through occupied country, took them down, and buried them (1 Sam. 31:11-13), because of one night decades earlier when Saul had saved their town. The first act of David's reign was a thank-you letter to those men for it (2:5-7).

So the chapter now has two acts of loyalty to the dead side by side: a town that walked all night to take four bodies off a wall, and a woman who sat on a rock for five months to keep the birds off seven more. Both for people who could do nothing for them, and both because bodies matter.

All of them go into the family tomb: Saul, Jonathan, and the seven. And note where the writer has put the last clause. And after that God responded to the plea for the land.

After what?

The executions were months earlier, in April. If the hangings had settled the matter, the rain should have come then. The writer says the answer came after that: after Rizpah, after the bones were fetched, after seven men and a king and a prince were laid in a grave in Benjamin. He does not draw the conclusion for us. But he has arranged the sequence with some care, and a reader is entitled to notice that God's answer is recorded immediately after a burial and not after an execution.

And the burial happened because a woman with nothing sat on a rock until somebody told the king.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: David grows weary in battle and is nearly killed by Ishbi-benob, but Abishai saves him, and his men swear he will no longer go out to battle (vv. 15-17). Three more giants fall to David's men (vv. 18-21), and the summary credits David and his servants together (v. 22).
verseByVerse.theology: The man who killed a giant as a boy is nearly killed by one as an old man, and is saved by his nephew. His army then keeps him from the field, and the name they give him, the lamp of Israel, becomes a word for God’s promise to David.
verseByVerse.examples: Verse 19 is a well-known difficulty, set out in the notes below. Saying a reading is uncertain is better than inventing a certainty.

verseByVerse.quote: There was war again between the Philistines and Israel, and David went down together with his servants, and they fought against the Philistines. And David grew weary. And Ishbi-benob, one of the descendants of the giants, whose spear weighed three hundred shekels of bronze, and who was armed with a new sword, thought to kill David. But Abishai the son of Zeruiah came to his aid and attacked the Philistine and killed him. Then David's men swore to him, "You shall no longer go out with us to battle, lest you quench the lamp of Israel." After this there was again war with the Philistines at Gob. Then Sibbecai the Hushathite struck down Saph, who was one of the descendants of the giants. And there was again war with the Philistines at Gob, and Elhanan the son of Jaare-oregim, the Bethlehemite, struck down Goliath the Gittite, the shaft of whose spear was like a weaver's beam. And there was again war at Gath, where there was a man of great stature, who had six fingers on each hand, and six toes on each foot, twenty-four in number, and he also was descended from the giants. And when he taunted Israel, Jonathan the son of Shimei, David's brother, struck him down. These four were descended from the giants in Gath, and they fell by the hand of David and by the hand of his servants.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And David grew weary. Three words, and they are the end of something. This is the man who ran at a giant with a sling and came back with the head, who broke the Philistines from Geba to Gezer. He is now an old man on a battlefield who cannot keep going.

A descendant of the giants, with a heavy spear and new equipment, sees the king of Israel struggling and moves in. The symmetry is unmistakable and the writer sets it up without a word of comment. A boy killed a Philistine giant in the Valley of Elah and made his name doing it. Decades later a Philistine giant nearly kills the same man because he is too tired to defend himself.

Abishai saves his life: the man who wanted to spear Saul in his sleep, and twice to behead Shimei, and whose brother murdered three men. When David is on the ground with a giant standing over him, Abishai is the one who gets there. The sons of Zeruiah were more severe than David, and they also kept him alive.

His own men take him off the battlefield. They swear it, which makes it binding, and they do it out of love and out of arithmetic. He is worth ten thousand of them, as they told him before the forest of Ephraim, and Israel would not survive his death in a skirmish. It is still a hard verse. Being told by the people who love you that you can no longer do the thing that defined you is one of the recognisable griefs of getting old, and the writer places it right after David grew weary.

And note the phrase they choose: the lamp of Israel. It becomes a word for God’s covenant promise. When the kingdom is torn away from Solomon, God keeps one tribe for his son that David my servant may always have a lamp before me in Jerusalem (1 Kings 11:36). It is said again of Abijam (1 Kings 15:4), and again when Judah deserves destruction: the LORD was not willing to destroy Judah, for the sake of David his servant, since he promised to give a lamp to him and to his sons forever (2 Kings 8:19).

The lamp is the promise of chapter 7 in a single image, a light God undertakes not to let go out. His soldiers used the word about a tired man on a battlefield, and Scripture carried it for centuries, and the promise it carries, I have prepared a lamp for my anointed (Psalm 132:17), is kept in the Son of David whose kingdom will have no end (Luke 1:33).

Then one of the best-known textual difficulties in the Old Testament, and the honest thing is to lay it out. This verse says Elhanan killed Goliath the Gittite, and describes his spear in the exact words used in 1 Samuel 17:7. But 1 Samuel 17 says David killed Goliath, in one of the most detailed narratives in the book. And 1 Chronicles, recording the same list, reads: Elhanan the son of Jair struck down Lahmi the brother of Goliath the Gittite, the shaft of whose spear was like a weaver's beam (1 Chron. 20:5).

There are three positions. The first, which most translators and commentators take, is that the Samuel text has suffered a copyist's slip and Chronicles preserves the original. The Hebrew words involved are easily confused in the older script, and a scribe's eye dropping the brother of is a recognised kind of error. On this reading Elhanan killed Goliath's brother, and there is no conflict. The second is that Chronicles is a later attempt to smooth out an awkward verse; that is the minority view. The third, occasionally suggested, is that Elhanan was David's original name. There is no real evidence for it, the men have different fathers, and it should be set aside.

What matters is not to pretend the difficulty is not there. The likeliest explanation is a copying error in a name. That is what textual criticism, the careful comparing of manuscripts, is for, and admitting it costs nothing; the account of David and Goliath in 1 Samuel 17 stands on its own.

When he taunted Israel. It is the same Hebrew verb as Goliath's defiance in the valley for forty days, and a nephew of David's kills this man for it.

The summary sentence is generous, and it is the point of putting these four skirmishes here at all. David did not kill any of them. He was nearly killed by the first, saved by his nephew, and then banned from the battlefield. Sibbecai, Elhanan and Jonathan killed the other three. And the credit is given to David and his servants together, in one phrase, without distinction.

That is what a reign looks like at the end of it. The work goes on and other men do it, and the old man who cannot go out any more is still named in the account, because he is the reason they are there. The next chapter is his psalm, and the one after that lists thirty-seven of his men by name.

The descendants of the giants were the Rephaim, a people of great stature in Canaan (Deut 2:11), like the Anakim; the six-fingered man was one of them. They are not to be confused with the Nephilim of Genesis 6.
verseByVerse.note: The father's name in v. 19, Jaare-oregim, probably shows a second copying slip: oregim means "weavers" and seems to have been picked up from "weaver's beam" at the end of the verse, while 1 Chronicles 20:5 has simply Jair.

22.title: David's Song of Deliverance
22.text: <sup>1</sup>And David spoke to the LORD the words of this song on the day when the LORD delivered him from the hand of all his enemies, and from the hand of Saul.<sup>2</sup>He said, "The LORD is my rock and my fortress and my deliverer,<sup>3</sup>my God, my rock, in whom I take refuge, my shield, and the horn of my salvation, my stronghold and my refuge, my savior; you save me from violence.<sup>4</sup>I call upon the LORD, who is worthy to be praised, and I am saved from my enemies.<sup>5</sup>"For the waves of death encompassed me, the torrents of destruction assailed me;<sup>6</sup>the cords of Sheol entangled me; the snares of death confronted me.<sup>7</sup>"In my distress I called upon the LORD; to my God I called. From his temple he heard my voice, and my cry came to his ears.<sup>8</sup>"Then the earth reeled and rocked; the foundations of the heavens trembled and quaked, because he was angry.<sup>9</sup>Smoke went up from his nostrils, and devouring fire from his mouth; glowing coals flamed forth from him.<sup>10</sup>He bowed the heavens and came down; thick darkness was under his feet.<sup>11</sup>He rode on a cherub and flew; he was seen on the wings of the wind.<sup>12</sup>He made darkness around him his canopy, thick clouds, a gathering of water.<sup>13</sup>Out of the brightness before him coals of fire flamed forth.<sup>14</sup>The LORD thundered from heaven, and the Most High uttered his voice.<sup>15</sup>And he sent out arrows and scattered them; lightning, and routed them.<sup>16</sup>Then the channels of the sea were seen; the foundations of the world were laid bare, at the rebuke of the LORD, at the blast of the breath of his nostrils.<sup>17</sup>"He sent from on high, he took me; he drew me out of many waters.<sup>18</sup>He rescued me from my strong enemy, from those who hated me, for they were too mighty for me.<sup>19</sup>They confronted me in the day of my calamity, but the LORD was my support.<sup>20</sup>He brought me out into a broad place; he rescued me, because he delighted in me.<sup>21</sup>"The LORD dealt with me according to my righteousness; according to the cleanness of my hands he rewarded me.<sup>22</sup>For I have kept the ways of the LORD and have not wickedly departed from my God.<sup>23</sup>For all his rules were before me, and from his statutes I did not turn aside.<sup>24</sup>I was blameless before him, and I kept myself from guilt.<sup>25</sup>And the LORD has rewarded me according to my righteousness, according to my cleanness in his sight.<sup>26</sup>"With the merciful you show yourself merciful; with the blameless man you show yourself blameless;<sup>27</sup>with the purified you deal purely, and with the crooked you make yourself seem tortuous.<sup>28</sup>You save a humble people, but your eyes are on the haughty to bring them down.<sup>29</sup>For you are my lamp, O LORD, and my God lightens my darkness.<sup>30</sup>For by you I can run against a troop, and by my God I can leap over a wall.<sup>31</sup>This God— his way is perfect; the word of the LORD proves true; he is a shield for all those who take refuge in him.<sup>32</sup>"For who is God, but the LORD? And who is a rock, except our God?<sup>33</sup>This God is my strong refuge and has made my way blameless.<sup>34</sup>He made my feet like the feet of a deer and set me secure on the heights.<sup>35</sup>He trains my hands for war, so that my arms can bend a bow of bronze.<sup>36</sup>You have given me the shield of your salvation, and your gentleness made me great.<sup>37</sup>You gave a wide place for my steps under me, and my feet did not slip;<sup>38</sup>I pursued my enemies and destroyed them, and did not turn back until they were consumed.<sup>39</sup>I consumed them; I thrust them through, so that they did not rise; they fell under my feet.<sup>40</sup>For you equipped me with strength for the battle; you made those who rise against me sink under me.<sup>41</sup>You made my enemies turn their backs to me, those who hated me, and I destroyed them.<sup>42</sup>They looked, but there was none to save; they cried to the LORD, but he did not answer them.<sup>43</sup>I beat them fine as the dust of the earth; I crushed them and stamped them down like the mire of the streets.<sup>44</sup>"You delivered me from strife with my people; you kept me as the head of the nations; people whom I had not known served me.<sup>45</sup>Foreigners came cringing to me; as soon as they heard of me, they obeyed me.<sup>46</sup>Foreigners lost heart and came trembling out of their fortresses.<sup>47</sup>"The LORD lives, and blessed be my rock, and exalted be my God, the rock of my salvation,<sup>48</sup>the God who gave me vengeance and brought down peoples under me,<sup>49</sup>who brought me out from my enemies; you exalted me above those who rose against me; you delivered me from men of violence.<sup>50</sup>"For this I will praise you, O LORD, among the nations, and sing praises to your name.<sup>51</sup>Great salvation he brings to his king, and shows steadfast love to his anointed, to David and his offspring forever."
22.overview:
This is Psalm 18, almost word for word, and its placement is the point of the chapter.

The heading dates the song to the deliverance from the hand of Saul, decades earlier, probably somewhere around chapters 5 to 8. Whoever assembled the book knew that, and still placed it here in the appendix, after ten chapters recording the collapse of David's household. The book does not end with the wreckage; it ends with his song.

The psalm moves from a fugitive's vocabulary (rock, fortress, stronghold, refuge, the words of a man who lived in actual caves) through one of the great appearances of God in Scripture, where the earth reels, the heavens bow, and God comes down riding a cherub with darkness under his feet. And the whole display arrives at one rescued man: he sent from on high, he took me; he drew me out of many waters. The reason given is not that the man deserved it, but that God delighted in him.

Verses 21-25, where David speaks of his own righteousness, are the hard part, and this commentary faces them rather than smoothing them over.
22.theology:
Why it is here (v. 1). An editor who had chapter 11 in front of him reached back decades and put this song at the end. He recorded the whole collapse without excusing a line of it, and then closed with what David believed the whole way through, because it was still true afterwards.

The righteousness claim, faced (vv. 21-25). The man who speaks of the cleanness of my hands is in the book that records what those hands did. The verse notes give three answers. The compilers placed the psalm after chapter 11, so they did not read it as a claim to sinless perfection. The heading names the deliverance from Saul, and on that question David's hands were clean. And blameless in the Old Testament means undivided allegiance, not sinlessness: David never served another god. Kings sums him up the same way: he did what was right all his days, except in the matter of Uriah the Hittite (1 Kings 15:5).

And what he did when he fell. The same man prayed Psalm 51, and any account of David that keeps only one of the two psalms is false. These verses are not comfortable and should not be made to seem so. Yet a Christian hears in them a voice that can say them without reserve. Only one Son of David had wholly clean hands, and it is his righteousness, not David's, that God credits to sinners who trust him (Romans 3:22; 2 Corinthians 5:21). David sang verses 21 to 25 as a forgiven man; believers sing them in Christ.

Your gentleness made me great (v. 36). After twenty verses of strength and equipment, the word David chooses for what made him is gentleness: God stooping down to a man who did not deserve it. That is the centre of the song.

The LORD lives (v. 47). The closing praise rests not on God's power or goodness, though the song praises both, but on his being alive. Paul quotes verse 50 first among four Old Testament texts showing that the nations coming in was always the plan (Rom. 15:9). Many readers hear Paul placing the words in the Messiah's own mouth: David's greater Son, having confirmed God's promises, praises the Father among the nations as they come in.
22.examples:
Then: The men who compiled Israel's history had recorded, without excusing a line of it, a king's adultery, the murder he arranged, his daughter's rape, the killing of one son by another, a rebellion that drove him barefoot out of his own capital, and a body left lying in a public road. Then they reached back decades to a song he had sung as a young fugitive and put it at the end of the book.

Now: Verse 36 is the one to take away. If you had to say in a few words what made you, what would you name? David had a great deal to choose from (the anointing, the giant, the throne, the empire, the trained hands and the bronze bow, all of which he mentions), and what he says is your gentleness made me great. The placement speaks too. Somebody who knew everything in chapters 11 to 20 decided that the last word on this life would not be the wreckage. Not because the wreckage was not real; they wrote ten chapters of it. Because what he had believed as a young man in a cave was still true about God after he had failed as badly as a man can fail. For anyone who has failed badly, that is where the way back begins.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–20 — He Drew Me Out of Many Waters
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: David sings this on the day when the LORD delivered him from the hand of all his enemies, and from the hand of Saul (v. 1), and it opens with a pile of names for God: my rock and my fortress and my deliverer, my God, my rock, in whom I take refuge, my shield and the horn of my salvation, my stronghold and my refuge, my savior (vv. 2-3). Then the trouble (waves of death, torrents of destruction, the cords of Sheol, the place of the dead) and the cry: in my distress I called upon the LORD... he heard my voice, and my cry came to his ears (vv. 5-7). And then the earth reels, the heavens bow, smoke goes up from his nostrils, he rides on a cherub and flies, the channels of the sea are seen and the foundations of the world laid bare (vv. 8-16). And all of it arrives at one man: he sent from on high, he took me; he drew me out of many waters (v. 17). He brought me out into a broad place; he rescued me, because he delighted in me (v. 20).
verseByVerse.theology: Psalm 18 is the same song with almost the same heading. The differences between the two are the sort that arise when a song is copied and sung for generations.
verseByVerse.examples: The theophany, God’s visible coming, shakes creation, and the point of it is a man being pulled out of water. That is the logic of the whole psalm: the God whose approach bows the heavens comes down for one person.

verseByVerse.quote: And David spoke to the LORD the words of this song on the day when the LORD delivered him from the hand of all his enemies, and from the hand of Saul. He said, "The LORD is my rock and my fortress and my deliverer, my God, my rock, in whom I take refuge, my shield, and the horn of my salvation, my stronghold and my refuge, my savior; you save me from violence. I call upon the LORD, who is worthy to be praised, and I am saved from my enemies. "For the waves of death encompassed me, the torrents of destruction assailed me; the cords of Sheol entangled me; the snares of death confronted me. "In my distress I called upon the LORD; to my God I called. From his temple he heard my voice, and my cry came to his ears. "Then the earth reeled and rocked; the foundations of the heavens trembled and quaked, because he was angry. Smoke went up from his nostrils, and devouring fire from his mouth; glowing coals flamed forth from him. He bowed the heavens and came down; thick darkness was under his feet. He rode on a cherub and flew; he was seen on the wings of the wind. He made darkness around him his canopy, thick clouds, a gathering of water. Out of the brightness before him coals of fire flamed forth. The LORD thundered from heaven, and the Most High uttered his voice. And he sent out arrows and scattered them; lightning, and routed them. Then the channels of the sea were seen; the foundations of the world were laid bare, at the rebuke of the LORD, at the blast of the breath of his nostrils. "He sent from on high, he took me; he drew me out of many waters. He rescued me from my strong enemy, from those who hated me, for they were too mighty for me. They confronted me in the day of my calamity, but the LORD was my support. He brought me out into a broad place; he rescued me, because he delighted in me.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The heading dates the song to the deliverance from the hand of Saul, decades earlier, and yet it stands here in the appendix, after everything: after the roof and Bathsheba and the letter Uriah carried; after Nathan and the dead child; after Amnon and Tamar; after the pit in the forest and a father over the gate saying my son five times; after a man with a trumpet splitting the country, a body lying in a road at Gibeon, and ten women shut in a house until they died. The book has spent ten chapters recording the collapse of this man's household, and it does not end there. It ends with his song. That is an editorial decision and a theological one: somebody who knew everything in chapters 11 to 20 chose to close the account with what David believed the whole way through.

Verses 2-3 give name after name for God, and every one of them is about safety. Rock is ground that does not shift under your feet. Fortress is the high strong place, and David spent years living in actual ones. Deliverer is the one who gets you out, and a shield is the thing between you and the blow. Horn of my salvation pictures a charging animal's strength turned to your side. Zechariah took up the phrase when he blessed God for raising up a horn of salvation for us in the house of his servant David (Luke 1:69): the strength David found in God came to his house in a person. Stronghold, refuge and savior complete the list.

And the possessive is on all of them: my rock, my fortress, my God. This is not a description of God in the abstract; it is what one man has found him to be. The vocabulary is a fugitive's. These are the words of a man who spent years in caves at Adullam and Engedi and the Wilderness of Ziph, and who learned that a stronghold is only as good as the God in it.

Then the trouble comes in pictures of water and rope, of drowning and being caught (vv. 5-6). He called, and God heard (v. 7). There was no temple yet, so his temple here is God's heavenly dwelling. A man cried out in trouble, and the answer is an earthquake.

The ground moves and the foundations of the heavens tremble. Smoke comes from God's nostrils and fire from his mouth, and he bends the heavens down like a man pushing a low branch aside, and comes through with darkness under his feet, riding a cherub, moving on the wind (vv. 8-11). The language is deliberately that of Sinai and the exodus. God came down on a mountain in smoke and fire and darkness, and he came down to Egypt for a nation of slaves, and David puts his own rescue in that vocabulary. The earthquake and storm are poetry for God's coming to rescue, and the point is that God is not detached. When his people cry out, he does not send a message. He comes, and creation notices him coming.

In verse 16 the sea bed is exposed and the foundations of the world are uncovered. That is the sea parting at the exodus, in the language of poetry: the whole created order pulled back like a curtain because God is angry at what has been done to his servant.

Then comes the sentence all of that was for (v. 17). The earth has shaken, the heavens have bowed, the sea bed has been laid bare, the Most High has thundered, and the object of the entire operation is one man: he took me. The verb drew me out is a rare one, the one behind the name Moses: I drew him out of the water (Ex. 2:10). God reaches down through all that machinery and picks one man out of a flood. That is the mystery at the centre of Old Testament prayer, and the psalm states it without apology. The God who shakes creation is the God who attends to one person's crisis, and his greatness is no reason to think he is not paying attention.

David admits that his enemies were too mighty for me (v. 18); he does not pretend otherwise. The rescue is into a broad place (v. 20). The Hebrew for distress is a word about narrowness: being hemmed in, squeezed, with nowhere to go. Rescue is the opposite, open ground and room to move. Anybody who has been in trouble knows exactly what the two words describe.

And the reason given is because he delighted in me: not because David was useful, or strong, or necessary to a plan. Deuteronomy says the same of Israel: God did not choose them because they were numerous, but because the LORD loves you (Deut. 7:7-8). The reason is in God, and it is affection.
verseByVerse.note: Psalm 18 opens with a line not found here: I love you, O LORD, my strength.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 21–37 — Your Gentleness Made Me Great
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The LORD dealt with me according to my righteousness; according to the cleanness of my hands he rewarded me. For I have kept the ways of the LORD and have not wickedly departed from my God (vv. 21-22), and the claim runs on for five verses. Then the character of God matched to the man: with the merciful you show yourself merciful; with the blameless man you show yourself blameless... and with the crooked you make yourself seem tortuous (vv. 26-27). You save a humble people, but your eyes are on the haughty to bring them down (v. 28). Then the equipping: he makes my feet like the feet of a deer, trains my hands for war, gives me the shield of his salvation, and your gentleness made me great (vv. 33-37).
verseByVerse.theology: The righteousness claim is the hard part of this psalm and should not be explained away, since the same book contains chapters 11 to 20. It concerns covenant loyalty (he never went after other gods) and the one vindication named in the heading: twice he refused to put out his hand against Saul when he could have.
verseByVerse.examples: Verse 36 is the sentence to carry out of this section. Amid the bronze bows and trained hands, he says what actually made him: your gentleness made me great.

verseByVerse.quote: "The LORD dealt with me according to my righteousness; according to the cleanness of my hands he rewarded me. For I have kept the ways of the LORD and have not wickedly departed from my God. For all his rules were before me, and from his statutes I did not turn aside. I was blameless before him, and I kept myself from guilt. And the LORD has rewarded me according to my righteousness, according to my cleanness in his sight. "With the merciful you show yourself merciful; with the blameless man you show yourself blameless; with the purified you deal purely, and with the crooked you make yourself seem tortuous. You save a humble people, but your eyes are on the haughty to bring them down. For you are my lamp, O LORD, and my God lightens my darkness. For by you I can run against a troop, and by my God I can leap over a wall. This God— his way is perfect; the word of the LORD proves true; he is a shield for all those who take refuge in him. "For who is God, but the LORD? And who is a rock, except our God? This God is my strong refuge and has made my way blameless. He made my feet like the feet of a deer and set me secure on the heights. He trains my hands for war, so that my arms can bend a bow of bronze. You have given me the shield of your salvation, and your gentleness made me great. You gave a wide place for my steps under me, and my feet did not slip;
verseByVerse.commentary:
The man saying the cleanness of my hands (v. 21) is in a book which has just spent ten chapters recording what those hands did. He committed adultery with the wife of one of his own officers, tried to disguise it, and then had the man killed with a letter the man carried himself. He failed to act when his daughter was raped and when his son was murdered. He let a general kill two commanders and never touched him.

Three things need saying, and the first is the most important: the editor knew. Whoever assembled this book had chapter 11 in front of him and put this psalm in anyway, afterwards, at the end. That is not an oversight. It means the people who compiled Israel's own Scriptures did not understand these verses as a claim to sinless perfection.

So what is it a claim about? The heading tells you which deliverance is in view: from the hand of all his enemies, and from the hand of Saul. On that question David has a specific record. For years he was hunted by a man he had not wronged, and twice he had him at his mercy: asleep at Hachilah with a spear in the ground beside his head, and in a cave at Engedi. Both times his men told him God had handed the man over, and both times he refused, saying the LORD forbid that I should put out my hand against the LORD's anointed. His conscience troubled him even for cutting a corner off a robe. On the question the song is about, his hands were clean, he knew it, and God had vindicated him.

The second thing is what blameless (v. 24) means in the Old Testament. It is not sinlessness but undivided loyalty: a man whose heart is not split, who has not gone off after other gods, who faces one way. It is the word used of Noah and of Job, and Job's friends spent thirty-odd chapters trying to prove it did not apply to him. That is true of David in a way it is true of hardly any other king of Israel. He was an adulterer and a murderer, and he never once served another god. The verdict passed on almost every king after him (that he made Israel to sin, set up high places, the hilltop shrines, went after the Baals) is never passed on David.

The third thing is what he did when he fell, and the psalter records that too: Have mercy on me, O God, according to your steadfast love... against you, you only, have I sinned and done what is evil in your sight (Ps. 51:1-4). The same man wrote both. Psalm 51 is not a correction of Psalm 18; they are two true things said by one person, and any account of David that keeps only one of them is a false account.

So verses 21-25 should not be made comfortable. A man who had genuinely kept covenant with God for decades, and had been genuinely vindicated against a king who hunted him, sang this; the same man did what chapter 11 records, and repented of it; and Scripture puts both in the same book without softening either.

Verses 26-27 do not claim that God changes character according to who is looking. They claim that how a person finds God to be depends on what that person is. To the merciful, God shows himself merciful. To the crooked he seems tortuous: twisted, hard to deal with, impossible to get a straight answer from. A devious man finds God devious because he reads God through himself, as a bent ruler measures everything bent. That is why Saul, at the end, could get nothing out of God by dreams or Urim (the priest’s sacred lot) or prophets, and went to a medium. And it is why Pharaoh met a God who kept hardening him.

Verse 28 holds the whole of Hannah's song and the whole of Mary's: God saves the humble and brings the haughty down. Both books that bear Samuel's name have been arguing it from their opening chapters.

In verse 29 David calls the LORD his lamp. His own men called David the lamp of Israel one chapter ago; here he says who the lamp actually is.

Verse 33 adds a clause that matters after verses 21-25: God made my way blameless. David is not claiming to have produced it himself. In verse 34 his feet are like a deer's, the animal that can run flat out on rock where a man would break an ankle. He spent years in that terrain being hunted, and the picture is exact.

Then verse 36: your gentleness made me great. Look at what surrounds it: trained hands, a bronze bow, feet like a deer's, the heights, a shield. Every image in twenty verses has been about strength and equipment and the ability to fight, and when he comes to say what actually made him, the word is gentleness. The Hebrew can be read more than one way (some render it as God's condescension, his stooping down), and the sense is close either way: God's willingness to be gentle with a man who did not deserve it.

Consider who is saying it: a man passed over by his own father and left with the sheep; hunted for years and sleeping in caves; an adulterer and a murderer, confronted and forgiven; a father who lost three sons, one of them a baby he had begged God for. He looks back over all of it, and what he names as having made him is that God was gentle with him.

The wide place for his steps in verse 37 is the broad place of verse 20 again. He keeps returning to the picture: room to stand.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 38–51 — To David and His Offspring Forever
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The battle section runs hard: he pursues and consumes his enemies, they cry and there is none to save, he beats them fine as the dust of the earth (vv. 38-43). Then the reign: you made me the head of the nations; people whom I had not known served me (vv. 44-46). And the closing praise: the LORD lives, and blessed be my rock, and exalted be my God, the rock of my salvation (v. 47). For this I will praise you, O LORD, among the nations, and sing praises to your name (v. 50). And the last verse: great salvation he brings to his king, and shows steadfast love to his anointed, to David and his offspring forever (v. 51).
verseByVerse.theology: The battle language is that of an ancient warrior king describing real campaigns. It should not be softened into metaphor, nor treated as a model for anybody's conduct toward their neighbours.
verseByVerse.examples: The song ends where chapter 7 ended, and reaches past its author. His anointed... David and his offspring forever is the covenant promise, and it runs on to David's greater Son.

verseByVerse.quote: I pursued my enemies and destroyed them, and did not turn back until they were consumed. I consumed them; I thrust them through, so that they did not rise; they fell under my feet. For you equipped me with strength for the battle; you made those who rise against me sink under me. You made my enemies turn their backs to me, those who hated me, and I destroyed them. They looked, but there was none to save; they cried to the LORD, but he did not answer them. I beat them fine as the dust of the earth; I crushed them and stamped them down like the mire of the streets. "You delivered me from strife with my people; you kept me as the head of the nations; people whom I had not known served me. Foreigners came cringing to me; as soon as they heard of me, they obeyed me. Foreigners lost heart and came trembling out of their fortresses. "The LORD lives, and blessed be my rock, and exalted be my God, the rock of my salvation, the God who gave me vengeance and brought down peoples under me, who brought me out from my enemies; you exalted me above those who rose against me; you delivered me from men of violence. "For this I will praise you, O LORD, among the nations, and sing praises to your name. Great salvation he brings to his king, and shows steadfast love to his anointed, to David and his offspring forever."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Verses 38-43 should be read as what they are: an ancient king describing real campaigns in the vocabulary of his own world. He fought the Philistines, the Ammonites, the Syrians, the Edomites and the Moabites; men died under his feet, and he says so.

Two things follow from taking it plainly. The first is that it is not a model for anybody's conduct toward their neighbours. It has been used as one, and it should not be. David was the anointed king of a covenant nation fighting national wars about a thousand years before Christ. The New Testament does not authorise a Christian to speak this way about anybody, and its instruction on the subject is the opposite: bless those who persecute you; bless and do not curse (Rom. 12:14). The second is that it should not be dissolved into metaphor to make it comfortable. These were real battles, the psalm is honest about them, and Scripture does not tidy up its own history. Even here the grammar keeps giving the work to God: you equipped, you made them sink.

Note the middle clause of verse 44: strife with my people. That is not the Philistines. That is Absalom, and Sheba, and the argument at the Jordan: the wars inside Israel. The song puts civil conflict among the things he was delivered from, and anyone who has read the previous twenty chapters knows that it was these, not the foreign wars, that nearly finished him.

The LORD lives (v. 47) is the foundation of the whole song. He is not an idea, or a national symbol, or a carved thing like Dagon in his temple at Ashdod, which fell on its face (1 Sam. 5:3). He is a living God who hears a man in trouble and comes.

Paul argues in Romans that Christ became a servant to the circumcised to confirm the promises given to the patriarchs, and in order that the Gentiles might glorify God for his mercy, and he stacks up four Old Testament texts to show that this was always the plan. The first of them is verse 50: therefore I will praise you among the Gentiles, and sing to your name (Rom. 15:9). David sang about praising God among the nations, and Paul reads it as a promise that the nations themselves would come in.

The last verse of the song goes past the man singing it. Look at its phrases. His king: not me, but the office, and it is God's, not David's. Steadfast love: hesed, the word this whole book has been built on, what Jonathan asked for, what Jabesh-gilead showed Saul, what David showed Mephibosheth and tried to show Hanun. Here it is God's, shown to his anointed, his mashiach or messiah, a word that simply means the man with the oil on him, and in this verse means David. And to David and his offspring forever is chapter 7: your house and your kingdom shall be made sure forever before me. Your throne shall be established forever (7:16).

So the song ends on the promise, and the promise runs past its singer. There is no way to sing of God's steadfast love to David and his offspring forever without the sentence travelling beyond one lifetime, and it did: through Solomon, through the long line of kings who mostly failed, through the exile when there was no son of David on any throne anywhere, and out the other side to a birth in the town this man came from.

The compilers of this book had every reason to end it differently. They could have closed with Absalom and written a tragedy about a man who ruined his own house, or with the body in the road at Gibeon and written a study in what a king cannot control. Instead, having recorded all of it without excusing a single line, they reached back decades and put his song at the end. Not because the wreckage was not real; it fills ten chapters and they wrote every one of them. Because this is what he believed the whole way through, and it was true the whole way through, and it was still true afterwards. The rock did not move when the man on it fell, and that is why the book closes with a psalm and not with a grave.

23.title: David's Last Words and His Mighty Men
23.text: <sup>1</sup>Now these are the last words of David: The oracle of David, the son of Jesse, the oracle of the man who was raised on high, the anointed of the God of Jacob, the sweet psalmist of Israel:<sup>2</sup>"The Spirit of the LORD speaks by me; his word is on my tongue.<sup>3</sup>The God of Israel has spoken; the Rock of Israel has said to me: When one rules justly over men, ruling in the fear of God,<sup>4</sup>he dawns on them like the morning light, like the sun shining forth on a cloudless morning, like rain that makes grass to sprout from the earth.<sup>5</sup>"For does not my house stand so with God? For he has made with me an everlasting covenant, ordered in all things and secure. For will he not cause to prosper all my help and my desire?<sup>6</sup>But worthless men are all like thorns that are thrown away, for they cannot be taken with the hand;<sup>7</sup>but the man who touches them arms himself with iron and the shaft of a spear, and they are utterly consumed with fire."<sup>8</sup>These are the names of the mighty men whom David had: Josheb-basshebeth a Tahchemonite; he was chief of the three. He wielded his spear against eight hundred whom he killed at one time.<sup>9</sup>And next to him among the three mighty men was Eleazar the son of Dodo, son of Ahohi. He was with David when they defied the Philistines who were gathered there for battle, and the men of Israel withdrew.<sup>10</sup>He rose and struck down the Philistines until his hand was weary, and his hand clung to the sword. And the LORD brought about a great victory that day, and the men returned after him only to strip the slain.<sup>11</sup>And next to him was Shammah, the son of Agee the Hararite. The Philistines gathered together at Lehi, where there was a plot of ground full of lentils, and the men fled from the Philistines.<sup>12</sup>But he took his stand in the midst of the plot and defended it and struck down the Philistines, and the LORD worked a great victory.<sup>13</sup>And three of the thirty chief men went down and came about harvest time to David at the cave of Adullam, when a band of Philistines was encamped in the Valley of Rephaim.<sup>14</sup>David was then in the stronghold, and the garrison of the Philistines was then at Bethlehem.<sup>15</sup>And David said longingly, "Oh, that someone would give me water to drink from the well of Bethlehem that is by the gate!"<sup>16</sup>Then the three mighty men broke through the camp of the Philistines and drew water out of the well of Bethlehem that was by the gate and carried and brought it to David. But he would not drink of it. He poured it out to the LORD<sup>17</sup>and said, "Far be it from me, O LORD, that I should do this. Shall I drink the blood of the men who went at the risk of their lives?" Therefore he would not drink it. These things the three mighty men did.<sup>18</sup>Now Abishai, the brother of Joab, the son of Zeruiah, was chief of the thirty. And he wielded his spear against three hundred men and killed them and won a name beside the three.<sup>19</sup>He was the most renowned of the thirty and became their commander, but he did not attain to the three.<sup>20</sup>And Benaiah the son of Jehoiada was a valiant man of Kabzeel, a doer of great deeds. He struck down two ariels of Moab. He also went down and struck down a lion in a pit on a day when snow had fallen.<sup>21</sup>And he struck down an Egyptian, a handsome man. The Egyptian had a spear in his hand, but Benaiah went down to him with a staff and snatched the spear out of the Egyptian's hand and killed him with his own spear.<sup>22</sup>These things did Benaiah the son of Jehoiada, and won a name beside the three mighty men.<sup>23</sup>He was renowned among the thirty, but he did not attain to the three. And David set him over his bodyguard.<sup>24</sup>Asahel the brother of Joab was one of the thirty; Elhanan the son of Dodo of Bethlehem,<sup>25</sup>Shammah of Harod, Elika of Harod,<sup>26</sup>Helez the Paltite, Ira the son of Ikkesh of Tekoa,<sup>27</sup>Abiezer of Anathoth, Mebunnai the Hushathite,<sup>28</sup>Zalmon the Ahohite, Maharai of Netophah,<sup>29</sup>Heleb the son of Baanah of Netophah, Ittai the son of Ribai of Gibeah of the people of Benjamin,<sup>30</sup>Benaiah of Pirathon, Hiddai of the brooks of Gaash,<sup>31</sup>Abi-albon the Arbathite, Azmaveth of Bahurim,<sup>32</sup>Eliahba the Shaalbonite, the sons of Jashen, Jonathan,<sup>33</sup>Shammah the Hararite, Ahiam the son of Sharar the Hararite,<sup>34</sup>Eliphelet the son of Ahasbai of Maacah, Eliam the son of Ahithophel the Gilonite,<sup>35</sup>Hezro of Carmel, Paarai the Arbite,<sup>36</sup>Igal the son of Nathan of Zobah, Bani the Gadite,<sup>37</sup>Zelek the Ammonite, Naharai of Beeroth, the armor-bearer of Joab the son of Zeruiah,<sup>38</sup>Ira the Ithrite, Gareb the Ithrite,<sup>39</sup>Uriah the Hittite: thirty-seven in all.
23.overview:
David's last words come as an oracle, the formula of prophecy rather than memoir, and he describes himself in four titles that end, where king or conqueror or founder might have gone, with the sweet psalmist of Israel.

His picture of what a king is for is unlike the way power usually describes itself: sunrise on a clear morning, and rain on new grass. Both are gifts people cannot produce for themselves, and neither is a display of force. That is what being governed by an honest man who fears God is like for the people under him, and no king in Israel was consistently that, including this one, so the sentence points past all of them.

At the end of a life in which his own house did nearly everything a house can do wrong, he does not list victories or rehearse failures. He goes back to chapter 7: an everlasting covenant, ordered in all things and secure. Its security does not depend on the man it was made with, which David of all people has reason to know.

Then come thirty-seven names, the men from the cave at Adullam. Three of them went through a Philistine garrison for a cup of water because their commander said he was homesick, and he would not drink it. And the last name on the roll of the finest soldiers in the kingdom is Uriah the Hittite, with no comment attached.
23.theology:
Presented as a word given (vv. 1-2). Oracle is the formula that introduces prophetic utterance, and the Spirit of the LORD speaks by me; his word is on my tongue claims inspiration outright. The New Testament agrees: Peter says the Holy Spirit spoke through David’s mouth, and at Pentecost calls him a prophet (Acts 1:16; 2:30).

The ruler who is the morning. No king of David's line was this sunrise for long, and the prophets said one would be: a righteous Branch raised up for David, who would reign as king and deal wisely (Jeremiah 23:5), a sun of righteousness rising with healing in its wings (Malachi 4:2). When that son of David was about to be born, Zechariah sang that the sunrise shall visit us from on high (Luke 1:78). And the everlasting covenant David rested on is the one Paul says God kept by raising Jesus from the dead: I will give you the holy and sure blessings of David (Acts 13:34). It is secure because its final King cannot die again.

What the list is (v. 8). The book is nearly over and the writer spends a long passage on soldiers' names and villages. These are the men from the cave: everyone who was in distress, and everyone who was in debt, and everyone who was bitter in soul (1 Sam. 22:2), four hundred failures in a hole in the ground. This is what became of them, and it is a picture of what God can make of people who come to his king with nothing.

Why he would not drink it (vv. 16-17). Pouring the water out to the LORD is a drink offering, not ingratitude. The cup had three men's lives in it, so he gave it to the only one worth what it cost, and accepted the rebuke in it: a leader’s passing wish is never harmless, because others will act on it.

And who else is on it. The roll includes Asahel, long dead; a man from Saul's own village; Zelek the Ammonite; Eliam, very probably Bathsheba's father; and last, Uriah the Hittite, one of the finest soldiers in the country, murdered by the man whose list this is. His name stands in a chapter that opens with David saying the Spirit of the LORD speaks by me. The book holds on to both facts and does not reconcile them for us.
23.examples:
Then: A hunted man in a cave twelve miles from the town he grew up in said aloud, to nobody in particular, that he wished he could have a drink from the well by the gate. Three of his men walked through an enemy army to get it, and he would not put it to his lips, but poured it out as an offering to God because it had their lives in it.

Now: Three things. Verse 5 is where to end up: at the close of a life in which nearly everything that could go wrong in a family did, what he rests on is not an achievement of his own but a covenant God arranged and God guards. Anyone looking back on a life with regrets can rest on the same thing. Second, the well, and the uncomfortable half of it: David never told anybody to go. People with any authority at all should notice how a passing remark lands on those who want to please them, and that somebody else pays the cost. And third, the last line. The book puts the name of the man David had killed at the very end of the roll of his finest soldiers, in the place he earned, and adds nothing. It is more devastating than any verdict it could have written.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–7 — Ordered in All Things and Secure
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Now these are the last words of David, and they come as an oracle: the oracle of David, the son of Jesse, the oracle of the man who was raised on high, the anointed of the God of Jacob, the sweet psalmist of Israel: "The Spirit of the LORD speaks by me; his word is on my tongue" (vv. 1-2). Then the vision of just rule: when one rules justly over men, ruling in the fear of God, he dawns on them like the morning light, like the sun shining forth on a cloudless morning, like rain that makes grass to sprout from the earth (vv. 3-4). And then the covenant: he has made with me an everlasting covenant, ordered in all things and secure (v. 5). Worthless men are like thorns, not gathered with the hand but burned where they lie (vv. 6-7).
verseByVerse.theology: This is prophetic formula, not memoir. The titles stack up in front of the claim to speak by the Spirit (raised on high, anointed of the God of Jacob, the sweet psalmist of Israel), and every one of them names something given to him.
verseByVerse.examples: At the end of a life he does not rehearse victories or failures. He goes back to chapter 7, a covenant ordered in all things and secure, and that is what he stakes everything on. It is not his own record.

verseByVerse.quote: Now these are the last words of David: The oracle of David, the son of Jesse, the oracle of the man who was raised on high, the anointed of the God of Jacob, the sweet psalmist of Israel: "The Spirit of the LORD speaks by me; his word is on my tongue. The God of Israel has spoken; the Rock of Israel has said to me: When one rules justly over men, ruling in the fear of God, he dawns on them like the morning light, like the sun shining forth on a cloudless morning, like rain that makes grass to sprout from the earth. "For does not my house stand so with God? For he has made with me an everlasting covenant, ordered in all things and secure. For will he not cause to prosper all my help and my desire? But worthless men are all like thorns that are thrown away, for they cannot be taken with the hand; but the man who touches them arms himself with iron and the shaft of a spear, and they are utterly consumed with fire."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The word is oracle, the formula used to introduce a prophetic utterance, the same one Balaam uses, and Agur in Proverbs. This is not offered as a memoir or a farewell speech. It is presented as a word given.

The four titles that follow are worth reading slowly. The son of Jesse is where he started, and it is the name Saul used when he would not say David, and the name Sheba used when he broke the country in half; he takes it first. The man who was raised on high is passive: somebody else raised him. The anointed of the God of Jacob says that he was anointed king, and whose choice that was. And then the sweet psalmist of Israel, for which the ESV margin offers "the favorite of the songs of Israel." Of everything that could have gone in that fourth place (the king, the conqueror, the founder of a dynasty), the one chosen is that he wrote the nation's songs. He then claims inspiration outright: the Spirit speaks by him.

Verses 3-4 give his picture of what a king is for, and it is unlike the way power usually describes itself. Both images are about things arriving that people cannot produce for themselves. The first is sunrise on a clear morning: light coming up over ground that has been in the dark all night, and everything becoming visible. It is not a display of force, just the end of not being able to see. The second is rain on new grass. In that country rain is the difference between a harvest and a famine, and nobody can make it happen. It arrives, and the ground goes green.

That is what a ruler who rules justly, in the fear of God, is like to the people under him: morning, and rain. He is not describing a strong king or a successful one. He is describing the effect on ordinary people of being governed by somebody who is honest and who is afraid of God. It describes what David was at his best (David administered justice and equity to all his people, 8:15) and what he failed to be, since Absalom built a rebellion on the claim that nobody at the gate was being heard. No king in Israel was consistently the morning light for his people, including this one. The sentence points past all of them. On just leadership in every sphere of life, see on Ephesians 5:21.

The Hebrew of the first clause of verse 5 is difficult. The older English versions read it as a concession, "although my house be not so with God": my household has not been what I have just described, and yet. Most modern versions read it as a question expecting yes: does not my house stand so with God? The two are further apart in tone than in effect, because the sentence after it is identical either way.

That sentence, the everlasting covenant, is chapter 7, and it is what the man goes back to at the end of his life. Look at what he does not do here. He does not list his victories or defend his record. He does not mention Goliath, or Jerusalem, or the empire from Egypt to the Euphrates. And he does not rehearse his failures either. He goes to the promise.

Ordered in all things uses a word for drawing up a battle line or setting out wood on an altar: things arranged deliberately, in position, nothing left loose. The covenant is not a general goodwill; it is an arrangement, put together with care, every part where it was meant to be. And secure means guarded and kept. It will not fail, and the reason it will not fail is that its security does not depend on the man it was made with, which David, of all people, has reason to know.

He is an old man who has watched his own house do everything a house can do wrong. His firstborn raped his daughter. His third son murdered his firstborn and then tried to kill him. He buried a child he had begged for. And what he stakes his hope on at the end is not one thing he did. He has made with me: God did it, God arranged it, God keeps it.

Verses 6-7 set the other picture beside it. The just ruler is morning light and rain on grass; worthless men are briars in a field. The detail is agricultural and exact. You cannot clear thorns by hand; you need tools, and in the end you burn them where they lie. They produce nothing and take up ground. The word for worthless is the one used of Nabal, of Sheba the son of Bichri, and of the men who would not have Saul as king: in this book, a settled name for the person who is simply no good to anybody.

So the last words of David are two pictures and a promise: what good government does for people, what is finally done with those who will not have it, and in the middle, holding both, a covenant ordered in all things and secure.

“The last words of David” are his last inspired words as psalmist and prophet, not his last speech; he still speaks in 1 Kings 2.

Is the just ruler of verses 3–4 Christ? David speaks of the righteous king God promised his house (7:12–16), and no king of David’s line fulfilled it but one. It points to Christ, the bright morning star (Rev 22:16).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 8–23 — Shall I Drink the Blood of These Men?
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The roll of the mighty men. Josheb-basshebeth killed eight hundred at one time (v. 8). Eleazar stood when the men of Israel withdrew and struck the Philistines until his hand was weary, and his hand clung to the sword. And the LORD brought about a great victory that day (vv. 9-10). Shammah took his stand in the middle of a plot of lentils when the people fled, and the LORD worked a great victory (vv. 11-12). Then the well: three of the thirty come to David at Adullam with a Philistine garrison in Bethlehem, and he says oh, that someone would give me water to drink from the well of Bethlehem that is by the gate! (vv. 14-15). They break through the Philistine camp and bring it, but he would not drink of it. He poured it out to the LORD (v. 16), saying shall I drink the blood of the men who went at the risk of their lives? (v. 17). Abishai and Benaiah follow, with Benaiah's lion in a pit on a snowy day (vv. 18-23).
verseByVerse.theology: The exploits of the Three all have one shape: a man refuses to run, and then the LORD brought about a great victory. The man’s courage holds the ground and God gives the victory, and the writer keeps both halves.
verseByVerse.examples: The water is the finest thing in the chapter. He said oh, that someone would: a longing, not an order, and three men went through an enemy army for it. Pouring it out was not refusing the gift but giving it to God instead.

verseByVerse.quote: These are the names of the mighty men whom David had: Josheb-basshebeth a Tahchemonite; he was chief of the three. He wielded his spear against eight hundred whom he killed at one time. And next to him among the three mighty men was Eleazar the son of Dodo, son of Ahohi. He was with David when they defied the Philistines who were gathered there for battle, and the men of Israel withdrew. He rose and struck down the Philistines until his hand was weary, and his hand clung to the sword. And the LORD brought about a great victory that day, and the men returned after him only to strip the slain. And next to him was Shammah, the son of Agee the Hararite. The Philistines gathered together at Lehi, where there was a plot of ground full of lentils, and the men fled from the Philistines. But he took his stand in the midst of the plot and defended it and struck down the Philistines, and the LORD worked a great victory. And three of the thirty chief men went down and came about harvest time to David at the cave of Adullam, when a band of Philistines was encamped in the Valley of Rephaim. David was then in the stronghold, and the garrison of the Philistines was then at Bethlehem. And David said longingly, "Oh, that someone would give me water to drink from the well of Bethlehem that is by the gate!" Then the three mighty men broke through the camp of the Philistines and drew water out of the well of Bethlehem that was by the gate and carried and brought it to David. But he would not drink of it.
