He poured it out to the LORD and said, "Far be it from me, O LORD, that I should do this. Shall I drink the blood of the men who went at the risk of their lives?" Therefore he would not drink it. These things the three mighty men did. Now Abishai, the brother of Joab, the son of Zeruiah, was chief of the thirty. And he wielded his spear against three hundred men and killed them and won a name beside the three. He was the most renowned of the thirty and became their commander, but he did not attain to the three. And Benaiah the son of Jehoiada was a valiant man of Kabzeel, a doer of great deeds. He struck down two ariels of Moab. He also went down and struck down a lion in a pit on a day when snow had fallen. And he struck down an Egyptian, a handsome man. The Egyptian had a spear in his hand, but Benaiah went down to him with a staff and snatched the spear out of the Egyptian's hand and killed him with his own spear. These things did Benaiah the son of Jehoiada, and won a name beside the three mighty men. He was renowned among the thirty, but he did not attain to the three. And David set him over his bodyguard.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The book is nearly over, and the writer spends most of the chapter listing soldiers. That is a decision. He could have summarised the reign, or given a genealogy, or ended on the psalm. Instead he writes down thirty-seven names, most of them with a village attached, and tells what four or five of them did. These are the men who gathered to David at Adullam in distress and debt and bitterness of soul, and this is what became of them.

Eight hundred here, three hundred in 1 Chronicles 11:11: numbers in Hebrew manuscripts were easily miscopied, and a copyist may have been influenced by Abishai’s three hundred in verse 18. The chief’s name differs too (Jashobeam in Chronicles; the KJV renders the Hebrew here “The Tachmonite that sat in the seat”), probably for the same reason. Such slips belong to the copying and leave the account itself trustworthy.

In verses 9-10 Israel ran and Eleazar did not. He fought until his hand seized around the grip and he could not let go of the sword, which is a soldier's detail and a true one: a man who has held a weapon through a long fight cannot open his fingers afterwards. Then the LORD brought about a great victory, not "Eleazar won a great victory." The man stood, and God gave the outcome. And the army that ran away came back to collect the plunder, which the writer records without comment.

Shammah's stand in verses 11-12 has the same shape, and the ground he defends is a lentil field. Not a pass, not a city gate, not a fortress, but a vegetable patch. It was somebody's food, the army decided it was not worth dying for, and one man stood in the middle of it. Then the same sentence again: the LORD worked a great victory. The writer does not say the men were irrelevant, and he does not let them keep the credit.

Verses 13-17 are the best scene in the catalogue, and everything turns on the word longingly. David is at Adullam, about twelve miles from Bethlehem, a fugitive. Bethlehem is his home town, where he watched his father's sheep and Samuel poured oil on his head, and a Philistine garrison is sitting in it. What he says is not an order, and the writer is careful to say so. It is what a homesick man says when he is tired, and it means: I wish I were home. He is not asking anybody for anything. He may not even know he said it aloud.

Twelve miles each way, through an occupied town, past a garrison, to a well in the open by the gate, the most exposed place in Bethlehem, and back again carrying water. Nobody sent them. There was no military purpose whatever. Their commander said he was thirsty for home, and they went through an enemy army for a cup of water because he wanted it.

And he will not drink it. This has occasionally been read as ingratitude, and it is the opposite. He poured it out to the LORD, which is the language of a drink offering: he does not tip it away, he offers it. The blood of the men is his reasoning, and it is exactly right. Three men nearly died to fill that cup, and whatever is in it now, it is not simply water; it has their lives in it. So he gives it to God, the only one worth what it cost.

And there is a rebuke in it that he takes on himself, and he is honest enough not to hide it. He said a careless thing where his men could hear it. A leader’s passing wish is never harmless; three of them risked everything for a remark he made without thinking, and he will not benefit from that.

Abishai (vv. 18-19) is the man who wanted to spear Saul in his sleep, who twice asked to behead Shimei, and who killed the giant standing over David in chapter 21. He has a name in this list and he earned it.

Benaiah's lion (v. 20) is killed on a snowy day, and snow in that country is rare enough to be worth recording. He went down into the pit, into the hole with the animal, on a day when the footing was bad and the sides were slippery, and killed it there. His Egyptian (v. 21) is, in Chronicles, seven and a half feet tall with a spear like a weaver's beam (1 Chron. 11:23), which is the Goliath description again: David’s men face giants as he did, and they learned it from him. The man set over the royal guard in verse 23 ends up commanding Solomon's whole army, and he is the man who finally executes Joab at the altar (1 Kings 2:34).
verseByVerse.note: The meaning of the word ariel is uncertain (ESV note).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 24–39 — Uriah the Hittite: Thirty-Seven in All
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The list of the thirty runs on: Asahel the brother of Joab, Elhanan of Bethlehem, and some thirty more names from all over Israel and beyond: Zelek the Ammonite, Naharai the Beerothite who carried Joab's armour, Ittai from Gibeah of Benjamin, Saul's own town (vv. 24-38). And the last line of the chapter: Uriah the Hittite: thirty-seven in all (v. 39).
verseByVerse.theology: The roll is a mixture. Israelites from every tribe, a man from Saul's own village, an Ammonite, a Hittite: the foreigners are on the list of Israel's most honoured soldiers, and so is the brother whose death started Joab's feud.
verseByVerse.examples: The last name on the roll of honour is Uriah. The book has already recorded what was done to him and by whom, and here it adds no comment at all.

verseByVerse.quote: Asahel the brother of Joab was one of the thirty; Elhanan the son of Dodo of Bethlehem, Shammah of Harod, Elika of Harod, Helez the Paltite, Ira the son of Ikkesh of Tekoa, Abiezer of Anathoth, Mebunnai the Hushathite, Zalmon the Ahohite, Maharai of Netophah, Heleb the son of Baanah of Netophah, Ittai the son of Ribai of Gibeah of the people of Benjamin, Benaiah of Pirathon, Hiddai of the brooks of Gaash, Abi-albon the Arbathite, Azmaveth of Bahurim, Eliahba the Shaalbonite, the sons of Jashen, Jonathan, Shammah the Hararite, Ahiam the son of Sharar the Hararite, Eliphelet the son of Ahasbai of Maacah, Eliam the son of Ahithophel the Gilonite, Hezro of Carmel, Paarai the Arbite, Igal the son of Nathan of Zobah, Bani the Gadite, Zelek the Ammonite, Naharai of Beeroth, the armor-bearer of Joab the son of Zeruiah, Ira the Ithrite, Gareb the Ithrite, Uriah the Hittite: thirty-seven in all.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The list begins with a dead man. Asahel was as swift of foot as a wild gazelle and would not turn aside, and Abner killed him with the butt of a spear at Gibeon in chapter 2, which started the feud that ended in a murder at the gate of Hebron. He is still on the roll.

Gibeah of the people of Benjamin (v. 29) is Saul's home town. A man from Saul's own village, of Saul's own tribe, is among the most honoured soldiers in David's kingdom. The war between Saul’s house and David’s did not set every man of Benjamin against David.

Eliam son of Ahithophel (v. 34) brings two earlier stories together. Ahithophel of Giloh is the counsellor who went over to Absalom and hanged himself, and chapter 11 said the woman on the roof was Bathsheba, the daughter of Eliam, the wife of Uriah the Hittite (11:3). So this man is very probably Bathsheba's father, and Ahithophel her grandfather, and both are in this chapter: one on the roll of honour, one at the end of a rope in Giloh.

Zelek the Ammonite (v. 37) comes from the nation whose king shaved David's envoys and whose capital David's army besieged.

And the last name in the list of the mighty men of David is Uriah the Hittite. The writer has already told us the story: a spring afternoon, a roof, a woman washing, a question asked and answered; a man brought back from the front who would not sleep in his own house because the ark and Israel and Judah dwell in booths, and my lord Joab and the servants of my lord are camping in the open field; a letter he carried to Joab with his own hands; a wall at Rabbah.

And now, at the end of the roll of the finest soldiers in the kingdom, thirty-seventh and last: Uriah the Hittite. There is no asterisk and no comment, no sentence explaining that this is the man the king had killed. The name simply stands where it has always stood, in the place it earned, on the list it belonged on.

That is the writer's whole method, and this is the purest example of it in either book. He seldom tells us what to think. He recorded Saul's spear and said nothing. He recorded the cart at Uzzah's death and said nothing. He recorded the new wives after 5:12 and said nothing. He put “the thing that David had done displeased the LORD” at the end of chapter 11 as the only editorial sentence in twenty-seven verses. Here he does not even do that. He writes the name and stops.

Consider the list as a whole. Its last few names are an Ammonite, two Ithrites and a Hittite. There is a man from Saul's home village and a son of Ahithophel; there is Asahel, dead for decades, and Joab's armour-bearer. Uriah was one of these. He was not a peripheral figure or a junior officer but one of the top thirty-seven soldiers in the country, a foreigner who had thrown in with Israel and Israel's God so thoroughly that his one recorded speech is about the ark being in a field. And he was murdered by the man whose list this is, and his name is on it. The book puts the last words and the last name in the same chapter and leaves the reader holding both.

“The thirty” was the name of the elite company, whose members changed over the years; with the Three, Abishai, Benaiah and replacements, the list reaches thirty-seven (v. 39).

24.title: The Threshing Floor of Araunah
24.text: <sup>1</sup>Again the anger of the LORD was kindled against Israel, and he incited David against them, saying, "Go, number Israel and Judah."<sup>2</sup>So the king said to Joab, the commander of the army, who was with him, "Go through all the tribes of Israel, from Dan to Beersheba, and number the people, that I may know the number of the people."<sup>3</sup>But Joab said to the king, "May the LORD your God add to the people a hundred times as many as they are, while the eyes of my lord the king still see it, but why does my lord the king delight in this thing?"<sup>4</sup>But the king's word prevailed against Joab and the commanders of the army. So Joab and the commanders of the army went out from the presence of the king to number the people of Israel.<sup>5</sup>They crossed the Jordan and began from Aroer, and from the city that is in the middle of the valley, toward Gad and on to Jazer.<sup>6</sup>Then they came to Gilead, and to Kadesh in the land of the Hittites; and they came to Dan, and from Dan they went around to Sidon,<sup>7</sup>and came to the fortress of Tyre and to all the cities of the Hivites and Canaanites; and they went out to the Negeb of Judah at Beersheba.<sup>8</sup>So when they had gone through all the land, they came to Jerusalem at the end of nine months and twenty days.<sup>9</sup>And Joab gave the sum of the numbering of the people to the king: in Israel there were 800,000 valiant men who drew the sword, and the men of Judah were 500,000.<sup>10</sup>But David's heart struck him after he had numbered the people. And David said to the LORD, "I have sinned greatly in what I have done. But now, O LORD, please take away the iniquity of your servant, for I have done very foolishly."<sup>11</sup>And when David arose in the morning, the word of the LORD came to the prophet Gad, David's seer, saying,<sup>12</sup>"Go and say to David, 'Thus says the LORD, Three things I offer you. Choose one of them, that I may do it to you.'"<sup>13</sup>So Gad came to David and told him, and said to him, "Shall three years of famine come to you in your land? Or will you flee three months before your foes while they pursue you? Or shall there be three days' pestilence in your land? Now consider, and decide what answer I shall return to him who sent me."<sup>14</sup>Then David said to Gad, "I am in great distress. Let us fall into the hand of the LORD, for his mercy is great; but let me not fall into the hand of man."<sup>15</sup>So the LORD sent a pestilence on Israel from the morning until the appointed time. And there died of the people from Dan to Beersheba 70,000 men.<sup>16</sup>And when the angel stretched out his hand toward Jerusalem to destroy it, the LORD relented from the calamity and said to the angel who was working destruction among the people, "It is enough; now stay your hand." And the angel of the LORD was by the threshing floor of Araunah the Jebusite.<sup>17</sup>Then David spoke to the LORD when he saw the angel who was striking the people, and said, "Behold, I have sinned, and I have done wickedly. But these sheep, what have they done? Please let your hand be against me and against my father's house."<sup>18</sup>And Gad came that day to David and said to him, "Go up, raise an altar to the LORD on the threshing floor of Araunah the Jebusite."<sup>19</sup>So David went up at Gad's word, as the LORD commanded.<sup>20</sup>And when Araunah looked down, he saw the king and his servants coming on toward him. And Araunah went out and paid homage to the king with his face to the ground.<sup>21</sup>And Araunah said, "Why has my lord the king come to his servant?" David said, "To buy the threshing floor from you, in order to build an altar to the LORD, that the plague may be averted from the people."<sup>22</sup>Then Araunah said to David, "Let my lord the king take and offer up what seems good to him. Here are the oxen for the burnt offering and the threshing sledges and the yokes of the oxen for the wood.<sup>23</sup>All this, O king, Araunah gives to the king." And Araunah said to the king, "May the LORD your God accept you."<sup>24</sup>But the king said to Araunah, "No, but I will buy it from you for a price. I will not offer burnt offerings to the LORD my God that cost me nothing." So David bought the threshing floor and the oxen for fifty shekels of silver.<sup>25</sup>And David built there an altar to the LORD and offered burnt offerings and peace offerings. So the LORD responded to the plea for the land, and the plague was averted from Israel.
24.overview:
The chapter opens with one of the hardest verses in the Old Testament: God incited David to do a thing for which seventy thousand people die, while the Chronicler, recording the same event, says that Satan stood against Israel and incited David (1 Chron. 21:1). God tempts no one to evil (James 1:13), and the theology below sets out how Scripture holds God's rule, Satan's malice and David's own guilt together.

Why a census is wrong is never stated, but the evidence all points one way: it is a count of fighting men, the law required a ransom at any numbering, and even Joab, who is not a scrupulous man, objects. It took nine months and twenty days, and every day of it a rider could have been sent to call it off.

Then David must choose one of three judgments and live with having chosen. He picks the one that comes straight from God, with no human hand in it, for his mercy is great, and standing on a hill watching his people die, the man who counted them as soldiers calls them sheep.

The angel stops at a particular threshing floor, and David buys it rather than take it free. The last sentence he speaks in this book is I will not offer burnt offerings to the LORD my God that cost me nothing. That ground is the temple mount, which Chronicles calls Mount Moriah.
24.theology:
Who incited David (v. 1)? Samuel says the LORD; Chronicles, written later, says Satan (1 Chronicles 21:1); and David says the choice was his own and takes the blame (v. 10). All three are true at different levels. Satan wanted David to fall and was the near tempter. God, already angry at Israel's sin, did not put evil into David's heart, for he tempts no one (James 1:13); he allowed Satan to work on a pride already there, within limits, and turned the outcome into a judgment. The pattern is Job's: Satan asks leave and executes the disasters, yet Job says the LORD gave, and the LORD has taken away, and the narrator approves the sentence (Job 1:21-22). Chronicles names the near agent and Samuel the ultimate governor, and neither cancels David's guilt. (The Hebrew of 1 Chronicles 21:1 has no article, and a few scholars read it as a human adversary; most translators take it as the name Satan.) Scripture will not let God be a bystander, nor the author of evil, and it does not explain the mechanism: the same tension stood at 17:14, where God ordained the outcome of a council in which every man freely did what he thought best.

These sheep, what have they done? (v. 17). He upgrades his own verdict (foolish in verse 10, wicked here) and then changes the word for the people. Shepherd is what this history has called the office from the day the elders came to Hebron (5:2) and in God's own words in the covenant (7:8). He counted them as soldiers and now calls them sheep, and that one word is the whole correction of the chapter: a census turns people into a figure on a tally, while a shepherd knows them as creatures that cannot look after themselves. Then he offers himself, not as a bargain, since he has nothing to trade, but asking that the judgment fall where the guilt is. The offer is refused, because a sinner cannot pay for other sinners. But there is a Son of David who stood over that same city, wept over it, and did what this man could only ask to do.

A threshing floor is the right place (v. 18). Grain is beaten and winnowed there, so it is the standard biblical picture of judgment; and it is also where the harvest is gathered. Judgment and provision happen on the same floor.

Where the book stops (v. 25). The threshing floor where judgment stopped is the ground where Solomon would build the temple, on Mount Moriah, where Abraham once offered Isaac and named the place the LORD will provide. One hill holds Abraham and Isaac and the ram, David and the angel and the fifty shekels, Solomon's temple, and, in the same city outside a wall, a Son of David on whom judgment stopped for good.
24.examples:
Then: A man was offered, free and sincerely, everything he needed to stop a plague that was killing his people (the land, the animals, and a farmer’s own working tools broken up for firewood), and he refused it and counted out fifty shekels of silver, because he would not give God something that had cost him nothing.

Now: Three things. Verse 1 is the one to hold carefully rather than solve: Scripture attributes the same event to God and to Satan and to a man's own choice, and refuses to let go of any of the three, and an account of God’s rule over events that drops one of them is not this book's account. Second, verse 14, which belongs in the memory against a bad day: not that God will go easy, but that if you must be dealt with, you would rather it were by the one whose mercy is great than by anyone else at their kindest. And third, the last sentence. Costless worship is the easiest thing in the world and does not feel like anything at all: nothing given up, nothing missed, nothing difficult. He was entitled to take the land. He paid for it. Not to buy God's favour: the plague stopped because God said it is enough, and the one sacrifice that answers for sin was paid by God himself, who did not spare his own Son. What we give is thanks, and the Spirit who has made us his own is the one who makes us glad to give it.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Again the anger of the LORD was kindled against Israel, and he incited David against them, saying, "Go, number Israel and Judah" (v. 1). Joab objects: may the LORD your God add to the people a hundred times as many as they are, while the eyes of my lord the king still see it! But why does my lord the king delight in this thing? (v. 3). The king's word prevails, and they go through the whole land for nine months and twenty days (vv. 4-8). The total is eight hundred thousand valiant men who drew the sword in Israel and five hundred thousand in Judah (v. 9).
verseByVerse.theology: Chronicles names Satan as the one who incited David; Samuel names the LORD. The Bible attributes one event to both without embarrassment, just as it says of the cross that men did what God's plan had predestined and that they were lawless men (Acts 2:23; 4:28).
verseByVerse.examples: The text never says what was wrong with a census, but the evidence converges: Joab objects; the count is of men who drew the sword; and the law required a ransom to be paid at any census, that there be no plague among them when you number them (Ex. 30:12).

verseByVerse.quote: Again the anger of the LORD was kindled against Israel, and he incited David against them, saying, "Go, number Israel and Judah." So the king said to Joab, the commander of the army, who was with him, "Go through all the tribes of Israel, from Dan to Beersheba, and number the people, that I may know the number of the people." But Joab said to the king, "May the LORD your God add to the people a hundred times as many as they are, while the eyes of my lord the king still see it, but why does my lord the king delight in this thing?" But the king's word prevailed against Joab and the commanders of the army. So Joab and the commanders of the army went out from the presence of the king to number the people of Israel. They crossed the Jordan and began from Aroer, and from the city that is in the middle of the valley, toward Gad and on to Jazer. Then they came to Gilead, and to Kadesh in the land of the Hittites; and they came to Dan, and from Dan they went around to Sidon, and came to the fortress of Tyre and to all the cities of the Hivites and Canaanites; and they went out to the Negeb of Judah at Beersheba. So when they had gone through all the land, they came to Jerusalem at the end of nine months and twenty days. And Joab gave the sum of the numbering of the people to the king: in Israel there were 800,000 valiant men who drew the sword, and the men of Judah were 500,000.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Verse 1 holds two problems. The first is why God is angry with Israel at all; the writer does not say, and the word again points back to the famine of chapter 21 without explaining anything. The second is much larger: God incited David to do a thing for which seventy thousand people then die, and the Chronicler, recording the same event, writes then Satan stood against Israel and incited David to number Israel (1 Chron. 21:1).

The theology above sets out the pattern from Job that makes sense of this: Satan is the near agent, God the one who governs, and David the one who chose. Neither account makes God the tempter, and neither excuses David, whose own confession in verse 10 owns the choice.

The New Testament does the same thing about the worst event in history without a flicker of discomfort. Jesus was delivered up according to the definite plan and foreknowledge of God, and in the same sentence was crucified by the hands of lawless men who are held responsible for it (Acts 2:23). What Scripture will not allow is either half alone.

What is being counted is stated in verse 9: men who drew the sword. This is not a population survey or a tax roll but a military inventory. He wants to know how many soldiers he has. And that is the exact thing this history has argued against from the beginning. Jonathan at Michmash said nothing can hinder the LORD from saving by many or by few (1 Sam. 14:6). David in the valley said the LORD saves not with sword and spear (1 Sam. 17:47). David hamstrung the captured chariot horses because the law said a king must not multiply them (8:4). The man who wrote some trust in chariots and some in horses is counting his soldiers.

There is also a law about this, and it is precise. When Israel took a census, every man counted had to pay a half-shekel ransom for his life, that there be no plague among them when you number them (Ex. 30:12). The people belong to God, not to the king, and numbering them without acknowledging that carries a stated penalty, plague, and plague is what falls in this chapter.

Joab objects (v. 3), which should make any reader stop and think. This is the man who murdered Abner at a gate, killed Absalom against a direct public order, knifed Amasa in a road, and told his king to stop grieving for his own son. He is not tender and he is not scrupulous. His argument is shrewd, too. He does not say the census is sinful; he says God can multiply the people a hundredfold anyway, so what is the point? Why does my lord the king delight in this thing? Delight is the word that gives it away. Joab has understood that this is not administration. It is the pleasure of a man wanting to see a large number with his name on it.

Nathan is not mentioned. Nobody in this chapter tells David it is a sin until after it is done, and the people best placed to stop him, the general and the commanders, tried and were overruled.

The count took nine months and twenty days (v. 8), and that detail makes this different from most sin in Scripture. Bathsheba was an afternoon. This took the better part of a year, with a national field operation crossing the Jordan, going up to Gilead and Dan and round to Beersheba, and every day of it David could have sent a rider to call it off.

The result in verse 9 is one million three hundred thousand fighting men, the largest number in the book, and what the whole exercise was for. The Chronicler gives 1,100,000 and 470,000 and notes that Joab did not finish the count because the command was abhorrent to him (1 Chron. 21:5-6); the two tallies are most plausibly counting slightly different things.

Why do the numbers differ from the parallel account? Numbers in Hebrew manuscripts were easily miscopied, since they were often written with letters or abbreviations; and the two accounts sometimes count different things, such as chariots and charioteers, or a total and a part. Neither touches what the passage teaches, and those who hold Scripture to be without error have always meant what was first written, not every later copy.
verseByVerse.note: Chronicles says Satan incited David (1 Chr 21:1); Samuel names the LORD, who rules even over Satan’s work (compare Job 1–2).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 10–17 — Let Us Fall into the Hand of the LORD
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: But David's heart struck him after he had numbered the people. And David said to the LORD, "I have sinned greatly in what I have done. But now, O LORD, please take away the iniquity of your servant, for I have done very foolishly" (v. 10). Gad brings three options: three years of famine, three months of flight before his enemies, or three days of pestilence (vv. 11-13). David answers: I am in great distress. Let us fall into the hand of the LORD, for his mercy is great; but let me not fall into the hand of man (v. 14). Seventy thousand die, and when the angel stretches out his hand toward Jerusalem the LORD relents: it is enough; now stay your hand (vv. 15-16). And David, seeing the angel at the threshing floor of Araunah: behold, I have sinned, and I have done wickedly. But these sheep, what have they done? Please let your hand be against me and against my father's house (v. 17).
verseByVerse.theology: Verse 14 is a real theological judgment and not an evasion. Two of the three options put him in the hands of people: famine means dependence on neighbours who sell grain, and flight means enemy soldiers. He chooses the one where the only hand on him is God's, and gives the reason: his mercy is great.
verseByVerse.examples: Verse 17 is shepherd language, the word this whole history has used for the office (5:2; 7:8). He asks for the judgment to fall on himself instead, and it is the last thing he asks for in this book.

verseByVerse.quote: But David's heart struck him after he had numbered the people. And David said to the LORD, "I have sinned greatly in what I have done. But now, O LORD, please take away the iniquity of your servant, for I have done very foolishly." And when David arose in the morning, the word of the LORD came to the prophet Gad, David's seer, saying, "Go and say to David, 'Thus says the LORD, Three things I offer you. Choose one of them, that I may do it to you.'" So Gad came to David and told him, and said to him, "Shall three years of famine come to you in your land? Or will you flee three months before your foes while they pursue you? Or shall there be three days' pestilence in your land? Now consider, and decide what answer I shall return to him who sent me." Then David said to Gad, "I am in great distress. Let us fall into the hand of the LORD, for his mercy is great; but let me not fall into the hand of man." So the LORD sent a pestilence on Israel from the morning until the appointed time. And there died of the people from Dan to Beersheba 70,000 men. And when the angel stretched out his hand toward Jerusalem to destroy it, the LORD relented from the calamity and said to the angel who was working destruction among the people, "It is enough; now stay your hand." And the angel of the LORD was by the threshing floor of Araunah the Jebusite. Then David spoke to the LORD when he saw the angel who was striking the people, and said, "Behold, I have sinned, and I have done wickedly. But these sheep, what have they done? Please let your hand be against me and against my father's house."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The word after in verse 10 does a great deal of work. Nine months and twenty days of surveying, and a general telling him not to, and only when the total is read out does his heart strike him.

The phrase has appeared once before in this history, of the same man. In the cave at Engedi, after he cut the corner off Saul's robe, David's heart struck him (1 Sam. 24:5). He had a conscience so finely set that cutting a piece of cloth troubled it. Here it takes nine months and a number.

But it does strike him, and he speaks without being told anything by anybody. I have sinned greatly. Nathan is not in this chapter; no prophet has spoken yet; nobody has confronted him. He works it out himself and says it to God. The last phrase is the one that stings: I have done very foolishly. Not wickedly, yet: stupidly. He is an old man who has just done something a young man would have known better than to do.

Gad has been with him since the cave: he turned up at Adullam and told him to leave the stronghold (1 Sam. 22:5), and here he is at the end of the reign, some forty years on. The choice he brings is itself part of the judgment. David is not told what will happen; he has to pick it, knowing the cost of each, and then live with having picked.

Verse 14 is the best sentence in the chapter, and it is a real theological judgment rather than an evasion. Famine means three years of buying grain, borrowing, and depending on neighbouring nations and whoever has stores, which puts Israel at the mercy of people. Fleeing before his enemies for three months means being hunted by soldiers, the hand of man in its plainest form, and he knows what that is like, having spent years being hunted. Pestilence has no human agent in it at all. There is nobody to negotiate with, nobody to be merciful or merciless, and nothing between the people and God.

He chooses the one where the only hand on him is God's, and he gives the reason: for his mercy is great. That is a considerable thing to say while choosing a punishment. He is not saying God will go easy. He is saying that he would rather be dealt with by God at his severest than by people at their kindest, because there is mercy in God and there may be none anywhere else. A man who has been hunted by Saul, betrayed by Ahithophel, cursed by Shimei, lied to by Ziba and driven out by his own son has good reason to expect little mercy from people.

Seventy thousand die (v. 15), and the phrase from Dan to Beersheba is the phrase used of the census route. The plague goes exactly where the counting went.

Then God says it is enough; now stay your hand (v. 16). The judgment stops because God stops it, and the writer records the geography with care because it is about to be the point of the whole chapter: the angel is standing at a particular threshing floor belonging to a particular man just outside Jerusalem.

In verse 17 David passes a harsher verdict on himself. In verse 10 he said he had been foolish; now, looking at what it has cost, he says I have done wickedly. And then: these sheep, what have they done? That is shepherd language, the word this history has used for the office from the day the elders came to Hebron, you shall be shepherd of my people Israel (5:2), and in God's own words in the covenant, I took you from the pasture, from following the sheep (7:8).

He counted them as soldiers. He now calls them sheep. A census turns people into a figure on a tally; a shepherd knows them as creatures that cannot look after themselves. He wanted to know how many swords he had, and he is standing on a hill watching them die and calling them a flock.

His offer of himself is not a bargain; he has nothing to trade. It is a man asking that the judgment fall where the guilt is, the one request he is entitled to make, and it is the same instinct that made him say I have occasioned the death of all the persons of your father's house to Abiathar decades earlier.

Verse 13’s three years of famine follow 1 Chronicles 21:12 and the Greek Old Testament (the Septuagint); the Hebrew text has seven, most likely a copying change.

Why did 70,000 die for David’s sin, and why was God angry with Israel? Verse 1 says the anger was already there: Israel itself had sinned, perhaps in the rebellions of Absalom and Sheba. The census was David’s pride, and the plague judged king and people together, as a nation stood or fell with its king. David himself says these sheep, what have they done? (v. 17), and offers himself in their place, a picture of the King who would.

Does God change his mind? His purposes never change (1 Sam 15:29); “relented” describes his real response of mercy in human terms.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Gad tells him to raise an altar on the threshing floor of Araunah the Jebusite, and he goes up (vv. 18-19). Araunah sees the king coming and bows: let my lord the king take and offer up what seems good to him. Here are the oxen for the burnt offering and the threshing sledges and the yokes of the oxen for the wood. All this, O king, Araunah gives to the king (vv. 22-23). But the king said to Araunah, "No, but I will buy it from you for a price. I will not offer burnt offerings to the LORD my God that cost me nothing." So David bought the threshing floor and the oxen for fifty shekels of silver (v. 24). He builds the altar, offers burnt offerings and peace offerings, and the LORD responded to the plea for the land, and the plague was averted from Israel (v. 25).
verseByVerse.theology: Araunah's offer is generous and entirely sincere, and David refuses it in the last sentence he speaks in this book. Worship that costs the worshipper nothing is not worship of this God, and he will not begin a national altar with a gift somebody else paid for.
verseByVerse.examples: The ground he buys is the site of the temple. The Chronicler says so outright (2 Chron. 3:1), and Moriah is where Abraham was sent with Isaac (Gen. 22:2). The book ends on that ground, at the place where God stopped the judgment.

verseByVerse.quote: And Gad came that day to David and said to him, "Go up, raise an altar to the LORD on the threshing floor of Araunah the Jebusite." So David went up at Gad's word, as the LORD commanded. And when Araunah looked down, he saw the king and his servants coming on toward him. And Araunah went out and paid homage to the king with his face to the ground. And Araunah said, "Why has my lord the king come to his servant?" David said, "To buy the threshing floor from you, in order to build an altar to the LORD, that the plague may be averted from the people." Then Araunah said to David, "Let my lord the king take and offer up what seems good to him. Here are the oxen for the burnt offering and the threshing sledges and the yokes of the oxen for the wood. All this, O king, Araunah gives to the king." And Araunah said to the king, "May the LORD your God accept you." But the king said to Araunah, "No, but I will buy it from you for a price. I will not offer burnt offerings to the LORD my God that cost me nothing." So David bought the threshing floor and the oxen for fifty shekels of silver. And David built there an altar to the LORD and offered burnt offerings and peace offerings. So the LORD responded to the plea for the land, and the plague was averted from Israel.
verseByVerse.commentary:
He is sent to the exact spot where the angel stopped, and a threshing floor is the right place for what is about to happen. It is a flat open area of rock on high ground, where grain is beaten and thrown into the wind so that the wheat falls and the chaff blows away. It is the standard biblical picture of judgment, which John the Baptist uses of Christ: his winnowing fork is in his hand (Matt. 3:12). And it is also where the harvest is gathered. Judgment and provision happen on the same floor.

Araunah is a Jebusite, one of the people who held Jerusalem before David took it, still living and farming just outside the city his people lost. His offer is complete and generous, and there is no reason to think it insincere. He offers the land, the animals and the wood, and the wood is his threshing sledges and ox yokes: his farm equipment. A man is offering to break up the tools of his own trade for firewood so that a sacrifice can be made. And he says may the LORD your God accept you, which from a Jebusite is remarkable.

David's answer in verse 24 is his last recorded sentence in the book of Samuel. Consider what he is refusing. There is nothing improper about the gift: a subject is offering his king land for a national emergency, freely, and David could have taken it with a clear conscience while the plague raged.

The principle is not about ownership, and it is not that God requires a receipt. It is that a sacrifice which costs the one offering it nothing is not a sacrifice. The whole meaning of the act is that something of yours is given up; take the cost away and what is left is a ceremony with somebody else's animal on it.

This is the man who counted his soldiers. The census was about accumulating: a large number, held and admired. His last recorded act is to spend money on ground he could have had free.

Then the LORD responded to the plea for the land (v. 25), the identical phrase used at the end of the Rizpah chapter (21:14). Both times it follows an act of costly obedience rather than an act of violence.

The Chronicler tells us plainly why the book stops here: Then Solomon began to build the house of the LORD in Jerusalem on Mount Moriah, where the LORD had appeared to David his father, at the place that David had appointed, on the threshing floor of Ornan the Jebusite (2 Chron. 3:1). The ground David buys in the last five verses of this book is the ground on which his son will build the house he was not allowed to build, where the sacrifices of Israel will be offered for nearly four centuries, and where the whole nation will come three times a year.

And Mount Moriah is where God sent Abraham with his son and a knife, telling him to go to the land of Moriah, and offer him there as a burnt offering on one of the mountains of which I shall tell you (Gen. 22:2): the place where a father raised a knife over a son and a ram was found caught in a thicket, the place Abraham named the LORD will provide.

1 Samuel ended on Mount Gilboa: a king dead on his own sword, his sons killed around him, his body nailed to a Philistine wall, and the men of Jabesh-gilead walking all night to bring the bones home. 2 Samuel ends on a different hill, with an altar, a plague stopped, and a man paying for ground he could have had for nothing.

Between them is everything: a boy with a sling, a spear thrown four times, a cave, a crown, an ark, a covenant, a roof, a letter, a forest, a room over a gate, a psalm, and a list of thirty-seven names ending with Uriah the Hittite. The writer has told all of it without excusing any of it. And he ends the history of Israel's greatest king not on a throne, not on a battlefield, and not on a deathbed, but on a rock outside the city, at an altar, at the place where God stopped the judgment. That is where the whole story was always going.

Fifty shekels of silver here, six hundred of gold in Chronicles: David paid fifty for the threshing floor and oxen, and Chronicles probably gives the price of the whole surrounding site, which became the temple mount. Araunah and Ornan are two spellings of one man's name; the Hebrew spells it more than one way even within this chapter.
verseByVerse.note: Compare 1 Chronicles 21:18-22:1, where David names this place as the site for the house of the LORD.
